en: ŪM. Salutations to the venerable Supreme Self.
Now begins the *Sāṃkhyapravacanabhāṣya*,
composed by the eminent scholar Śrīmad Vijñānabhikṣu.
Regarding the Person (*puruṣa*), there are scriptural declarations such as "one, without a second."
For its liberation, by means of turning back all conceit.

They say that there is an absence of distinction characterized by difference, but not an indivisibility (akhaṇḍatā), because it is not contradictory for [the one] to possess hundreds of attributes, just as in the case of space. ||1||
Because that would contradict the fact that hearing has reflection as its purpose.
The author of the Sāṃkhya system appeared here with a web of sound reasoning.
Salutations to that Nārāyaṇa who, in the form of Kapila, exists for the sake of the total destruction of the suffering of the multitude of living beings. || 2 ||
That which appears in various forms through diverse limiting adjuncts, like fire or the sun.
We worship that universal consciousness which is equal toward all beings. || 3 ||
Attributes such as being the Lord or not being the Lord [are superimposed] upon the reality whose sole essence is consciousness.
That which the deluded perceive is this supreme light.
The Sāṃkhya scripture, which is a moon of the nectar of knowledge, has been devoured by the sun of Time.
I shall once again fill that which is distinguished by its artistic merit with the nectar of my words.
By breaking the knot of the conscious and the unconscious, I shall liberate even the conscious self.
Through this work under the guise of a commentary on Sāṃkhya, may Hari, the bestower of liberation, be pleased. || 6 ||
That indeed is you; you alone are this—thus it is declared by hundreds of scriptural texts.
The complete dissimilarity [of all things] in every respect is the exclusive domain of this very treatise.

In such scriptural passages as, "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon," the triad of hearing and so forth is enjoined as the means for the direct realization of the Self, which is the instrument for attaining the supreme human goal. In that regard, when there arises a requirement for the means to hearing and the rest, it is stated in the Smṛti: "It is to be heard from the sentences of the Śruti, and it is to be reflected upon by means of logical arguments;
having reflected, it must be constantly meditated upon—these are the causes of [direct] vision."

The phrase "is to be meditated upon" implies "according to the method of the Yogaśāstra. In that regard, the Blessed One in the form of Kapila taught, by means of the Vivekaśāstra consisting of six chapters, logical reasonings (*upapatti*) that are not in contradiction with the Vedas, concerning those matters heard from the Śrutis—namely, the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*), their causes, the knowledge thereof, and the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the Self which is its object.

[Objection: But surely, since the principles regarding these matters have also been demonstrated by the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika systems, this [system] would be redundant; furthermore, because its arguments for establishing the Self through contradictory forms such as possessing qualities and being devoid of qualities conflict with the arguments found here, the validity of both systems would be untenable. [Response: Not so, because there is neither redundancy nor contradiction due to the difference in their respective objects—namely, the conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and the ultimate (*pāramārthika*) levels.

Indeed, by means of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika systems, through the discourse on pleasure and pain, the Self is inferred in the first stage as being distinct from the body and so forth alone, because at that time it is impossible to enter into the supreme subtlety; and its knowledge—by way of dispelling the notion of the body and such being the Self—is conventional knowledge of reality (*vyāvahārika-tattvajñāna*). Just as the knowledge of possessing hands, feet, and so on serves to dispel the delusion of a post in a man, and is thus conventional knowledge of reality, so it is here. Therefore: "Those who are deluded by the qualities of *prakṛti* become attached to the actions of the qualities.
One who knows the whole should not disturb those dull-witted ones who do not know the whole."

Thus, in the *Gītā*, it is stated that the logician (*tārkika*) who identifies with agency possesses only incomplete knowledge (*akṛtsnavit-tva*) in comparison to the Sāṃkhya who possesses complete knowledge (*kṛtsnavit*); it is not, however, said that he is entirely ignorant. Likewise, even his knowledge becomes a means to liberation through a succession of stages by way of secondary detachment (*apara-vairāgya*). Therefore, compared to that [logician’s] knowledge, the Sāṃkhya knowledge alone is ultimate (*pāramārthika*), and it becomes a direct means to liberation by way of supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*). By the aforementioned *Gītā* passage, it is established that [the Sāṃkhya] possesses the knowledge of the self's non-agency.

The state of possessing all knowledge is established by hundreds of authoritative scriptural passages such as: "For then he has crossed beyond the sorrows of the heart; thinking that the mind itself [is the agent] of desire and so forth, he moves through both worlds, as if meditating, as if moving about; whatever he sees here, he remains untouched by it. And:
"All actions are performed in every way by the qualities of nature (prakṛti);
the self, deluded by egoism, thinks, 'I am the doer.'"
This self is indeed composed of nirvāṇa, consisting of knowledge and stainless;
however, the phenomena (dharmas) consisting of suffering and ignorance belong to primordial nature (prakṛti), not to the self.

This is also established by hundreds of such authoritative scriptural texts (*tāttvika-smṛti*). Furthermore, the knowledge propounded by the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika systems is sublated at the level of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-bhūmi*). Nevertheless, this does not imply that the Nyāya and other systems lack authority. This is because there is no sublation regarding the intended meaning—the aspect of the self's distinction from the body and so forth—according to the maxim: "Whatever a word intends to convey is its meaning. Since the possession of pleasure, pain, and so on by the self is already established in common worldly experience, there is no need for another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) in that regard; thus, that portion [of the teaching] is merely a restatement (*anuvāda*) and is not the primary subject matter of the scripture’s purport.

It might be argued: "There is no contradiction here with the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika systems; however, there is indeed a contradiction with the Brahmamīmāṃsā and Yoga, because those two establish an eternal Īśvara, whereas here Īśvara is denied. Nor should it be said that even here there can be no contradiction between the theistic and atheistic doctrines by distinguishing between the conventional (*vyāvahārika*) and the ultimate (*pāramārthika*), on the grounds that the theistic doctrine may be intended for the purpose of meditation (*upāsanā*). This is because there is no decisive evidence (*vinigamaka*) [to favor such an interpretation].

Since God is indeed difficult to know, even the absence of God (*nirīśvaratva*)—which is established by worldly convention—can be restated for the sake of detachment from power, just as the possession of qualities (*saguṇatva*) is attributed to the Self; however, nowhere in the Śrutis or other scriptures is God explicitly denied, such that one could conclude that the doctrine of the existence of God (*seśvaravāda*) is merely conventional.
To this it is replied: here too there exists the distinction between the conventional and the ultimate:
"They say the world is unreal, without foundation, and without God."

Since the doctrine of non-divinity (nirīśvaravāda) is censured by such scriptures, and since within this very treatise the negation of an Īśvara is merely a restatement (anuvāda) for the sake of cultivating detachment from sovereignty and so forth regarding the conventional (vyāvahārika) level, the intention of the Sāṃkhya teachers is as follows: if eternal sovereignty were not negated in accordance with the Lokāyata view, then, through the perception of a perfect, eternal, and faultless sovereignty, the mind might become absorbed therein, thereby creating an obstacle to the practice of discrimination (viveka). Thus they argue.

There is no censure or the like of the doctrine of a personal God (Seśvaravāda) anywhere [in this system], by which that scripture might be restricted to being merely concerned with meditation and so forth. As for the statement:
"There is no knowledge equal to Sāṅkhya, there is no power equal to Yoga;
let there be no doubt in you regarding this: Sāṅkhya is considered the supreme knowledge."

This statement and others like it demonstrate that the superiority of Sāṃkhya knowledge over other systems of philosophy lies solely in its portion concerning discriminative discernment (*viveka*), and not even in its portion regarding the negation of God. Likewise, from the consensus of all learned authorities such as Parāśara and others, it is determined that the doctrine of the existence of God alone is ultimately real. Furthermore: "In the systems composed by Akṣapāda, Kaṇāda, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga, those who take refuge solely in the Śruti must discard whatever portions contradict the Śruti."
In the system of Jaimini and that of Vyāsa, there is not the slightest contradiction;
for both have reached the further shore of the Vedas through their mastery of the Vedic scriptures and the knowledge of their meaning.

Thus, even from sources such as the *Parāśara Purāṇa*, the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* is most authoritative regarding the aspect of the Lord. Likewise: "The systems of logic (*nyāya*) are many, propounded by various disputants; that which is consistent with reason, scripture, and the conduct of the virtuous should be followed."

Even from such statements in the *Mokṣadharma*, as well as from the practice of all the learned (*śiṣṭa*) beginning with Parāśara, the very logic that establishes the Lord (*īśvara*) as set forth in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, the *Nyāya*, the *Vaiśeṣika*, and other systems must be accepted, because of its superior strength. Thus:
"Seek refuge in Him alone—the Great Lord (*Maheśvara*), the Brahman without beginning or end, whom the lords of yogis and even the Sāṃkhyas do not perceive."

This is because, according to such statements from the *Kūrma Purāṇa* and others, it was Nārāyaṇa and others who taught the Sāṅkhya system itself as being the ignorance of the Lord. Furthermore, it is established through the introductory passages (*upakrama*) and other criteria that the primary subject matter of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā is the Lord alone. If that portion were sublated, the scripture itself would become invalid, according to the maxim: "That which a word primarily intends to signify is its true meaning."

Furthermore, since the primary subject matter of the Sāṅkhya treatise is precisely the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, along with the human goals and their means, the Sāṅkhya system does not lose its authority even though it contradicts the portion concerning the negation of God (*īśvara*), according to the maxim: "Whatever a word aims at, that is its meaning. Therefore, because it has [other] scope, the Sāṅkhya alone is weak regarding the portion that negates God. Nor can it be said that in the Brahma-Mīmāṃsā as well, the primary subject is God alone rather than eternal sovereignty;
for this would result in the untenability of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) concerning the fault of leaving no room for certain Smṛtis.

This is because the subject matter of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā is determined precisely as being characterized by eternal sovereignty; for although the word "Brahman" is primarily applied to the Supreme Brahman, the aphorism was not formulated as "Now, therefore, the inquiry into the Supreme Brahman. By this, one should not suspect that the Yoga and Sāṅkhya systems refer to an *īśvara* who is a product [of nature], due to their contradiction with the Sāṅkhya, nor because of the impossibility of the world's construction if [the Lord] were dependent on *prakṛti*, and because of the inconsistency with the succession of Brahma-sūtras beginning with "Not through inference" (*nānumānam*).

Likewise, from the *Yogasūtra-bhāṣya* of Vyāsa, which clearly states, "He is the teacher even of the ancients, for he is not limited by time," the eternity of the Lord (*Īśvara*) is understood. Therefore, since the Sāṃkhya school’s denial of a conventional Lord (*vyāvahārikeśvara*) is merely a provisional argument (*abhyupagamavāda*) and not a definitive position, there is no contradiction between it and the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* or Yoga systems. Furthermore, such a provisional argument is considered flawed within the scriptures. As stated in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa*: "O Daitya! These various conceptualizations have been described for those of divergent views; having provisionally accepted them, now hear my summary."

Or rather, let it be that for the purpose of obstructing the knowledge of sinners, even within the systems of the orthodox (āstika-darśanas), there exists validity regarding their primary subjects, provided they are not in partial contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti. For this very reason, the censure of philosophical systems other than the Brahma-yoga-darśana found in the Padma Purāṇa is also justified. As therein, the Lord says to Pārvatī:
"Listen, O Goddess! I shall explain in due order the Tāmasa systems, by the mere hearing of which even those possessed of knowledge fall."
For first, the Śaiva systems such as Pāśupata and the rest were spoken by me alone; thereafter, they were proclaimed by brahmins who were possessed by my power.
The great Vaiśeṣika scripture was proclaimed by Kaṇāda,
likewise the Nyāya by Gotama, and the Sāṅkhya indeed by Kapila.
By the twice-born Jaimini, through a doctrine devoid of a Lord, was composed the most extensive scripture concerning the meaning of the first part of the Veda.
Likewise, the highly censurable Cārvāka doctrine was proclaimed by Dhiṣaṇa;
and for the sake of destroying the Daityas, Viṣṇu, assuming the form of Buddha,
proclaimed the false Buddhist scriptures concerning the naked ones, those clad in blue garments, and so forth.
O Goddess, this Māyāvāda, a false scripture that is actually a concealed form of Buddhism,
was taught by me alone in the Kali age under the guise of a Brāhmaṇa.
Demonstrating that the literal meanings of Vedic statements are purposeless and censured by the world, the nature of action as something to be abandoned is established here;
and therein, "actionlessness" (naiṣkarmya) is taught as resulting from the total relinquishment of all action.
The identity of the Supreme Self and the individual soul is established here by me.
I have revealed this supreme, attributeless form of Brahmā for the purpose of destroying this entire world in the Kali age;
it is a great treatise appearing like the meaning of the Vedas, yet it is the non-Vedic doctrine of Māyāvāda.
"O Goddess! I myself have spoken this for the sake of the destruction of the worlds.

Thus it has been further elaborated by us in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*. Therefore, there is no lack of authority or contradiction in any of the scriptures of the orthodox (Āstika) tradition, because all of them remain uncontradicted and non-contradictory within their respective domains.

But in that case, would not this scripture also be considered a mere *abhyupagamavāda* (an admission for the sake of argument) regarding the plurality of *puruṣas*? It would not, because there is no contradiction. Even in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*, the plurality of individual selves (*jīvātman*) is established by a series of sūtras such as "A part [of Me], on account of the declaration of diversity" (*Aṃśo nānāvyapadeśāt*). However, the status of the selves established by the Sāṅkhya as being the ultimate Self is indeed sublated by the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*; for by the sūtra "But they recognize Him as the Self" (*Ātmeti tūpagacchanti*), it is determined that only the Supreme Self is the Self in the realm of ultimate reality.

Nevertheless, the Sāṅkhya system is not invalid; for there is no contradiction regarding the intended meaning—that the knowledge of the discrimination between the transmigrating self (jīva) and the other [the Primal Nature] is the means to liberation—within the context of the empirical self. By this, we have already explained in detail in the Brahmamīmāṃsā that there is no conflict between the plurality of selves and the oneness of the Self as established by Śruti and Smṛti, due to the distinction between the empirical and the ultimate levels. This is the direction of the argument.

If it be objected that even so, there is redundancy between this work of six chapters and the aphorisms known as the *Tattvasamāsa*, we say: not so. For there is no redundancy between the two, as they differ in their form—being respectively concise and detailed. For this very reason, this work of six chapters is entitled *Sāṅkhyapravacana* (The Thorough Exposition of Sāṅkhya), just as the *Yogadarśana* is. Indeed, since this work provides a detailed exposition (*prakarṣeṇa nirvacanam*) of that very same concise Sāṅkhya philosophy which is called the *Tattvasamāsa*, the distinction is simply this: that in the six-chapter work there is merely an expansion of the meanings already stated in the *Tattvasamāsa*.

In the Yoga system, however, by defining Īśvara—who is not prohibited by the doctrine of *abhyupagama-vāda* (the acceptance of a position)—through these two [means], the deficiency is also avoided. Furthermore, its designation as "Sāṅkhya" is etymologically justified:
"They perform enumeration (*saṅkhyā*) and they explain primordial nature (*prakṛti*);
because they [enumerate] twenty-four principles (*tattva*), they are celebrated as Sāṅkhyas."

This is [known] from such statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts. The meaning of "enumeration" (*saṅkhyā*) is the correct description of the self through thorough discrimination. Therefore, because the word *sāṅkhya* possesses both etymological (*yoga*) and conventional (*rūḍha*) meanings, in Vedic texts such as "That cause is to be attained through Sāṅkhya and Yoga," and in Smṛti texts such as "This wisdom has been declared to you in Sāṅkhya; now hear this regarding Yoga," the word *sāṅkhya* must be understood as referring specifically to the Sāṅkhya scripture itself, and no other meaning should be imagined.

This treatise on liberation (mokṣa-śāstra), like the science of medicine (cikitsā-śāstra), consists of four divisions. Just as the four divisions of the science of medicine—disease, health, the cause of disease, and the remedy—are its subjects of exposition, so too the four divisions of the treatise on liberation—what is to be abandoned (heya), the abandonment itself (hāna), the cause of what is to be abandoned (heyahetu), and the means of abandonment (hānopāya)—are its subjects of exposition, because they are what those seeking liberation desire to know. Among these, the threefold suffering is that which is to be abandoned; its absolute cessation is the abandonment.

And through the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heya*); discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), however, is the means of abandonment. By the word "array" (*vyūha*), the collection of their instruments is indicated. In that context, since cessation (*hāna*) is the most venerable as the fruit, the author of the treatise—intending to demonstrate the object to be abandoned (*heya*) precisely by way of its opposite—announces the commencement of the scripture for the sake of the student’s attention: "Now, the absolute cessation of the threefold suffering is the ultimate goal of human life. (YS 1.1)

This word *atha* (now/then) is auspicious by its mere utterance; for this very reason, he himself will state in the fifth chapter that "the performance of an auspicious rite follows from the practice of the learned. However, the meaning of the word *artha* here is specifically "commencement" (*adhikāra*). This is because [meanings such as] "question," "immediacy," and so forth cannot be construed with the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and because the immediacy following knowledge and the like will be explained by the sūtras themselves, making it redundant to explain it here. Furthermore, if it were to mean something other than commencement, there would be the undesirable consequence of failing to obtain the formal promise (*pratijñā*) regarding the beginning of the treatise.

Therefore, since the commencement and conclusion [of the treatise] are seen to concern the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), it is appropriate that its purpose is indeed to establish the qualification (*adhikāra*). As for the conclusion, "The cessation of that [ignorance] is the human goal," it will follow accordingly. Furthermore, *adhikāra* (qualification) means an undertaking (*ārambha*) characterized by preeminence or primacy. And although this undertaking pertains directly to the scripture itself, it nevertheless extends—by way of that—to the subject matter of the scripture and to the inquiry into it as well.

And thus, the meaning of the aphorism is this: we have commenced the primary exposition of the human goal as previously described, together with its means and auxiliary instruments, for the sake of the qualified person. Suffering is threefold: internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, that which operates with reference to the self (*ātman*)—that is, one's own aggregate—is "internal," namely, bodily and mental. Bodily suffering arises from disease and the like; it is produced by the imbalance of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*).

Suffering arising from the provocation of desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, envy, and so forth is mental (*mānasika*). Likewise, that which occurs with reference to living beings (*bhūta*) is physical (*ādhibhautika*), such as that arising from tigers, thieves, and the like. That which occurs with reference to divine agents (*deva*), such as fire, wind, and so forth, is supernatural (*ādhidaivika*), meaning it arises from rain, cold, and the like—this is the sense. Although all suffering is indeed mental, there is nevertheless a distinction between what is mental and what is non-mental based on whether or not it is produced by the mind alone.

The intermediate meaning of the sentence is as follows: the absolute cessation (*atyantanivṛtti*) of these three kinds of suffering—that is, their complete cessation without remainder, common to both the gross and the subtle—is the ultimate, supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), which is desired by the intellect of persons. In this context, "gross" suffering is that which exists in the present state; and that, from the second moment onward, will perish of its own accord.

Therefore, there is no dependence on knowledge in that regard; and since the past has already perished, there is likewise no dependence on a means of accomplishment for it. By process of elimination, it follows that in this context, the cessation of subtle suffering in its future state alone culminates as the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*). Thus says the *Yogasūtra*: "That which is to be abandoned is future suffering. Furthermore, this cessation is not destruction, but rather the past state, because the proponents of the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) do not admit the existence of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or annihilative non-existence (*dhvaṃsa*), as these are merely the nature of the past and future states respectively.

[Objection: Is it not the case that future suffering, which never exists in the present, lacks any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇika*)? Therefore, just like the cessation of a sky-flower, its cessation cannot logically be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). [Reply: Not so. For it is established in the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-bhāṣya] that the capacity to produce its respective effects resides in every substance as long as that substance exists; for fire and the like are never observed anywhere to be devoid of the power to burn and so forth. And that capacity exists in the form of those various effects in their future state. This very thing is also called the "fitness" (*svarūpa-yogyatā*) of the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*).

Therefore, as long as there is the existence of the mind (*citta*), so long is the existence of future suffering inferred; and the cessation of that [suffering] is the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Furthermore, in the state of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), there is the burning away of the seeds—that is, the destruction of the latent impressions—of those sufferings existing in a future state, excluding the fruits of *prārabdha* karma; whereas in disembodied liberation (*videhakaivalya*), there is destruction along with the mind itself. This is the internal distinction. Moreover, the "burning of the seed" is merely the cutting off of ignorance (*avidyā*) and its auxiliaries, because it is established in the world that knowledge has the power to destroy ignorance alone.

For this very reason, suffering is destroyed simultaneously with the mind; for there is no evidence that knowledge directly destroys suffering and the like. Now, one might object: even so, the cessation of suffering cannot be a human goal (puruṣārtha), because since suffering is a property of the mind, its cessation is impossible for the Puruṣa. Even if the term "cessation of suffering" means the non-arising of suffering, that too is eternally established for the Puruṣa. As for the claim that it may be a human goal due to the delusion of its being unestablished despite being established—like a golden necklace around one's own neck—that is not correct.

Even so, it would be untenable for a person to engage in practices such as *nididhyāsana* (meditative contemplation) after hearing and reflecting (*śravaṇa-manana*) for the sake of destroying suffering, on the grounds that they are already free from suffering. For engagement in a means that requires great effort occurs only when there is certainty regarding the result. In the present case, however, because the state of being established is known through hearing and reflection, there is no certainty that the result is unestablished—a certainty that is not undermined by the cognition of invalidity.

Furthermore, even if the absence of suffering were at some time the object of a person's desire due to error or the like, how could the Śruti—which destroys delusion—contradict the fact that it is an established fruit? For it says: "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow," and "The wise man abandons joy and sorrow," and so forth.

To this it is replied: "There is no connection for that which is by nature eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, except through such a connection"—by this very sūtra, which determines the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heya*), this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is resolved. For instance, pleasure and pain exist in the *puruṣa* as well, in the form of reflections; otherwise, their status as objects of experience (*bhogyatva*) would be untenable. Indeed, experience (*bhoga*) is the apprehension (*grahaṇa*) of pleasure and so forth, and apprehension is the assumption of that [object's] form.

Furthermore, since a transformation (*pariṇāma*) consisting of the form of an object cannot occur within the intellect (*buddhi*), which is by nature like a deceptive vessel, there is no other recourse but to conclude that it must consist of a reflection (*pratibimba*). This very reflection of the mental modification (*vṛtti*) is what is stated in the *Yoga Sūtra*: "In other cases, there is conformity with the modification" (*vṛttisārūpyamitaratra*). Moreover, in the *Yoga Bhāṣya*, the reflection of suffering such as pain is specifically mentioned by the term "conformity with its form": "When the *sattva* is afflicted, the *puruṣa* also appears as if afflicted, due to conforming to its form."

For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras will state that the crystal serves as an illustration for the coloring of the Puruṣa by the modifications of the intellect: "And like a gem with a flower. Even by the Vedāntins, that which appears as superimposed upon consciousness is so described. And that superimposition (adhyāsa) is not possible without a reflection. If superimposition were merely knowledge, it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (ātmāśraya), because knowledge arises from superimposition, and superimposition is itself knowledge. This is also recorded in traditional scripture: "In that expansive mirror of Consciousness, all perceptions of objects [are reflected]."

"These [reflections] reflect [in it], like trees on a bank in a lake. Here, the word *dṛṣṭi* (vision) refers generally to the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), due to the similarity of the underlying logic. And "reflection" (*pratibimba*) is a transformation of the mind (*citta-pariṇāma*) in the form of the original object (*bimba*) within its respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, there exists for the *puruṣa* a connection with suffering called "experience" (*bhoga*) by way of being a reflection. Consequently, it is logical that the purpose of the *puruṣa* consists in the cessation of that [suffering] through that very same form [of reflection]. For this very reason, since the purpose of the *puruṣa* cannot exist as something subordinate to another, that [cessation of suffering] alone is the *puruṣārtha* (the goal of man) in itself.

The cessation of suffering, however, like the removal of thorns and the like, is not in itself a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) by virtue of its mere existence. Likewise, pleasure (*sukha*) also is not a human goal in itself; rather, it attains the status of a human goal only through its experience. This fact—that the cessation of the experience of suffering constitutes a human goal—was stated by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Yogabhāṣya*: "When that [ignorance] has ceased, one no longer experiences these three types of affliction."

Therefore, even in the Śruti, the fact that the cessation of suffering is the human goal (puruṣārtha) must be understood as being through the relation of objecthood (viṣayatā-sambandha) alone. This has been elaborated by us in the *Yogavārttika*; this is the direction [of the argument].
Thus, by this sūtra, two arrangements have been briefly indicated; their detailed exposition, however, will follow later. ||1||

Henceforth, in order to create an expectation for the systematic presentation of the means of abandonment (hānopāya) that is about to be described, [the author] refutes the status of other things as such means through a series of sūtras:
"Its accomplishment is not achieved by the seen [means], because its persistence is observed even when [the seen means] have ceased. (Sūtra 2)

The absolute cessation of suffering cannot be accomplished through worldly means such as wealth and the like. Why? Because it is observed that even when suffering is temporarily removed by means of wealth and so forth, suffering recurs once that wealth and the rest are exhausted. Thus says the Śruti: "There is no hope for immortality through wealth," and so on. || 2 ||
Now, if the acquisition of wealth and so forth does not bring about the cessation of suffering—just as bathing an elephant does not remove its dirt—how can there be any inclination toward it?
To this he replies: It possesses the status of a human goal because it is an endeavor to counteract [suffering], just like the daily countering of hunger. (3)

In the cessation of suffering produced by visible means, there is no absolute human purpose (*atyantapuruṣārthatva*); however, it certainly possesses some form of human purpose in one way or another. Why? Because, just as one seeks to remove the daily (*prātyahika*) suffering of hunger—meaning that which occurs day after day—one likewise strives for and seeks the removal of suffering through wealth and other such means. Thus, the point is that engagement in the acquisition of wealth and so forth becomes logically consistent.
Even acts such as bathing with elephant-ichor serve as a minor human purpose, precisely because they remove immediate suffering. || 3 ||
And since that [means] arising from what is seen results in meager human effort, the wise should abandon it; thus he says:
"Because of the impossibility of all [means], and even if possible, because of the impossibility of its existence, it should be abandoned by those skilled in the means of valid cognition. (4)

And that remedy for suffering arising from perceived means, which is to be abandoned by those proficient in the treatises on the discrimination between suffering and non-suffering, is to be designated as a form of suffering.

Why? Because of the impossibility of [remedying] everything—because there is no possibility of a remedy for all sufferings by means of perceived (empirical) instruments. Even where such a possibility exists, he states that suffering arising from the sin of accepting gifts and the like is inevitable: "Even when possible" (*sambhave’pi*). The meaning is that even when possible, there is an unavoidable connection with suffering inherent in other perceived means and so forth. Thus says the *Yoga-sūtra*: "To the discerning person, all is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of acquisition, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the guṇas. (4)

Now, one might object: in every remedy for suffering produced by visible means, the rule that it is inevitably accompanied by suffering is not a necessary factor; and thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"That happiness which is unmixed with suffering, which is not immediately swallowed up by it, and which is brought about by desire—that is the state of heaven. To this, he replies:
Also because liberation is superior, as it is heard in scripture to be the highest of all things. || 5 ||

Because liberation—which is to be accomplished by means that are not perceived [in the ordinary sense]—is superior to sovereignty and the like, which are accomplished by perceived means, the existence of suffering therein is established. By the word "also" (api), qualities such as being composed of the three *guṇas* are also included. The proof for the superiority of liberation is stated as: "on account of the scriptural declaration of its absolute superiority. This means that the superiority of disembodied absolute isolation (*videhakaivalya*) is declared in such passages as: "For one who is embodied, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who is indeed disembodied, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him. || 5 ||

[Objection: "Granted that the cessation of absolute suffering may not result from visible means; however, it could result from invisible means, namely Vedic ritual action, because of scriptural texts such as 'We have drunk [the Soma]' (apāma somam). To this, he replies:
'And there is no distinction between the two. (6)

The meaning is that when both [the visible and the audible] are equally incapable of effecting the absolute cessation of suffering, and are likewise causes of that [suffering] as previously described, they must be regarded as being exactly the same. This very point has been stated in the verse:
"For the audible [means], like the visible, is joined with impurity, decay, and excess."

That which is heard from a teacher is *āmnāya*, which is the Veda; that which is prescribed by it, such as sacrifice and the like, is *ānuśravika*. The meaning is that this [Vedic path], like the perceived means [of worldly attainment], is characterized by impurity, by sins such as violence, and by having perishable and limited results. Now, one might object: "If ritual violence (*vaidha-hiṃsā*) produces sin, then the meaning of the injunction—which consists in being a means to a desired end unaccompanied by a more powerful undesired consequence—would be untenable. This is not so.

The scriptural injunction (*vidhi*) remains intact because the undesirable result produced by ritual killing (*vaidha-hiṃsā*) is invariably concomitant with the production of a desired result; thus, it does not produce excessive suffering, which constitutes the "lack of connection to a powerful undesirable consequence" (*balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva*), a necessary component of a scriptural injunction. As for the claim that only violence other than ritual killing produces sin—that is incorrect. There is no evidence for such a restriction, and furthermore, we hear of expiations (*prāyaścitta*) for Yudhiṣṭhira and others even when performing their own duty (*svadharma*) such as battle, in order to avoid the transgression (*pratyavāya*) resulting from violating known injunctions.
Therefore: "O Father! I shall go, having seen this presence of suffering."
The dharma of the three Vedas is rich in unrighteousness and resembles the fruit of the kimpāka tree.

This is also supported by the words of Mārkaṇḍeya. As for the Vedic scripture stating, "Not harming any living beings, except at sacred sites (*tīrtha*)," it expresses only that the cessation of non-scriptural violence is a means to achieve a desired end; it does not, however, state that scriptural violence lacks the status of being a means to an undesirable end. Such details should be consulted in the *Yogavārttika*. This is the general direction.

However, because it contradicts such scriptural passages as, "Neither by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality," and "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey," it must be understood that the immortality resulting from the drinking of Soma and similar acts is merely figurative.
"For the state that lasts until the dissolution of all beings is indeed called immortality," according to the Viṣṇupurāṇa. (6)

Thus, having established that neither perceptible nor imperceptible means directly accomplish the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and since there is a desire for a means to that end, the means consisting of discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) must be stated. With the intention that discriminative knowledge is the means to liberation only by way of severing the cause of suffering known as non-discrimination (*aviveka*), the author first isolates discrimination alone—by negating everything else—as the cause of what is to be abandoned (*heya*), through the following section:
"There is no instruction on the method of the means to liberation for one who is bound by nature. (7)

Since liberation has been defined as the absolute cessation of suffering, bondage here consists solely in the conjunction with suffering. This bondage does not possess the nature of being inherent (*svābhāvikatva*) in the person (*puruṣa*), as will be explained by its definition later. For if one were bound by nature, it would be impossible for those enjoined to perform the practice of the Vedic injunctions intended for the means to liberation; indeed, liberation is not possible from the natural heat of fire. This is because that which is inherent persists as long as the substance exists. As it is said in the *Īśvaragītā*:
"If the self were by nature impure, untransparent, and subject to modification..."
For indeed, there would be no liberation for him even in hundreds of other births. Thus [it is said].

The definition of being intrinsic (*svābhāvikatva*) is this: when something exists, that whose production does not undergo delay due to a delay in its cause is said to be intrinsic to it. [Objection: But since suffering would then be perceived at all times, its being intrinsic—this definition of intrinsicness—is untenable. [Reply: If you say, "In that case, there is no suspicion at all that suffering is intrinsic because it would have to be perceived at all times," we say no.

Although the mind (*citta*) is by nature suffering because it consists of the three *guṇas*, its constant non-perception as suffering is possible due to its being overwhelmed by the predominance of *sattva*; likewise, the non-perception of that [suffering] by the self (*ātman*) is also possible. Furthermore, the Buddhists, who maintain that suffering is inherent, accept that the mind itself is the self. If it is argued that liberation (*mokṣa*) should thus consist simply in the destruction of the self, we say no; for liberation is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) precisely through its co-referentiality with bondage, as expressed in the thought, "I, who am bound, shall become liberated. || 7 ||
Let there be non-performance; what follows from that? To this he says:
"Because its nature is unchanging, non-performance constitutes invalidity. (8)

The meaning is that, since intrinsic nature (svabhāva) persists as long as the substance exists, liberation would never occur; consequently, the scriptural teaching on the means for achieving it would lack authority in terms of its practical application (anuṣṭhāna). || 8 ||

Now, one might object that performance [of the rite] would proceed solely by the force of scripture; to this he replies: "There is no injunction for what is impossible; even when taught, it is as if not taught. (9)

The performance of an instruction is not possible for an impossible result; for even if an impossible means has been taught or prescribed, that instruction does not truly constitute an instruction, but is merely a semblance of one—according to the principle that "even the Veda does not teach a sublated matter. This is the meaning. || 9 ||
Here he raises an objection: "If it is like a well-prepared cloth or like a seed. (10)

"Objection: Even that which is innate is seen to be removed. For example, the innate whiteness of a white cloth is removed by dye; and likewise, the innate power of a sprout in a seed is removed by fire. Therefore, just as in the case of the white cloth and the seed, the removal of even innate bondage is possible for the *puruṣa*; thus, instruction on the means for its [bondage's] removal should be given accordingly. This is the meaning of the word 'yadi' (if). || 10 ||
He provides the resolution:
"Because of the emergence and non-emergence of power, there is no teaching of the impossible. (11)

Even in the two examples mentioned, the instruction regarding the removal of what is impossible or inherent does not apply to worldly beings. Why? Because of the manifestation and suppression of power (*śaktyudbhavābhyām*). For in the two examples, there is merely the appearance and disappearance of whiteness and so forth; it is not that the potential for whiteness or the potential for the sprout ceases to exist. This is because, through the actions of washermen and the like, or through the volitions of yogis and the like, the potential for whiteness and the potential for the sprout manifest once again in the dyed cloth and the scorched seed, respectively. This is the meaning.

[Objection: "In that case, let liberation for the *puruṣa* also consist merely in the concealment (*tirobhāva*) of the power of suffering. [Reply: No; for in the world, it is experienced that the absolute cessation of suffering alone constitutes the human goal (*puruṣārtha*), and its status as a human goal is established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, but not merely through concealment as in the two examples [of the jar and the tree]. Furthermore, if liberation were merely the concealment of the power of suffering, then since that power could at some time arise again even in liberated souls—due to the volition of the Lord of Yogins and so forth, just as in the case of parched seeds—there would follow the consequence of non-liberation (*anirmokṣa*). || 11 ||

Having refuted bondage by way of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), [the author] now refutes bondage even from the perspective of adventitious causes (*nimitta*) through a series of aphorisms. Even if suffering in the *puruṣa* were adventitious, its cessation through means would not be possible because it is beginningless; for a subtle suffering in its future state exists as long as the substance itself does. With this intention, adventitiousness is refuted:
"Not due to connection with time, because that which is all-pervading and eternal is connected to everything. (12)

Nor is the bondage of the person caused by connection with time. Why? Because since time—which is all-pervading and eternal—is connected at all times and in every respect with all persons, both those who are liberated and those who are bound, it would follow that all persons are bound at all times and in every respect. This is the sense. And in this context, the general status of time, space, karma, and so forth as causal factors is not denied, for that is established by scripture, tradition, and reasoning; rather, what is [denied] is that specific kind of causality...

That very state of being produced by a cause—namely, possessing color and other qualities born of maturation—is denied in the case of bondage, because it is accepted that bondage belongs to the *puruṣa* only as a result of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). If it is argued that even if time and other factors are the causes, the distinction [between bondage and its absence] could be established through the presence or absence of other auxiliary conditions (*sahakārin*), [we reply: this being so, since bondage necessarily occurs whenever there is conjunction with that specific auxiliary condition, it is more parsimonious (*lāghava*) to attribute bondage to that very condition. Since the conventional usage of "bondage" in relation to the *puruṣa* is explained by its being merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), there is no need for a "caused" (*naimittika*) status; thus, bondage does not arise from connection with space either. || 13 ||

Bondage also results from spatial connection (deśa-yoga). Why? Because, due to this aforementioned connection with all puruṣas—both those liberated and those unliberated—bondage would follow even for one who is liberated; such is the meaning. || 13 ||
Not from a state [of existence], because that state is a property of the body. || 14 ||

The state consisting of the body, which is designated as a specific form of aggregation, is also a cause of bondage for the *puruṣa*. Why? Because that state possesses the attributes (*dharma*) of the body; that is to say, it possesses the attributes of the insentient (*acetana*). The meaning is that if the attribute of one thing were to directly cause bondage for another, there would be an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), resulting in the undesirable consequence that even a liberated soul (*mukta*) would be bound. || 14 ||
Now, what is the subverting argument against the state of the Puruṣa as well? To this he says:
"This Puruṣa is unattached" (Kārikā 15).

The word *iti* is used in the sense of a reason. The connection with the preceding sūtra is as follows: because the Puruṣa is unattached (*asaṅga*), states of being are merely attributes of the body. The meaning is that if the Puruṣa were to accept modifications in the form of these states, attachment—known as the conjunction with the cause of change—would necessarily follow. Regarding this lack of attachment, there is the Śruti: "Whatever he sees here, he remains untouched by it."

"For this Puruṣa is indeed unattached" (asaṅga)—here, "attachment" (saṅga) does not mean mere conjunction, because the connection with time and space has already been explained previously. Furthermore, in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, the example of water on a lotus leaf is heard as an illustration for the Puruṣa's lack of attachment, showing that the water does not affect the lotus leaf; nor can it mean the performance of action, because that would result in the over-extension (atiprasakti) of attributing other qualities to him. || 16 ||

For there is no bondage of the person (puruṣa) even by means of enjoined or prohibited actions, because actions are not properties of the Self (anātmadharma). Furthermore, if one thing were to be directly bound by a property belonging to another, it would follow that even a liberated being could be bound. Now, with the intention of showing that this fault does not apply if bondage is accepted as being caused by the actions of one's own respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi), he states another reason: "And because of over-extension" (atiprasakteśca). This means that there would be the consequence of bondage—in the form of conjunction with suffering—even during the dissolution of the universe (pralaya) and other such times. Moreover, the hypothesis that the delay [in liberation] is due to the delay of other auxiliary factors has already been refuted in the Sūtra beginning with "na kālayogaḥ" (Sūtra 3.2.40). || 16 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, since bondage consists of the conjunction with suffering, let it belong to the mind alone, in accordance with its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with karma; for it is established that suffering is an attribute of the mind. Why then is it postulated for the *puruṣa* as well? To this doubt, he says:
"If [bondage] were an attribute of something else, the experience of diverse enjoyments would be impossible" (Sūtra 17).

If bondage, which consists of the conjunction with suffering, were a property belonging solely to the mind (*cittamātra*), then the variety of experiences would be untenable. For if it were admitted that a person (*puruṣa*) undergoes experience—defined as the direct perception of suffering—even without being conjoined with suffering, then all the sufferings and so forth of every person would become objects of experience for every person, since there would be no restrictive factor. Consequently, the variety of experiences in the form of "this person is an experiencer of suffering" and "that person is an experiencer of pleasure," and so on, would not be possible. This is the meaning.

Therefore, for the sake of accounting for the diversity of experiences, bondage—in the form of conjunction with suffering and so forth as that which determines experience—must be admitted even in the *puruṣa*. And it has already been stated that this conjunction with suffering in the *puruṣa* is of the nature of a reflection (*pratibimba*) alone. Furthermore, since a reflection arises only from the activity of its own limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it follows that not all *puruṣas* experience all sufferings; thus, this established doctrine is proven by the *Yogabhāṣya* and other texts. Moreover, the *puruṣa*'s ownership of the mind (*citta*) consists in its possessing the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the mental modifications (*vṛtti*) experienced by itself.

As for the fact that it is proclaimed in the Śrutis and Smṛtis that bondage and liberation belong to the mind alone and not to the Puruṣa, that should be understood as referring to ultimate bondage in the form of association with the suffering inherent in the nature of the reflected image (bimba). ||17||
He also refutes the view that bondage is directly caused by primordial nature (prakṛti):
"If it is argued [that bondage arises] from being bound by primordial nature, no; for even that [nature] possesses dependence. (18)

If it is argued that bondage arises from *prakṛti* as its cause, we say no; for even in that case, *prakṛti* possesses dependence upon conjunction (*saṃyoga*), which will be explained later. The meaning is that if it were a cause of bondage even without a specific conjunction, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the bondage of suffering even during the dissolution (*pralaya*) and other such states. However, in the reading "if [bondage] is based on *prakṛti*" (*prakṛtinibandhanā cet*), the meaning is: "if bondage is dependent upon *prakṛti*. || 18 ||

Therefore, since it is possible that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) could be the cause of bondage, he establishes his own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) right here in the midst of this discussion: "Bondage is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), arising from that very specific conjunction [with impurities], just as the heat of water arises from contact with fire;
there is no such conjunction for that which is by nature eternally pure, awakened, and liberated, except through that [adventitious] conjunction. (19)

Therefore, apart from that connection—that is, without the conjunction with *prakṛti*—there is no "connection" (*yoga*) for the *puruṣa*, meaning no contact with bondage; rather, that [conjunction] itself is the bondage. This elliptical expression using two negatives is employed to establish that bondage is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). For if bondage were produced by the conjunction with *prakṛti*, like a color produced by baking (*pākaja-rūpa*), then it would persist even after that conjunction has ceased, just as that color does. Nor can it be postulated that the second moment and subsequent moments possess the power to destroy suffering.

Since the destruction of the cause is already established as the cause of the destruction of the effect, we do not postulate anything else when that [destruction of the cause] itself suffices. For the *vṛtti* (mental modification) is the material cause (*upādāna*) of suffering and the rest; therefore, because the *vṛtti* is momentary—like the flame of a lamp—its own destruction occurs through its very nature of rapid perishing, and thus the destruction of its attributes, such as suffering, desire, and so forth, is possible. Consequently, since there is no bondage upon separation from *prakṛti*, bondage is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), and neither innate (*svābhāvika*) nor incidental (*naimittika*).
Likewise, the result of this indirect statement (*vakrokti*) is that the cessation of conjunction alone is the direct means of liberation. And so says the *Smṛti*: [The Smṛti verse follows here.]
"Just as a house adjacent to one engulfed by flames is preserved by being separated from it, so too, this [person], when severed from the defiled nature, does not grieve. Thus it is said.

The phrase "eternal" (*nitya*) and so forth is used so that there may be no delusion—such as that held by the Vaiśeṣikas—that the connection with suffering is ultimate (*pāramārthika*). Just as a naturally pure crystal cannot be joined with redness without the proximity of a *japā* flower, even so, for the *puruṣa*, whose nature is eternally pure and so forth, a connection with suffering is not possible without the conjunction with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), because suffering and the like cannot exist inherently. As it is said in the *Saura*: "Just as a crystal, though pure, is perceived by people as red due to the proximity of a coloring substance and the like, so too is the Supreme Person."

Eternality (*nityatva*) is the state of being unconditioned by time. Furthermore, the nature of being pure and so forth refers to the six qualities beginning with eternal purity (*nitya-śuddhatva*). Among these, eternal purity is the state of always being devoid of both demerit and merit. Eternal enlightenment (*nitya-buddhatva*) is the state of having a nature of consciousness that is never lost. Eternal liberation (*nitya-muktatva*) is the state of always being dissociated from ultimate suffering. The point is that while the association with suffering in the form of a reflection is not ultimate, such bondage is indeed [illusory].

Regarding the eternal purity and other attributes of the Self, there is scripture: "This Self is pure existence alone, eternal, pure, enlightened, true, liberated, stainless, and all-pervading," and so forth. If it is argued that, since this is a treatise on reflection (*manana-śāstra*), reasoning (*yukti*) must also be stated regarding this matter, that is true. However, by the statement "Not from that [scripture] is its connection [with the goal], but from the connection with that [reasoning]," reasoning regarding eternal purity and the rest has indeed already been stated. For instance, the eternality, omnipresence, and so forth of the Self have been established even within the systems of Nyāya and others.

In this regard, since the eternal and omnipresent self cannot be joined with all transformations such as suffering and so forth without a conjunction [with something else], it is more logical that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—which is accepted by all as the cause [of experience]—is indeed the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of those [transformations], on account of parsimony (*lāghava*). This is further supported by the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) of the internal organ alone in all transformations. It is not, however, logical to posit the mind (*manas*) as the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and the self as the material cause for these internal transformations; for that would involve the cumbersome assumption of two distinct causes.

If it is argued that the self’s status as the material cause of modification is established by the experience "I am happy," "I am miserable," and so forth, we say no. This is because those aforementioned perceptions are undermined by the suspicion of invalidity, as they fall within hundreds of such errors as "I am fair-complexioned"; thus, they are weaker than the inference supported by the aforementioned reasoning. Furthermore, the argument for the self being pure consciousness will be stated later; this is the general direction.

Therefore, through conjunction with that [Purusha], the insentient linga appears as if it were sentient; and likewise, while the gunas are the actual agents, the indifferent [Purusha] appears as if he were the agent. Thus [ends verse 20].

In this context, "agency" (kartṛtva) is an indicator for all modifications, such as suffering and so forth. Likewise, the meaning of this very aphorism is stated in the Yoga Sūtra: "The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned. And in the Gītā: "For the Puruṣa, abiding in Prakṛti, experiences the qualities born of Prakṛti."
"Abiding in nature" means being conjoined with nature. And so it is said in the Śruti as well:
"The wise say that the Self, when joined with the senses and the mind, is the enjoyer."

Nor should it be argued that, like time and other factors, the conjunction with *prakṛti* is common to both liberated and unliberated persons and thus cannot be the cause of bondage. For here, the term "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) refers specifically to a particular kind of conjunction with *prakṛti* which has assumed the form of one's own respective intellect (*buddhi*)—this being synonymous with birth—as explained by Vyāsa in the *Yogabhāṣya*. Furthermore, it is only through the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that suffering is joined to the *puruṣa*.

Just as in the case of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, we also accept a specific distinctness (*vaijātya*) in the conjunction with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-saṃyoga*), by virtue of its being the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the production of experience. Therefore, there is no possibility of bondage during deep sleep (*suṣupti*) and other such states. Furthermore, like the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the various mental modifications (*vṛtti*) experienced by each individual, the stream of certain modifications and their latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) is also beginningless; thus, the established relationship between the self and its owner (*svasvāmibhāva*) remains intact.

However, some might argue that if one accepts a conjunction (*saṃyoga*) between primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and the spirit (*puruṣa*), it would follow that the spirit is subject to transformation and attachment; therefore, in this context, the meaning of the word "yoga" is merely non-discrimination (*aviveka*), and not conjunction. That is not correct, because the author of the Sūtras will state in the aphorism, "That [bondage] is due to yoga, which is non-discrimination," that non-discrimination alone is the cause of yoga.

Furthermore, according to the two Sūtras in the Pātañjala [Yoga system], "Conjunction is the cause of the cognition of the essential nature of the self and the master (Puruṣa and Prakṛti)" and "Its cause is ignorance," it is stated that ignorance alone is the cause of conjunction. Moreover, if non-discrimination (*aviveka*), which consists in the absence of discrimination, were conjunction, then since the conjunction of Prakṛti and Puruṣa exists even during dissolution (*pralaya*) and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of experience and so on occurring at those times as well. And if non-discrimination, which consists in false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*), were conjunction, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*), because the conjunction of Puruṣa and Prakṛti is itself the cause of ignorance and the like.

Therefore, yoga must be explained as something distinct from non-discrimination (*aviveka*). And that is indeed conjunction (*saṃyoga*), since no other [definition] is supported by authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, conjunction is not transformation (*pariṇāma*), because the conventional usage of "being subject to transformation" occurs only upon the arising of a property distinct from general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*). Otherwise, it would be impossible for the immutable (*kūṭastha*) to possess omnipresence (*vibhutva*) in the form of being all-pervading. Nor is conjunction in its mere sense "attachment" (*saṅga*), because the term "attachment" must be understood as referring specifically to that conjunction which is the cause of transformation.

[Objection: Even so, how can a non-eternal conjunction be possible as the cause of the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, given that both Nature (prakṛti) and Spirit (puruṣa) are eternal? [Reply: This is not so; for since Nature consists of a collection of three kinds of qualities—both limited and unlimited—it is possible for a conjunction with the Spirit to arise through the limitation of the limited qualities. This is because the conjunction and the agitation of Nature are established by Śruti and Smṛti. And this has been explained by us in detail in the *Yogavārttika*.

Another, however, says that the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of these two is simply their mutual fitness as the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer. That too is not correct; for if this fitness were eternal, its cessation through knowledge would be impossible. If it were non-eternal, what harm has been done by conjunction? For the consequence of being subject to modification (*pariṇāmitva*) applies equally to both. Furthermore, since the view that the fitness of the object and the enjoyer constitutes conjunction is not stated in the Sūtras and other authoritative texts, it lacks scriptural authority.

Therefore, it is determined that the author of the Sūtras intended here a specific kind of conjunction alone as the cause of bondage—which is to be abandoned—as he himself identified it as the cause of bondage. (19)

Now, even those causes of bondage intended by the nihilists (nāstika) must be refuted. In this regard, certain sects of Buddhists who maintain that the self consists of momentary consciousness—established through such teachings as "The Guide is possessed of the six superknowledges, the ten powers, and speaks of non-duality"—assert the following: There is no external entity such as primordial matter (prakṛti) or anything else, by conjunction with which there could be either a conditional or a real bondage. Rather, the sole reality is the non-dual stream of momentary consciousness; everything else is merely conventional (sāṃvṛttika).
Conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) is ignorance (*avidyā*), known as false cognition (*mithyājñāna*); from that alone comes bondage. And so it has been said by them:
"For although the nature of the Buddha is undivided, through the perceptions of those who are deluded, it appears as if possessed of the consciousness of the grasped and the grasper."
That view is refuted first:
bondage cannot arise even from ignorance, because that which is non-existent cannot produce bondage. (20)

The word "api" (even/also) refers back to the previously mentioned time and other factors; for even from ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no direct connection with bondage. This is because, according to those who maintain non-duality (*advaitavādins*), since ignorance itself is unreal, it is illogical for bondage to arise through it. The meaning is that one does not observe binding by means of a rope seen in a dream. If it is argued that bondage itself is unreal, we say no; for the author of the Sūtras himself will refute this later, and because it contradicts the acceptance of the practice of yoga for the cessation of bondage following the hearing of the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (*vijñānādvaita*).

Because, upon hearing about bondage and falsehood, one becomes certain that the fruit called the cessation of bondage has already been accomplished; consequently, it is impossible to practice the limbs of yoga, which must be achieved through great exertion for that purpose. || 20 ||
If it were a real entity, there would be a loss of the established tenet. || 21 ||
And if the reality of ignorance (avidyā) were admitted, then the unreality of ignorance that one has accepted for oneself would be abandoned; such is the meaning. || 21 ||
And there would be the consequence of a duality of heterogeneous natures. || 22 ||

Furthermore, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were a real entity, it would follow that there is a duality consisting of something of a different genus from the stream of momentary consciousnesses; and this is undesirable for you—this is the meaning. The qualification "of a different genus" is used with the intention that, since the individuals included within the stream are infinite, a duality of the same genus is indeed accepted [by them]. If it is objected: "Since ignorance is also a specific kind of cognition, how can there be a duality of a different genus even with respect to ignorance?"—the answer is no.

This is because ignorance in the form of cognition occurs subsequent to bondage, whereas they admit that only ignorance in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) is the cause of bondage; and that [ignorance as latent impression] is indeed of a different genus from cognition.

One should not fall into the error of thinking that the established doctrine of the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* is refuted by these sūtras; for in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, bondage is nowhere stated to arise from mere ignorance (*avidyāmātra*). Furthermore, through sūtras such as "Non-distinction [is established] because of the scriptural statement" (*avibhāgo vacanāt*), there is no contradiction even if the non-dualism characterized by non-distinction intended in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* were real despite the existence of ignorance and so forth.
As for the claim that a sign of the modern Māyāvāda of those who merely call themselves Vedāntins is seen here, that is entirely appropriate, since they too are but a branch of the Vijñānavādins.
O Goddess, this false scripture of Māyāvāda, which is actually concealed Buddhism,
was taught by me alone in the Kali age while assuming the form of a Brāhmaṇa.

This is established from the succession of Śiva’s statements found in the *Padma Purāṇa* and elsewhere, such as: "The Māyāvāda is a non-Vedic great system, though it claims to be the meaning of the Vedas"—this being evident from the remainder of that very statement. Furthermore, the proponents of Māyāvāda are not the direct opponents here, because the qualification "of a different kind" (*vijātīya*) would otherwise be redundant; for in the Māyāvāda, even non-duality of the same kind (*sajātīya-advaita*) is not accepted. Therefore, in this context, it is specifically the Vijñānavādins' own systematic account of the cause of bondage that is directly refuted.

In this very manner, it should be understood that the view of the modern "crypto-Buddhists" (pracchanna-bauddhas), the proponents of Māyā (māyāvādins), who hold that mere ignorance (avidyāmātra)—which is insubstantial—is the cause of bondage, is also refuted. In our own system, however, although ignorance lacks ultimate reality in the form of immutable permanence, it is nonetheless real in the same way as a jar or other objects; thus, there is no room for the aforementioned contradiction regarding its being the cause of bondage through the conjunction to be described later. This applies equally to the Yoga system and the Brahma-Mīmāṃsā system. || 22 ||
Again, he raises an objection: "If it were of two contradictory natures. (23)

The meaning is as follows: [the opponent argues] that if both [existence and non-existence] are contradictory, or if it is something distinct from both existence and non-existence, then ignorance (*avidyā*) itself must be described as having such a nature; therefore, there is no subversion of ultimate non-duality (*advaita*) by means of it. However, the term "contradictory" (*viruddha*) is employed in order to establish that the existence and non-existence of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), which he himself will later describe, do not actually constitute a contradiction, since they consist respectively of the states of being manifest and unmanifest. || 23 ||
He refutes this: "No, because such an entity is not perceived. (24)

This is easy to understand. Furthermore, if ignorance (*avidyā*) were the direct cause of bondage known as the connection with suffering (*duḥkhayoga*), then immediately after the destruction of ignorance by knowledge, the experience of the *prārabdha* (commenced) karma would be untenable; for the experience of suffering, which is synonymous with bondage, would cease due to the destruction of its cause. However, in our school’s view, this fault does not arise. This is because ignorance, karma, and so forth, are causes of bondage only through the medium of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). And the conjunction known as birth does not perish until the completion of the *prārabdha* [karma]. || 24 ||
Again, he raises an objection: "We are not proponents of six categories like the Vaiśeṣikas and others. (25)

The point is this: unlike the Vaiśeṣikas and other proponents of realism who assert a fixed number of categories—such as six or sixteen—we do not maintain such a restriction. Therefore, even if it is not perceived, a category that is of the nature of both being and non-being, or distinct from both being and non-being, must be accepted as avidyā. || 25 ||
He refutes this: "Even though it is indeterminate, that which is irrational cannot be included; otherwise, there would be equality with children, the insane, and so forth. (26)

Let it be granted that there is no fixed rule regarding categories (padārtha); nevertheless, the inclusion of a category consisting of both existence and non-existence—which contradicts reason due to the mutual exclusion of being and non-being—is not possible for your disciples based on your mere word alone. Otherwise, even irrationalities such as those held by children would have to be accepted; this is the meaning. Furthermore, there is no clear scriptural authority (śruti) or other evidence for this point. The implication is that when a scripture is doubtful due to its contradiction with reason, another interpretation must be established.
Māyā is neither of the nature of non-existence nor of the nature of existence, nor is it of the nature of both;
it is indefinable as either existent or non-existent, illusory in nature, and eternal.
The meaning of such passages from the *Saura Purāṇa* and other texts is as follows:

The primordial nature (*prakṛti*), known as *māyā*, which is established by such Vedic scriptures as "the producer of transformations, *māyā*, eightfold, unborn, and eternal," is not ultimately real (*paramārthasatī*), because it perishes moment by moment through the forms of successive transformations. Nor is it ultimately unreal, because it possesses causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*) and is thus distinct from a hare's horn. Nor is it both [real and unreal], due to the contradiction involved. Therefore, it is indefinable as either existent or non-existent; it cannot be definitively taught as being "only real" or "only unreal."

However, it possesses a conventional existence characterized by the so-called illusory substrate (mithyābhūtālaya), as well as a conventional existence consisting of a transforming eternity (pariṇāminityatā). We shall elaborate upon this further ahead; this is the general direction.
Furthermore, all the refutations set forth in this context should be applied even to the modern doctrine of Māyā. || 26 ||

Other nihilists say: "External objects exist as momentary; through their latent impressions (vāsanā), there is bondage for the individual soul (jīva). He refutes that as well: "Nor is this [bondage] caused by the coloring of various beginningless objects. (27)

The meaning is that bondage, which would be caused by the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) regarding objects belonging to this self in its form as a continuous stream, is also not possible. The reading *nimittato 'py asya* is the correct one. || 27 ||
He states the reason for this:

"There is not even a relationship of the colored and the colorer between the external and the internal, because of the separation of space, just as in the case of those residing in Sādhna and Pāṭaliputra. (28)

In that view, the self is limited and situated within the body. For such an internal [self], even the relationship of the colored and the colorer (uparajyoparañjakabhāva) with external objects is not possible. Why? Because of the separation of location, like [the relationship] between one staying on Mount Sumeru and one staying in Pāṭaliputra; this is the meaning. Indeed, it is only when there is conjunction (*saṃyoga*) that the coloring known as latent impression (*vāsanā*) is observed, as in the case of madder and cloth, or as in the case of a flower and crystal. By the word "even" (*api*), the absence of contact and so forth in our own view is also included. Sumeru and Pāṭaliputra are two distinct, distant locations. || 28 ||

[Objection: "But surely, just as for you [the Sāṃkhyas] the senses [reach the object], so for us [the Naiyāyikas] the self must be said to become colored by the object through contact with the object due to its movement to the location of the object. To this, he says:
"There is no fixed rule [regarding the experience of objects], because the coloring is obtained in only one part of both [the self and the sense]. (29)

If both the bound and the liberated selves were located in the same objective space, there would be no distinction between bondage and liberation, because both would equally come into contact with the objects present in that location; the meaning is that even the liberated self would incur bondage. || 29 ||
Here he raises an objection: "If [it is argued] that it is due to the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). (30)

The meaning is: if it is argued that, even though the contact with the object is equal due to the connection with one part [of the sense organ], the acquisition of the coloring (uparāga) occurs solely through unseen merit or demerit (adṛṣṭa). || 30 ||
He refutes [this objection]: "There can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary between two things because they cannot exist at the same time. (31)

Because both the agent and the enjoyer are admitted to be momentary, they do not exist at the same time; therefore, there can be no relationship of benefactor and beneficiary. The meaning is that it is impossible for an objective coloring (viṣayoparāga) residing in the enjoyer to arise from unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa) residing in the agent. || 31 ||
He raises an objection:
"If it is argued that it is like the action of a son. (32)

Now, the meaning is this: just as there is a benefit to the son through a rite performed by the father residing in the father, so too would the coloring of the object (viṣayoparāga) occur through an unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) whose locus is the substance itself. || 32 ||
He refutes [the opponent's position] by showing that the example is unestablished:
"For there exists no permanent, single self which is consecrated by the rite of impregnation and so forth. (33)

In that view, even by means of the *putreṣṭi* sacrifice, the benefit to the son is not possible. For, according to that view, there exists no single, enduring self from conception until birth who could be consecrated by the *putreṣṭi* for the sake of entitlement to ritual acts subsequent to birth; thus, the meaning is that the illustrative example is unestablished. The intention is that, in our own view, there is no lack of an illustrative example, because the benefit to the son occurs through the son's limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) by means of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) residing in that adjunct, which is produced by the *putreṣṭi*.

Now, another nihilist objects with the intention that since bondage itself is momentary, let bondage be either without a fixed cause or have non-existence as its cause: "Because a stable effect is not established, [all things] are momentary. (34)

The word "of this" (*asya*) is to be understood as referring to "bondage" (*bandha*). The meaning [of the term *bhāva*] has already been stated. Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: that which is the subject of dispute, such as bondage and so forth, is momentary because it exists, like the flame of a lamp and the like. Nor is there a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of a jar or similar objects, since those too are equivalent to the subject of the proposition (*pakṣasama*). This very point has been stated [in the verse] by the words "because a permanent effect is not established. (34)
He replies: No, because it is sublated by recognition. (35)

The remainder [of the argument] is that nothing whatsoever is momentary. This is because stability is established through recognition such as "I touch that very same thing which I saw before," and because momentariness is thereby sublated by an inference that serves as a counter-argument. For example: "Bondage and so forth must have a stable substratum, like a jar and other such objects. Since this favorable reasoning exists precisely within our own system, there is no "counter-balanced opposition" (satpratipakṣatā). Furthermore, in the case of a lamp and similar phenomena, the opponents' notion of momentariness is merely an illusion arising from their failure to perceive the subtle succession of multiple moments. || 35 ||
And because it contradicts both scripture and logic. || 36 ||

The meaning is that because there is a contradiction with such Vedic texts as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and "In the beginning, this was indeed darkness alone" (Ṛgveda 10.129.3), as well as with scriptural reasonings such as "How could Being be born from Non-being? (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.2), momentariness does not belong to anything within the entire phenomenal world consisting of cause and effect;
