furthermore, the illustrative example [for momentariness] is unestablished. || 37 ||
The meaning is that, because momentariness is not established in the examples such as the flame of a lamp, there can be no inference of momentariness. || 37 ||

Furthermore, for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatāvādin*), even in cases such as clay and a jar, the causal relation—which is established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for engagement and withdrawal—would not be tenable; thus he says:
"There is no causal relation between two things that arise simultaneously. (38)

Is the relationship of cause and effect between two things that arise simultaneously, or between those that arise sequentially? On this point, the sense is that it cannot be the first, due to the absence of a determining factor (*vinigamaka*) and other such reasons. (38)
He says that it is not the latter [case]: "Because when the preceding [moment] ceases, the succeeding one arises. (39)

Furthermore, the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) is not possible in the theory of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda), because it is illogical for the subsequent effect to arise at the very time the preceding cause ceases;
the meaning is that the effect is experienced only as following upon its material cause (upādānakāraṇa). || 39 ||

Concerning the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) itself, he states another refutation: "Because that [effect] is impossible when that [cause] exists, and because both [the cause and the effect] are subject to deviation. (40)

The meaning is that because the latter is non-existent at the time of the former's existence, there is no relation between them; therefore, due to the deviation of both—namely, the deviation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*) and negative concomitance (*vyatireka*)—there is no causal relationship. To explain: the causal relationship between material cause (*upādāna*) and its effect (*upādeya*) is grasped precisely through positive and negative concomitance, such that when the effect arises, the material cause exists, and when the material cause is absent, the effect does not arise. In that regard, because those two are momentary, they exist at contradictory times; thus, due to the deviation of positive and negative concomitance, the causal relationship cannot be established. || 40 ||

"Is it not the case that the status of being a cause should belong to the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) as well, just by its mere prior existence, in the same way as the efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*)? To this, he says:
'There is no certainty based on mere prior existence. (41)

If one were to accept merely prior existence [as the definition of a cause], there would be no restriction that "this alone is the material cause," because instrumental causes (nimittakāraṇa) also possess the same quality of prior existence. The meaning is that the distinction between the material cause and the instrumental cause is established by the consensus of all the world. || 41 ||

Other nihilists (nāstika) say: "Since there is no entity apart from consciousness, bondage too is mere consciousness, like the objects in a dream. Therefore, because it is absolutely false, there is no cause for it. He refutes that view: "Nor is it mere ignorance, because external perception occurs. (42)
The meaning is that consciousness alone is not the reality, because external objects, like consciousness itself, are established by cognition as being real. || 42 ||

[Objection: Surely, by means of the light reasoning [of the Advaitin], through analogies such as dreams, and by the inference of falsity based on the reason of being an object of perception (*dṛśyatva*), the experience of external objects should be sublated. Furthermore, for your venerable selves, there are even the Śruti and Smṛti texts: "All is the vibration of consciousness" (*ciddhādaṃ sarvam*), and "Therefore, only consciousness exists; there is neither the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) nor transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*)," and so forth. To this, he states another refutation:
"In the absence of that [consciousness], because of the absence of that [object], it would then be a void (*śūnyam*). (43)

In that case, if external objects do not exist, it would follow that only emptiness remains, and not even consciousness. Why? Because in the absence of that [object], there is the absence of that [consciousness]; for if external objects are absent, it follows that consciousness is also absent, since it can be inferred that the apprehension of consciousness—just like the apprehension of external objects—has a non-existent thing as its object. Furthermore, the validity of consciousness is unestablished anywhere; thus, the meaning is that even the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are denied within consciousness because they are [regarded as] external.

If it is argued that since there is no dispute regarding experience (*anubhava*) itself, there is no need for a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with respect to it—this is not so; for the Śūnyavādins themselves do indeed dispute its existence. Furthermore, if it is argued that an object is established even by a non-existent means of valid cognition, because what makes something a valid cognition is simply the non-sublation of the object and not the ultimate reality of the cognition itself—this is also not so; for if that were the case, since a non-existent means of valid cognition would be easily available everywhere, it would be impossible to ever seek a valid cognition for any given object.

If it is argued that even within the midst of non-existence, a distinction consisting of empirical reality (*vyāvahārikasattva*) must be sought in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth—then you have arrived at our own path. But what, then, is this "empirical reality"? If it is the state of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*), then we too accept exactly such a thing, since we deny [only] such a nature to the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). If, on the other hand, it is merely the state of being perceived (*pratīyamānatāmātra*), then by such same means of valid cognition, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of establishing external objects as well.
Furthermore, a sublation (*bādha*) by some kind of inference supported by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*) applies equally to consciousness as well.

By this, the view of the moderns who merely profess to be Vedāntins is also refuted, as it shares the same logical fate as the Vijñānavāda (Idealist school). Furthermore, those Śruti and Smṛti passages that establish the reality of consciousness alone refute only the ultimate existence (*pāramārthika-sattā*) of external objects in the sense of their being immutable (*kūṭastha*), but they do not refute even their conventional existence (*vyāvahārika-sattā*) in the sense of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*).
O King, what indeed is that thing which, even after the lapse of time, does not undergo another designation arising from transformation and the like? And what is that?
O King, that which is called "king" in the world, as well as the king’s soldiers and so forth, and likewise other things—none of this is real; it consists merely of mental construction.

Thus, from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other sources, it is understood that the state of being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) is non-existent [in the ultimate sense]. "Consisting of volition" (*saṅkalpanāmaya*) means fashioned by the volition of the Lord and others. By this—namely, by the passage in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* beginning with "Understand all this to be consisting of consciousness alone"—the truth was indeed taught even to the Asuras by Viṣṇu in the form of Māyāmoha; however, due to defects such as lack of qualification, they grasped the meaning perversely and thus became nihilists who propound a doctrine of mere consciousness (*vijñānavādinaḥ*).
This must be understood as having been fully explained. All of this has been elaborated by us in the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya in the context of refuting the doctrine of Māyā. || 43 ||

"Now, let it be so that emptiness alone is the reality; then, for that very reason, it is not at all proper to search for a cause of bondage, because of its insubstantiality. Thus the crest-jewel of nihilists objects: "If emptiness is the reality, then an entity perishes, because perishing is a property of real things. (44)

Emptiness alone is the reality, because every entity perishes. That which is perishable is false, like a dream. Therefore, since all things consist merely of non-existence at their beginning and end, their momentary existence in the interim is conventional (*sāṃvṛttika*), not ultimate; bondage and so forth are likewise not ultimate. Consequently, the intention is: what could be bound by what? The reason for the perishability of entities is that perishing is the very nature of things (*vastudharmatvāt*). This means that because perishing is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of an object, no entity can remain once its own nature has departed. || 44 ||
He refutes this: "It is merely a denial for those who lack understanding. (45)

The claim that "because of existence there is perishability" is merely a denial by the ignorant and is nothing but a false doctrine; for, due to the absence of a cause of destruction, the destruction of partless substances is impossible, and the destruction of effects is likewise unestablished. Just as from the cognition "the jar is worn out," so too from the perception "the jar has passed away," it is established that the jar and other things simply possess a state called "past. Furthermore, if one accepts that the "pastness" of an effect is merely its non-manifestation, one enters precisely into our own position. Moreover, even if one accepts that destruction is the true nature of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), destruction itself could indeed be the goal of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*) regarding bondage.

However, someone explains: "The doctrine that 'the reality is void' is merely a contemptible claim of the ignorant; there is no logic here, because [the concept of] voidness cannot withstand the conceptual alternatives of the existence or non-existence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). If one accepts a means of valid cognition regarding the void, then by that very fact the voidness is destroyed; if one does not accept it, then due to the absence of a means of valid cognition, the void is not established. Furthermore, if it were self-established, it would entail its being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) and so forth. And it is not the case that:
"There is neither cessation nor arising, neither the bound nor the seeker, neither the one desiring liberation nor the liberated—this is the ultimate truth (*paramārthatā*)."
That state in which one's own nature is contemplated as entirely empty and without support is declared to be the yoga of non-existence (abhāvayoga), by means of which one perceives the Self.

Thus, it should not be said that emptiness (*śūnya*) is taught as the ultimate reality even by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* scriptures; for in such *Śruti* passages, it is the very absence of the cessation and so forth of persons (*puruṣa*) that is stated to be the reality. This is because, through both the preceding and following sentences, the person alone is the subject of the context (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, in such *Smṛti* texts, it is the very space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) in which the universe has dissolved that is presented as the reality.
Meditating on the three worlds as having the form of space, his own body as equal to the sky,
and his mind as moving through the void, the yogi is proclaimed as Brahman itself.

Because of the syntactic unity with such other statements as these, and because "space" (ākāśa) and "void" (śūnya) are synonyms, the entire internal organ—including the mind, the intellect, and so forth—dissolves into the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa). 45.
He states another objection: "This [argument] also [is subject to the same fault], because it is equally precarious for both sides. (46)

Since the two positions—that external objects are momentary and that consciousness is momentary—are equally precarious and share the same grounds for refutation, this position also perishes; thus, the logical consequence (*anuṣaṅga*) applies because it is common to all [the preceding cases], as stated by Jaimini: "The connection [of a word] follows [from a previous context] because of its equal application to all. However, in this case, because there is no interruption of the preceding section, the rule "due to intervention, the connection does not follow" does not apply.

This is stated with the intention that, since the word "perishes" (*vinaśyati*) mentioned in the preceding sūtra can be syntactically connected here, it is more appropriate to supply (adhyāhāra) the very word stated in the sūtra rather than relying on a worldly or imagined insertion (*anuṣaṅga*). For the reasons for rejecting the position of momentariness—such as the impossibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth—are common even to the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*). Likewise, the reasons for rejecting the position of consciousness-only (*vijñānavāda*), such as the perception of external objects and so forth, are equally applicable here. ||46||
As for their view that emptiness alone constitutes the human goal—either by virtue of being the cessation of suffering itself or by being its means—that too is untenable; thus he says:
"In either case, it would not be a human goal. (47)

In no other way can emptiness constitute the human goal (puruṣārtha), whether from its own side or from the perspective of another, because the status of pleasure and so forth as human goals exists only by virtue of being grounded in the self; furthermore, this is because a permanent person (puruṣa) is not admitted [to exist]. This is the meaning. || 47 ||

Thus, the nihilistic views regarding the cause of bondage have been refuted. Now, other possible causes of bondage that might be conceived by theists, though already rejected previously, are being refuted:
"Not from a particular state of motion. (48)
Bondage is understood from the context; the meaning is that there is no bondage for the person even due to specific states of existence (gati), such as entering a body and so forth. || 48 ||
He states the reason for this: "Because that is impossible for one who is devoid of activity. (49)
The meaning is that motion is impossible for the omnipresent Puruṣa because he is devoid of action. || 49 ||

One might object: "Since the Śruti and Smṛti speak of the coming and going of a person between this world and the next, let it be that the person is indeed limited; for even the Śruti says, 'The person is thumb-sized, the inner self,' and so forth. To dispel this doubt, [the author] states:

"Because of having form, like a jar and so forth, there would be the contingency of sharing common properties [with material objects], which constitutes an abandonment of one's own tenet (apasiddhānta). (50)

And if the person (puṃs) were accepted as being material and limited like a jar or similar objects, then, by the consequence of possessing qualities identical to those of a jar—such as having parts and being subject to destruction—there would be a contradiction with one's own established tenets (apasiddhānta); such is the meaning. || 50 ||
He establishes the scriptural teaching regarding movement:
"The scriptural teaching regarding movement also [occurs] due to connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), like space. (51)

The meaning is that even the scriptural mention of "going" (transmigration) in relation to the person must be understood as being due solely to the connection with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as in the case of space, in accordance with the scriptures on omnipresence (*vibhutva*) and with reasoning. And the proof for this is: "Just as when a jar containing space is moved, it is the jar that is moved and not the space; in the same way, the individual soul (*jīva*) is like the sky."

The scriptural authority is such as: "By the quality of the intellect and by the quality of the self, it is indeed seen to be even smaller than the tip of an awl," and so forth; and the traditional authority (smṛti) is such as: "It is eternal, all-pervading, and subtle," and so forth. As for the reasoning: if it were of intermediate dimension, it would follow that it possesses parts and is therefore perishable; furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya school, even an atom is merely an effect—as will be stated in the fifth chapter in the sūtra: "There is no eternality of the atom, because scripture declares it to be an effect. Moreover, if it were non-material (amūrta), there would be the impossibility of consciousness pervading the body and so on.
For this very reason: "Prakṛti performs action consisting of auspicious and inauspicious fruits."
And Prakṛti devours it, moving at will through the three worlds.
By such Smṛti passages as these, it is established that the movement in the form of action belongs specifically to *prakṛti* alone. || 51 ||
Nor by action, because that is not its nature. || 52 ||

Even by means of unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) arising from action, there is no direct bondage of the Puruṣa. Why? Because [the adṛṣṭa] lacks the nature of being an attribute of the Puruṣa; this is the meaning. Previously, it was stated that bondage is not caused by the Puruṣa through action in the form of enjoined or prohibited activities; here, however, it is stated that [bondage is not caused] by the unseen merit produced by that [action]. Thus, due to this implicit distinction, there is no tautology. || 52 ||
But surely, there might be bondage of one thing by means of the attribute of another; to this he replies:
"If it were the attribute of another, there would be an over-extension. (53)

The meaning is that if bondage and its cause possessed different properties, there would be an over-extension of the principle (atiprasakti), resulting in the undesirable consequence that even one who is liberated would still be subject to bondage. || 53 ||

What need is there for much? Whether by means of inherent nature (*svabhāva*) and so forth, by karma, or by any other cause whatsoever, the arising of bondage for a person is not tenable, because it contradicts the sacred scriptures (*śruti*). Thus, he states the general refutation:
"And because it contradicts the scriptures concerning the one devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*)," etc. (54).

The meaning is that if the bondage of the person (*puruṣa*) were not due to limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), it would contradict such scriptural passages as, "He is the witness, the knower, solitary, and devoid of qualities" (*asākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaśca*). The word *iti* marks the conclusion of the investigation into the cause of bondage. || 54 ||

Thus, by this section beginning with "not [bondage] of one already bound by nature," it has been determined through the negation of other alternatives that the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* alone is the direct cause of bondage. Here, the following doubt arises: "But surely, the conjunction with *prakṛti* in the *puruṣa* is also subject to the same set of options, such as being inherent (*svābhāvika*) and so forth; why is it not [subject to the same critique]? For if conjunction were inherent or caused by time and the like, the faults—such as the consequence of bondage even for one who is liberated—are equally applicable, as the case may be.
He dispels this doubt: "That conjunction also [is not inherent], because of non-discrimination; there is no equality [of the two cases]. (55)

The previously mentioned conjunction of the Puruṣa also occurs precisely due to non-discrimination (aviveka), which is the cause that will be described hereafter. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no equality between this [conjunction] and the aforementioned defects. Furthermore, since that non-discrimination does not exist in those who are liberated, there is no further conjunction for them. Now, one might object: "In this context, non-discrimination is the direct perception of the identity between Prakṛti and Puruṣa, because it does not exist prior to conjunction; rather, it is either the antecedent non-existence of discrimination or the latent impression of the knowledge known as discrimination."

If it is argued that both of these are not attributes of the *puruṣa*, but rather attributes of the intellect (*buddhi*) alone—and thus the objection regarding the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) remains the same because one thing’s attribute is being joined to another—this is not so. For non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is an attribute of the *puruṣa* by virtue of the relation of "objectness" (*viṣayatā*). Thus, there is no over-extension due to the established rule that Nature (*prakṛti*), assuming the form of the intellect, joins its body to whichever master-*puruṣa* it serves. As it has been stated in the *Kārikā*:
"For the sake of the *puruṣa*'s perception, and likewise for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of Nature;
the conjunction of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man, and from that, creation proceeds."

Thus, the meaning is that [the intellect] exists in order to show itself to the Lord, the Puruṣa, through the medium of the Pradhāna, and for the sake of their isolation (kaivalya). As for the claim that non-discrimination (aviveka) is a modification (vṛtti), that is a mere verbal assertion and not the actual reality; we shall explain this in the forthcoming sūtra beginning with "cittisthiteḥ. Furthermore, non-discrimination is the cause of bondage only by way of conjunction (saṃyoga), because bondage is not observed during the dissolution (pralaya), and because even when non-discrimination has ceased, the experience of suffering is observed in one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta). Therefore, non-discrimination was not previously stated to be the direct cause of bondage.

If it is objected: "Since the beginningless relationship between owner and owned (svasvāmibhāva) has already been established as the regulator of the state of being the enjoyer and the enjoyed, or alternatively, since karma and so forth may serve as the cause of conjunction, why is non-discrimination (aviveka) also accepted as a cause of conjunction? We reply: No. For it is said:
"The Self, situated in Nature, indeed experiences the qualities born of Nature;
attachment to these qualities is the cause of its births in good and evil wombs. (Gītā 13.21)

Thus, because the *Gītā* records that the conceit known as attachment (*saṅga*) is the cause of bondage, and because otherwise the liberation established by the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* through knowledge would be untenable, [non-discrimination is the cause]. Now, one might object: "Even so, one's own limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), such as karma and the like, are also causes of bondage; why then is non-discrimination alone stated to be the cause there, setting those aside? It is replied: In comparison with non-discrimination, even karma and the rest have a connection with the *puruṣa* only through a mediated succession.

Likewise, non-discrimination (*aviveka*) alone can be directly severed by the person; however, action and the like are severed only through the severance of their cause, which is called non-discrimination. With this intention, non-discrimination alone is stated to be the primary cause of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Furthermore, this non-discrimination is intended as the very cognition of the two [the Self and the intellect] without grasping their non-relation (*asaṃsarga*), which is designated as the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*).

This is because of the two subsequent sūtras stating, "Bondage consists of the five varieties of error," and because even in the Yoga Sūtra, it is stated that "its cause is ignorance" (Yoga Sūtra 2.24), thereby declaring that ignorance alone—with its five aspects—is the cause of the conjunction between the intellect and the self; thus, the distinction here [in the Sāṃkhya] is appropriate precisely because it does not accept any theory other than *anyathākhyāti* (the misapprehension of one thing as another).

Furthermore, non-discrimination (*aviveka*) here is neither mere non-existence nor the prior absence of discrimination; for if it were so, bondage would accrue even to one who is liberated, and even for one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), there would be the contingency of renewed bondage through the production of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*) by means of the prior absence of the manifestation of future discrimination. Moreover, the analogy of darkness found in the subsequent sūtra would be untenable, since non-existence cannot function as an obscuring agent like darkness. Likewise, the increase and decrease of non-discrimination mentioned in scripture would also be inexplicable.

In our view, since it is precisely non-discrimination in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that is the cause of birth—termed "conjunction"—its qualities such as obscuration, increase, and decrease are easily established, just like those of darkness. As it is said: "Its cause is ignorance (*avidyā*)."

In the *Pātañjala-sūtra*, the commentators have explained that by the term "ignorance" (*avidyā*), the seed of ignorance is intended, because knowledge cannot produce conjunction since it occurs subsequent to conjunction. Furthermore, in such statements as "The Puruṣa, situated in Prakṛti, experiences," it is understood that the very conjunction called "egoism" (*abhimāna*) is the cause of the conjunction known as being "situated in Prakṛti. For this very reason, the venerable Vyāsa has established with great effort in the *Yoga-bhāṣya* that ignorance is not a mere absence, but rather another form of cognition opposed to knowledge.

Therefore, since non-discrimination (*aviveka*) and ignorance (*avidyā*) share the same status regarding their acquisition and maintenance, it is established that discrimination (*viveka*) is also a specific form of knowledge. This non-discrimination, known as *saṃyoga* (conjunction), is the cause of birth; it occurs both directly through the production of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), and indirectly through the visible means such as the household and so forth. This is according to the *Yogasūtra*: "When the root exists, there is its fruition," and the *Smṛti*: "One is bound by the thought, 'I am the doer,'" and the *Nyāyasūtra*: "Because no birth is observed for one who is free from passion. This has also been stated in the *Mokṣadharma*: "The objects of the senses do not approach the one who is devoid of thirst [for them]."
And the embodied soul, being deficient in its instruments, does not deserve a body again.

"Therefore, living beings are born from the seed of passion (*rāga*), which consists of thirst. And "passion is the effect of non-discrimination (*aviveka*). This should also be understood from two *Yoga-sūtras*, according to the principle of a common system (*samānatantra-nyāya*). Those two sūtras are: "The latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) has its root in the afflictions (*kleśa*); when the root exists, there is its fruition, namely birth, lifespan, and experience"; and "the afflictions are the pentad beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, the collection of gateways through which non-discrimination produces bondage is stated in the *Īśvara-gītā*:
"The cognition of the self in what is not-self; from that arise suffering and likewise the other [states]."
All defects, such as attachment, aversion, and the rest, are rooted in delusion.

"For there would indeed be fault for him [the agent], namely merit and demerit; such is the Vedic revelation. From that very fault arises for all [beings] the manifestation of all the Vedas. This very point has been formulated in the Nyāya-sūtra: "Pain, birth, activity, faults, and false knowledge—in the absence of each subsequent one, there is the absence of the one immediately preceding it, leading to liberation. Thus, it has been established that non-discrimination (aviveka) is the root cause of that which is to be abandoned—bondage—by means of birth, which is termed conjunction; this is the cause of what is to be abandoned. || 55 ||

From this point forward, he sets forth the systematic arrangement of the means for abandonment (*hānopāyavyūha*) in great detail until the completion of the treatise; furthermore, he will expand upon the arrangements mentioned here and there as well.
"Its cessation [occurs] due to a specific cause, like darkness" (verse 56).

In cases such as the [misapprehension of] silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, that which is established in the world as the specific cause for its cessation—namely, the direct realization of discrimination (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*)—is what brings about the destruction of that non-discrimination (*aviveka*), just like darkness. Just as darkness perishes only through its specific cause, light, and not by any other means, so too non-discrimination perishes only through discrimination and not directly from ritual action (*karman*) and the like. This is stated in the *Yoga Sūtra*: "The means of abandonment is the unflinching discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*)."

Actions and the like, however, are the means for knowledge alone; for the *Yogasūtra*—in the aphorism, "From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there arises the illumination of knowledge leading to discriminative discernment"—determines that all actions included within the limbs of yoga are means for knowledge itself by way of purifying the *sattva*.
The ancient Vedāntins, however, maintain that even with respect to liberation, action serves as an auxiliary to knowledge:
"He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together—
having crossed over death by means of ignorance, he enjoys immortality by means of knowledge."

Thus it is heard; and because the Vedānta Sūtra states, "And by way of being a cooperative cause," it is determined that knowledge and action are cooperative through the relationship of principal and subordinate. Therefore, whether one is a knower or a non-knower, as long as the body is sustained, action prescribed for one's caste and stage of life must be performed for the sake of liberation.

This is also because of such Smṛti passages. Furthermore, the Vedānta Sūtra, "And the sublation [of dharma]" (Upamardaṃ ca), merely restates that the renunciation of action for one who has ascended to Yoga is logically established, in order to establish that knowledge is the primary cause of liberation. For if action were an obstacle to the practice of knowledge due to its nature as a distraction, then—according to the maxim "when a quality is lost, the possessor of the quality is not [lost]"—action, being merely a subordinate factor, would have to be abandoned for the sake of preserving the primary factor, just as in the case of Jaḍabharata and others; this is the underlying intention.

Even in their view, since the capacity of karma to destroy discrimination cannot be established without its being a door to discrimination, there is no contradiction with that [scriptural] position. In this sūtra, because darkness is stated to be destroyed by light, *tamas* (darkness) is indeed a substance and not the mere absence of light; for in the absence of a subverting factor (*bādhaka*), it is inappropriate to consider cognitions such as "darkness is blue" to be erroneous. Nor should it be argued that the subverting factor is simply the "cumbrousness" (*gaurava*) of postulating an additional entity when the phenomenon is already explained by what is already established; for if that were the case, then by means of consciousness alone—just as in a dream—[all appearances would be accounted for].

Because, in order to account for the occurrence of all worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*), the assumption of an excessive complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*) would result in the subversion of the very cognition of external objects. Therefore, since this [assumption] is based on authoritative means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), such complexity is not a fault. If it is asked: "Why is it maintained that cognition is the destroyer of those individual instances of cognition called 'non-discrimination' (*aviveka*), given that even without a cognition of discrimination, those instances of non-discrimination necessarily perish at their own third moment?

The answer is: because in the previous aphorism, the term 'non-discrimination' was explained as referring specifically to its latent impression (*vāsanā*); and furthermore, in our system, the destruction of non-discrimination in its future state is possible. || 56 ||

Now, if it is argued that the non-discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* alone is the cause of bondage through the medium of their conjunction, and that the discrimination between them alone is the cause of liberation, then liberation would occur even while there is the conceit of being the body and so forth; and that is contrary to the *śruti*, *smṛti*, and logic. To this he says:
"Other than the discrimination from *pradhāna*, there is no other non-discrimination; when that [non-discrimination] is abandoned, [all others] are abandoned. (57)

The meaning is that since the non-discrimination of the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—which arises from the cause, namely the non-discrimination of *puruṣa* from *pradhāna*—is rooted in the non-discrimination of the primordial cause (*anādi-kāraṇa*), when the non-discrimination of *pradhāna* is abandoned, that [non-discrimination of the intellect and so forth] must necessarily be abandoned as well.

Just as when the self is distinguished from the body, no non-discrimination regarding the body’s functions—such as form and so forth—is possible, so too, when the Puruṣa is distinguished from Pradhāna by its attributes such as immutability (*kūṭasthatva*), no misconception can arise regarding its effects—the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—which possess attributes such as transformation (*pariṇāma*), because the same logic applies and because the cause has ceased to exist; this is the intended meaning. Thus it is recorded in the Smṛti: "When the canvas that supports the painting is discarded, the painting itself is abandoned; likewise, when Prakṛti ceases, what [remains] for meditators—desire and the rest?"* *The verse is cited from the *Mokṣadharma-parvan* of the *Mahābhārata* (12.203.24).*

Cessation (*virāma*) means cessation, which is abandonment. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), modifications in the form of material objects (*dravya*) are also to be understood. Furthermore, as for the statement made in some places that liberation arises solely from the discrimination between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*puruṣa*), there, by the inclusion of both gross and subtle intellects, *prakṛti* is also included; otherwise, even upon the discrimination of the intellect, the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding *prakṛti* would still be possible.

If it is objected: "What is the proof for a conceit regarding *prakṛti* distinct from the conceits regarding the intellect and so forth? For all conceits, such as 'I am ignorant,' are accounted for simply by having the intellect and its derivatives as their objects," we reply: No.
Dying again and again, may you be purified; may you dwell in heaven and never in hell.

This is because such forms of self-identification (abhimāna) would be inexplicable without having the *pradhāna* as their object, and because there is no re-creation of all past effects, such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth. For the *pradhāna*, this very process—discarding its single transformation in the form of the intellect and so on, and transforming again into another form of intellect and so on—is what constitutes "birth" after dissolution.

Nor should it be argued that the cognition of birth and so forth regarding the Self is not indeed a form of self-identification, since for the *puruṣa* as well, birth and death consist in the real union with and separation from the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*).
It is never born nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be again.

By such statements as these, through the negation of birth and so forth, it is established that the cognition of birth and so forth—which consists of the conceit (abhimāna) regarding production and destruction—pertains to the self. Since this [conceit] is already established, its negation is improper because it has not been previously suspected. Furthermore, it cannot be said that the conceit of persons toward the intellect (buddhi) and other faculties is beginningless, because the intellect and the rest are effects. Therefore, when there is a requirement for a regulator to account for the systematic distribution of conceit toward effects, the conceit regarding the cause itself is established as that regulator, because this is observed in the world and because conceptual construction follows what is observed.

Just as in the world, from the conceit regarding a field arises the conceit regarding the grain and other crops produced therein, and from the conceit regarding gold arises the conceit regarding the bracelets and other ornaments produced therefrom; and with the cessation of those two, their respective effects cease—so too, because the primary conceit and its latent impressions (vāsanā) are beginningless like a seed and its sprout, no further regulating cause is required for that conceit. 57.

When the fourfold manifestation (*caturvyūha*) has been thus established, this further doubt arises: "If bondage and liberation, as well as their respective causes—discrimination and non-discrimination—belong to the *puruṣa* and are produced by himself, then there is a contradiction with your own statement that [the *puruṣa*] is eternally pure, awakened, and liberated. And so it is said:
"There is no opposition, no origination, no bound one, and no seeker;
no one desiring liberation, and no one who is liberated—this is the ultimate reality (*paramārthatā*)."
"There is a contradiction with such scriptural passages," he says; he resolves that [objection] as follows:
"It is a mere matter of words, not the reality, because of the stability of the mind. (58)

Since all states, such as bondage and the rest, reside only in the *citta*, their presence in the *puruṣa* is merely verbal; it is a mere reflection like the redness of a crystal, and not its actual nature (*tattva*). The meaning is that it is not superimposed [upon the *puruṣa*], unlike the redness of a *japā* flower. Therefore, there is no contradiction with what was stated above—this is the sense. The scriptural passages, such as "Being the same, he wanders through both worlds, as if thinking, as if moving," serve as the authority here. The *puruṣa* is "the same" (*samāna*), having one and the same form in both worlds. By the two uses of the word "as if" (*iva*), it is indicated that the possession of various forms is due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). As it has been said:
"Bondage and liberation, suffering and the onset of delusion, are manifested through Māyā;
just as the appearance of a self in a dream, this cycle of existence (saṃsṛti) is not real. Thus it is said.

The meaning is that [bondage] is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) called *māyā-prakṛti*. Now, one might ask: "If this is so, how can the abandonment of a void (*tuccha*) bondage be a human goal (*puruṣārtha*), or how can there be no lack of systematic order (*avyavasthā*)—as in the case of karma and other factors—when the bondage and liberation of one thing are accepted as belonging to another? To this, although it has already been largely stated, it is explained again in detail.

Although bondage in the form of conjunction with suffering, as well as discernment and non-discernment in the form of mental modifications, belong to the *citta* alone, nevertheless, for the *puruṣa*, experience (*bhoga*) consists solely in the reflection of suffering; thus, even though this [bondage] is not a real entity, its cessation is the purpose of the *puruṣa*, because of the prayer: "May I not experience suffering. Likewise, nature (*prakṛti*), having shown herself through non-discrimination to whichever *puruṣa*, binds that very one—through the gateway of conjunction—by the force of its latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and not another.

Likewise, the systematic arrangement is also consistent in that she liberates only him to whom she has shown her self through discrimination, by means of her own separation [from him], because of the eradication of latent impressions (*vāsanā*). However, if bondage were admitted to arise from karma and other such factors, this systematic arrangement would not hold; for since karma and the rest are not manifest to the witness-consciousness (*sākṣin*), they do not directly reflect upon the Puruṣas. || 58 ||

Now, if bondage and so forth are merely words regarding the Puruṣa, then let their sublation occur through hearing or through reasoning; for the Śruti and Smṛti teach discriminative knowledge up to the point of direct realization as the cause of liberation. To this, he says:
"Even by reasoning it is sublated, like one confused about directions, but not without direct perception. (59)

Reasoning (*manana*) is reflection. The word "also" (*api*) serves to include hearing (*śravaṇa*). Even mere verbal [instruction] regarding a person's bondage and so forth is not sublated by hearing and reasoning alone without direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*). The meaning is that, for example, for a person who is disoriented regarding directions, even mere verbal instruction about the reversal of directions is not sublated by hearing and reasoning without direct realization. In the present context, this very thing constitutes "sublatability": namely, the cessation of the cognition of bondage and so forth in the person, and not the direct realization of non-existence, because there is not even the possibility of such [realization] arising through hearing and the like.

Or rather, it should be explained as follows: Now, by the statement "its cessation [occurs] through a specific cause," it was stated that discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*) is the destroyer of non-discrimination (*aviveka*). In response to the inquiry—whether that knowledge is common to all means such as hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, or if there is some distinction—the author states the sūtra beginning with "also by reasoning" (*yuktitaḥ api*). Non-discrimination is neither sublated nor destroyed by reasoning or by hearing alone, because it lacks opposition [to them] in the absence of the direct perception (*aparokṣa*) of discrimination. || 59 ||

Thus, having established that liberation results from the direct realization of discrimination (*viveka*), hereafter discrimination itself must be explained. To that end, the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for establishing the distinction between primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the spirit (*puruṣa*), and so forth, are first set forth:
"The cognition of things imperceptible to the eye occurs through inference, just as fire is known by means of smoke and the like. (60)

"Of those that are non-visual" means not perceptible to the eye. First, certain categories of objects—such as the stable elements, their effects, and the body—are indeed established through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). However, for those things not established by perception, such as *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and so forth, there is cognition through the means of inference (*anumāna*), which results in the attainment of the fruit residing in the person (*puruṣa*). The meaning is that, for example, fire is established by an inference produced from smoke and other signs. It should also be understood that even what is not established by inference may be established through scripture (*āgama*).

Since this treatise prioritizes inference (*anumāna*), it presents inference alone as the primary means, rather than disregarding scripture (*āgama*). Thus, the *kārikā* states: "The cognition of supersensuous things arises from inference based on what is perceived in a general way; furthermore, that which is imperceptible and not established by that [inference] is established through the scripture of a reliable authority."
Thus, by this sūtra, it is understood that this is a treatise on reflection (manana). 60.

By means of the aforementioned proofs, he presents a summary aphorism for the categories that serve as the counter-correlates and correlates of the discernment to be established, and also demonstrates the causal relationship (kāryakāraṇabhāva) useful for the inferences to be stated hereafter:
"Prakṛti is the state of equilibrium of sattva, rajas, and tamas; from Prakṛti comes Mahat;
from Mahat comes Ahaṅkāra; from Ahaṅkāra come the five subtle elements (tanmātras) and both types of sense organs; [the gross elements arise] from the subtle element."
From these [subtle elements] arise the gross elements and the Puruṣa; thus, there is a group of twenty-five. ||61||

The substances, such as *sattva* and the others, are not Vaiśeṣika qualities because they possess conjunction and disjunction. Their properties include lightness, mobility, heaviness, and so forth: "Sattva is desired to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. And their functioning is for the sake of a purpose, like a lamp."

Thus it has also been stated by Īśvarakṛṣṇa. Furthermore, the word "guṇa" (quality) is applied to these [factors] in this treatise and in the Śrutis and other texts because they are instruments for the Puruṣa, and because they act as the makers of the rope consisting of the three guṇas that binds the Puruṣa like a sacrificial animal. The state of equilibrium of those substances—sattva and the others—which is a state of neither deficiency nor excess, meaning a state in which they are not combined through the relation of deficiency and excess; the essential point is that it is a state that is not an effect (*akāryāvasthā*). The meaning is that *prakṛti* is the commonality of the guṇas characterized by this state of non-effect. For if taken according to the literal sense, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of *prakṛti* during its state of disequilibrium.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—this indeed is the eternal primordial nature (prakṛti).
This very thing is the cycle of worldly existence for living beings; beyond it lies the supreme state.

This is because such Smṛti passages state that only the *guṇas* (constituents) constitute primordial nature (*prakṛti*). The term "universal" (*sāmānya*) is used to include *sattva* and the other *guṇas*; "constituent" (*guṇa*) is used to exclude the *puruṣa* (spirit); and "characterized by the final limit" (*upalakṣitānta*) is used to exclude the intellect (*mahat*) and the rest. This is because the intellect and the others, being of the nature of the effect-aspect of *sattva* and so on, are also *guṇas* by virtue of being instruments for the *puruṣa*. Thus, in this context, the very essential nature of *prakṛti* has been stated; its specific details, however, will be explained later. The effect of *prakṛti* is the Great One (*mahān*), which is the principle of the Great (*mahattattva*).

The essential nature and the specific distinctions of the Great Principle (mahat) and the others will now be explained. The effect of the Great Principle is the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). The effects of the ego-sense are twofold: the subtle elements (tanmātras) and the two types of sense organs. Among these, the two types of sense organs are elevenfold, distinguished as external and internal. The effects of the subtle elements are the five gross elements. By the term "gross," it is acknowledged that the subtle elements possess the nature of subtle elements. The Spirit (puruṣa), however, is distinct from both cause and effect.

Thus, the group consists of twenty-five categories (*padārtha*). The meaning is that there is no category existing beyond these. Alternatively, the word "group" (*gaṇa*) expresses the infinity of individual manifestations of *sattva* and the other [constituents]. This very group of twenty-five is of the nature of substance (*dravya*) alone; however, due to the non-difference between attribute and substrate (*dharmadharmy-abheda*), qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*karman*), universals (*sāmānya*), and so forth, are included herein. For if there were the existence of a category beyond this, then because one would have to distinguish the *puruṣa* from that as well, there would result the deficiency of failing to grasp what is non-existent.

By this, the foolish prattle of the Sāṅkhyas—that they accept an indefinite number of categories—should be disregarded. Space and time are indeed [the same as] ether; thus there is no contradiction with the scriptural statement, "The ear is space" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.2.2), because of the forthcoming sūtra: "Space and time are merely ether" (VS 2.2.34). These very categories, through mutual inclusion or non-inclusion, are taught in some systems as only one [in the Vaiśeṣika view], in others as six, in others as sixteen [in the Nyāya system], and in others they are taught even by other numbers.

However, it should be understood that the distinction consists merely in similarity and dissimilarity. Thus it is stated in the Bhāgavata: "Even in a single [principle], all other principles are seen to be entered in their entirety, whether in the preceding or in the succeeding principle."
Thus, the various enumerations of the principles (tattvas) have been made by the seers;
since all are logical and possess sound reasoning, what in them is unseemly for the wise? Thus it is said.

These categories are also enumerated in the Śrutis. For instance, in the Garbha Upaniṣad: "Eight are the primary natures (prakṛtis), and sixteen are the transformations (vikāras). And in the Praśna Upaniṣad: "The earth and the subtle element of earth," and so forth. The same is found in the Maitreya Upaniṣad and others. Furthermore, the eight primary natures are explained by the Kārikā: "Root-nature is unevolved; the seven beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) are both nature and evolution;
the group of sixteen is only evolution; and the Puruṣa is neither nature nor evolution."

As for the declaration of the Śruti and Smṛti that "Reality is one alone, without a second," there is no contradiction, because all principles (tattvas) are dissolved into the Puruṣa through the non-difference of power and the possessor of power (śakti-śaktimator-abheda). Furthermore, dissolution (laya) is abiding in a subtle state, not destruction. As it has been said:
"There was indeed an object consisting of knowledge alone, one and undifferentiated."

It is undifferentiated and indivisible. This has been established in detail in the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya* in the context of non-dualism (*advaita*). However, there is this distinction: in the doctrine that accepts a Lord (*seśvaravāda*), since other principles are not distinct from Him, the consciousness of the Lord alone is the single reality. In the doctrine that rejects a Lord (*nirīśvaravāda*), however, because the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest are indivisible from Nature (*prakṛti*) in its subtle state—like the three channels of a braid being inseparable within a single mass of hair, or like the solar orb containing the solar disc—one principle consisting of this very indivisibility is the sole reality.
And so he will state: "There is no contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality, because [the statement] has the universal (jāti) as its referent. || 61 ||
Regarding these categories, he establishes the cognition of those things that are not perceptible to the eye through inference by means of a series of aphorisms:
"From the gross, [one infers] the five subtle elements. (62)

The term "understanding" (bodha) is understood to carry over [from the previous sūtra]. First, the gross [element] is indeed the eye; and that has been described as being an effect of the subtle element (tanmātra). Therefore, the meaning is: through the discernment of the gross, there arises understanding by means of the inference of its cause—the subtle element—from that gross effect. Here, "grossness" is defined for the sake of consistency with space as the state of possessing qualities perceivable by the external sense organs.

Or rather, [the definition of the *tanmātras*] is their possession of specific qualities such as tranquility (*śānta*) and so forth. And these *tanmātras* are subtle substances that serve as the substrata for those classes of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell in which the threefold distinction of tranquility and so forth does not reside; they are the "non-distinct" (*aviśeṣa*) causes of the gross elements.
Regarding this, it is said: "In each respective case, they are called *tanmātras* because they consist of that alone.
They are neither tranquil nor terrible, nor are they deluded; they are non-distinct."

Thus, from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other sources. The meaning of this is as follows: because the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) reside within those respective gross elements, the state of being subtle elements is attributed to the substances themselves by virtue of the non-difference between a quality and its possessor (*dharmadharmyabheda*). Furthermore, those categories [the gross elements] are devoid of the specific qualities of sound and so forth—such as those found in a "lump" (an aggregate)—which are termed "tranquil," "fierce," and "deluded. This is because they possess a single uniform nature. Thus, the intention is that the state of being a subtle element of sound and so forth for the gross elements consists precisely in their possessing sound and the rest while being devoid of such specific qualities as tranquility and the like. Therefore, they are called "non-specific" (*aviśeṣa*) because they lack these specificities.

The peaceful is of the nature of pleasure, the terrible is of the nature of pain, and the deluded is of the nature of delusion. Furthermore, the subtle elements (tanmātras) consist solely of pleasure, because they are exclusively objects of enjoyment for the gods and others, owing to the predominance of pleasure.

Herein lies the inference: gross elements that have reached the limit of refinement (apakarṣakāṣṭhā) must have as their material cause a substance possessing its own specific quality, because they are gross, like jars, cloths, and so forth. In this case, the conclusion is established by taking recourse to the subtle [cause], as otherwise an infinite regress (anavasthā) would result. The supporting argument (anukūlatarka) here is that the production of qualities in an effect occurs through the sequence of qualities in the cause, which cannot be avoided unless there is a sublation; furthermore, there are the Śruti and Smṛti texts [to support this]. However, there is a sublation regarding the claim that primordial matter (prakṛti) possesses sound, touch, and so on:
"It is devoid of sound and touch, and unendowed with color and the rest."
That source of the world consists of the three qualities; it is without beginning, being both the origin and the dissolution [of all things].

Such is the collection of passages from the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other texts. Furthermore, regarding the possession of qualities such as sound and touch by the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the very *śruti* and *smṛti* scriptures that declare them to be the causes of the elements serve as their sublation. This is because the defining characteristic of an element is precisely the possession of specific qualities belonging to the same class as those perceivable by the external senses; consequently, if the intellect and ego were also elements, it would be logically impossible for them to be the causes of themselves.

If it is asked: "In that case, since color and other qualities are absent in the causal substances, what is the cause of the subtle elements (tanmātra) such as color?"—the answer is: it is simply a specific kind of mutual conjunction resulting from the relative deficiency or excess of their own causal substances. This is because we observe that the conjunction of turmeric and other substances is the cause of red color and so forth in the substance produced by those two. Since it is possible for conjunctions—which are the causes of their own substrates—to be the causes of color and other qualities in accordance with observed facts, the logicians' postulation of color in atoms is to be rejected.

Furthermore, even for them, there is no such rule that only a quality of a cause belonging to the same genus (sajātīya) initiates a quality in the effect; for they also admit that in cases such as the magnitude (mahattva) of a triad (tryaṇuka), the multiplicity of parts (avayavabahutva) and so forth are the causes. This is the general direction [of the argument].

Inference regarding the sense organs (*indriyānumāna*) is [established] solely through direct perceptions such as the observation of space and the act of speaking; therefore, it has not been mentioned here. Since the subject at hand is specifically the inference of one principle (*tattva*) from another principle, there is no deficiency [in the treatment]. Furthermore, regarding the production of the subtle elements (*tanmātras*), the process described in the *Yogabhāṣya* should be adopted. As it is said: from the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) arises the subtle element of sound (*śabdatanmātra*). Then, from the subtle element of sound, aided by the ego, arises the subtle element of touch (*sparśatanmātra*), which possesses the qualities of both sound and touch. In this manner, the subtle elements are produced through the successive addition of one quality each. As for that [which follows]—
But space, undergoing transformation, produced the subtle element of touch;
from that, the powerful wind arose, and thus touch is considered its quality.

By such statements in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, the creation of the subtle elements (tanmātras) beginning with touch is described as proceeding from the four gross elements beginning with ether. That [creation] must be understood as being of the nature of transformation into the form of the elements themselves. For the gross elements beginning with ether and ending with water transform their own inherent subtle elements into the form of each respective subsequent element through their own support. || 62 ||
And by means of those [elements], both external and internal, there is the manifestation of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). 63.

The meaning is that there is an inferential cognition of the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) by means of the external and internal senses and their effects, the five *tanmātras*, because [the latter] have it as their cause. Furthermore, the *ahaṅkāra* is a substance (*dravya*) whose function (*vṛtti*) is self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and not merely self-conceit itself; for in the world, it is observed that only a substance can be the material cause (*upādāna*) of another substance. Moreover, if it were merely a function, then upon the destruction of the function of the *ahaṅkāra* during deep sleep and so forth, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the destruction of the elements; thus, the substance called *ahaṅkāra* is established precisely as the substratum (*āśraya*) of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Herein lies the following inference: the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the sense organs (*indriya*) have as their material cause a substance possessed of *abhimāna* (egoity), because they are substances that have *abhimāna* as their effect; for whatever is not thus [i.e., does not have *abhimāna* as its effect] is not thus, like the *puruṣa* and so forth. If it is objected that it is unestablished (*asiddha*) that these are indeed substances having *abhimāna* as their effect, we reply: they are established as such by virtue of being the material causes of mental modifications (*vṛtti*) such as "I am fair," just like the eyes and other senses. And by this inference, the mere transcendence of the mind (*manas*) and the rest is established as their causal basis. In this regard, the following is the favorable argument (*anukūlatarka*).

From such Vedic and Smṛti texts as "May I be many, may I procreate," it is established that since the creation of the elements and so forth is preceded by self-identification (*abhimāna*), this identification functions as the cause in a creation preceded by a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*). And in that case, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), the causality of identification toward creation is postulated through its proximity by way of inherence in a single substrate. Now, an objection: if this were so, the *ahaṅkāra* (ego-sense) of a potter would also have to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the jar; consequently, upon the liberation of the potter and the destruction of his internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the jar produced by him would necessarily be destroyed. But this is not tenable, because another person would still perceive, "This is that very same jar."

"Because it is recognized [to persist]"—do not say so. For it is only the transformation that serves as the cause for the experience of the liberated person which is destroyed after the liberation of that internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); it is not the destruction of transformation in general, nor of the very nature of the internal organ itself. This is because the *Yoga Sūtra* states: "Though it has perished for one whose purpose is fulfilled, it has not perished, since it is common to others," thereby establishing that even the instrument of a liberated person continues to serve the purposes of other persons.

Alternatively, let even in the case of jars and the like, the *ahaṃkāra* of Hiraṇyagarbha alone be the cause, and not the *ahaṃkāra* of the potter; even so, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the general pervasion (*sāmānyavyāpti*). For it is taught in the Purāṇas and in Sāṅkhya-Yoga that creation has as its material cause only the collective intellect (*samaṣṭibuddhi*) and so forth, and not the individual intellect (*vyaṣṭibuddhi*) and so forth which are parts thereof. Just as the great earth alone is the material cause of stationary and moving beings, and not a clod of earth or other fragments of the earth. || 63 ||
Therefore, [the cognition] belongs to the internal organ. || 64 ||

The meaning is that through that effect, namely the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), there is an understanding by means of inference of the primary internal organ, the intellect (*buddhi*) known as *mahat*, because [the former] has that [intellect] as its cause. Here too, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the substance of the ego-sense has as its material cause a substance possessing the function of determination (*niścaya-vṛtti*), because it is a substance that is the effect of determination; for whatever is not so [is] not thus, like the Self (*puruṣa*) and so forth. Here too, this is the reductio ad absurdum (*tarka*).

It is already established that every person in the world first ascertains an object in its own nature and subsequently conceives of it in such forms as "this," "I," "by me," "this must be done," and so forth. In this regard, when there is a requirement for the material cause of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), the relationship of cause and effect is postulated between the two substrates themselves on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), rather than between the two functions (*vṛtti*), because it is a general rule that the manifestation of the function of the effect follows from the manifestation of the function of the cause.

Even in the Śruti, in passages such as "He thought" (sa īkṣāñcakre) and "He thought [then]" (tadaikṣata), it is understood that the entire creation other than Him proceeds from the intellect produced at the beginning of creation. Although, for the sake of parsimony, there is only one internal organ which is threefold according to its different functions—as it is said:
"When the agitation of the Guṇas arose, the Mahat appeared;
the Manas and the Mahat are to be known as one, due to the difference in their functions."

This is because of the *Laiṅga Purāṇa* passage; and because the Vedānta Sūtra, "The fivefold function [of the mind] is designated like that of the mind," establishes the plurality of the mind through its various functions by way of the analogy of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Otherwise, there would result an infinite number of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), each equal in number to its own functions—such as error, doubt, sleep, anger, and so on—just as there are functions such as ascertainment. Furthermore, it would be untenable in all scriptures, such as those of Patañjali, to apply terms like "mind" (*manas*) and so forth to the intellect (*buddhi*) and others indifferently.

Nevertheless, it should be understood that the sequence and the relationship of cause and effect among the three internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) have been stated by resorting to internal subdivisions, as if they were the joints of a bamboo stalk, in accordance with the technical terminology of the scriptures useful for Yoga. As it is said in the *Vasiṣṭha*: "O Great-minded One, know that this which arises as the sense of 'I', consisting of the mind and characterized by cognition, is the seed of this tree of the mind."
From this first sprout that has emerged,
which possesses a manifest form and is of the nature of certainty yet devoid of external shape, the term "intellect" (buddhi) is designated.

"The swelling of this sprout called 'intellect' (buddhi), which consists of volitional construction (saṅkalpa), is designated by the terms 'mind-stuff' (citta), 'consciousness' (cetas), and 'mind' (manas). Thus it is said.

The referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in its general sense. In this statement, according to the logic of the seed and the sprout, the various successive states of that single tree of the internal organ—namely, those designated as *citta* and so forth—are described as threefold modifications (*pariṇāma*) consisting merely of its functional modes (*vṛtti*). Furthermore, in the Sāṅkhya treatises, the *citta*, which has the function of reflection (*cintā*), is included within the *buddhi* itself; and in this statement, the *ahaṅkāra* is likewise included within the *buddhi*. (64)
Then [the dissolution occurs] from primordial nature (prakṛti). 65.

The meaning is that from the Great Principle (*mahattattva*), which is an effect, there arises an understanding of *prakṛti* by means of inference as its cause. Furthermore, the fact that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) in general is an effect is established—just like the body and so forth—by its intermediate dimension, since at times the cognitions of the five senses do not arise simultaneously; this is also established by the authority of the Śruti, Smṛti, and the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).

And regarding its being an effect of primordial nature (prakṛti), the formal argument is as follows: "Intellect (buddhi) possesses the qualities of pleasure, pain, and delusion; it is produced from a substance characterized by the qualities of pleasure, pain, and delusion, because, while being an effect, it consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, like a beloved woman and so forth. Furthermore, the supporting logical reasoning here is that the qualities of an effect must conform to the qualities of its cause, and it should be understood that the Śruti and Smṛti scriptures also confirm this.

[Objection: Surely there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for the fact that objects possess pleasure and so forth, since experience is only of the form "I am happy" and the like; how then can objects such as a beloved woman serve as an illustration? [Reply: This is not so. Because they are the effects of cognitions whose nature is pleasure and so forth, and because of the experience "the pleasure of a garland," "the pleasure of sandalwood," and so on, it is established that objects also possess the attributes of pleasure and so forth, as is also confirmed by Śruti, Smṛti, and inference. Furthermore, that very thing whose positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with pleasure and so forth is observed is postulated to be the material cause (*upādāna*) of that pleasure.

Since it would involve the conceptualization of two causes—by first postulating that [the external object] is the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and then postulating that something else is the material cause (*upādāna*)—such a theory is cumbersome. Furthermore, through mutual corroboration and recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the existence of stable pleasure common to all persons regarding objects is established. In our system, the conceptualization of the restriction of mental modifications (*vṛtti-niyama*) and so forth for the sake of grasping that pleasure is not a defect, as it is a matter of secondary importance (*phalāmukhatvāt*). Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that recognition could not establish the composite whole (*avayavin*), due to the resulting burden of postulating its causes and so forth. Regarding the presence of pleasure and the like in the object itself, it is stated in the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa*:
"Whether those pleasures or pains exist in the mind or in the body, what concern is it of mine? Thus [it is said].

The cognition "I am happy," and so forth, like the cognition "I am wealthy," has as its object a relationship termed the relation between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*). However, in order to dispel the misconception that these cognitions have the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) as their object, the Puruṣa is distinguished from those who are happy, miserable, or deluded in the scriptures. Furthermore, the conventional usage of terms such as sound as being "of the nature of happiness" and so forth arises from inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*).

Or let it be that pleasure exists directly in sound and other objects according to the aforementioned rule; furthermore, let the pleasure inherent in the object be grasped by the intellect alone due to the force of the resulting experience. As for the sattvic peace-pleasure (*śānti-sukha*) manifested during deep sleep and so forth at times when there is no contact with objects—that very thing, being an attribute of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*), is called the "pleasure of the self" (*ātma-sukha*).

Although logicians such as the Vaiśeṣikas and others also infer the arrangement of cause and effect in the phenomenal world in other ways, nevertheless, it is precisely this arrangement inferred by us—supported by numerous Śruti and Smṛti texts—that should be accepted by those seeking liberation (mumukṣu). This is because the inferences of others are weak due to the defect of having shaky foundations. For this very reason, the Vedānta Sūtra states, "Because reasoning is unestablished" (tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt), thereby rejecting mere reasoning on account of its instability. Likewise, Manu also says:
"And one should examine the instruction on Dharma given by the Ṛṣis with [reasoning] that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures..."
He who investigates by means of reasoning knows the Dharma, and no other.

Thus, it has been stated that only reasoning (*tarka*) which is not in conflict with the Vedas is determinative of the truth. Therefore, based on such scriptural statements as "It is to be heard from the words of the Śruti and reflected upon through reasonings" (*śrotavyaḥ śrutivākyebhyo mantavyaścopapattibhiḥ*), reflection (*manana*) that has the same object as hearing (*śravaṇa*) is indeed more authoritative. However, reflection of a different nature, as held by others, is weak. Similarly, regarding the person (*puruṣa*) as well, an inference based on the existence of pleasure, pain, and so forth is weak because it contradicts numerous Śruti passages and other authorities; this is the general direction. We shall discuss the specific distinctions regarding *prakṛti* later.

If it is asked: "Since the discrimination of the *puruṣa* from all insentient things (*jaḍa*) alone is the cause of liberation, for what purpose is the mutual discrimination among insentient things shown here?"—the answer is that discrimination is also required for the purification of the *sattva* through the meditation on the principles (*tattva*), beginning with *prakṛti*. Having stated the establishment of the principle up to *prakṛti* through inference based on the relationship of cause and effect, he now states the establishment of the *puruṣa*—who is devoid of such a cause-and-effect relationship—in another way through inference:
"Because of being for the sake of another, since [all things] are composite, [there must be] a *puruṣa*. (66)

*Saṃhanana* is the conjunction that initiates [a composite]. And because there is no distinction between the part (*avayava*) and the whole (*avayavin*), it is common to both the primordial material cause (*prakṛti*) and its effects. Thus, the meaning is that through the inference that the combined *prakṛti* and its effects exist for the sake of another, the consciousness of the *puruṣa* is established. For example: "The subject of dispute, namely *prakṛti*, the *mahat*, and so forth, exists for the sake of another—that is, it results in the experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) of something other than itself—because it is a composite, like a bed, a seat, and so forth. By this inference, the *puruṣa* is established as being distinct from *prakṛti* and non-composite.

Furthermore, if that [composite] were itself composite, it would lead to an infinite regress. And in the *Pātañjala*, the author of the Sūtras established an inference by stating: "Because they act by combining for the sake of another. That [inference], however, as it stands literally, applies to the ultimate constituents (*antyāvayava*), since the meaning of the term "acting by combining" (*saṃhatyakāritā*) is precisely the capacity to produce purposeful action through association with others.

The Puruṣa, however, requires nothing else for its own purposeful activity, which consists in the illumination of objects, because the Puruṣa is of the nature of eternal luminosity; it depends only upon the modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) for the mere connection with an object. Furthermore, this connection is not a unique purposeful activity. In this regard, scriptural and traditional texts such as "Verily, it is not for the sake of the desires of the body that everything becomes dear, but for the sake of the Self that everything becomes dear," serve as supporting arguments.

Furthermore, if Pradhāna and the like, which possess pleasure and so forth, were for the sake of their own enjoyment of pleasure and so forth, then there would be a contradiction between the object and the agent, since it would have to be its own direct object of cognition. For the manifestation of pleasure is not possible without the manifestation of its substratum (dharmī), because the experience of pleasure occurs only in the form "I am happy."

Moreover, since it would involve excessive complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a plurality of consciousness-attributes for the many constituent parts and their various effects, it is more appropriate—on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*)—to postulate a single Puruṣa, whose nature is conscious illumination, as that which transcends all composite entities. Thus, the Sūtra establishes the inference of the Puruṣa as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), because it states that the purpose of the Puruṣa (*puruṣārtha*) is the motive for the conjunction of all things.

For this very reason, with reference to the Puruṣa produced at the beginning of creation, it is recorded in the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts: "He is merely the efficient cause in the act of creating those things to be created."
For it is from that which has become the primary cause that the powers of the objects to be created indeed proceed.

O Sage, O best of the twice-born, from that state where the qualities are in equilibrium, when presided over by the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), there arises at the time of creation the manifestation of the qualities and their effects.

Thus, the locus of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) is the Great Principle (mahattattva), which is a mere conjunction for one whose human purpose is not yet fulfilled and which manifests the qualities (guṇas); it is so called because, as a cause, it manifests Pradhāna, whose nature consists of the three qualities. In this way, the establishment of those things that are beyond the range of sight through inference has been stated. || 66 ||

Now, in order to establish that Prakṛti is the cause of all things, its eternity is demonstrated for the sake of proving the immutability of Puruṣa: "Since there is no root at the root, the root is rootless. (67)

The root material cause (upādāna) of the twenty-three principles is Pradhāna, which is itself rootless; the meaning is that because it would lead to an infinite regress, no further root for it is possible. || 67 ||

Now, an objection: since the production of even the *pradhāna* from the *puruṣa* is heard in such passages as, "From that, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest was produced, consisting of the three *guṇas*," let the *puruṣa* alone be the root of *prakṛti*. Furthermore, because the *puruṣa* is eternal, there is no infinite regress; and because this occurs through the medium of *avidyā*, there is no loss of the *puruṣa*'s immutability. Thus it is recorded in Smṛti:
Therefore, this cycle of existence for human beings is rooted in ignorance. Thus [it is said].
Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Even in the case of a lineage, there is a finality in one [source]; thus, it is a mere name. (68)

Although the Puruṣa is the root cause of the world through a succession beginning with ignorance (avidyā) and so forth, this succession must terminate in some eternal entity such as ignorance; for the Puruṣa is unchanging (apariṇāmin). Therefore, that in which the succession terminates is itself the eternal Prakṛti. The meaning is that "Prakṛti" here is merely a name for the root cause. || 68 ||

[Objection: "In that case, it would not be tenable that there are twenty-five principles (tattvas), because even in relation to the unmanifest (avyakta), which is the cause of the principle of the Great One (mahat), another insentient principle would result. With this intention, he states the fundamental solution: "The same [is the case] for both with respect to primordial nature (prakṛti). (69)

In reality, however, when investigating the fundamental cause of *prakṛti*, our positions as both proponent and opponent are identical. This is what is meant: just as the origination of *prakṛti* is heard [in scripture], so too is that of *avidyā* heard in such statements as, "This fivefold *avidyā* has manifested from the Great Self. Therefore, for one of these two, a figurative origination must necessarily be asserted.
