And in that case, it is logical that the figurative origination of *prakṛti* alone consists in its manifestation through conjunction with the *puruṣa* and other factors.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa* it is stated: "The origination characterized by conjunction is said to belong to action and knowledge.

Since this scripture records a secondary (gauṇa) origination for *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, and since no such secondary origination is heard of anywhere regarding *avidyā*, the latter is beginningless (*anādi*). Furthermore, the [Yoga] Sūtras define [ignorance] as being of the nature of false cognition and a property of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*); therefore, there is no addition to the fundamental principles (*tattva*). Alternatively, the meaning is that the same logic applies equally to both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, because [it is said]:
"From which the Pradhāna and Puruṣa arise, and from which this world of moving and unmoving things proceeds."
May that Viṣṇu, the cause of this entire universe, be gracious to us.

The sense is that, because the birth of the *puruṣa* is also heard of in such passages as these, the birth of *prakṛti* is likewise merely figurative (*gauṇī*), just as that of the *puruṣa* is; for the scriptural hearing of their eternity is equally applicable to both. Therefore, it is established that *prakṛti* alone is the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, while *avidyā*, which is an attribute of *prakṛti*, is the instrumental cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) of the world; and the same applies to the *puruṣa*. As for the statement:
"They call *avidyā* the unmanifest (*avyakta*), characterized by creation and dissolution;
they call the twenty-fifth principle, which is free from creation and dissolution, indeed *vidyā*."

Thus, in the *Mokṣadharma*, there is the statement regarding *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* as "ignorance" (*avidyā*) and "knowledge" (*vidyā*). However, that [statement] is merely figurative (*upacarita*), because it refers to both subjects. For, since *prakṛti* is subject to transformation (*pariṇāmin*), it is unreal from the perspective of the *puruṣa*; thus, its status as the object of ignorance has been stated. In the same way, in that very section, the entire collection of effects among the elements (*bhūta*) is called "ignorance" with respect to their respective causes, while each respective cause is called "knowledge" with respect to its own [effect].

It should be understood that the Puruṣa’s status as the material cause of the world in the form of transformation is due solely to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of Prakṛti, just like his agency and so forth; this is merely restated for the purpose of meditation in the Śruti and Smṛti. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as "neither gross nor subtle, neither short nor long. Furthermore, by the word *māyā*, it is Prakṛti itself that is denoted, because in the Śruti passage, "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti," the nature of Māyā—which was introduced previously in the verse, "The Illusionist (Māyin) creates this universe from this [Māyā], and another is bound therein by Māyā"—is stated to be Prakṛti.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the three qualities belonging to Prakṛti;
and Prakṛti, which consists of these, is known as the Māyā of Viṣṇu.
Red, white, and black—such was her offspring, vast in number.

This is also established by such Smṛti passages as these. However, ignorance (*avidyā*) and *māyā*—the referents of those terms—are not things to be destroyed by knowledge, for that would entail the impossibility of their being eternal. Furthermore, if ignorance were a substance (*dravya*), there would be a mere difference in terminology [from *prakṛti*]; if it were a quality (*guṇa*), then *prakṛti* would be established as its substratum, since the Puruṣa is devoid of qualities and so forth. If it is argued that we must describe ignorance as something distinct from substance, quality, and action, we say no; for it has already been stated that no such category is perceived. (69)

If this is so, and there exists such a method of inference regarding primordial nature (prakṛti), the person (puruṣa), and so forth, then why does discriminative reflection not arise for everyone? To this he replies:
"There is no such restriction because of the threefold nature of qualification. (70)

Just as in the case of hearing (*śravaṇa*) and so forth, there are three types of qualified persons for reflection (*manana*)—namely, the dull, the mediocre, and the superior; therefore, the rule of reflection does not apply to everyone. The meaning is that because sublation (*bādha*) and counter-balancing (*satpratipakṣatā*) are possible for the dull and the mediocre through fallacious reasoning (*kutarka*) and the like. For by the multitude of fallacious arguments propounded by the Buddhists and others, the stated inferences are sublated by the dull-witted. And by the mediocre, those very inferences are rendered counter-balanced by contradictory and unreal middle terms (*liṅga*) derived from the same Buddhist teachings.

The meaning is that such reflection occurs only for those of the highest qualification (*uttamādhikārī*). The essential nature of *prakṛti* as the equilibrium of the qualities (*guṇasāmya*) has already been stated; and the subtle elements (*sūkṣmabhūta*) and so forth are indeed well known. || 70 ||

He states the essential nature of the remaining two, the Great Principle (mahat) and the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), by means of two aphorisms: "The first effect, called the Great Principle, is that mind. (71)

The first effect, called the Great (mahat), is that mind whose function is deliberation (manana). Here, "deliberation" means ascertainment; thus, the meaning is that the intellect (buddhi) has that as its function. That which is the expanded seed, consisting of both Pradhāna and Puruṣa, is proclaimed as the Great Principle (mahattattva); it is called the principle of intellect (buddhitattva).
For from such statements as these, it is understood that the intellect alone is the effect of fire. || 71 ||
The final ego-sense. || 72 ||
That which follows immediately after that is called *ahaṅkāra*; the meaning is that its function (*vṛtti*) is self-identification (*abhimāna*). || 72 ||
Since the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) functions as self-conceit (abhimāna), it is therefore logical that the subsequent [categories] are its effects; thus he says:
"The subsequent ones have that as their effect. (73)
This is easy to understand. Having thus explained the three sūtras, the suspicion of redundancy has been dispelled. || 73 ||

Now, anticipating the objection that "in this way, [the doctrine] contradicts the Śruti and Smṛti which state that Prakṛti is the cause of creation," he says: "The status of being a non-direct cause exists through that [intermediary], even in a traditional succession, just as in the case of atoms. (74)

Even though there is no direct causality in the case of the succession, the primordial *prakṛti* possesses causality toward the *ahaṅkāra* and so forth by means of the *mahat* and the rest. The meaning is that, just as in the Vaiśeṣika system, atoms possess causality toward jars and other objects only through the medium of dyads (*dvyaṇuka*) and so on. || 74 ||
Now, since both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are eternal, what is the determining factor for Prakṛti alone being the cause? To this he replies:
"If both were antecedent, there would be the abandonment of one and the conjunction with the other. (75)

The meaning is that although both the Spirit (*puruṣa*) and Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) precede all effects, since one of them—the Spirit—is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*), it lacks the status of being a cause; therefore, it is appropriate for the other—Primordial Matter—to be the cause. And this is the reason for the Spirit’s immutability: if the Spirit were to act through association (*saṃhatya-kāritva*), it would follow that it exists for the sake of another, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). If it were to act without association, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the effects, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*), arising at all times. Furthermore, if one were to postulate transformation by means of Primordial Matter, then by the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), let that [Matter] alone be the subject of transformation.

However, the designation of "creator" is applied to the Puruṣa only figuratively, by virtue of its sovereignty. Just as victory and defeat, though residing in the soldiers, are attributed to the king because he is their master by being the enjoyer of their resulting pleasure and pain; likewise, since the primary means of cognition that establishes the subject (the *dharmigrāhakapramāṇa*) establishes Prakṛti solely as the cause, there is no further requirement for another cause. Just as when the Puruṣa is established as the seer by that same primary means of cognition, there is no requirement for another seer.

Furthermore, if the Puruṣa were subject to transformation (pariṇāmin), it would occasionally become as incapable [of cognition] as the eyes, the mind, and so forth. In that case, even though pleasure, pain, and the like exist, they would not be known. Consequently, there would arise the possibility of doubt, such as "Am I happy or not? Therefore, because its nature as perpetual luminosity is never lost, the non-transformative nature of the Puruṣa is established. As it is stated in the Yoga Sūtra: "The fluctuations of the mind are always known to its Lord, the Puruṣa, because of his non-transformative nature."

And by that very remedy [the author] says: "The fact that the Puruṣa is always the object of knowledge demonstrates his unchanging nature. We shall explain later how, even though its essential nature is eternal luminosity, it does not manifest the entire universe at all times. || 75 ||
He also establishes the all-pervasiveness [of Prakṛti] in order to justify its simultaneous causality:
"That which is limited cannot be the material cause of everything. (76)

The meaning is that the primary cause (pradhāna) is the material cause of everything; it is not limited, but all-pervasive. Here, "being the material cause of everything" is a qualifying attribute containing a logical reason, because such a status is impossible for something that is limited.

Now, it may be objected that the unlimitedness (*aparicchedatva*) of *prakṛti* is untenable; for *prakṛti* is not something distinct from the three qualities (*guṇa*), namely *sattva* and the rest, as is clearly established by both the *Yoga-sūtra-bhāṣya* and the forthcoming sūtra: "The fact that *sattva* and the others are not properties of that [Prakṛti] is because they are its very nature. Furthermore, if [Prakṛti] were all-pervasive (*vibhu*), the properties of those *sattva* and the others—such as lightness, mobility, and heaviness—which will be mentioned later, would be contradicted; and causes such as conjunction and disjunction, which are the grounds for creation and so forth, would also be untenable.

To this it is replied: here, "limitedness" (paricchinnatva) means being delimited by the delimitors of the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitāvacchedaka) of spatial non-existence (daiśikābhāva). And its absence is pervasiveness (vyāpakatva). Thus, since the causality of the world is not a delimitant of the counter-correlativity of spatial non-existence, it follows that Prakṛti is pervasive.

Just as the all-pervasiveness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) throughout all bodies, whether stationary or moving, is stated by virtue of its common nature as "vital breath"—since individual instances of the vital breath are connected to every body—in the same way, the pervasiveness of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is established. Furthermore, we shall demonstrate in the *Sādharmya-vaidharmya-sūtra* that primordial matter possesses such qualities as being inactive and unitary. || 76 ||
Not only because it is the material cause of everything, but also because of the scriptural statement regarding its production [from that]. || 77 ||

And because there is scriptural testimony regarding the origination of those [limited things]; for in such scriptural passages as "Now, that which is small is mortal," it is understood from their nature as subject to death that limited things originate, as well as from other scriptural texts—this is the meaning. || 77 ||
Now, in order to establish that primordial matter (prakṛti) is the cause, he refutes non-existence and other such things as being the cause:
"The establishment of a real entity does not proceed from a non-entity. (78)

The meaning is that since a non-entity has no existence, there can be no establishment of an entity, nor the arising of an existent; for if the world were to arise from a hare’s horn, liberation and so forth would be impossible, and such a thing is never observed. || 78 ||
Now, one might object: "Let the world also be unreal, like a dream and so forth. To this, he says:
"Because it is uncontradicted and because it is produced by causes free from defects, it is not unreal. (79)

The meaning is this: there is no sublation (*bādha*) of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of authoritative sources such as the Vedas, as there is for the objects of a dream; nor does it arise from defective sense organs and the like, as is the case with the yellowness perceived in a conch shell. Since there is no evidence for the postulation of such a defect (*doṣa*), the effect is not unreal. If it is argued that the sublation of the phenomenal world is established by scriptural texts such as, "Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," and that because of this sublation a defect called ignorance (*avidyā*) must exist in its own cause [Brahman], we say no.

This is because such statements are intended to convey the non-existence of things in the form of instability, which depends upon their own causes, as established by the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the analogy of clay; furthermore, it would otherwise contradict statements regarding creation and so forth. Moreover, if the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) were sublated by scripture, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*); since the scripture itself is included within the phenomenal world, its sublation would lead to the recurrence of doubt regarding the very meaning it seeks to establish.

For this very reason, two Vedānta sūtras emphatically reject the view that the waking state is equivalent to dreams, sky-flowers, and the like, on account of the difference in their characteristics—such as sublation and non-sublation—and because they are actually perceived: "And because of the difference in nature, it is not like a dream, etc. and "And because of perception. Furthermore, statements such as "not this, not this" (neti neti) are intended solely for the purpose of discernment (*viveka*), and do not intend to negate the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in its own right; for the Vedānta sūtra states: "It negates the limitedness of what has been previously described."
In this manner, other statements as well have been explained by us in the Brahmamīmāṃsābhāṣya. || 79 ||
Regarding what was stated—that the establishment of a real entity does not occur from that which is non-real—he states the reason for this:
"If [the entity] exists, its establishment occurs through connection with it; if it does not exist, because that [connection] is absent, how much less could there be its establishment? (80)

If the cause exists—that is, if it possesses the nature of being—then the accomplishment of the effect would be possible through its connection with that [existence], namely, through its connection with *sattā*. But if the cause is non-existent—that is, if it lacks the nature of being—then due to the absence of that [cause], the effect also lacks existence; how, then, could there be the accomplishment of an effect that is a real entity? The meaning is that the effect must be consistent with the very nature of the cause. || 80 ||
[Objection: Even so, let karma alone be the cause of the world because it is necessary; what is the use of postulating a primal matter (pradhāna)? To this, he replies:
"Because karma cannot be the material cause. (81)

Even regarding action (*karman*), the establishment of a real entity [as a material cause] is not possible; for action, being an instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), cannot be a fundamental material cause (*mūlakāraṇa*), since qualities (*guṇa*) cannot logically serve as the material cause of a substance (*dravya*). Indeed, conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) occurs only in accordance with what is observed. Furthermore, the status of being a material cause for the "qualities" mentioned by the Vaiśeṣikas is nowhere seen in experience—this is the meaning. Here, the word "action" (*karman*) is also indicative of ignorance (*avidyā*) and so forth, because they too, being equally "qualities," cannot logically function as material causes.
If ignorance were a substance residing in a conscious being, like a cataract in the eye, then it would be a mere difference in nomenclature for the Pradhāna. || 81 ||

Thus, the distinction between the Puruṣa and Prakṛti has been shown by means of their being subject to transformation and not subject to transformation, and their being for the sake of another and not for the sake of another. Now, he elaborates—using five sūtras—that which was previously stated in the sūtra "And there is no difference between the two"—namely, that discriminative knowledge itself, through the destruction of non-discrimination, is the cause of the supreme human goal (puruṣārtha), and that Vedic rituals have no direct causality therein: "Nor is its accomplishment [of liberation] achieved even through the revealed (Vedic) means, because [those results] are things to be accomplished and are thus subject to recurrence; therefore, they do not constitute the supreme human goal. (SK 82)

By the word "api" (also/even), there is a conjunction with what was previously stated—that the goal is not established through what is seen (*dṛṣṭa*). That which is heard from a teacher is *anuśrava*, namely the Veda; the ritual acts such as sacrifice prescribed therein are *ānuśravika* acts. From these as well, the aforementioned human goal is not established. The meaning is that because they are accomplished through effort (*sādhya*) and are thus connected with rebirth, they lack the quality of being the ultimate human goal.

Regarding the impermanence of that which is accomplished through action, there is a scriptural text: "Just as here the world acquired by action perishes, even so in the hereafter the world acquired by merit perishes. Since bondage through action was previously refuted by the Sūtra, "Not by action, because it is of a different nature," there is no tautology in now refuting liberation [through action].

If it is argued that—since the causality of action (*karman*) with respect to liberation has already been effectively refuted by the previously stated reason that [action] is a property of something else, no further doubt should arise—[we reply]: No. For once non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is established as the cause of bondage, it is logically consistent to determine that action belongs to a particular person because it is born from that person’s own non-discrimination.

But then, how is the scriptural teaching of "no return" (*anāvṛtti*) for one who has gone to the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) through ritual action known as meditation (*upāsanā*), such as the *pañcāgni-vidyā*, or through actions like dying at a sacred ford (*tīrtha-maraṇa*), to be explained? To this, he says:
"In that case, the scriptural teaching of no return applies to one who has attained discrimination. (Sūtra 83)

In that regard, the scriptural statement concerning non-return for those who have gone to the world of Brahmā through ritual action (*anuśravika-karman*) should be understood as applying only to one who has attained discrimination (*viveka*) while still there. For otherwise, there would be a contradiction with other scriptural passages which establish that there is indeed a return even from the world of Brahmā; this is the meaning. Nevertheless, even that non-return is the fruit of discriminative knowledge alone, and not directly of ritual action. This he will demonstrate in the sixth chapter. Furthermore, in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*, we have already explained these two sets of passages by citing them. (83)
He then states the fruit of that action:
"From suffering to suffering, like bathing in water, there is no release from dullness. (84)

However, because of the defects such as violence inherent in what is revealed by tradition (*ānuśravika*), and because its enjoyment consists of suffering, from suffering there arises only further suffering—a continuous stream of pain—and not liberation from insentience (*jāḍya*) or the cessation of non-discrimination (*aviveka*). Liberation from suffering remains exceedingly remote. The meaning is that just as for one afflicted by cold, sprinkling with water results only in the non-cessation of suffering and not in liberation from the cold. As it has been said:
"Just as mud cannot be cleansed by mud, nor water by water, nor a liquor by liquor, so too a single act of killing a living being cannot be wiped away by sacrifices."

And it is heard that even for Jayavijaya and others, who are attendants of Viṣṇu residing in the world of Brahmā, there is again a descent into the womb of a Rākṣasa, which is a stream of suffering. This has been stated in a kārikā:
"The scriptural (ānuśravika) [means] is like the perceptible (dṛṣṭavat), for it is characterized by impurity, decay, and excess. (84)

Now, one might object: "Surely there is no suffering from action consisting of internal sacrifice, recitation, and so forth when performed without desire; on the contrary, liberation is heard in scripture as its fruit. To this, he says:
"Whether with desire or without desire, because there is no difference in the fact that [the result] is something to be accomplished. (85)

Whether the action is performed with desire or without desire, it results in suffering from suffering. Why? Because there is no difference in their being things to be accomplished (sādhya). The meaning is that even knowledge—which is to be accomplished through action by means of the purification of the *sattva*—is of the nature of suffering, since it consists of the three *guṇas*. Furthermore, based on such scriptural passages as, "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone some have attained immortality," the point is that liberation is not the direct fruit of action.

By renunciation—that is, by the abandonment of egoism—some alone, and not all, have attained immortality; the meaning is that because the abandonment of egoism arises from the knowledge of reality, it is difficult to achieve. || 85 ||
[Objection: But even in your own view, why is that which is to be accomplished by knowledge not itself suffering, since there is no difference in their being "to be accomplished"? To this he says:
"For one who is liberated by nature, there is merely the destruction of bondage; therefore, there is no equality [between liberation and suffering]. (86)

For that which is liberated by its own nature—that is, liberated by its very essence—the mere cessation of bondage as previously described through the destruction of the cause called ignorance (*avidyā*) is the supreme and absolute fruit of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*). And this destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) is imperishable; it is not, like pleasure and so forth, an effect in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*) such as karma, which, by being subject to destruction, would itself become a source of suffering. Furthermore, it is not possible for karma to directly destroy ignorance without the presence of a visible auxiliary cause.

Therefore, because knowledge is inexhaustible, there is no equality between knowledge and action; this is the meaning. It is established that a return to worldly existence is not possible through knowledge, because the cause known as non-discrimination has been destroyed. Thus, it has been stated that discriminative knowledge alone is the direct means to liberation. || 86 ||

Now, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which are the direct methods for discriminative wisdom (*vivekajñāna*), will be examined. For, through scriptural statements such as "The Self, indeed, my dear, is to be seen, heard, and reflected upon," it is understood that knowledge of the Self is attained by means of the three instruments of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Ritual action and other such things, however, serve merely to purify the mind and the other instruments of knowledge. The cognition of an object not [otherwise] present to the senses is *pramā* (valid knowledge). That which is the most effective instrument for its production is the threefold *pramāṇa*. (87)

"Not proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*) means not mounted upon the cognizer, that is to say, not already apprehended. The determination or ascertainment of such an object—that is, a real entity—is valid cognition (*pramā*). And let that [determination] be a property of both, namely both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*puruṣa*), or let it belong to either one alone; in either case, that which is the most efficient cause (*sādhakatama*) of that valid cognition—being the cause whose connection with the result is not excluded—is threefold, according to the nature that will be described hereafter. The term "not already apprehended" is used to exclude memory (*smṛti*).

The word "object" (*vastu*) is used to exclude error; the restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇa*) is used to exclude doubt. In this context, if the fruit in the form of valid cognition (*pramā*) is said to reside solely in the person (*puruṣa*), then the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And if it is said to reside solely in the intellect, then the aforementioned contact with the sense organs and so forth is the means of valid cognition; the person, however, is merely the witness of the cognition, not the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). And if the cognition belonging to the person is [the result]...

Both the [instrument] and its function are called "valid cognition" (pramā); thus, it has been stated that both constitute the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) through their respective distinctions as cognitions. However, the conventional usage of the term "means of valid cognition" with respect to the eyes and other [senses] occurs only in an indirect sense; this is the intended meaning. In the *Pātañjalabhāṣya*, however, the venerable Vyāsa has stated that cognition residing in the self (puruṣa) is valid cognition. Since the instruments (karaṇas) operate solely for the sake of the self, it is appropriate that the result resides in the self alone. Therefore, even here, that very [view] is the primary established doctrine.

Nor should it be argued that, because the essential nature of the person's defect is eternal, how can it be a "fruit" (result); for although the defect in its isolation is eternal, it becomes an effect when colored by an object, or rather, the fruit consists precisely in its coloring by the purpose of the person.

The process here is as follows: through the channel of the sense organs, by means of contact with an object or by means of the cognition of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so forth, a modification (*vṛtti*) of the intellect (*buddhi*) arises in the form of that object. Among these, the perceptual modification born from sensory contact rests upon the intellect as qualified by the sense organ; the distinction is that it may take on the form of bile (*pitta*) and other such things due to defects like bile located in the eyes and other organs. And that modification, colored by the object, appears having mounted upon the *puruṣa* in the form of a reflection.

Because the Puruṣa, being unchanging, cannot possess the form of an object by itself—unlike the intellect (buddhi)—and because the apprehension of an object occurs precisely through the assumption of that object’s form, it is difficult to explain [the cognition] in any other way. This very point will be stated later: "There is no actual coloring as between a hibiscus flower and a crystal, but rather a misconception. And the Yoga Sūtra says: "In other cases, there is conformity with the mental modification (vṛtti). Smṛti also says:
"In that expansive mirror of consciousness, all perceptions of objects are reflected, just as trees on a riverbank are reflected in a lake."

And from the *Yogabhāṣya*: "The Puruṣa is the perceiver of the intellect (*buddhi*). The term "perceiver" (*pratisaṃvedī*) means that which serves as the locus for the reflection of consciousness (*saṃvedana*), like an echo. By this, although the Puruṣas are of the nature of immutable, all-pervading consciousness, there is no contingency of their manifesting everything at all times; for, being unattached, they do not by themselves assume the form of objects. Furthermore, without assuming the form of an object, the apprehension of an object through mere conjunction is not observed in the case of the intellect in instances such as supersensuous objects.

Furthermore, it is inferred on the strength of the resulting effect that the capacity to project a reflection belongs only to the respective modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) within the Person (*puruṣa*). This is just as the capacity to reflect in water and other media belongs only to those things possessing color-form (*rūpavat*), and not to anything else. Moreover, possessing color-form is not the general cause for reflection, since we observe that even sound has a reflection in the form of an echo. Nor should it be argued that an echo is merely another sound produced by the original sound.

Otherwise, since even the redness of a crystal and similar phenomena would result from being produced by proximity to a hibiscus flower (*japā*), the established doctrine of the falsity of reflections would be undermined. Furthermore, it should be understood that a reflection is merely a particular transformation (*pariṇāma*) of the intellect itself, taking the form of the original object (*bimba*) while residing in water or other media.

However, some maintain that consciousness itself, when reflected in a mental modification (*vṛtti*), illuminates that modification; thus, it is the reflection residing within the modification that constitutes the objectivity of consciousness toward the modification, and not that there is a reflection of the modification within consciousness. This is incorrect, because mere reasoning is inconclusive when it contradicts the scriptures already cited, and because—given the absence of any decisive criterion—the mutual reflection between the modification and consciousness is established by their very nature as a relationship consisting of mutual objectivity.

Since the nature of being an object (*viṣayatā*) is established in the external world precisely by way of having the form of the object (*arthākāratā*), it is appropriate that even in the internal [cognition], the nature of being an object consists precisely in that same having of the form of the object.

As for those logicians who do not accept the objectivity of cognition, in their view, because there is no common property (*anugamaka-dharma*) unifying individual instances of cognition, the occurrence of uniform linguistic usage such as "the cognition of a jar" or "the cognition of a cloth" would be untenable.

Some logicians, however, on account of this very lack of logical consistency, claim that objectivity (*viṣayatā*) is a distinct category (*padārtha*). That too is incorrect; for it involves unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*) to postulate a separate objectivity apart from the form of the object as it is being experienced.

[Objection: Even so, let there be a mutual objectivity between the mental modification (*vṛtti*) and consciousness (*caitanya*) consisting simply in their occurring within their respective adjuncts (*upādhi*), since they are subsumed under the very fact of occurring within their own adjuncts; what is the use of these two reflections called "aspects" (*ākāra*)? [Reply: No, because without a reflection, even "belongingness" (*svatva*) is difficult to define. For belongingness consists in possessing the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the modifications experienced by oneself. And experience (*bhoga*) is cognition (*jñāna*). Thus, since the definition of objectivity is constituted by the causal complex of the object, it would result in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Therefore, the mutual reflection of the unconscious and the conscious within each other—consisting in their being objects of one another—is established. For further details, one should consult the *Yogavārttika*; this is the direction. Herein lies the division of the knower and so forth:
"The knower is the pure consciousness; for us, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is only the mental modification (*vṛtti*).
The reflection of the modifications, which take the form of the object of knowledge, occurs within consciousness."
The object of the mental modifications that have been reflected [in the Self] is called the "object of knowledge" (meyam).
Furthermore, he himself will later describe the nature of being the Witness (sākṣitvam) as consisting in direct perception.
Therefore, due to the absence of a cause for [active] functioning, the conscious one is indeed the witness;
thus, Viṣṇu and others possess only a figurative status as witnesses of all, because of the absence of indicative marks [of such activity]. || 87 ||
But surely— it is said: "Just as the one sun illumines this entire world,
so too, O Bhārata, does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire Field."

In such statements as these, the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) consisting of analogy and so forth have been set forth for the sake of discerning between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; how then can it be said that there are only three [means of knowledge]? To this, he says:
"Since everything is established when that [the Veda] is established, there is no failure to establish anything additional. (88)

Furthermore, since every object is established once the threefold means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are established, no additional means of valid cognition is proven; the meaning is that it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). For this very reason, Manu also presented only the three means of valid cognition: "Perception, inference, and scripture consisting of various traditions—these three must be well understood by one who desires purity in dharma. Thus it is said.

Comparison (*upamāna*), presumption (*arthāpatti*), and the like are included within inference (*anumāna*), while non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) and others are included within perception (*pratyakṣa*). In the statement previously mentioned, this is the intended inference: "The entire [world], from its base to its summit, must be illuminated by a single entity distinct from itself, because it is not self-luminous, like the three worlds. Here, luminosity (*prakāśatva*), common to both light and consciousness, is established as an indivisible adjunct (*akhaṇḍopādhi*) by virtue of being the regulating factor for the linguistic usage of "luminosity. || 88 ||
Relying on the primary tenet that valid cognition (pramā) resides in the person, he begins to state the specific definitions of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa):
"That cognition which, being connected [with its object], reflects its form—that is perception (pratyakṣa). (89)

The meaning is that a cognition which, being connected, bears the form of the connected object—that is, the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*)—is the means of valid perception (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*). Here, the phrase ending with "existent" (*sat*) is a qualification containing a reason. Thus, the essential conclusion is: the modification (*vṛtti*) which is the substratum of the form produced by the contact with its own object is the means of valid perception. Since the forthcoming sūtra states, "the modification moves toward the object for the sake of connection," the modification itself is not produced by the contact; therefore, the mention of the "substratum of the form" is made.

Furthermore, the expansion of the function through the doors of the eyes and other senses is like the flame of a lamp; because it assumes the form of the external object immediately after contact with that object, there is no impossibility [of its occurrence]. || 89 ||

One might object: "Is there not a lack of pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of yogis perceiving past and future objects, because of the absence of the form of a connected entity? Anticipating this, he resolves it by stating that such cases are not subject to the definition: "There is no fault, because for yogis, [these are] non-external perceptions. (90)

In this context, only sensory perception (*aindriyakapratyakṣa*) is the object to be defined. Since yogis possess perceptions that are not external, there is no fault; the meaning is that there is no lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of such perception. || 90 ||
He states the actual resolution: "Or there is no fault because of the connection with the excellence obtained from the merged object. (91)

Alternatively, even that [past and future object] is indeed the object of perception (*lakṣya*); nevertheless, there is no fault, nor is there a lack of pervasion (*avyāpti*). For the meaning is this: a connection is possible for the yogic mind—which has acquired an excellence produced by the dharma born of yoga—with objects that are latent (*līna*). Here, the word "latent" (*līna*) expresses what is intended by the opponent as "non-proximate" (*asannikṛṣṭa*). Since, according to the proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists (*satkāryavādin*), even the past and so forth exist in their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), such a connection could occur; therefore, the qualification "having acquired an excellence" is provided as the cause for the connection with things that are obstructed or remote.
Furthermore, this "excellence" (*atiśaya*) consists of all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*), the removal of *tamas* which obstructs mental modifications (*vṛtti*), and so forth.

And this point should be noted here: since the preceding sūtra states "that which, being related, exists," it follows that for perception in general, the contact between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the object alone is the cause, as this is common to all external objects. The contacts with the sense organs (*indriya-sannikarṣa*), however, are causes specifically for visual and other types of perception.

[Objection: But in this case, even in the absence of sense-object contact, yoga-born dharma (*yogaja-dharma*), and so forth, there would follow the perception of external objects by the intellect (*buddhi*). [Reply: Not so; because at that time, due to the obstruction of *tamas*, the activity (*vṛtti*) of the *sattva* of the intellect is impossible. And that *tamas* is sometimes dispelled by the contact between the object and the senses, and sometimes by yoga-born dharma, just as the impurity of the eye is removed by the application of collyrium (*añjana*).

Nor should it be argued that, by the principle that "let it be so because of that very cause," sense-object contact and the like alone should be the cause for the general category of perception of external objects; for it is established that in states such as deep sleep, darkness acts as an obstacle to the functioning of the intellect.
One should know that wakefulness arises from sattva; one should indicate sleep as resulting from rajas;
deep slumber results from tamas; and the fourth state is continuous throughout these three.

This follows from such Smṛti texts as these, and because no other obstacle to the mental modification (vṛtti) is possible during deep sleep and similar states; furthermore, it is observed that even in visual perception, darkness acts as an obstacle.

As for the fact that dry logicians (śuṣka-tārkika) postulate the contact between the skin and the mind as the cause for the general cognition [of touch] in order to prevent the arising of mental modifications during deep sleep—that is incorrect. For it is heard in scripture that even prior to the emergence of the sense-organ of touch, Svayambhū perceives everything through his intellect alone. Furthermore, even in the absence of the contact between the skin and the mind, darkness itself must be stated to be the cause [of non-perception]. Moreover, mere logic is beset by the defect of being unestablished (apratiṣṭhā). This is the direction of the argument. || 91 ||
But even so, is there not non-pervasion (avyāpti) in the case of God's perception, since that, being eternal, is not produced by sensory contact? To this, he says:
"Because God is unestablished. (92)

The phrase "there is no fault because there is no proof for a Lord" is understood to carry over [from the previous argument]. Furthermore, it has already been established that this negation of a Lord is merely a bold assertion (*prauḍhivāda*) made by the partial proponents (*ekadeśin*). Otherwise, one would simply have said, "because of the non-existence of a Lord. However, if a Lord were admitted, then the intended definition of perception would be "that which belongs to the same class as what is produced by sense-object contact" (*sannikarṣajanyajātīyatva*). And the meaning is that this "belonging to the same class" (*sājātya*) consists in a universal (*jāti*) that is directly pervaded by the universal "cognition-ness" (*jñānatva*). (92)
In response to the inquiry, "How is it that the Lord is not established by means of the Śruti and Smṛti?", he states a worldly contradiction as a subverting argument:
"Because neither of the two—the liberated nor the bound—exists, He is not established. (93)
Is this intended Lord free from afflictions and the like, or bound by them? Since neither possibility is tenable, the meaning is that the existence of a Lord is not established. || 93 ||
In both cases, there is a lack of respect. || 94 ||

The meaning is that even when liberated, there is an incapacity for creation and so forth due to the absence of the pride and attachment that are the causes thereof; likewise, even when bound, there is no capacity for creation and so forth because of being deluded. || 94 ||
If this is so, what then is the status of those scriptural passages that establish the existence of God? To this he says:
"They are either praises of the liberated soul, or [instructions for] the meditation of one who has already attained perfection. (95)

Accordingly, some scriptural passage (śruti) is intended for praise and incitement by means of the mere proximity [of the liberated soul], in order to declare that the liberated self—the universal self alone—is an object of knowledge. And another scriptural passage, which establishes [the soul's] status as a creator preceded by volition (saṅkalpa), refers to the worship of the eternal nature and so forth of those who are already established as lords such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara, even though they possess egoism and are non-eternal lords; the meaning is that it is devoted to the worship of their secondary (gauṇa) eternity and other qualities. || 95 ||

[Objection: Even so, the fact that He is heard in scripture to be the presiding director (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*) of all things, such as primordial matter (*prakṛti*), remains unproven and untenable; for in the world, the term "presiding director" is conventionally applied only to one who effects transformation through volition (*saṅkalpa*) and the like. To this, he says:
"His state of being the presiding director is due to His proximity, like a magnet. (96)

If being a creator and a presiding controller were said to consist in volition (*saṅkalpa*), then this fault would indeed apply. However, we maintain that the Puruṣa’s status as a presiding controller and creator, etc., arises solely from his proximity (*sannidhāna*), like a magnet (*maṇi*). Just as a magnet possesses the power of extracting iron merely by its presence and not through volition or the like, so too does Primordial Matter (*prakṛti*) undergo transformation into the form of the Great Principle (*mahat*) through mere conjunction with the First Person (*ādi-puruṣa*). And this very thing is what is meant by "being a creator of one's own limiting adjunct" (*svopādhi-sraṣṭṛtva*).
Thus it has been said:
Just as iron moves when a wishless jewel is present,
so does this world of living beings [move] by the mere existence of the Divine.
Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside in the Self;
because it is devoid of desire, it is a non-agent, yet it is an agent by virtue of its mere presence. Thus it is said.

The scriptural passage beginning with "Then He thought: 'May I be many'" is figurative (*gauṇī*), like the expression "the bank wishes to fall," because of the proximity of Prakṛti to a multitude of qualities.

Alternatively, such a collection of statements refers to a creation preceded by conscious intent (*buddhipūrvaka*), and does not concern the original creation (*ādisarga*), since that is remembered as being unconscious (*abuddhipūrvaka*). As it is said in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Thus has this primary creation (*prākṛtasarga*) been briefly described by me."
"Understand that their creation by Brahmā was not preceded by conscious intention. Thus [it is said].
And because this statement is produced by the intellect of the Primordial Person, any restriction [of its scope] would entail unnecessary complexity (gaurava). || 96 ||

It is not only at the beginning of creation that the Puruṣa possesses the status of creator and so forth merely through conjunction; rather, he states that for all Puruṣas, this applies even to all other specific effects, such as the elements and so on, which are preceded by volition and the like: "Even in specific effects, [the agency belongs] to those who are born. (97)

The phrase "the state of being a presiding agent [is due] to proximity" is to be supplied [to the previous verse]. It will be explained in the sixth chapter that the meaning of the word *jīva* is precisely that which is characterized by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, even in the specific activity called emission—the individual creation—the presiding agency of the *jīvas*, who are consciousnesses reflected in the internal organs, arises solely from their proximity, and not through any action, because they consist of immutable pure consciousness alone. This is the meaning. || 97 ||

If it be objected that, since there is no eternally omniscient Lord, then the teaching of the discrimination that constitutes the meaning of the great Vedāntic statements would be rendered invalid due to the suspicion of a "tradition of the blind," he replies to this: "Because it possesses the nature of imparting knowledge of an already established reality, the instruction on the meaning of the statement [is authoritative]. (98)

The implication is that the instruction regarding the meaning of their sentences is authoritative, because Hiraṇyagarbha and others possess the status of realized beings who know reality as it is, and because this is established by the authority of the Āyurveda and other sciences taught by them. || 98 ||

Now, if the Puruṣa possesses a secondary (gauṇa) status as a presiding agent merely by virtue of his proximity, then, in response to the inquiry as to who possesses the primary (mukhya) status of presiding agent, he says:
"The internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) possesses the status of a presiding agent because it is ignited by that [Puruṣa], like iron. (99)

The non-figurative status of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as a presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) should be understood as being mediated by volition (*saṅkalpa*) and other such functions. Now, one might object that presiding agency is not appropriate for something insentient, like a jar; to this he replies: "Because it is ignited by the conscious [Self], like iron. For the internal organ becomes ignited by the conscious [Self] just like heated iron. Therefore, the meaning is that its status as a presiding agent—which distinguishes it from objects such as jars—is established by its being animated by consciousness.

[Objection: But if this were so, the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) being illumined by consciousness would result in consciousness becoming attached [to it], just as fire [is attached] to iron. [Reply: This is not so. For the "illumination" of the internal organ consists merely in its specific conjunction with eternally luminous consciousness, or rather, in the reflection of consciousness produced by that specific conjunction; consciousness itself does not migrate into the internal organ, whereby it would become attached. Indeed, even in the case of fire, its light and so forth do not migrate into the iron; rather, the illumination of the iron is simply a specific effect of its conjunction with fire.

If it is argued that even so, there is transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) due to conjunction (*saṃyoga*), we say no; for the conventional usage of "transformation" applies only when there is the production of a property distinct from general qualities (*sāmānyaguṇa*). And this particular conjunction of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is postulated on the strength of the observed result, as it arises from a transformation consisting in the increase of *sattva*. This is because, since the Spirit (*puruṣa*) is unchanging (*apariṇāmin*), no such particularity can be produced in it by conjunction. Furthermore, this very particular conjunction is the cause of the mutual reflection between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the Self (*ātman*).

If it is argued that since a specific conjunction is necessary as the cause of reflection, the postulation of a reflection is redundant—because the effects of reflection, such as the cognition of objects and so forth, can arise from that specific conjunction alone—it is not so. The reflection of consciousness in the intellect is postulated for the purpose of perceiving consciousness, just as the reflection of a face occurs in a mirror; otherwise, due to the contradiction between agent and object, it would be impossible for consciousness to perceive itself directly.

This very reflection of consciousness in the intellect (buddhi)—its falling into the shadow of consciousness—is termed the superimposition of consciousness (caitanyādhyāsa), the penetration by consciousness (cidāveśa), and so forth. Furthermore, this reflection of the intellect in consciousness is held to exist together with the objects mounted [upon the intellect] for the sake of the manifestation of the intellect. This is because it is improper to assume that the apprehension of objects occurs in the Puruṣa (Spirit) through the assumption of the form of the object itself; and because the very meaning of the term "apprehension of an object" consists precisely in the assumption of the object's form.

Since such a transformation of the object's form within the Puruṣa is impossible, it follows by implication that it must result in the nature of a reflection. Such is the general direction of the argument.
This mutual reflection has been established as a definitive conclusion by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Yogabhāṣya*:

"The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*), which is unchanging and non-transferring, appears as if transferred into an object that is subject to change; it follows the modifications (*vṛtti*) of that [object]. And because it merely conforms to the modification of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is to receive the reflection of consciousness, the modification of consciousness is described as being indistinguishable from the modification of the intellect," and so forth. This has been explained by us in detail in the *Yogavārtika*.

However, some maintain that the intellect itself possesses the status of being the knower of all objects through the reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā) residing within it; for they argue that experience shows knowledge is in grammatical apposition with desire and so forth, and it is improper for one thing to act based on the knowledge of another. This view should be disregarded because it is rooted in a misconception regarding the self. For, in this way, [it would follow that] the intellect alone...

If [the self] were a knower, there would be a contradiction with the two subsequent sūtras stating that "experience consists in the finality of the non-conscious" (YS 2.20) and so forth. Furthermore, there is a lack of evidence for the existence of the *puruṣa*; for experience, which is the mark (*liṅga*) of the *puruṣa*, is admitted to reside in the intellect (*buddhi*) alone. Nor should it be argued that the *puruṣa* as the original object (*bimba*) is established by the impossibility of the reflection otherwise; for this would involve circular reasoning (*anyonyāśraya*). If the separate existence of the original object is established, then the status of consciousness residing in the intellect as a reflection is established; and if the status of the reflection is established, then the original object is established as its correlate.

In our view, once the self (puruṣa) is established as the knower, its status as the object of knowledge is established through the impossibility of any other way [of accounting for cognition]; thus, when the reflection is established, there is no circularity (*anyonyāśraya*). If it is argued that the conscious being is established as the original object (*bimba*) by virtue of being the witness (*sākṣin*) of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), then it is more appropriate to attribute the status of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) to the witness alone. This is because postulating the status of knower for both would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*), and because we experience the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the cognition of a mental modification and the cognition of a jar.

Furthermore, this being the case, the proof of the *puruṣa* as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) by means of the forthcoming sūtra, "Because [otherwise] there would be the state of non-enjoyment" (*abhoktṛbhāvāt*), given that the intellect alone is the enjoyer, would be contradicted. Now, if its intention were described merely as follows—that cognition belongs to the original object (*bimba*) itself through a connection consisting of the reflection of the intellect, and that no reflection of the intellect is postulated within consciousness (*cit*)—that too is incorrect.

Since it is not observed that the sun or other luminaries illuminate water and the objects situated therein through a relationship consisting of their own reflected images—because both are illuminated by their rays alone—it is seen, however, in cases such as a mirage (*marumarīcikā*), that they do indeed illuminate water and so forth superposed upon themselves. Therefore, following empirical observation, we postulate that the relationship whereby the reflection in the intellect (*buddhipratibimba*) is the cause for the manifestation of all objects is precisely this [superposition]. As for what was said—that the activity of one person toward an object is untenable through the cognition of another—that too is not the case.

This is because the future sūtra, "The experience of the fruit belongs even to one who is not the agent, like food and so forth," will establish the difference in locus between knowledge and activity by means of an illustration; for here too, the specific conjunction and other factors alone serve as the determinants of bodily action through the volition of the intellect. || 99 ||
Having defined the means of valid cognition that is perception, he defines inference: "Inference is the knowledge of the related [sādhya] by one who perceives the connection [pratibandha]. (100)

The connection is pervasion (*vyāpti*). The meaning is that inference as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consists of the knowledge of the pervader (*vyāpaka*) arising from the observation of pervasion, which takes the form of a mental occurrence (*vṛtti*). Inference, however, is the human cognition [resulting therefrom]. || 100 ||
He defines verbal testimony (śabdapramāṇa): "Verbal testimony is the instruction of a reliable person" (sūtra 1.1.7).

In this context, "attainment" (āpti) means fitness (yogyatā). Since the authorlessness (apauruṣeyatā) of the Veda will be explained in the fifth chapter, the meaning is that the valid means of knowledge called verbal testimony (śabda) consists of a word that is fit [to produce knowledge] and the cognition generated by it. And the result is the understanding produced by a human word. || 101 ||
He states the very fruit of establishing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) himself:
"The establishment of both [the self and the world] arises from the means of valid cognition; therefore, there is the teaching of it. (102)

The accomplishment of the distinction between the two—the self and the non-self—occurs through valid cognition alone; therefore, the meaning is that the instruction on that valid cognition has been given. || 102 ||
In this regard, he describes how those two [the self and the body] are primarily to be established here by means of a specific type of inference:
"The establishment of both occurs through *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* [inference]. (103)

Inference (*anumāna*) is of three kinds: *pūrvavat*, *śeṣavat*, and *sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*. Among these, *pūrvavat* has as its object something belonging to a class previously perceived. For example, the inference of fire from smoke [“the mountain possesses fire because it possesses smoke”]. Indeed, fire of that same class was previously perceived in the kitchen and other such places. *Śeṣavat* is negative inference (*vyatirekānumāna*). It is called *śe�śavat* because its object is a "remainder" (*śeṣa*), meaning a novel (*apūrva*) matter; that is to say, it is one whose probandum (*sādhya*) is not yet established.

For example, there is the inference of the earth's difference from other things: "The earth is distinct from others because it possesses odor; for whatever is not so, is not thus. Indeed, the earth's distinction from others was previously unestablished. And that inference which is distinct from both [the aforementioned types] is the *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*. This is where, by grasping a pervasion (*vyāpti*) through a general perception or similar means, an object of a different class—such as something imperceptible—is established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). For example, in the cognition of color and so forth, one infers the possession of an instrument (*karaṇavattva*) by virtue of its being an action (*kriyātva*).

For here, having apprehended the pervasion by taking as the instrument [of action] something belonging to the same class as an axe and the like—such as "earth-ness" (pṛthivītva)—one establishes the sense-faculty (*indriya*) as an instrument of cognition that is of a different class and beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). In this context, the meaning is that the establishment of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* occurs through inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). Among these, the inference based on general observation regarding *prakṛti* is as follows: [The text continues: ...In this regard, the inference based on general observation concerning *prakṛti* is: "That which is not perceived directly but whose effects are perceived must have a cause, because it is an effect, just like a pot. From this, the existence of *prakṛti* is established. As for *puruṣa*, the inference is: "The aggregate of the elements and organs exists for the sake of another, because it is an aggregate, just like a bed, a seat, or a chariot. From this, the existence of *puruṣa* is established. Thus, the meaning is that the proof of both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* proceeds from inference based on general observation.

Just as the principle of Mahat has for its material cause a substance characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion, because, while being an effect, it is characterized by pleasure, pain, and delusion.

"Like earrings and so forth produced from gold," and so on. Although there is no need for inference regarding the Puruṣa (the Self) because it is universally accepted, nevertheless, for the sake of distinguishing it from Prakṛti and the rest, only that which is "seen through general observation" (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭam*) is required. For example: "Pradhāna exists for the sake of another, because it acts by means of combination, like a house and such. Here, having taken as an instance the fact that houses and the like exist for the sake of bodies and so forth—which is established by perception—one infers that the Puruṣa, being of a different class [from those objects], exists as the "other" (the enjoyer) in relation to Pradhāna and the rest. Furthermore, since the state of being an enjoyer has previously been grasped [erroneously] due to non-discrimination with respect to the body and other such things, this is established for both parties.

Regarding the doubt that the person undergoes transformation through that accomplishment called "valid cognition" (pramā), which was described as the fruit of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa), he states its true nature:
"Experience terminates in consciousness. (104)

The meaning is that enjoyment and accomplishment (siddhi) have their ultimate culmination in the form of the Puruṣa. The term "culminating in consciousness" (cid-avasāna) is used to distinguish this from the enjoyment of the intellect (buddhi). The word "culmination" (avasāna) is employed to dispel doubts regarding the possibility of consciousness undergoing transformation or possessing attributes. The intention is that since enjoyment culminates in the form of consciousness, there is no loss of its immutability (kauṭasthya) and other such qualities. For instance, the objects of knowledge (prameya), such as Prakṛti and Puruṣa, which are presented by the mental modification (vṛtti) known as valid cognition (pramāṇa), appear when they are reflected along with that modification in the Puruṣa.

Therefore, it is the self-nature consciousness (svarūpa-caitanya) itself, as delimited by the reflection in the mental modification colored by the object, that constitutes manifestation; this is the experience of the person (puruṣa) and the fruit of the means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Consequently, since the mental modifications serve as the medium for the connection with the object in the form of a reflection, they possess the status of instruments (karaṇa). As it is said in the Viṣṇupurāṇa: "Salutations to her who is the self of the universe, the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), to whom the objects grasped by the senses are presented in their essential nature."

For it is observed that the administrative department of a king delivers the objects of enjoyment to the master; and the meaning of the word *bhoga* (enjoyment) is "consuming," which is to say, "making one's own. This [process] is common to all things from the body up to consciousness. However, there is this distinction: because the *puruṣa* is unchanging (*apariṇāmī*), its enjoyment of objects consists merely in the reception of a reflection; for others, however, because they are changing (*pariṇāmī*), it also includes nourishment and so forth.

Furthermore, it should be understood that this very enjoyment in the form of transformation is denied in the case of the *puruṣa* by such statements as "like the enjoyment of the intellect [is attributed] to the Self. In this sūtra, the fact that the *puruṣa* is also pervaded by the result (*phala-vyāpyatā*) is established, because it is stated that the state of terminating in consciousness (*cid-avasānatā*) is admitted by both parties. || 104 ||

An objection may be raised: "In the world, it is observed that only the agent experiences the fruit of an action, just as one who is walking alone experiences the suffering arising from that walk. Therefore, how can the experience of pleasure and so forth—which are the fruits of merit (dharma) and other qualities produced by the intellect—be attributed to the Puruṣa, given that they consist of the fluctuations of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) colored by objects? In response to this doubt, he says:
"Even for one who is not the agent, there is the enjoyment of the fruit, like [the taste] of food and drink. (105)

The enjoyment of the fruit of the intellect’s activity is also appropriate for the *puruṣa*, even though he is not its agent; this is like food and so forth. The meaning is that just as a king enjoys food and other things prepared by others, so it is here. However, there is no over-extension [of this principle] because non-discrimination (*aviveka*) or the relationship between owner and owned (*svasvāmibhāva*) serves as the regulator of enjoyment. Having accepted that pleasure, pain, and so forth are the fruits of karma, it was stated that the *puruṣa* experiences the fruit of karma residing in the intellect. || 105 ||

Now, having accepted that the enjoyment acquired by the person alone is the fruit of karma, he states the primary established doctrine—that it is the person himself who produces the fruit through the activity of the intellect:
"Or, because its accomplishment [arises] from non-discrimination, the agent experiences the fruit. (106)

Alternatively, the fruit does not belong to the agent at all. Since the desire "May I enjoy happiness" and so forth indicates that enjoyment itself is the fruit, the fruit therefore resides only in the enjoyer; for it is said that "the fruit prescribed by the scriptures belongs to the performer. However, the understanding of the fruit as belonging to the agent found in the scriptures arises because the accomplishment of that [enjoyment]—namely, the accomplishment known as experience—resides in the non-agent (the Self), due to a lack of discrimination on the part of the agent's intellect. For the common worldly experience is: "I, who am the doer, am the very same one who enjoys."

The desire expressed in such thoughts as "May happiness be mine" is logically established only as a means to an end, just like the thought "May a son be born to me. Pleasure itself, however, is not a means to anything else; therefore, it alone is the primary result (*phala*). Although pleasure is of the very nature of the self (*puruṣa*), according to the Vaiśeṣika school, it must be understood as something produced (*kāryatā*), similar to the sense of hearing. This is because consciousness delimited by pleasure and so forth is precisely what constitutes "experience" (*bhoga*). In this view, where experience is regarded as the result, liberation (*apavarga*) should be understood as simply the absence of the experience of suffering.

Alternatively, let pleasure (*sukha*), pain (*duḥkha*), and the absence of these alone be the fruits, by virtue of their connection with ownership (*svattva*) in the form of being objects of experience (*bhogyatā*). For, through that connection, pleasure and the like reside in the person (*puruṣa*), just as wealth and so forth do.

Thus, having established the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and the establishment of the objects of knowledge (*prameyasiddhi*) which constitute the fruit of the means of knowledge, he states the fruit of that very establishment of the objects of knowledge:
"And neither [is the fruit] in the proclamation of reality" (107).

When the reality of both nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) has been declared by means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), and when there is direct realization of that reality, neither pleasure nor pain occurs for either of them. This is the meaning, based on the scriptural authority of "The wise man abandons joy and sorrow" and on logical reasoning as well. || 107 ||

In brief, primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa) have been inferred through their distinction. From this point until the end of the chapter, the intermediate specific details regarding the inference of that primordial nature and the person are to be investigated. In that regard, he first removes the objection of non-perception against the inferences of primordial nature and so forth: "An object, even if it is not within range due to excessive distance and the like, [is known] by the organ of sense through its rejection or acquisition. (108)

The Cārvākas cannot establish the non-existence of *prakṛti* and so forth merely on the grounds of their not being perceived by the senses, as in the case of the non-existence of a jar; for even an existing object may not be perceived due to a defect in the sense organs or because it is beyond the range of perception. It is only when there is a failure of perception despite the presence of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) that such non-perception serves as the cause for the perception of non-existence. However, in the case of *prakṛti* and the like, the causal complex is not present due to the obstacles that will be mentioned later. Furthermore, defects such as excessive distance and others are specifically enumerated in the verse: [Verse omitted] The meaning is that these defects prevent the meeting of the causal conditions. Thus, the intention is that although *prakṛti* exists, it is not perceived because the necessary causal complex is absent due to these aforementioned impediments. Finally, the defects such as being too far away are specifically listed in the verse.
"Due to excessive distance, extreme proximity, impairment of the sense organs, the mind being elsewhere, subtlety, obstruction, being overwhelmed, and the withdrawal of dreams. Thus [it is said].

"Samānābhihāra" (the merging of equals) is the blending with that which is of the same class; for example, when buffalo milk is mixed with cow's milk, the "buffalo-ness" is no longer perceived. || 108 ||
Now, among [the causes of non-perception] such as extreme distance and so forth, what is the obstacle to the perception of primordial matter (prakṛti) and the rest? To this he says:
"Its non-perception is due to subtlety" (SK 8).

The meaning is that the non-perception of those two previously mentioned—the *prakṛti* and the *puruṣa*—is due to their subtlety (*saukṣmya*). This subtlety does not consist in atomicity (*aṇutva*), because they pervade the entire universe; nor does it consist in being difficult to grasp, for that would be indefinable. Rather, it is a universal property (*jāti*) that acts as an obstacle to perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣapramā*). Through the role of an auxiliary factor (*uttejaka*) played by merit born of yoga (*yogajadharma*), perceptual cognition of *prakṛti*, *puruṣa*, and so forth, does occur. Furthermore, the commingling of universals (*jātisaṅkara*) does not constitute a logical fault. Alternatively, subtlety here may simply be defined as the state of being a partless substance (*niravayavadravyatva*), and the merit born of yoga remains merely the auxiliary factor. (109)

Now, one might object: "Since non-perception is possible simply through non-existence, why postulate subtlety? Otherwise, why would even things like a hare's horn not be unperceived due to their subtlety? To this, he says:
"Because that [subtlety] is perceived through the observation of its effects. (110)

The meaning is as follows: once the existence of *prakṛti* and the rest has been established through the impossibility of otherwise accounting for the effects (*kāryānyathānupapatti*), their subtlety (*sūkṣmatva*) is postulated. Since prior to the inference there was doubt regarding subtlety and so forth, and thus no determination of non-existence, the inference is valid.
(110) Regarding this, an objection is raised: "If it is argued that [the inference] is unestablished because of conflicting views among disputants" (111).

Now, if the effect were already established prior to its production, then primordial matter (prakṛti) would be established as its eternal substratum; for it will be stated later that the inference of a cause is possible only through its association with an effect. The meaning of "if" is that, due to the disagreement among disputants, the pre-existent effect (satkārya) itself remains unestablished. || 111 ||
Having conceded this, he refutes it:
"Even so, there is no denial [of the other], because one is established through the perspective of the other. (112)

Let it be granted that the effect does not pre-exist; nevertheless, since one cause is established through the observation of its corresponding effect, there is no denial of causality at all, and thus the cause is indeed established. For this very reason, liberation is possible through the discernment of the Puruṣa as unchanging from the transforming [Prakṛti]. It is by means of this very provisional argument (abhyupagamavāda) that the Vaiśeṣika and other orthodox (āstika) scriptures proceed. Therefore, it should not be thought that because they contradict the Śruti and Smṛti of those who maintain the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), they lack authority in their other parts. || 112 ||
He states the refutation from the perspective of ultimate truth: "And because it would entail a threefold contradiction" (113).

Now, it is established by all disputants that every effect is of three kinds: past, future, and present. In this regard, if an effect is held to exist eternally, then its threefold nature is untenable; for since a jar or the like does not exist at times such as the past, it would be impossible for the jar to possess the properties of being past and so forth. Furthermore, a relationship between the existent and the non-existent is impossible. Moreover, if the nature of being a counter-correlate were identical to the form of the counter-correlate itself, the aforementioned defect would remain unchanged.

If its nature were merely non-existence, then the absence of a cloth would be the absence of a jar, and so on, because there would be no distinction between one non-existence and another. Even among absences, if one admits a specific intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-viśeṣa*), it follows that "non-existence" would be nothing more than a mere technical designation (*paribhāṣā-mātra*). If it is argued that the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) itself is what distinguishes the absence, we say no; for an unreal counter-positive cannot function as a distinguisher in cases such as antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*). Therefore, one must maintain that it is precisely an eternal effect that possesses distinct states of past, future, and present.

This is because it is appropriate that the cognitions "the jar is past," "the jar is present," and "the jar will be" possess an identical form; it is not the case that one has existence as its object while the other two have non-existence as their objects. It is those very states of pastness and futurity that generate the conventional usage of "destruction" (dhvaṃsa) and "prior non-existence" (prāgabhāva), since there is no evidence for a pair of non-existences distinct from them. This is the general direction of the argument.

However, more [on this matter] is to be seen in the *Pātañjala*. In this way, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) are also merely the nature of the locus itself (*adhikaraṇasvarūpa*). Nor should it be argued that, in this case, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition of absolute non-existence even at a time when the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) exists, because the nature of the locus does not depart; for even by others (the Naiyāyikas), the absolute non-existence of that [object] is admitted in a place where its counter-positive is present, and because the status of occasional absolute non-existence (*sāmayikātyantābhāva*) is possible only in the past and future states of the relation with the counter-positive.

Therefore, in our system, negation (*abhāva*) is not an additional entity. Furthermore, when there is a requirement for some real thing to account for such cognitions as "the jar is destroyed," "the jar will come into being," or "there is no jar here," it is more parsimonious to postulate that very thing in the form of a positive entity (*bhāva*). One should understand that this is because postulating an unperceived negation would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). || 113 ||
For this reason as well, he states that the pre-existence of the effect is established: "There is no production of the non-existent, because [the non-existent] is like a human horn. (114)
The meaning is that even the arising of a non-existent thing, such as a human horn, is not possible. || 114 ||
He states the reason for this:
"Because of the restriction of the material cause" (115).

The restriction that a jar arises only from clay and a cloth only from threads—such a restriction regarding the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) of effects is not possible. For prior to its production, there is no distinction whatsoever in the non-existence of the effect within the cause by which one [cause] might produce a certain non-existent effect and not another. If such a distinction is admitted, then because it would possess the nature of an entity (*bhāvatva*), it is lost to the status of non-existence. And that very distinction is what we call the "future state" (*anāgatāvasthā*) of the effect.

By this, the position of the Vaiśeṣikas—who postulate *prāgabhāva* (prior non-existence) alone as the regulator of the production of an effect—is also refuted. This is because there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in postulating an entity (*bhāva*) rather than a non-entity (*abhāva*), since entities are observed and do not depend on anything else. Furthermore, if non-entities possessed an intrinsic distinction, they would necessarily become entities. Moreover, any distinction consisting of the nature of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) does not exist at the time when that counter-correlate is absent. Therefore, since non-entities are indistinguishable [from one another], it is not logical for them to serve as regulators in the production of an effect. ||115||
He states the authoritative proof for the restriction of the objects of appropriation:
"Because everything is not possible at all times and in all places" (116).
This is easy to understand. The intention is that if there were no restriction on the causes of appropriation, then everything would arise from everything, at all times, and in all places. || 116 ||
For this reason as well, there is no arising from non-existence; so he says:
"Because that which is capable produces only that which is possible for it to produce. (117)

The state of being a material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*) is simply the possession of the capacity for the effect; this is because no other [definition] can be easily stated and because of parsimony (*lāghava*). That capacity is nothing other than the future state of the effect itself; therefore, since that which possesses the capacity produces the effect for which it is capable, there is no production of what is non-existent. This is the meaning. || 117 ||
And for this reason as well: "and because of the nature of being a cause" (kāraṇabhāvāt). || 118 ||
