Even prior to its origination, the non-difference of the effect from the cause is heard in scripture. Therefore, by the establishment of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is no production of what was previously non-existent; this is the meaning. For if the effect were non-existent, the non-difference between the existent and the non-existent would be untenable. And regarding the non-difference of effects from their causes prior to origination, there is scriptural authority: "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest"; "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone"; "In the beginning, this was the Self alone"; "In the beginning, this was water alone," and so forth. [At the end, some read a variant text: "In the beginning, this was heat alone"; "In the beginning, this was this very one alone. || 118 ||
He raises an objection:
"If there is no connection with existence in that which exists" (verse 119).

Now, if the effect were thus eternal, then in the case of an effect that is of the nature of an existent (bhāvarūpa), the connection with existence—that is, the connection with origination—is not possible; for the conventional usage of "origination" applies only to the coming into being of what was previously non-existent. This is the meaning. || 119 ||
He refutes this: linguistic usage and non-usage are not based on manifestation. || 110 ||

The linguistic usage (vyavahāra) of "origination" and the absence of such usage regarding an effect are caused by its manifestation (*abhivyakti*). From manifestation arises the linguistic usage of "origination," and from the state of being unmanifest arises the absence of the linguistic usage of "origination. The meaning is not that there is existence through the coming-to-be of what was previously non-existent. Furthermore, manifestation is not cognition; rather, it is the present state. The operation of the cause also produces only a transformation characterized by the present state of the effect. Moreover, in the world as well, we observe that for an effect which already exists, there is merely manifestation due to the operation of the cause.

Just as there is merely a manifestation of an image situated within a stone through the act of inference, of oil from sesame seeds by pressing, and of rice from grain by threshing; so it is said in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"Just as the lines of wheels and lotuses exist within a stone and other such objects during the state of deep sleep, even so does this series of worlds exist within Consciousness."
The meaning is: "by way of the primordial nature. || 120 ||

Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be some kind of origination for that which exists prior to its arising, but how can there be destruction of an entity that is beginningless? In response to this expectation, he says:
"Destruction is the dissolution into the cause. (121)

The meaning is as follows: based on the instruction "līṅ means to adhere," *laya* (dissolution) is the non-distinction [of the effect] within its causes by way of subtlety. That very state, when past, is called "destruction" (*nāśa*). The remainder of the sense is that dissolution termed "future" is called "prior non-existence" (*prāgabhāva*). Furthermore, there is no re-manifestation of a dissolved manifested effect, because such a view has been rejected in the Pātañjala [Yoga-bhāṣya] due to the undesirable consequence of [the necessity of] recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and so forth; and because, just as for our opponents, for us too, the state of being future—known as prior non-existence—is the cause of manifestation.

But what is the proof that the past also exists? For, unlike the existence of the future, scripture and other authorities are not clearly perceived even regarding the existence of the past. This is not so; for the existence of both the future and the past is established by the fact that the direct perception of yogins would otherwise be inexplicable, since the object must serve as the cause for any direct perception in general. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even the present could not be established through direct perception.

Therefore, by virtue of the inherent validity (*autsargika-prāmāṇya*) of cognitions, provided there is no sublation, it is established that even the past exists through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of yogis. Furthermore, regarding the direct perception of the past and future by yogis, the *Yogavārttika* has elaborated upon the authority of the *Śruti*, *Smṛti*, *Itihāsa*, and so forth; this is the general direction. Thus, the conventional usage of the "arising" and "destruction" of effects has been explained by means of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) and dissolution (*laya*).

Now, is manifestation also existent or non-existent prior [to the operation of causes]? In the first case, the activity of the cause would be fruitless. In the latter case, the very doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is undermined, because one would be admitting the manifestation of something that is itself non-existent.

To this it is replied: Since it is accepted that all effects exist eternally prior to the operation of their causes, there is no room for the aforementioned alternatives. For, like a jar, even its manifestation is non-existent in its present state prior [to that operation]; therefore, the operation of the cause is required for the purpose of removing that non-existence. And by way of its future state...

This is because the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) remains unimpaired. If it is objected that there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence at one and the same time, we reply that this is not so, because a distinction of modes has already been stated. If it is further argued that even so, since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is not admitted, it is difficult to explain the prior non-existence of effects, we say: do not speak thus; for the various states themselves consist in mutual negation. (121)

One might object: "In order to defend the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), one must admit that even manifestation itself has a manifestation; thus, there would be an infinite regress. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"The search [for a cause] proceeds through a succession, like the seed and the sprout. (122)

The pursuit [of the series] must be carried out through a succession, by way of a continuous chain of manifestation, just like the case of the seed and the sprout; the meaning is that this is not a fault because it is established by valid authority (*prāmāṇika*). And the only distinction here between the seed and the sprout is that in the case of the seed and sprout there is an infinite regress through a temporal succession, whereas in the case of manifestation it is through a simultaneous succession; however, their status as being established by valid authority is exactly the same.

Vyāsadeva, in his *Pātañjalabhāṣya*, while stating that all effects are eternal in their essential nature (*svarūpa*) yet perishable through their states (*avasthā*), has likewise accepted this infinite regress as being authoritative. Here, the analogy of the seed and the sprout is presented from a worldly perspective; however, the actual intent lies precisely in the understanding of birth, karma, and so forth. Therefore, even if there is no infinite regress—since the stream of seeds and sprouts is limited by the beginning of creation rather than being beginningless—there is no deficiency in the argument.
For it is well known from both Śruti and Smṛti that at the beginning of creation, a tree arises even without a seed, [produced] from the body and other parts of Hiraṇyagarbha through his volition—
just as a tree, endowed with roots, trunk, branches, and so forth, originates from its primary seed,
and from it, indeed, other seeds [arise].
Thus, by such statements from the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other texts. || 122 ||
In reality, however, there is no such thing as "without interval" (anavara); thus he says:
"There is no fault because of the door of origination. (123)

Just as the production of a jar’s production is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others who maintain the theory of the production of the non-existent (*asadutpāda*) as being its very own nature for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), so too must we accept that the manifestation of a jar’s manifestation is its very own nature for the sake of parsimony. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) even in the case of manifestation, just as in the case of production. Now, if it is argued that by not accepting a manifestation of manifestation in this way, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) would be undermined because the existence of that [manifestation] prior to the operation of the cause would be untenable—the answer is: no.

In this view, the intention is that the doctrine of *satkāryavāda* (the pre-existence of the effect) consists precisely in the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of that which already exists. Furthermore, because manifestation itself lacks manifestation, even though it is non-existent prior [to its own occurrence], there is no consequence of falling into the position of *asatkāryavāda* (the non-existence of the effect). If it is objected: "In that case, let it be accepted that the great principle (*mahat*) and the rest are simply non-existent prior [to their production]; what is the point of postulating a state called 'manifestation'?", we reply: No. This is because, according to such scriptural passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed unmanifest (*avyākṛta*)," the manifestation of effects is established as being only those things that already exist in an unmanifest state.

If it is argued that even so, one would still be forced to accept the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and other types of absence, we say no. This is because the three states—future and so forth—are said to be mutually constitutive of one another's absences; and it is precisely through the cessation of such absences that the efficacy of causal operations becomes possible. For this indeed is the distinction of the proponents of the theory of the pre-existent effect (*satkāryavāda*) from the proponents of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavāda*): what the latter call prior non-existence and destruction are, for the former, stated to be the future and past states of the effect, which are positive entities (*bhāvarūpa*).

Furthermore, the state known as "presentness," which is the stage of manifestation, is held to be distinct from the jar; this is because we experience that the jar and other such things possess three states. Everything else, however, is the same. Therefore, there is no room for further suspicion against us. This is the direction [of the argument]. || 123 ||

By the sūtra, "Because it is perceived through the observation of its effect," it is stated that the primal cause is to be inferred by means of its effect. In this regard, in order to determine the limit of what constitutes an effect, [the author] states the common characteristic of all effects:
"An effect is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, and indicative. (1.2.4)

In this context, the term *liṅga* refers to the entire aggregate of effects, because it either leads to the inference of its cause or undergoes dissolution [into that cause]; however, the *mahat-tattva* alone is not intended here, since properties such as "having a cause" (*hetumattva*) and so forth are common to all effects.
The manifest is causal, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composite, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite.

Thus, in this very verse, it is stated that everything called "manifest" (vyakta) is indeed an effect (kārya) and serves as a logical mark (liṅga). Accordingly, the meaning of the sentence is that this logical mark possesses such properties as having a cause (hetumattva) and so forth. Among these, "having a cause" means possessing a causal agent. "Impermanence" (anityatva) means the state of being subject to destruction. "Non-pervasiveness" (avyāpitva) is the opposite of the pervasiveness previously attributed to the Pradhāna. "Activity" (sakriyatva) refers to the performance of specific functions in the form of determination (adhyavasāya) and the like.

However, because *pradhāna* is the cause by virtue of being common to all activities (*kriyā*), it does not possess the property of performing only a single portion of an effect. Nor can activity be said to be nothing other than action (*karman*); for since scripture declares that creation arises from the agitation of *prakṛti*, it would follow that *prakṛti* also possesses activity here, as it too would be characterized by action. "Multiplicity" (*anekatva*) means being differentiated by different creations; that is to say, it refers to the uniqueness of each pair of creations, and not to the existence of multiple individual instances of the same kind.

Because there is over-extension [of the definition] to *prakṛti*, since *prakṛti* also possesses multiple forms such as *sattva* and so forth; for this reason, it will be stated in a future sūtra: "The quality of not being attributes of that [the Puruṣa] belongs to *sattva* and the others, because they have that [Puruṣa] as their form. Furthermore, the state of being dependent resides in the parts [of the body]. || 124 ||

Since properties such as having a cause (hetumattva) and so forth are established only when there is a distinction between cause and effect, he states the means of valid cognition for establishing an effect distinct from its cause:
"Its establishment [is known] either through directness or non-difference, or through qualities, universals, and so forth, or by the designation 'pradhāna'. (1.125)

The establishment of that [effect] is the proof of the effect called the "mark" (liṅga) as being distinct from its cause. In some cases, this occurs directly through perception (*pratyakṣa*) without effort due to its manifest nature, as in the case of cloth and the like being established as distinct from threads and the like by means of properties such as grossness. In other cases, it occurs through inference based on the mark consisting of the identity of qualities, universals, and so forth—as in the case of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, which are established by means of their difference from their causes in the form of having qualities such as being the Great Earth and so on.

And just as earth and the other elements possess a nature consisting of universals such as "earthiness" (*mahāpṛthivītva*), which is a dissimilarity to the *tanmātras*, or—as included by the word "etc."—possess a nature consisting of action and so forth, which is a dissimilarity [to the *tanmātras*], for example, a mobile whole that is distinct from its stable parts; likewise, from the designation "pradhāna" (primary matter), the existence of an effect distinct from its cause is established even by the scriptural mention of "pradhāna. For it is called "pradhāna" because the collection of effects is deposited (*pradhīyate*) within it.

And that [identity] is not possible without both difference and non-difference between cause and effect; the meaning is that if there were absolute non-difference, it would be impossible for something to be its own substratum. || 125 ||

The definition of effects as having the nature of similarity, and the proof for an effect that is distinct from its cause, have been shown by the two preceding sutras. Now, in order to infer the cause through its similarity to the effect, he demonstrates the similarity between effect and cause as well: "Both possess the qualities of consisting of the three guṇas, being insentient, and so forth. (126)

The meaning is that the similarity between the two—the effect and the cause—consists precisely in their possessing the three *guṇas* and so forth. Those qualities included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) have been stated in the *Kārikā*: "The manifest and the Pradhāna are composed of the three *guṇas*, non-discriminative, objective, common, insentient, and subject to transformation; the Spirit (*puruṣa*) is the opposite of these and likewise [possesses] those [qualities]."

It is called "triguṇa" (composed of the three qualities) because the three qualities—sattva and the others—exist here in the form of substances. Among these, sattva and the other qualities exist within the intellect (*mahat*) and the subsequent principles in the form of causes; however, sattva and the others exist in *pradhāna* as a collection of the three qualities. [In this regard, an additional variant reading is seen: it should be understood to be like trees in a forest.

Alternatively, since the terms *asattva* (non-existence) and so forth also refer to pleasure, pain, and delusion, it is consistent that both cause and effect possess the three *guṇas*. Thus, the description [of nature] as "non-discriminating" (*avivekin*) and "object" (*viṣaya*) is to be seen by the ignorant alone; that is to say, it is the "enjoyable" (*bhogya*). Furthermore, the compound *avivekiviṣaya* is to be analyzed as "that which is non-discriminating" and "that which is an object. In this analysis, "non-discrimination" means acting in combination, while "object-ness" is simply the state of being enjoyable. It is "common" (*sāmānya*), meaning shared by all *puruṣas*; that is to say, it remains undivided even when there is a distinction between *puruṣas*. It is "productive" (*prasavadharmin*), meaning subject to transformation. The "manifest" (*vyakta*) is the effect.

The meaning is that it is the primary cause. The mutual difference between the effect and the instrument (the manifest and the unmanifest) is also shown by the *kārikā*: "The manifest is caused, non-eternal, non-pervasive, active, manifold, dependent, indicative, composed of parts, and subordinate; the unmanifest is the opposite. Thus [it is said].

In this context, "oneness" (ekatva) means non-difference even amidst the diversity of manifestations; therefore, although Nature (prakṛti) consists of multiple individuals, its oneness is not impaired.
Enveloping the Great Principle (mahat), it exists as the Pradhāna;
for that infinite one, there is no end, nor is its number known.
Thus, from the statement in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa regarding its being "innumerable," the multiplicity of individual instances of the Pradhāna is established. || 126 ||

In order to distinguish between the qualities (guṇas) called *pradhāna* which constitute the cause of the world, [the author] establishes their internal differences as well, and for the sake of proving that they can serve as the cause of a manifold world—for indeed, diverse effects cannot arise from a single uniform cause—the mutual dissimilarity of the qualities through pleasure, pain, dejection, and so forth, is stated. (127)

The meaning is that there is a mutual difference between the qualities (*guṇas*)—the three substances beginning with *sattva*—due to pleasure, pain, and so forth, because these are observed in their effects. Furthermore, pleasure and the like are attributes (*dharma*) of even objects such as jars, just like color and so forth, because they have the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) as their material cause; thus it is said, "of other effects. The categories included by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here were stated by the teacher Pañcaśikha: for instance, that which is called *sattva* consists of an infinite variety of forms such as clarity, lightness, attachment, joy, forbearance, and contentment, and is, in brief, of the nature of pleasure.

In this way, *rajas* also consists of various distinctions such as grief and so forth, and in brief, its nature is suffering (*duḥkha*). Likewise, *tamas* also consists of various distinctions such as sleep and so forth, and in brief, its nature is delusion (*moha*). Here, because it is stated that pleasure (*prīti*) and the others are attributes of the *guṇas*, and because lightness (*laghutva*) and other qualities will be mentioned in a future sūtra, it is established that *sattva* and the other *guṇas* are substances (*dravya*). However, their nature as pleasure and so forth belongs to the mind (*manas*).

The fact that [the qualities] consist of volition (saṅkalpa) is established precisely because there is no difference in their essential nature (dharmyabheda). It is not the case, as the Vaiśeṣikas claim, that pleasure and so forth are themselves the qualities of *sattva* and the rest. Furthermore, the triad beginning with *sattva* is infinite due to the diversity of individual manifestations (*vyaktibheda*). Otherwise, if they were merely all-pervasive (*vibhu*), the established doctrine—that the diversity of effects arises from the diversity of the friction between the qualities—would be untenable; for in the case of mere pervasiveness, internal differentiation within the friction would be impossible. (127)

If the qualities (guṇas), such as sattva and the others, were each merely a single individual entity, then increase, decrease, and so forth would not be possible. Likewise, if they were limited in extent, it would follow that the Pradhāna—which consists of their aggregate—would also be limited; consequently, the countless cosmic eggs and other entities established by Śruti and Smṛti could not be accounted for at one time. Therefore, since the qualities are infinite in number, [the author] sets forth their common characteristics (sādharmya) for the purpose of establishing their number as three and for the sake of their discrimination (viveka) and so on:
"The qualities possess common characteristics and differences through properties such as lightness and the rest. (128)

The meaning is as follows: the term "lightness and so forth" (*laghv-ādi*) is an indication where the abstract quality (*bhāva*) is the primary referent. Through the property of lightness and the like, there is both similarity and dissimilarity among all individual manifestations of *sattva* in relation to *rajas* and *tamas*. Thus, just as individual particles of earth possess the nature of earth, it is logical that individual manifestations of *sattva*, by virtue of belonging to a single genus, possess unity; and through the support of their own kind and other such factors, their increase, decrease, and so forth are likewise appropriate—this is the intended sense.

Thus, there is similarity among the manifestations of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* through properties such as mobility (*cañcalatva*), while there is dissimilarity between them and *sattva* and *tamas*. The rest is as before. Likewise, all manifestations of *tamas* share similarity through properties such as heaviness (*gurutva*), while there is dissimilarity with *sattva* and *rajas*. The rest is as before. Since dissimilarity has already been stated previously, the repetition of the discussion of dissimilarity here is merely incidental. In this context, the reading "and dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyaṃ ca*) is indeed a mere scribal error.

Now, it is established by the Sūtra that each of the causal substances, such as *sattva* and the others, possesses multiple individual instances; otherwise, it would be impossible for lightness (*laghutva*) and the rest to constitute a common property (*sādharmya*), since a common property is defined as a quality belonging to things that are alike. Nor should it be argued that lightness and so forth could be a common property based on the multiplicity of the *sattva* and other qualities belonging to their effects.

Since even objects such as jars possess the nature of being composed of the three *guṇas*, it would be untenable for qualities like lightness to constitute a common property (*sādharmya*) with *sattva* and the others by virtue of their being effects that exist [in the cause]. Therefore, it is the qualities of the causes themselves that are here described as having common properties and so forth. Furthermore, the qualities of *sattva* and the others, such as lightness, have been stated in the *Kārikā*: "Sattva is held to be light and illuminating; rajas is stimulating and mobile; tamas is heavy and enveloping. Their functioning is for a purpose, like a lamp. (SK 13)

"In terms of purpose"—that is, by reason of being the cause for the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*). Now, if it is asked: "In that case, what is the distinction here from the Vaiśeṣika doctrine regarding the fact that the primal cause consists of either finite, infinite, or innumerable individual manifestations? [The answer is: It is precisely the absence of qualities such as sound and touch in the causal substance.
But that which is devoid of sound and touch, unjoined with form and the other [qualities],
consisting of the three guṇas, is the womb of the world, its beginningless source and place of dissolution.
Thus it is from the Viṣṇupurāṇa and other sources; and this has been explained by us in detail in the Pātañjala [Yogasūtra-bhāṣya]. 128.

Now, one might object: even if the nature of the Great One (mahat) and the other principles is established, there is no proof for their being effects, since they are not observed to arise through direct perception; by what means, then, could they possess the common property of having a cause? To this he replies:
"Because it is distinct from both [the eternal and the non-eternal], the Great One and the others are effects, like a jar and so forth. (129)

The series beginning with Mahat and ending with the five elements, which is the subject of dispute, is not the Puruṣa, because it is an object of experience (bhogya). Nor is it Primordial Matter (prakṛti), because it is perishable, as would otherwise be impossible for liberation (mokṣa) to occur. Therefore, the meaning is that it is distinct from both Prakṛti and Puruṣa, and because it is distinct from them, it is an effect (kārya), like a jar or similar objects. || 129 ||

Now, one might object that since liberation and so forth are established simply by the burning away of the power of transformation (vikāra-śakti), their perishability is also unproven; in response to this doubt, he states further reasons for their being effects:
"Because of [their] limited size" (parimāṇāt) || 130 ||

The meaning is: "because of being delimited" (paricchinnatvāt), that is, because of possessing a genus (jāti) which is the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) for the counter-correlativity (pratiyogitā) of spatial absence (daiśikābhāva). By this, there is no fallacy of deviation (vyabhicāra) even though individual instances of qualities (guṇavyakti) are delimited. || 130 ||
Furthermore: because of the harmony [of all things with Brahman]. 121.
For the reality of the intellect and so forth, which has been diminished by fasting and the like, is replenished again through the association with food and other such things; therefore:

The meaning is that the state of being an effect is inferred from "conjunction" (samanvaya). For in the case of an eternal [substance], conjunction—consisting of the entry of parts—is not possible due to its partless nature. And regarding this conjunction, scripture is the authority; with reference to the mind, it says: "In this way, my dear, of those sixteen parts, one part remained. That was replenished by food and blazed up. And there is a Yoga Sūtra: "Transformation into another species occurs through the influx of primordial matter (prakṛti). || 131 ||
Furthermore: "And because of power" (śaktitaḥ). || 132 ||

The meaning is "by way of being an instrument" (karaṇataḥ). The intention is that whatever function belongs to the Person (puruṣa) is like that of the eyes and other sense organs. Since Primordial Matter (prakṛti) does not directly present objects to the Person, it is not an instrument. Therefore, once it is established that the Great Principle (mahattva) is an effect by virtue of its being an instrument, the fact that the others are also effects follows all the more easily. The word "iti" serves to indicate the conclusion of the section on reasons. || 132 ||

And if some effect whatsoever among the Great One (mahat) and the rest is admitted, then that very thing is established as being either Nature (prakṛti) or Spirit (puruṣa); for our intention is precisely this: having established Nature and Spirit, they are to be distinguished by their being subject to transformation and being unchanging, respectively. Thus he says: "In its absence, it must be either Nature or Spirit. (133)

If, upon the abandonment of that [causality], its status as an effect were abandoned, then if it were transformative, it would be *prakṛti*; or if it were non-transformative, it would be the experiencer, the *puruṣa*—this is the meaning. (133)
Now, one might object that even the eternal [Self] could be distinct from both; to this he says:
"If it were different from those two, it would be a mere nothingness. (134)

If the unproduced (akārya) were distinct from primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa), it would be a mere nothingness, like the horn of a hare, because there is a lack of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). For the unproduced is established either as a cause or as an enjoyer; it cannot be established otherwise—this is the meaning. || 134 ||

Thus, having established the state of being an effect in the Great Principle (mahat) and the others, he now states a specific point not mentioned regarding the inference of Primordial Matter (prakṛti) by means of them:
"One may infer a cause from that [effect], because of its association with it. (135)

Regarding the inference of a cause from an effect—such as the *mahat*-principle and so forth—which was described as being based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*), that must be performed through the concomitance of the effect together with its accompaniment [of a conscious agent], in order to remove the notion of mere indifference [on the part of the cause]. This is in accordance with such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," and "In the beginning, this was indeed darkness alone. For example: the *mahat* and other principles have for their material cause a substance consisting of the three *guṇas* inherent within them, because they are effects, like a statue existing within a stone, or like oil [from sesame seeds].
The supporting argument (*anukūlatarka*) for this has already been shown previously. || 135 ||
To distinguish that primordial nature from its effects by means of their dissimilarity, he says: "The unmanifest is distinct from the manifest [which consists of] the three qualities. (136)

The unmanifest (*avyakta*), which is the root cause, is subtler even than the Great Principle (*mahattattva*) from which the three qualities (*triguṇa*) are manifested. For while the qualities such as pleasure and so forth belonging to the Great Principle are directly perceived, the qualities of *prakṛti* are not directly perceived; thus, the Pradhāna is the supreme unmanifest. The meaning is that the Great Principle, by comparison, is manifest. To the objection—"If it is supremely subtle, then its non-existence (denial) would be more appropriate"—the author recalls what was stated previously:
"Because it is established through its effects, there is no denial [of it]. (1.137)
This is easy to understand. || 137 ||

The specific points regarding the inference of *prakṛti* have been examined in detail. From here until the end of the chapter, the specific points regarding the inference of *puruṣa* are to be examined. Regarding that, he states a certain particular point at the outset:
"Because there is no dispute in a general sense, it is not a means of proof, unlike [the case of] *dharma*. (138)

The meaning is this: where there is no dispute regarding a thing in its general form, its proof in terms of its specific nature (*svarūpa*) is not required, just as in the case of a property (*dharma*). This is the point: just as in the present context, a proof for primordial matter (*prakṛti*) is required because there is dispute even regarding its general existence as a substratum (*dharmin*), it is not so for the Person (*puruṣa*). For if consciousness were denied, the world would fall into blindness; thus, even among Buddhists, there is no dispute regarding the Person in its general form as the enjoyer and the referent of the word "I" (*aham*), just as there is none regarding a property.

For *dharma* is accepted in a general sense even by Buddhists, since they admit that practices such as climbing upon heated stones constitute *dharma*. Therefore, inference should be employed merely as a means to establish qualities such as the discernment and permanence of the Person (*puruṣa*). || 138 ||

By the aphorism already stated, "Because of being for the sake of another who is an aggregate," it is intended that there is an inference of discrimination (*viveka*), and not that the Puruṣa is in every respect entirely imperceptible. In that regard, the initial aphorism asserting discrimination is:
"The Person is distinct from the body and so forth. (1.139)

The meaning is that the person (*puruṣa*) is the enjoyer, distinct from the reality consisting of the twenty-four principles beginning with the body and ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). And this state of being an enjoyer consists in being a seer (*draṣṭṛ*). || 139 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason through the sūtras: "Because they exist for the sake of another who is a composite. (240)

Since everything that is composite, such as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest, exists for the sake of another—just like a bed and so forth—it follows that the Puruṣa is established as distinct from the non-composite body and other such things; this is the meaning. Furthermore, this reason has already been explained under the statement "because the Puruṣa is for the sake of the composite. The restatement of the reason, though already mentioned, is for the purpose of summarizing the group of reasons. || 140 ||
Furthermore: "Because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth. (141)

The meaning is that it is due to the opposite nature [of the Self], such as consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion. For the property of the body and so forth—which consists in being the nature of pleasure and the like—is not possible in one who is the enjoyer of pleasure and the like; because if [the enjoyer] were itself to grasp pleasure and the like, there would be a contradiction between the object and the agent, since the experience of pleasure and so on occurs precisely by way of the subject (dharmin). Now, if it is argued: "Let the Puruṣa grasp its own pleasure and the like as reflected in the modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), just as one grasps oneself," we say no. For if that were the case, it would be more appropriate to postulate that pleasure and the like belong to the intellect alone.

It is cumbersome to postulate that pleasure and other qualities residing in the *puruṣa* are reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*). Furthermore, cognitions such as "I am happy," "I am miserable," or "I am deluded" do not prove the existence of pleasure and so forth in the *puruṣa*, because they can be accounted for by the *puruṣa* being the owner of those states. They can also be accounted for by the intellect itself possessing pleasure and other qualities. For in the worldly notion of "I," the intellect is necessarily an object; this is due to the persistence of defects in the form of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of false knowledge, and because postulating a reflection [of the *puruṣa*] therein is cumbersome.

By the word "etc. (*ādi*) here, the properties such as non-discrimination (*avivekitva*) mentioned in the *kārikā*—namely, "consisting of the three guṇas, non-discriminative, objective," and so forth—are to be understood. Likewise, the physical attributes of the body and so on, such as form (*rūpa*) and the rest, are to be understood. 142.
Furthermore:
"And because of superintendence" (adhiṣṭhānāt). || 142 ||

The meaning is that because the enjoyer is the presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛ*), he is distinct from all things subordinate to him, ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*). For "presiding" is the conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of the enjoyer; and this [conjunction] is the cause for the transformations of primordial nature and the rest which serve as the means for experience. This is because of the sūtra to be stated later: "From the presiding of the enjoyer, there is the construction of the locus of experience. And the implication is that conjunction occurs only when there is difference (*bheda*). The word "iti" marks the conclusion of the reason. || 142 ||
He demonstrates the supporting argument (anukūlatarka) for the stated inference by means of two aphorisms:
"Because of the existence of an enjoyer" (1.1.14).

For if the enjoyer were of the very nature of the body and so forth, then the status of being an enjoyer would be contradicted due to the contradiction between being the object of action and being the agent. The meaning is that it is impossible for [the self] itself to be its own direct enjoyer; and this impossibility has already been explained. It should be remembered that in this sūtra, the enjoyment of the *puruṣa* is accepted. Furthermore, the enjoyment of the unchanging *puruṣa*—that enjoyment which terminates in consciousness (*cidavasāna*)—has been explained in this context. || 143 ||
Furthermore: "And because activity is for the sake of isolation (kaivalya). (144)

If the body and so forth were themselves the enjoyer, then no one’s activity for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*)—that is, for the absolute cessation of suffering—of the enjoyer would be possible. This is because the body and other such things are perishable, and because *prakṛti* is established by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its existence as being of the nature of suffering; thus, isolation would be impossible. For the absolute destruction of an inherent nature (*svabhāva*) is not tenable; this is the meaning. Here, the reading of the sūtra as “for the sake of the isolation of *prakṛti*” (*prakṛteḥ*) should be disregarded due to its being a scribal error.

The Puruṣa exists because the composite is for the sake of another; because there is a reversal of the three guṇas and so forth; because there must be a presiding controller; because there is the state of being an enjoyer; and because of the activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya).
Thus, from the verse, because of the reading "and because of the activity for the sake of isolation," and because of the lack of consistency in meaning. || 144 ||

The Puruṣa has been established as distinct from the twenty-four principles; now, a specific quality residing in the Puruṣa is inferred in order to clarify the discrimination [between it and Prakṛti]: "Because it cannot be the illumination of the insentient, it is luminous. (145)

The Vaiśeṣikas say: "In the case of the soul, which is insentient and of a non-luminous nature, a light called 'knowledge' arises from its conjunction with the mind. This is not so, because in the world, one does not observe the production of light in insentient and non-luminous things such as clods of earth; therefore, that [theory] is untenable. Consequently, the meaning is that the *puruṣa* is of the very nature of light, like the sun and other luminaries. And thus says the Smṛti:
"Just as a connection between light and darkness is not possible, so too oneness is not possible for the phenomenal world and the Supreme Self."
"Just as a lamp, whose nature is light, whether small or great, so should one know the Person (puruṣa) within all living beings, whose nature is knowledge. Thus it is said.
And luminosity is an indivisible adjunct (akhaṇḍopādhi) that persists through fire, sattva, and consciousness, because of the persistence of its corresponding linguistic usage. || 145 ||
Now, even if its nature is luminosity, does the relation of attribute and substrate exist as it does in the case of light, or not? To this he says:
"Because it is devoid of qualities, consciousness has no attributes. (146)

This is easy to understand. Furthermore, it should be understood that once it is established that the Self (puruṣa) has the nature of luminosity (prakāśa), and that the functioning of other things is possible through mere connection with it, the postulation of a separate attribute consisting of luminosity would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (kalpanā-gaurava). Moreover, since light is perceived by way of its touch even when its specific quality called "luminosity" is not grasped, the difference between luminosity (prakāśa) and physical light (tejas) is established.

Since there is no apprehension of the self at the time of apprehending its manifestation known as cognition, it is postulated—on the grounds of parsimony—that the substance of the self is of the nature of manifestation alone, devoid of the relation of attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*). Furthermore, this [self] does not possess the status of a quality (*guṇatva*), because it possesses conjunction and other qualities, and because it is non-dependent (*anāśritatva*). Thus it is remembered:
"Cognition is by no means an attribute or a quality of the self;
the self is of the very nature of cognition, eternal, complete, and always auspicious."

If it is asked, "What is the reasoning for [the Puruṣa] being devoid of qualities (nirguṇatva)? it is replied as follows: First of all, qualities such as desire and so forth cannot be eternal in the case of the Puruṣa, because they are perceived as being produced. If one were to admit that the Puruṣa possesses produced qualities, it would follow that he is subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva). Furthermore, it would be cumbersome (gaurava) to postulate that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are causes of transformation. Moreover, since blindness is a form of transformation, there would occasionally arise the consequence of ignorance, which in turn would lead to the occurrence of doubt regarding objects such as knowledge and desire.

Furthermore, since it has already been stated that the manifestation of an insentient entity is impossible, eternal cognition cannot belong to an eternal [self]. Desire and the like are established as residing in the mind alone, on account of parsimony, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). It is cumbersome to assume that the conjunction of the mind and the self are both causes of those qualities; moreover, it has already been stated that the word "quality" (*guṇa*) here refers specifically to "specific qualities" (*viśeṣaguṇa*). Therefore, the self is devoid of qualities.

Furthermore, for those logicians who maintain that the self is an agent, liberation is untenable; for it is stated in the *Gītā* and other texts that the very notion "I am the agent" is the cause of the production of unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). And according to their view, since this notion is not false ignorance (*mithyājñāna*), it cannot be sublated by the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Therefore, because liberation as described in the Śruti would otherwise be impossible, we maintain that the self is a non-agent. And due to its being a non-agent, there is an absence of unseen merit, pleasure, and so forth.

Furthermore, since the mind must be postulated as the cause of volition and other such functions, it is more parsimonious to postulate this [agency] by delimiting it to the quality of internal perception (*antaḥkaraṇaguṇatva*). Therefore, the Self is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*). And the nature of this aforementioned, most subtle Self has been explained and demonstrated with analytical clarity in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, like a myrobalan fruit in the palm of one's hand, as follows: "Just as the stainless form of light remains when all objects of illumination—consisting of the directions, the earth, and space—are removed."

"When the three worlds, as well as 'you' and 'I', have attained existence within the field of the visible, there would be for the seer of such a pure self only absolute non-existence [of that field]. (146)

[Objection: Surely the fact that consciousness is an attribute of the person is established by the experience of the relationship between the attribute and its substratum in the cognition "I know," for this is not a defect since it is validated by authoritative means of knowledge (pramāṇa). To this, he replies:
"There can be no denial of what is established by scripture, because that [scriptural authority] sublates direct perception. (147)

It might be argued: "Let it be so if we were to establish the absence of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), the nature of consciousness (*ciddharmatva*), and so forth, by mere reasoning alone; however, [we establish them] by scripture (*śruti*) as well. Therefore, the denial of the absence of qualities and other attributes established by scripture is impossible, because the perception of those [attributes], such as the perception of qualities, is sublated by scripture itself—just like the perception 'I am fair-complexioned' and the like. This is the meaning.

Otherwise, even those arguments intended to establish a self distinct from the body—such as "I am the cow"—would be sublated by the force of perception; thus, the nihilists would be victorious. Regarding its being devoid of qualities (*nirguṇatva*), there are scriptural passages such as: "The witness, the cognizer, solitary and devoid of qualities. Regarding its being pure consciousness (*cinmātratva*), however, there are scriptural passages such as: "It is a non-agent, consciousness, pure consciousness; for this Self is of the single essence of existence and consciousness. As for the scriptural passages concerning omniscience and so forth, they are merely restatements of worldly conceptualizations, like the expression "the head of Rāhu."

Because among the scriptural texts consisting of injunctions and prohibitions, the prohibitory texts are more powerful—according to the Śruti: "Now, therefore, follows the instruction: 'Not this, not this'; for there is nothing else higher than this 'not this'"—and furthermore, because in the cognition "I know," validity is the default rule, whereas this [perception] is undermined by the suspicion of invalidity due to being included among hundreds of errors; therefore, even inference, when supported by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava*) and other factors, is capable of subverting this perception.

If it is asked, "In what way is there simplicity (lāghava) if the self has the nature of eternal knowledge? it is replied: The Naiyāyikas and others postulate four categories—the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), the primary cognition (vyavasāya), the secondary cognition (anuvyavasāya), and their substratum. We, however, postulate only three categories: the internal organ, its modification in the form of primary cognition, and the self, which is of the nature of eternal, unitary knowledge and serves as the locus for infinite secondary cognitions. || 147 ||

Now, one might object: if the Self is indeed of the nature of light alone, then the distinction between states such as deep sleep and so forth would not be possible, because light would never cease to exist. To this, he says:
"The state of not being the witness of deep sleep and so forth" (Kārikā 148).
The meaning is that the person's state of being the witness (*sākṣitva*) alone pertains to these three states—waking, dreaming, and deep sleep—which reside in the intellect (*buddhi*).
As it has been said:
"Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are, by virtue of the [guṇas], fluctuations of the intellect."
The individual soul (jīva), being distinct from them, is established as their witness. Thus [it is said].

The meaning is that [the Self] is determined to be distinct from those modifications of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti) by virtue of being their witness, and thus devoid of states such as waking and the rest. In this context, the state called "waking" is a modification of the intellect into the form of an object through the door of the senses. The state of "dreaming" is a similar modification produced solely by latent impressions (saṃskāra). And the state of "deep sleep" (suṣupti) is twofold, distinguished by partial dissolution and total dissolution.

In that state of partial dissolution (*ardhalaya*), there is no mental modification (*vṛtti*) taking on the form of an external object; rather, the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) takes on only the forms of pleasure, pain, and delusion pertaining to itself. Otherwise, for one who has arisen [from sleep], the recollection of pleasure and so forth experienced during deep sleep—such as "I slept happily"—would be impossible. This has been stated by Vyāsa in the Sūtra: "In the case of the swoon, there is partial attainment [of dissolution], because of the remainder. In total dissolution (*samagralaya*), however, there is an absence of all modifications of the intellect, as occurs in death and similar states.

Otherwise, the subsequent sūtra stating that "the state of being Brahman exists in samādhi, deep sleep, and liberation" would be untenable. Furthermore, since that [state] consists in the absence of all mental modifications (*vṛtti*) during deep sleep, the Puruṣa is not its witness; for the Puruṣa is the witness only of mental modifications. Otherwise, it would follow that even the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and other attributes of the intellect (*buddhi-dharma*) would be manifest to the witness. We shall explain later that the Puruṣa’s witnesshood with respect to deep sleep and so forth consists in the illumination of such mental modifications as they are reflected within it.
Therefore, for the purpose of cognition, the Puruṣa does not depend upon modification.

It might be argued as follows: "If it is maintained that in deep sleep there is a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) having pleasure, pain, and so forth as its object, then it would be more logical to accept that even in the waking state and others, all modifications are themselves apprehended by other modifications; thus, the postulation of a witnessing Puruṣa (*sākṣi-puruṣa*) would be useless. For it can be stated in general that the cause of the empirical usage of a thing is simply the existence of a modification whose object is that very thing. This is not so. If one were to necessarily postulate a modification for every object of experience, there would result an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and excessive complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, in cognitions such as "I am happy," a non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition of the pleasure and so forth must first be required, wherein these qualities function as qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*).

In that regard, for the sake of simplicity, the nature of the Self is postulated as a single, eternal consciousness, with reference to its infinite non-conceptual (nirvikalpa) states. For the sake of specific cognitions such as "I am happy," it is the mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) itself that assumes such a form; this is because, by accepting merely the conformity of the Puruṣa to the modification (*vṛtti-sārūpya*), one does not admit any form over and above the form of the modification, lest there be the consequence of the Puruṣa undergoing transformation (*pariṇāma*) through an independent form of its own. || 148 ||

Now, since the oneness of the Puruṣa is thus established by his being the mere witness of states such as deep sleep, a doubt arises as to whether he is one or many. Regarding this, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) view is as follows: aided by the logic of parsimony (lāghava), the Self is established as being only one, based on the scriptural texts declaring non-difference. This is because the differences consisting of the states of waking and so forth belong to the attributes of the intellect (buddhi).

Although a single Self is the witness of all cognitions, nevertheless, whichever cognition undergoes a particular modification (*vṛtti*), that very cognition, as qualified by that modification, apprehends the Witness in such forms as "I know the jar" and so forth. Therefore, when the modification of one cognition occurs in the form "this is a jar," there is no experience through the medium of a modification of another cognition, such as "I know the jar."
In this regard, he states the established conclusion: "The plurality of Puruṣas follows from the fixed order of birth and so forth. (149)

The meaning is that there are many persons (*puruṣas*), because otherwise the distinction established by the scriptures and traditional law (*śruti-smṛti*)—such as "the meritorious is born in heaven, the sinner in hell, the ignorant is bound, and the wise is liberated"—would be inexplicable. Furthermore, birth and death here do not refer to origination and destruction, since these do not reside in the *puruṣa*. Rather, they are the conjunction with and the disjunction from a specific aggregate consisting of a new body, sense organs, and so forth, which determine experience and its absence. Regarding this regulation of birth and so on, the scripture says:
"The one unborn [Prakṛti], red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form..."
For one unborn, delighting [in her], lies along with her; another unborn leaves her, whose enjoyments have been experienced.
"Those who know that become immortal, while others enter only into suffering," and so forth. || 149 ||

[Objection: "But surely, even if the Puruṣa is one, the distinction between birth and so forth could be established through the difference in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which serve as delimiters. To this, he says:
"Even when there is a difference in adjuncts, there is no manifold connection for a single [entity], just as space [is not manifold] due to jars and the like. (150)

Even when there is a difference in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), it is indeed possible for a single person to be associated with various adjuncts, just as a single space is associated with various things such as jars and walls. Therefore, the claim that there is no established order—such as "one person is born and another is not"—regarding the occurrence of diverse births, deaths, and so forth for the one Self alone due to the difference in limiting adjuncts (as in the case of the multiplication of bodies, *kāyavyūha*), is untenable. For an established order does not hold in the case of a single tree which possesses both the conjunction with a monkey and its absence due to the difference in limiting adjuncts.

"One tree is conjoined with a monkey, and another is not. [If you argue that this distinction is possible through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), we reply: Even for one who is liberated, since a particular region of the Self might again become bound by other limiting adjuncts, the lack of a fixed order regarding bondage and liberation remains exactly as it was. This is just like the case where a region of space, though freed from one jar, becomes designated as "the space within a jar" due to its connection with another jar. Nor should it be said that the scriptural teaching on the distinction between bondage and liberation is merely a restatement of worldly delusion; for liberation is not a worldly phenomenon, and because [otherwise] the scripture would incur the charge of being a deceiver by propounding a false human goal. (150)

But surely, even if there is unity of consciousness, the systematic arrangement [of experiences] can be established by admitting that each [consciousness] qualified by its respective limiting adjunct (upādhi) is distinct; to this, he replies: "The adjunct is differentiated, but not that which possesses it. (151)

The meaning is this: it is only the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) that is manifold, but the possessor of that adjunct—the self as qualified by the adjunct—is not to be accepted as manifold; for if the qualified entity were something distinct [from the self], it would follow that even other scriptures would have to accept its very nature as being manifold. Furthermore, there are other refutations: if the one who experiences bondage were the qualified entity, then upon the separation from the adjunct, the qualified entity would perish, and thus liberation would be impossible. If it is argued: "But surely the status of being the individual soul (*jīvatva*) belongs to the qualified entity, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*)," and that the author himself will state in the sixth chapter that the status of the soul belongs only to that which is qualified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), we say no.

This is because the state of being a living being (*jīvatva*), which consists in the sustaining of the vital breaths, is specifically stated to be that which is superposed [upon Brahman]; however, the distinction between bondage and liberation is not something residing in the qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa*), since at the time of liberation the qualified entity does not exist.

Furthermore, some moderns who call themselves Vedāntins have said: "The individual souls (jīvas) and the Lord (īśvara) are merely reflections of the one Self within the limiting adjuncts (upādhis) of cause and effect; and because of the mutual difference among these reflections, the entire system of distinctions such as birth and so forth is logically established."

That too is incorrect, because it cannot withstand the dilemma of difference or non-difference. If there were a difference between the original image (*bimba*) and the reflection (*pratibimba*), then, since the reflection is insentient, its status as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and its bondage or liberation would be untenable; furthermore, this would undermine the established doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman are non-different. Moreover, a self distinct from both the individual soul and the Lord (*īśvara*) would lack any basis in valid authority (*prāmāṇika*). On the other hand, if there were non-difference, the problem of confusion (*sāṅkarya*) could not be avoided. If one were to accept both difference and non-difference, it would result in the abandonment of the established doctrine as well as the contradiction of difference and non-difference.

In our view, however, there is no contradiction, because non-difference is characterized by indivisibility (*avibhāga*), whereas difference is mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). We shall explain the illustrative statements regarding delimitation (*avaccheda*), reflection (*pratibimba*), and so forth later on.

It might be argued: "We merely say that the distinction between bondage and liberation is a conceptual construction imagined by the scripture based on the postulated distinction between the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*); however, we do not maintain that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there exists a relationship of original and reflection, nor a difference between them, nor even bondage, liberation, and so forth.

This is not so. If that were the case, then rather than requiring the sublation of both sets of scriptural passages—those concerning bondage and liberation, as well as those concerning difference—it would be more logical, on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*), to restrict the scope of the set of passages concerning non-difference alone to the sense of mere non-distinction (*avibhāga*). Furthermore, this non-distinction is already established by other scriptural and traditional (*smṛti*) texts. (151)
He concludes the refutation stated against those who maintain the identity of the self:
"Thus, for that which revolves as a single unity, there is no superimposition of contradictory attributes. (152)

The meaning is that, in this manner, for the Self which exists as one and the same everywhere, the occurrence of contradictory attributes such as birth and death is not logical. Alternatively, there is a word-break at *ekatve* (in oneness): "If oneness is accepted, then for that which exists all around, everywhere, and is pervasive through all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), there is no superimposition of contradictory attributes; rather, on the contrary, the confusion of contradictory attributes is unavoidable in every respect."

[Objection: But surely the *puruṣa* is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmaka*). In that case, how can there be a confusion of contradictory attributes such as birth, death, bondage, and liberation? For even you [Sāṃkhyas] admit that all attributes reside in the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). [Reply: This is not so. Because those aforementioned attributes—consisting of conjunction, disjunction, and experience—are accepted as belonging to the *puruṣa*. It has been stated that only attributes in the form of transformation (*pariṇāma*) are prohibited in the *puruṣa*.

Just as there is a distinct determination of qualities such as redness or blueness even when they are superimposed upon a crystal, so too in the case of persons, there is a determination of the qualities of the intellect (buddhi) such as pleasure and pain, as well as the qualities of the body and so forth—such as being a Brahmin or a Kṣatriya—even though these are superimposed upon the Self, as established in the scriptures. As it is said in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:

"Just as when the space within one jar is covered by dust, smoke, and the like, all [other jars] are not affected by them, so it is with living beings (jīvas) regarding pleasure and the rest. || 152 ||
He says that even that [distinction] is not tenable when there is a single selfhood, just like the distinction of birth and so forth:
"Even if it were a property of another, its establishment would not occur through superimposition because of [the soul's] unity. (153)

Even if the qualities such as pleasure and so forth were distinct from the Self, their attribution (*āropa*) to the Person (*puruṣa*) would not establish a fixed distinction [between them]. This is because the Person, who is the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of that attribution, is one. Just as space is one, yet the spaces delimited by jars (*ghaṭāvacchinnākāśa*) appear distinct due to the differences between the jars, and thus a distinction of conditioned properties (*upādhikadharma*) is possible; however, properties such as "selfhood" (*ātmatva*) or "individual soul-ness" (*jīvatva*) do not belong to that which is delimited by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). For if they did, then upon the removal of the adjunct—just as the space within a jar perishes when the jar is destroyed—the individual soul (*jīva*) would perish as well, which would result in a contradiction with scriptural texts (*śruti*) such as, "The individual soul does not die."

However, it has already been stated that this applies to pure consciousness alone. Moderns who merely claim to be Vedāntins, failing to understand this subtle inconsistency regarding the arrangement of bondage, liberation, and so forth, assert that even in the case of the Self, the distinction between bondage and liberation is maintained through the difference of limiting adjuncts (upādhi). They too are refuted by this [very argument].

Even those partial proponents who, seeing this very same inconsistency, claim that bondage and so forth belong only to the reflections of consciousness residing in limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), are utterly deluded; for they are subject to the aforementioned defects such as the inability to withstand the alternatives regarding difference and so on, and because of the defect already stated here: "because the internal organ is illumined by that [consciousness]. Furthermore, nowhere in the Vedānta Sūtras is the absolute identity of all selves ever taught.

On the contrary, difference has been stated in such sūtras as: "And because there is a designation of difference [He is] other," "But [He is] superior because of the mention of difference," and "[The soul is] a part [of Him], because of the designation of multiplicity. Therefore, the views of modern thinkers regarding reflection and the like are indeed non-tenets (apasiddhānta). This is because, regarding doubtful matters not explicitly stated in one's own scripture, the tenet established by another system is not accepted as a tenet; this and more has been set forth by us in the *Brahmamīmāṃsābhāṣya*. [Objection: But if there is thus a plurality of persons—[it is said]: "For the single Self of beings is situated in every being."
It is seen as one and also as many, like the moon reflected in water.
The Self is indeed eternal, omnipresent, immutable, and free from defects;
it is one, yet it appears divided through power—that is, through māyā—and not by its own nature.

"If such scriptural and traditional texts (śruti and smṛti) teaching the oneness of the Self are thus rendered untenable," to that he replies: "There is no contradiction with the teaching of non-duality, because [those texts] have the genus as their intended meaning. (1.2.154)

There is no contradiction, however, with the scriptural texts concerning the identity of the Self, because those [texts] have the universal (jāti) as their purport. The universal is the commonality, the state of having a single form; it is precisely in that sense that the non-duality (advaita) scriptures intend their meaning, and not in the sense of being partless (akhaṇḍatva), because there would be no purpose [in establishing such a thing]. Furthermore, the fact that the word "universal" (jāti) signifies the state of having a single form is understood from the subsequent sūtra.

Regarding the respect for the word *jāti* as it is heard [in the scriptures]: the Sūtra must be explained solely as establishing non-duality (*advaita*) through such Śruti passages as, "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone," and "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. "Because it refers to the genus" (*jātiparatvāt*) means that its purpose is the negation of dualism consisting of heterogeneous things (*vijātīya*). In the first interpretation, the underlying idea is this: in the Śruti texts concerning unity, words such as "one" (*eka*) refer merely to the uniform nature of consciousness, while words such as "difference" (*bheda*) refer to difference characterized by dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*).
The Self should be understood as one and the same throughout the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep;
for one who has transcended these three states, rebirth no longer exists.

This is because, in such statements as these, it is necessary that the meaning be uniform. Otherwise, even if one had knowledge of the mere oneness of the Self throughout the three states, the cessation of the conceit of the three states—expressed by the term "transcending the three stations"—would be impossible. Likewise, only through the demonstration of this uniformity can all selves be directly conveyed by the word "Brahman" via the discernment of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), since words have only the universal (*sāmānya*) as their objective domain.

Once it has been established that the Self is of a single nature from the pillar of Brahma down to the blades of grass, the disciple himself first proceeds to discern this for the sake of its realization, until he arrives at the essential nature which is beyond all distinctions and transcends the reach of words. Thereupon, through the complete cessation of all conceits (*abhimāna*), he becomes one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛtakṛtya*). However, if the non-dual statements were intended merely to convey an undifferentiated unity, then the cessation of conceit would not be possible through them.

Just as various sounds exist in space despite its being indivisible, so too pleasure, pain, their absence, and so forth are possible within the self, which is indeed indivisible, due to the distinctions of their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Furthermore, for a single sentence to intend both indivisibility and non-difference would result in a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*); and if one assumes it intends only indivisibility, there is no resulting benefit, because all conceits (*abhimāna*) are removed simply through the knowledge of non-difference. Therefore, sentences concerning non-duality (*advaita*) do not intend indivisibility, given the support of sound reasoning.

Furthermore, [the opponent's view] is contradicted by powerful Śruti and Smṛti passages that apprehend difference. However, those [passages cited by the opponent] are actually intended to express non-difference characterized by the absence of dissimilarity (avaidharmya), because they form a single syntactical unit with the Śruti passages that teach equality, and because of the Brahma-sūtra passage:

"But on account of the commonality" (B.S. 3.2.31). Regarding that equality, the Śruti passages are as follows: "Just as pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it; so, O Gautama, does the Self of the sage who knows become—stainless, he attains supreme equality," and so forth. And the Smṛti passages are:
Light resides in the Self and nowhere else; it is equal in all beings.
And it can be perceived by oneself through a mind that is perfectly concentrated.
To the extent that the nature of consciousness exists in oneself, to that same extent it exists in the Supreme Self.
"He who knows thus, even while remaining among people, does not become deluded"—and so forth.

Since it is stated in the *Uktaśruti* that even in the state of liberation there is a statement of equality constituted by difference, it is established that there exists a difference of essential nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) among selves. Furthermore, in our system, the purport of statements such as "I am Viṣṇu, I am Śiva" should be understood as referring to non-difference through non-contradictory attributes (*avaidharmya-abheda*), but not even for statements such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) or "I am Brahman" (*ahaṃ brahmāsmi*).

In that regard, according to the Sāṅkhya view, since the very Self at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*)—which is eternally pure, liberated, and free from attributes—is the referent of terms such as "That" (*tat*), the meaning of sentences such as "Thou art That" (*tattvamasi*) is exactly as it is heard in the text. However, if the person produced at the beginning of creation, named Nārāyaṇa, were indeed the referent of the term "That," then let it be that sentences such as "Thou art That" have as their sole purpose the expression of non-difference (*avaidharmya*). If it is argued that the Śrutis cannot possibly intend to convey difference because there would be no purpose for doing so, we say: no.

This is because the sole purpose [of the scriptures] is the attainment of liberation (*mokṣa*). Since creation and dissolution continue in the form of an uninterrupted stream, liberation would be impossible if they were one and the same. If it is argued that, since the plurality of selves is established by worldly experience, it is not tenable for the Śrutis to have that as their purport—this is not so. For, while the oneness of the self is suggested through the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava-tarka*)—just like space—it is negated by the Śrutis and other authorities. Furthermore, the difference between one's own consciousness and that of another is not perceived directly, as such an experience occurs only with respect to bodies and the like.

As for the condemnation of difference found in passages such as, "He who perceives even a slight difference in this [reality] has cause for fear," that is intended to convey the distinction characterized by either dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) or spatial division (*vibhāga*). Now, if it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the scriptural texts concerning the reflections and limitations of the liberated souls?"—it is replied as follows:

Just as the solar orb consists of many rays of light, so too the solar orb of Consciousness (cid-āditya-maṇḍala), though composed of many selves, is of a single essence and undivided. Having unified it into a single mass, its differentiation into innumerable parts within innumerable limiting adjuncts (upādhis) through innumerable individual souls (puruṣas)—who are like its own rays—is demonstrated by such analogies as reflections and the like. This is intended to show that the apparent difference characterized by division is merely a matter of verbal designation (vācārambhaṇa-mātra), and not to deny its indivisibility (akhaṇḍatva). As it is said: "Just as the one wind, having entered the world, assumes a form corresponding to every form..."
This is because such scriptural passages concerning the illustration of [the world] having parts possess greater force when supported by reasoning. And as it is stated in the Smṛti:
"Even though he is the self of all, his unity as a single mass is never divided."

In the Brahmamīmāṃsā, however, non-duality is also explained through the dissolution of others into the eternally manifest consciousness of the Supreme Lord in a state of non-distinction, as stated in the sūtra: "Non-distinction [results] from scriptural statement. We have explained this in detail in our commentary on the Brahmamīmāṃsā; this is the direction of the argument.

In the second interpretation of the Sūtra, however, the intended meaning is as follows: At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), everything that is of a different class from the Spirit (*puruṣa*) is non-existent, because it lacks causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). Since the Spirits, being immutable (*kūṭastha*), do not possess causal efficiency at all, they [the Spirits] exist even during dissolution. Therefore, there is an absence of dualism consisting of a different class with respect to those whose nature is the Spirit.

Likewise, even at the time of creation, because there is no other reality due to the ultimate existence (*pāramārthikasattva*) characterized by immutability, there is an absence of dualism consisting of a different class; thus, the scriptural texts concerning non-duality (*advaita*) pertaining to the time of creation are also justified. || 154 ||

But surely, just as the oneness of the self, its uniformity is also contradicted by the perception of manifold forms; so how can it be said that [the scripture] refers to the universal (jāti)? To this he replies:
"From the perspective of one who has understood the cause of bondage, it appears as not having that [manifold] form."

The cause of bondage is clearly understood to be non-discrimination (*aviveka*), wherein there is a perception of form where there is no form among persons; the meaning is that there is a distinction of forms [where none exists]. Therefore, through erroneous vision, the establishment of a distinction of forms does not occur. || 155 ||
[Objection: "Even so, the absence of a single form will be established through non-perception. To this, he says:
"The non-perception [of the blind] does not constitute [non-existence] for those with sight. (156)
Non-apprehension itself is unestablished; the meaning is that even when it is not perceived by the ignorant, its uniform nature is perceived by those possessing knowledge. || 156 ||
Having resolved the inconsistency regarding the scriptural texts on non-duality (advaita), he states another objection against the doctrine of undivided non-duality (akhaṇḍādvaita):
"Vāmadeva and others were liberated; there is no non-duality. (157)
Vāmadeva and others were liberated; nevertheless, bondage is still experienced by them in themselves even now. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no absolute non-duality (akhaṇḍādvaita).
Moreover, he [Vāmadeva], having attained awakening through the recollection of his past lives (jātismaraṇa), achieved liberation in that very birth.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "and there would be contradiction with hundreds of such scriptural passages. Nor should it be understood that bondage and liberation belong to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) alone, for that would contradict the established tenets of Śruti and Smṛti. Furthermore, because we observe the desire, "May I not experience suffering," liberation is the supreme human goal (*puruṣārtha*) known as the liberation of the person (*puruṣa*). Moreover, the removal of suffering belonging to the adjunct is a human goal only insofar as it serves that [liberation of the person], just like [the well-being of] a son or others.

As for what is asserted by modern proponents of Māyāvāda—that the scriptural texts concerning bondage, liberation, creation, dissolution, and so forth, are sublated because they contradict the scriptures on non-duality (advaita)—that too is incorrect. For if the very absence of the fruit called liberation were ascertained at the time of hearing [the scriptures], it would follow that the injunctions for reflection (manana) and other practices subsequent to hearing would be invalid due to their non-performance. Furthermore, if even the Vedānta, being part of the phenomenal world (prapañca), were sublated by the scripture on non-duality, then doubt would arise once again regarding the non-duality understood from the Vedānta, just as there is doubt regarding the meaning of a dream-utterance when it is sublated upon waking.

Furthermore, according to the instruction that "false cognition leads to nihilism," it is precisely the Buddhists who hold false views regarding dharma and so forth, as if in deep sleep; for they accept the world of phenomenal manifestation (*prapañca*) as being merely conventional (*sāṃvṛttika*) and rooted in ignorance (*avidyā*). This is the general direction of the argument. || 157 ||
"Is it not to be admitted that even for Vāmadeva and others, supreme liberation has not occurred? To this he replies:
'Because of its non-existence from the beginningless past up until now, it will likewise be so in the future. (158)

If liberation has not occurred for anyone from beginningless time until today, then the future time as well would likewise be devoid of liberation; the meaning is that there is no difference in the performance of the correct means of accomplishment. || 158 ||
Regarding this, he states the application:
"Just as now, so everywhere there is no absolute destruction. (159)
The meaning is that the inference could be possible: "At no time whatsoever is there an absolute cessation of bondage for any person, just as it exists in the present time. (159)

In response to the inquiry—whether that uniformity of persons, which is determined by the meaning of the scriptural texts establishing oneness, exists only at the time of liberation or at all times—he says: "Having both forms withdrawn. (160)

And that person is "of both excluded forms," meaning he is one from whom distinct forms are excluded; the ellipsis is to be supplied as "because his existence and form are established through Śruti, Smṛti, and reasoning. As it has been said:
"By means of manifold Māyā, he appears as if possessing many forms;
sporting among the Guṇas, he becomes bound by the notions of 'mine' and 'I'."
"In the great dream called the world, as one passes from one dream to another, the peaceful form of Brahman—augmented by its own peace—is not abandoned. Thus it is said. (160)
