But surely, since the state of being a witness is impermanent, how can the goals of the person (puruṣārtha) possess eternal uniformity? To this he says:
"The state of being a witness [is established] through direct connection. (161)

The witnesshood of the Puruṣa that has been mentioned arises from a direct connection alone, and not through transformation; this is the meaning. By means of a direct connection, the Puruṣa is understood to be the witness of the intellect alone, because the word *sākṣin* (witness) is etymologically derived as "one who sees directly" (*sākṣād-draṣṭari saṃjñāyām*). And "seeing directly" means seeing without any intervention.

Furthermore, the direct connection with the *puruṣa* occurs only through the modification of its own intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*); therefore, the scriptural distinction is that the *puruṣa* is directly [connected] only to the intellect, while for others it is merely a witness (*draṣṭṛ-mātra*). Moreover, the relationship that determines cognition is precisely the form of a reflection (*pratibimba-rūpa*), which stands in the place of the assumption of the object's form; it is not mere conjunction (*saṃyoga-mātra*), as this would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), as has been stated repeatedly. As for the universal witnesshood (*sarva-sākṣitva*) attributed to Viṣṇu and others, that is only figurative (*gauṇa*), based merely on the absence of any intervention by the senses and so forth.

In the reading "sākṣitvam akṣasaṃbandhāt," however, "akṣa" here refers to the intellect (buddhi) because it shares the common property of being an instrument (karaṇatva). The meaning is: "due to its connection with the aforementioned reflection. || 161 ||
To establish the absence of the nature of both [bound and liberated], he states two further specific characteristics of the Puruṣa by means of two sūtras:
"eternal liberation" (nityamuktatva). || 162 ||

The meaning is that the person (puruṣa) is always devoid of the bondage called suffering, because suffering and the like are transformations of the intellect (buddhi). Furthermore, it has already been stated that the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha) is simply the cessation of the experience of suffering. || 162 ||
And indifference as well. || 163 ||

Indifference is non-agency (*akartṛtva*). By this, other qualities such as desirelessness (*niṣkāmatva*) and so forth are also to be indicated, according to the Śruti: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, intellect, shame—this whole [group] is nothing but the mind. The word "iti" marks the end of the section establishing the attributes of the person (*puruṣadharma*). || 163 ||

Now, if the distinction between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is thus established through their mutual difference, how can the agency of the *puruṣa* and the cognitive capacity (*jñātṛtva*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), as stated in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, be justified? To this he says:
"Agency [belongs to the Self] due to coloring; and cognitive capacity [belongs to the intellect] due to proximity to consciousness. (164)

Here, the construction [of the sentence] is according to what is appropriate: that which is the agency of the Puruṣa arises from the coloring (uparāga) by the intellect; and that which is the thinking of the intellect arises from its proximity to the Puruṣa. The meaning is that both of these are not real. The sense is that just as there is a transfer of each other's attributes due to a particular conjunction between fire and iron, or just as there is a superimposition of each other's attributes due to the conjunction of water and the sun, so it is with the intellect and the Puruṣa. This has also been stated in a verse: "Therefore, through that conjunction, the insentient principle (liṅga) appears as if it were sentient."
"And likewise, while the qualities are the agents, the indifferent one appears as if he were the agent. Thus [it is said].
The repetition of the phrase "due to the proximity of consciousness" (citsānnidhyāt) is for the purpose of indicating the conclusion of the chapter. || 164 ||
The causes for the abandonment and the removal of these two are the [four] arrangements, respectively.
The four principal subjects of the treatise are elaborated upon in this chapter. || 1 ||
Because the meaning of the *Saṃkṣipta-sāṃkhya-sūtras* is elaborated upon here.
This treatise, titled the Exposition of Sāṅkhya, is indeed like Yoga itself.
Thus ends the first chapter, on the Objects of Knowledge, in the commentary on the *Kāpila Sāṅkhya-pravacana* composed by the venerable teacher Vijñāna. 1.
Now begins the second chapter. || 2 ||

The subject matter of the treatise has been defined. Now, in order to establish the unchanging nature of the *puruṣa*, the author will explain in detail in the second chapter the process of creation from *prakṛti*. It is precisely there that the nature of the effects of *pradhāna* must be explained in detail, so that the *puruṣa* may be distinguished from them with the utmost clarity. Therefore it is said: "He who knows correctly both the transformation (*vikāra*), the primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the eternal *puruṣa*, becomes free from craving and is liberated."

Thus, in the *Mokṣadharma* and other texts, there is the statement that only these three are to be known. Regarding this, with the intention that if the insentient primordial nature (*prakṛti*) were to create without purpose, it would follow that even one who is liberated would be bound, [the author] states the purpose for the creation of the world:
"For the sake of the liberation of those already liberated, or for its own sake, [is the activity] of the Pradhāna. (1)

The term "agency" (*kartṛtvam*) is supplied from the concluding sūtra of the previous chapter. It means that the Pradhāna acts as the creator of the world either for the sake of liberating the Puruṣa—who is by nature already free from the bondage of suffering—from the suffering of its reflection (by effecting the release of that reflection), or for the sake of liberating itself; that is to say, for the sake of its own ultimate liberation from suffering. Although enjoyment (*bhoga*) is also a purpose of creation just like liberation, liberation alone is mentioned here because it is the primary goal. || 1 ||
Now, if creation is for the sake of liberation, then since liberation would be possible through a single creation alone, there would be no need for repeated creations; to this he replies:
"Because that [liberation] is accomplished for one who is dispassionate. (2)

The meaning is that liberation from creation does not occur at any single time; rather, it occurs only for one who has been intensely tormented by the manifold sufferings of birth, death, disease, and so forth, many times over, and for whom the practice of liberation is established through supreme detachment born from the discriminative discernment between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. || 2 ||
He states the reason why dispassion is not established by a single act of creation:
"Its establishment does not result from mere hearing alone, because beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are powerful. (3)

Even hearing [the teachings] occurs only through merit accumulated over many births. Furthermore, detachment is not accomplished by mere hearing alone, nor does direct realization occur instantaneously—because beginningless false tendencies (*mithyā-vāsanā*) are powerful—but rather through steadfastness in yoga (*yoga-niṣṭhā*). Since there are many obstacles to yoga, the meaning is that detachment and liberation are achieved only for some rare individual after many births. (3) He states another reason for the continuity of creation:
"Or, like one who has many servants, [it occurs] with each [individual]. (4)

Just as for householders there are many individuals to be supported, distinguished by wives, sons, and so forth, even so for each of the qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, there are countless *puruṣas* who must be liberated. Therefore, even when some *puruṣas* have been liberated, the stream of creation continues for the sake of liberating other *puruṣas*, because *puruṣas* are infinite. Thus says the *Yogasūtra*: "Though it has fulfilled its purpose and perished [for one], it has not perished, because it is common to others. (4)

[Objection: But how can it be said that the power of creation belongs to *prakṛti* alone, given that the Śruti, stating "From this Self, space was produced," establishes that the Puruṣa also possesses the power of creation? To this, he says:
"And when *prakṛti* is real, the superimposition of [agency] upon the Puruṣa is established. (5)

The meaning is as follows: once it is established that the capacity for creation belongs to *prakṛti* and that this is a reality, the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the status of creator upon the *puruṣa* is established in the scriptures, since the intent of the scripture lies solely in [instructing] meditation (*upāsanā*). This is because the capacity for creation is established for *prakṛti* by another scriptural passage such as "the one unborn," and because it would contradict other scriptural passages which teach that persons (*puṃs*) are immutable consciousness (*kūṭastha-cit*). Furthermore, this superimposition exists in the world as a well-established form of metaphorical usage (*upacāra*).

Just as victory and defeat, which actually reside in the warriors according to their own capacities, are metaphorically attributed to the king, so too the power of creation and the like, which resides in the primordial nature (prakṛti) as its capacity, is metaphorically attributed to the Puruṣas who possess that capacity, because of the non-difference between the capacity and the possessor of the capacity. As it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa: "Yogis who contemplate reality perceive the difference between the capacity and the possessor of the capacity from the ultimate standpoint, yet they also perceive their non-difference."

The meaning is that those who worship the principles (tattvas) such as Primordial Matter (prakṛti) perceive both difference—the distinction consisting of mutual non-existence—and non-difference, which is of an undivided nature. The scriptural illustrations for these two are, respectively: the Śruti passage beginning with "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this'" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.6), and the Śruti passage beginning with "All this is indeed the Self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 7.25.2). This is the intended sense. || 5 ||

[Objection: But in that case, why is it determined that even in the case of primordial nature (prakṛti) the status of being a creator is real, given that scripture also hears of creation being similar to a dream and so forth? To this, he says:
"Because its establishment [as real] follows from the effect" (sūtra 6).

The meaning is that because effects possess reality by virtue of their causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), the reality of Nature’s status as a creator is established precisely through its effects, by means of the very instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that apprehends the subject (*dharmin*). As for the scriptural passages stating that [the world] is like a dream and so forth, they should be understood as referring either to the aspect of non-existence in the form of impermanence, or to the aspect of being superimposed upon the Spirit (*puruṣa*); otherwise, there would be a contradiction with those scriptures that establish creation. Furthermore, even dream-objects lack absolute non-existence, since they are transformations of the mind (*manaḥ-pariṇāma*). || 6 ||

But surely, if the view that [Nature] acts for its own sake is maintained, then it would proceed even toward a liberated person; to this he replies: "The restriction [of Nature's activity] is due to the aim of a conscious being, like the removal of a thorn. (7)

By the etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) from "consciousness" (*saṃjñāna*), the "conscious one" (*cetana*) here refers to the one who possesses discriminative knowledge (*abhijña*). Just as [the thorn] acts toward even a single person, so too does *prakṛti*—having accomplished its purpose through that conscious one who possesses discriminative knowledge—become liberated from him. It is not of the nature of suffering for him alone; however, the rule or established order is that it remains of the nature of suffering for others who lack such discriminative knowledge.
By this, it is shown that although *prakṛti* is bound by its own nature, its own liberation is possible; therefore, it does not function toward a person who has already been liberated. || 7 ||

Now, as for the statement that agency in the Puruṣa is merely superimposed, that is not tenable; for through conjunction with Prakṛti, it is logical that the Puruṣa too undergoes transformations such as Mahat and the rest. Indeed, it is observed that through contact with earth and other elements, wood and the like undergo transformations resembling those elements. To this, he replies: "Even when there is conjunction with another, that [agency] is not established [in him] directly, as in the case of the burning of iron. (8)

Even when there is a conjunction with *prakṛti*, the agency (*sraṣṭṛtva*) of the *puruṣa* is not established directly or immediately. In this regard, the example is "like the burning of iron" (*ayodāhavat*). The meaning is that iron does not possess the quality of being a burner directly; rather, it is mediated through the fire conjoined with it, and is thus merely intermediate. In the aforementioned example, however, the transformation of both [iron and fire] is accepted because it is established by direct perception. But in a case where there is doubt, since the explanation is possible through the transformation of only one, to postulate the transformation of both is cumbersome (*gaurava*). Otherwise, it would follow that a crystal undergoes a transformation into redness due to its conjunction with a hibiscus flower (*japā*). || 8 ||
It was stated previously that liberation is the fruit of emanation. Now, he states the primary efficient cause of emanation: "Emanation is the conjunction of passion and dispassion. (9)

In passion (*rāga*) there is creation; in dispassion (*vairāgya*) there is yoga, which is to say, abiding in one's own true nature—that is, liberation—or else, the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛttinirodha*). Thus, through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*), the intention is that passion is the cause of creation. Accordingly, the Śruti also, having described the various courses of karma beginning with Brahmā, says: "But he who desires thus—yet he who is without desire, his vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) do not depart. Passion and dispassion are indeed attributes of *prakṛti* alone. || 9 ||
From here onwards, he begins to describe the process of creation—the five elements in the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (mahat). 10.

The term "creation" (*sṛṣṭi*) is carried over from the preceding sūtra. Although in such scriptural passages as "From this Self, space was produced," the creation of the five elements is heard of at the very beginning, nevertheless, the intended meaning is that the creation of the five elements occurs precisely through the sequence beginning with the Great Principle (*mahat*). The sense is that, just as the creation of space and air is supplied in the scriptural accounts of the creation of fire and so forth, so too in the stated scripture, the creation of the Great Principle and the rest must be supplied at the outset.
And here the proof is the inference that all creation other than the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is preceded by a modification of the internal organ, just like the creation of a jar.
Furthermore—
From this is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;
as well as space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe.

Thus, in accordance with the sequence of the reading found in another Vedic text (*śrutyantara*), and by means of another scriptural passage stating, "He created *prāṇa*, from *prāṇa* [he created] faith, space, wind," and so forth, it is determined that the creation of the *mahat*-tattva and the rest occurs prior to the creation of the five elements. Furthermore, he will state that *prāṇa* is a specific modification (*vṛttibheda*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); therefore, in this scripture, *prāṇa* itself is the *mahat*-tattva. Likewise, even the Vedānta Sūtra describes the creation according to the very sequence beginning with the *mahat*.

"Between the intellect (*vijñāna*) and the mind (*manas*), [the ego arises] in succession because of its characteristic mark. This means that the intellect and the mind are produced in sequence between [Nature and] Space. Furthermore, the entry of the ego into the mind implies that the agency of creation belongs to Nature alone for the sake of its own liberation, because Nature is eternal; whereas the agency of creating their respective transformations belongs to the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the others, not for the sake of their own liberation, because they are non-eternal. He states this distinction:
"Since creation is for the sake of the Self, their undertaking is not for their own sake. (11)

Because the agency of these [principles], beginning with Mahat, is for the sake of the Self—that is, for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa—their undertaking is not for their own sake. The meaning is that since agency implies perishability, it would be incompatible with liberation. Furthermore, since the purpose of another's liberation is necessary, it is logical that it must be for the liberation of the Puruṣa alone, and not for the liberation of Prakṛti; for the latter is subordinate to the Puruṣa. || 11 ||
He states the creation of space and time: "Space and time [arise] from ether and so forth. (12)

The eternal space and time are essentially of the nature of ether (ākāśa) and are merely specific qualities of primordial matter (prakṛti). Therefore, the omnipresence of space and time is established. Furthermore, the omnipresence of ether as stated in such scriptural passages as "It is like the sky, all-pervading, and eternal" is thus justified. As for the limited space and time, however, they arise from ether through conjunction with their respective limiting adjuncts (upādhi); this is the meaning, since the word "etcetera" (ādi) includes the adjuncts. Although limited space and time are indeed ether itself as qualified by those respective adjuncts.

Nevertheless, according to the doctrine that accepts the distinctness of the qualified [whole] as something over and above its parts, its being an effect is stated here—just as the ear is an effect in the Vaiśeṣika system. || 12 ||
Now, having stated [the sequence] by way of the order beginning with the Great Principle (mahat), he shows their nature and their properties in succession:
"Intellection (buddhi) is determination (adhyavasāya). (13)

The synonym for the principle of Mahat is *buddhi* (intellect). Furthermore, the meaning is that determination (*adhyavasāya*), which is termed "ascertainment" (*niścaya*), is its specific function (*asādhāraṇī vṛtti*). The designation in terms of non-difference, however, is due to the non-distinction between the attribute and the substratum (*dharmadharmyabheda*). And the greatness of the intellect (*buddhi*) is to be understood from its pervading all effects other than itself, as well as from its being like the Great Lord (*maheśvara*).
From the Pradhāna, which is subject to modification, the Mahat-tattva was born;
it is called "Mahat" because from it the manifestation (khyāti) of the worlds always arises.

This is because of the Smṛti: "The Ṛgveda and so forth are the breath of this Great Being. Furthermore, in the Śrutis and Smṛtis such as these, even though Hiraṇyagarbha is sentient, the word "Great" (mahān) is applied to him solely by virtue of his being the presiding deity of the intellect (buddhi). Just as the word "earth" is used for the sentient being who presides over the earth, so too should the words "ego" (ahaṅkāra) and so forth be understood in the case of Rudra and the others.

Starting from the deities who preside over the primordial nature (prakṛti) up to those who preside over the gross elements, the specific limiting adjuncts consisting of their respective intellects are all indeed portions of the principle of Mahat alone. || 13 ||
He states other attributes of the principle of Mahat as well: "Its effects are dharma and so forth. (14)

The knowledge of dharma, dispassion, and sovereignty are also derived from the intellect (buddhi) as their material cause, not from the ego (ahaṅkāra) or other such principles; the meaning is that these are the effects of the intellect alone when it is characterized by unsurpassed sattva. || 14 ||

[Objection: But if this is so, how can the predominance of unrighteousness (*adharma*) be established for those portions of the intellect (*buddhi*) residing in humans, animals, and so forth? To this he says:
"The opposite [occurs] due to the influence of the Great One (*mahat*). (15)

The meaning is that this very Great Principle (Mahat-tattva), due to its coloring by *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes the opposite—possessing the qualities of unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), non-detachment (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). By this, the scriptural and traditional assertion that "all persons are indeed lords" (*īśvara*) is also established, because the natural sovereignty of all limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is merely veiled by *rajas* and *tamas*. Now, if it is objected: "In that case, since the intellect (*buddhi*) is also eternal for the sake of the persistence of dharma and so forth, how can it be an effect?"—it is not so.

Since the impressions of karma and other factors reside within the Great Principle (*mahat-tattva*)—which is a specific form of *sattva* existing in the state of a seed and is of the nature of a constituent of primordial nature (*prakṛti*)—it is accepted that this very principle arises like a sprout during its state as the cause of knowledge. Thus, the intellect (*buddhi*) is of both eternal and non-eternal natures, just like space; for, according to the power of primordial nature, it assumes its own form in accordance with its cause. (15)
Having defined the principle of Mahat, he now defines its effect, Ahaṅkāra:
"Ahaṅkāra is self-conceit. (16)

It is called *ahaṅkāra* because it performs the function of "I-making" (*ahaṅkaroti*), like a potter; the suffix *aṇ* is applied according to the rule [Pāṇini 3.2.1] *karmaṇyam*, and the feminine form is derived from its ending in *aṇ*. It is the substance of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). And that is called "egoism" (*abhimāna*) by identifying the attribute with the substratum, in order to indicate its specific function. Egoism and the sense of "mine-ness" arise only regarding an object already determined by the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, as has been stated previously, the causal relationship between the two possessors of the functions (*vṛttimat*) is inferred from the causal relationship between the two functions themselves. Furthermore, it has also been stated before that [the intellect] "attains the state of the internal organ. For this very reason, in the *Vāyumātsya*:
Mind, the Great One, intellect, Brahmā, the ancient wisdom, renown, and the Lord.
Thus, it has been stated that "manas" and "buddhi" are synonyms. || 16 ||
He states the effect of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) that has come down in succession: "The eleven [faculties] and the five subtle elements (tanmātras) are its effects. (17)

The meaning is that the eleven organs and the five subtle elements (tanmātras), such as sound and the rest, constitute the body of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra). Because of the production of the organs and their objects during the creation of the gods and others—based on the conceit, "I shall enjoy this form and so forth through this organ," or "this alone is the means to happiness"—the ego-sense is the cause of the organs and the rest. This is because in the world, we observe that one who possesses the conceit of enjoyment creates the instruments of enjoyment through the medium of passion (rāga).

The intention is that, as stated in the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata* in the passage beginning "From attachment to form, the eye arose," it is recorded that the collective eyes and other organs of Hiraṇyagarbha originated from attachment (*rāga*) alone. Therefore, between the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*), the specific distinction is that the mind (*manas*), characterized by attachment, arises first from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), because the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) and the rest are effects of attachment. || 17 ||
Regarding that, he states the distinction:
"The group of eleven, characterized by sattva, proceeds from the *vaikṛta* ego. (18)

The eleventh, which completes the group of eleven, is the mind (*manas*); among the group of sixteen [senses], it is *sāttvika*. Therefore, the meaning is that it is born from the *vaikṛta*, which is the *sāttvika* ego (*ahaṅkāra*). Consequently, it should be understood that the organs of perception arise from the *rājasa* ego, and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) from the *tāmasa* ego.
"I am threefold: *vaikārika*, *taijasa*, and *tāmasa*.
From the *vaikārika* [ego], while performing the function of the principle of egoity (*ahaṃtattva*), the mind was produced."
The gods who are the vaikārika (transformative) are from that which manifests objects;
from the taijasa (energetic) arise the very senses consisting of knowledge and action.
The subtle elements and so forth, beginning with space, are characterized by tamas, for they are the sign of the self.
This is determined precisely by such Smṛti passages as these. For this very reason, it has also been stated in the *Kārikā* in accordance with the Purāṇas and other sources:
"The group of eleven [senses] proceeds from the *vaikṛta* (modified) *ahaṃkāra* as *sāttvika*;
the *tanmātras* proceed from the *bhūtādi* (elemental) *ahaṃkāra* as *tāmasa*; and both proceed from the *taijasa* (radiant) *ahaṃkāra*."

The *taijasa* is the *rājasa*. Both [classes of organs] consist of the organs of cognition and the organs of action. Now, it may be objected: since the author will state in a future aphorism that "the deities are the abode" (*devatālayaśruti*), he will speak of the deities as the presiding divinities of the instruments; why then has the Kārikā not also stated that the deities are the products of the *sāttvika* ego? It is replied: the deities of the eyes and so forth are heard of in scripture as being the conscious beings such as the Sun who possess the collective (universal) bodies of the eyes and so on. Therefore, with the intention of establishing the identity between the individual (*vyaṣṭi*) and the collective (*samaṣṭi*), the deities are not mentioned separately from the instruments in this treatise.

Therefore, the collective sense organs (*samaṣṭīndriyāṇi*) are designated as being the effects of the *rājasa* ego because they possess less *sattva* than the mind (*manas*). It should be understood that there is no contradiction with the principle stated in the *Smṛtis*, which describe them as the effects of the *sāttvika* ego due to their possessing more *sattva* than the individual sense organs (*vyaṣṭīndriyāṇi*). Thus, since the ego is threefold, its cause—the Great Principle (*mahat*)—must also be considered threefold.
The Great Principle (Mahat) is threefold: characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), and darkness (tāmasa).

Thus it is from the traditional authority (smṛti). Furthermore, that these two possess a threefold nature is due to the distinction between their individual instances; this is another matter. || 18 ||
He shows the eleven faculties:
"The internal [group] consists of eleven, [namely] the organs of action and the organs of perception. (19)

The organs of action—speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—are five; and the organs of knowledge—known as the eye, ear, skin, tongue, and nose—are five. Together with these ten, the internal mind (*manas*) makes eleven; this is the meaning of "the eleventh organ. An *indriya* is the instrument (*karaṇa*) of *Indra*, the Lord of the aggregate [of the body]. Thus, the definition of an organ is: being an instrument while being an effect of ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*). || 19 ||
He refutes the view that the sense organs are elemental:
"The sense organs are not elemental, because scripture states they are derived from the ego-principle. (20)

The sense organs are the remainder [of the context]. Regarding their being derived from *ahaṅkāra*, the scriptural authority (*śruti*), though lost at some point in time, is inferred from the words of the Teacher (Vyāsa) and from all the *smṛtis* of Manu and others [as stated clearly in the first chapter, second section of the Pūrva-mīmāṃsā: "From practice one knows the *smṛti*; from the *smṛti* one infers the *śruti*; this inference is *anumāna*"]. Direct scriptural evidence (*pratyakṣā śruti*) includes such passages as: "May I become many."

If it be objected that there is indeed scriptural authority for their material nature, such as "For the mind, my dear, consists of food" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.5.4), we say no. Since it is more appropriate for the internal organs to have the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) as their material cause—given the commonality of their illuminating nature—the scriptural statement regarding their being derived from the ego is primary. Furthermore, since even the gross elements are produced by the will of Hiraṇyagarbha, food is produced from the mind; thus, the scriptural reference to them as "material" (*bhautika*) is secondary, meaning that individual bodies and so forth exist only through their association with the elements and are merely manifested from them. || 20 ||

But even so, one might object that the determination of [the senses] as being derived from *ahaṅkāra* is not tenable; for in such scriptural passages as, "Of this person, speech merges into fire, breath into wind, and sight into the sun," it is understood that the senses have the deities (*devatā*) as their material cause (*upādāna*), since the effect must merge into its very cause. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The scriptural statement regarding the merging of the deities does not refer to the originator. (21)

The scriptural statement regarding dissolution into the deities does not refer to that which is non-originative; the meaning is that it does not concern the non-originative [deity]. This is because, for example, the dissolution of a drop of water is observed even upon a ground that is not its originative cause, and because the dissolution of the self is heard of even in elements that are not its originative causes, as in such scriptural passages as: "Being a mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13). This is the intended sense. || 21 ||
Some maintain that the mind is eternal and included among the sense organs; he refutes this [view] with the sūtra:
"Because its origination is heard in scripture and because its destruction is observed. (22)

There is indeed the origination of all these very faculties, according to such scriptural passages as, "From this [Self] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense-faculties. The meaning is that, just as the eyes and other organs undergo deterioration in states such as old age, the mind is also determined to perish through decay and so forth. Thus it has been said: "The mind and all the sense-faculties depart along with the group of ten. Furthermore, those statements regarding the eternity of the mind refer to the seed known as *prakṛti*. || 22 ||
He refutes the materialist view that the sense organ is merely the physical globe by stating:
"The sense organ is supersensible; for those who are deluded, it [appears] in its physical substrate. (23)

Every sense organ (*indriya*) is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*); it is not perceptible. However, for those who are deluded, the sense organ is [erroneously perceived] as being identical with its physical substrate (*golaka*), which is called the "seat" (*adhiṣṭhāna*). The reading is indeed *adhiṣṭhāna*. (23)
He refutes the view that there is only one sense-faculty which produces diverse effects due to a difference in its powers:
"Even if there is a difference in powers, since a difference [in the entity itself] is established, there can be no unity. (24)

Even if one accepts that there is a differentiation of powers within a single sense organ, the distinction between sense organs is nonetheless established; for those powers themselves are also sense organs. Therefore, there is no unity [of the sense organ] on the basis of its being a sense organ. Thus, the meaning is that the sense organ is not a single entity. || 24 ||
But surely, if one postulates the production of various kinds of sense organs from a single ego-principle (ahaṅkāra), there is a contradiction with logic; to this he replies:
"There is no contradiction with the conceptual construction, for it is seen through valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). (25)
This is easily understood. || 25 ||
He states that the other ten are merely different powers of the single primary sense, the mind:
"The mind is of a dual nature. (26)
Therefore, the mind consists of the organs of cognition and the organs of action. || 26 ||
He himself explains the meaning of "consisting of both" [nature and spirit]:
"The multiplicity [of the world] arises from the differences in the transformations of the qualities (guṇas), like various states. (27)

Just as a single man assumes various forms through association—becoming a lover through association with a woman, a detached ascetic through association with the detached, and something else through association with others—so too the mind becomes manifold through association with the eyes and other senses, appearing distinct by virtue of its specific functions such as seeing, due to its identification with the eyes and so forth. The reason for this is stated in the verse beginning with "guṇa": it means by virtue of the capacity [of the mind] during the various transformations of the *guṇas*, namely *sattva* and the rest.

And this is inferred from the fact that the eyes and other senses are incapable of functioning without conjunction with the mind, as established by such scriptural passages as, "My mind was elsewhere, I did not hear," and so forth. || 27 ||
He states the object of both the organs of knowledge and the organs of action:
"From form up to the impurity of taste is the object of both. (28)

The impurity of food-essences consists of feces and so forth; likewise, form, taste, smell, touch, and sound, as well as that which is to be spoken, grasped, gone toward, rejoiced in, and emitted—these are the ten objects of both the organs of knowledge and the organs of action. Furthermore, the object of the generative organ (*upastha*) is the pleasure to be experienced (*ānandayitavya*), which is distinct from the other [five] objects. || 28 ||
He states both that sense-organ by which [the soul is assisted] and that assistance by means of which these are called "senses":
"The seer, the visual faculty, and so forth, constitute the instruments for the self; they are the senses. (29)

The meaning is that the pentad beginning with "the state of being a seer" (draṣṭṛtva) and the pentad beginning with "the state of being a speaker" (vaktṛtva), as well as the state of being a "conceiver" (saṅkalpayitṛtva), belong to the Self (puruṣa); whereas the instruments (karaṇatva) for the functions of seeing and so forth belong to the sense organs. Now, one might object: while the states of being a seer, a hearer, and so on may be possible even for the changeless Puruṣa because they ultimately terminate in mere experience, how can the states of being a speaker and so forth [be attributed to him]?

If it is objected: "How can mere activity belong to that which is immutable (kūṭastha)? We say no; for here, the meaning of words such as "seer" and so forth is simply the agency of the functions of seeing and so on by virtue of mere proximity, like a magnet. Just as a great king, though not himself engaged in action, becomes a warrior by means of his army as an instrument through his mere command, so too the immutable Puruṣa becomes a seer, a speaker, a volitional agent, and so forth, by means of all the instruments such as the eyes and the rest.

They act as instigators merely by their proximity, which is termed "conjunction," like a magnet. And here, agency is like that of a craftsman using an axe or similar tools. As for the fact that agency such as seeing and so forth is denied in the scriptures regarding the *puruṣa*, that refers to the possession of a volition conducive to action, or the actual performance of those respective actions. Thus it has been said:
"Therefore, both agency and non-agency reside in the Self."
"Because it is devoid of desire, it is a non-agent; yet, being merely present, it is an agent. Thus [it is said].

For this very reason, because the power to employ the entire circle of causal factors (*kāraka-cakra*) is the very nature of the Self (*ātman*), it is heard in scripture that seeing, speaking, and so forth are eternal for the Self. This is expressed by such passages as: "There is no loss of the seer’s sight, nor is there any loss of the speaker’s speech," and so on. Now, one might object: "In the classification of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-vibhāga*), it was stated that the instruments (*karaṇa*) are only the functions (*vṛtti*) of perception and the rest; how then can the sense organ (*indriya*) be spoken of [here] as the instrument? To this, we say: No.

In this context, since the instruments (karaṇas) of the senses are said to be the mental modifications (buddhi-vṛttis) consisting of seeing and so forth, which operate through the doors of the eyes and other organs—and because it has been stated therein that these modifications function as instruments with respect to the fruit called "awareness" (bodha) residing in the Puruṣa—the author now states the specific functions (asādhāraṇa-vṛtti) of the three internal instruments:
"The specific characteristic of the three [is their respective nature]. (30)

The term *svālakṣaṇya* refers to the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—that is, the unique function (*asādhāraṇī vṛttiḥ*)—of each of the three: the Great Principle (*mahat*), the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the mind (*manas*). This is a compound formed by eliding the middle term (*madhyamapadalopī vigrahaḥ*). Its state (*bhāva*) is its essence (*tattva*). In common usage, the characteristic of the Great Principle is the possession of preeminent qualities such as determination (*adhyavasāya*). That of the ego-sense is the superimposition upon the self of qualities not actually present there. And that of the mind is the acceptance [of objects] in the form "let this be."

And thus it follows that determination (*adhyavasāya*) is the function (*vṛtti*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), egoism (*abhimāna*) is that of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and volition (*saṅkalpa*) and doubt (*vikalpa*) are those of the mind (*manas*). Volition is the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*), according to the traditional teaching: "Volition is mental action" (*saṅkalpaḥ karmamānasam*). Doubt is either uncertainty or a specific type of error mentioned in Yoga; it is not qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*), because the latter is a function of the intellect. || 30 ||
He also states the common function of the three [internal organs]:
"The common function of the organs is the five vital airs, beginning with prāṇa. (31)

The five well-known vital airs (*vāyu*), such as *prāṇa* and the rest, which circulate like wind, constitute the common or general function (*sāmānyā vṛttiḥ*) of the three instruments; that is to say, they are specific modifications [of those instruments]. This has been stated in the following verse: "The function of the triad is its own non-commonality; this indeed is its uncommon [function]. The common function of the instruments consists of the five vital airs, beginning with *prāṇa*. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, someone says: "The vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth are merely specific modifications of air. Since they function through the activity of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) by means of the effort that is the source of life (jīvanayoni-prayatna), the statement that 'the vital breaths and so forth are functions of the organs' is an indication of non-difference. This is not correct. For, by the Vedānta Sūtra, "Neither air nor function [is the prāṇa], because of the separate teaching," the status of the prāṇa as air or as a transformation of air is clearly negated; therefore, it is appropriate here as well to maintain consistency with that same [Sūtra]. Furthermore, it is more appropriate for the qualities of the mind, such as desire and so forth—which cause the agitation of the prāṇas—to be expressed in grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with them.
As for the scriptural passages that teach the wind (*vāyu*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as distinct—such as:
"From this [Brahman] are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs;
as well as space, wind, light, water, and the earth which supports the universe"—[these refer to their functional differentiation].

"Thus, and so forth. For this very reason, there is no deficiency even when the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are enumerated within the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), because it is the intellect (*buddhi*) itself, through its power of action (*kriyāśakti*), that receives the designations of the "thread-self" (*sūtrātman*), the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and so on. Furthermore, although these are modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the application of the term "air" (*vāyu*) is justified due to their specific mode of movement resembling air and because they are presided over by the deity Vāyu. || 31 ||
Unlike the Vaiśeṣikas, for us there is no such rule that the functioning of the senses must occur only sequentially and never simultaneously; thus he says:
"The functioning of the senses is both sequential and non-sequential. (32)

This is easy to understand. The point is that for us, there is no fault in the mixing of classes (*jātisaṅkara*), because when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present, there is no obstacle to the simultaneous production of a single function even by multiple sense organs. Furthermore, the division of the functions of the sense organs has been explained by the following verse:
"The function of the five [organs] with respect to sound and the other [objects] is held to be mere perception (*ālocana*).
And speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure belong to the five [organs of action]."
And *ālocana* has been explained by the former teachers as follows:
"Indeed, *ālocana* is the first cognition, which is indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*);
but subsequently, it is likewise [determinate] through the properties of the object, such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth."

The meaning is that subsequently, cognition becomes conceptual (*savikalpaka*) through the properties of objects—that is, through properties consisting of substance as well as [qualities] such as genus (*jāti*) and so forth—and likewise becomes what is called "mere observation" (*ālocana*). Thus, it is established that sensory cognition is of two kinds—non-conceptual and conceptual—and is designated as "observation. However, some explain the meaning of the verse as follows: only non-conceptual cognition is observation and is produced by the senses, whereas conceptual cognition is produced by the mind alone. That is not correct.

This is because Vyāsadeva, in the *Yogabhāṣya*, has established that even distinguished cognition (*viśiṣṭajñāna*) can be sensory in nature, and because there is no sublation regarding distinguished cognition produced by the senses. He explains the meaning of the Sūtra as follows: "The functioning [of the internal organ], beginning from the external senses and ending with the intellect, occurs sequentially as a general rule. However, at times—such as when seeing a tiger or similar object—due to a particular intensity of fear, the functioning occurs simultaneously across all the instruments, like a flash of lightning; such is the meaning. That too is incorrect.

Since the Sūtra speaks only of the sequential and non-sequential nature of the functions of the sense organs (*indriya*), there is no occasion for the functions of the intellect (*buddhi*) or the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) to be included. Furthermore, since there is a dispute among disputants regarding the simultaneous functioning of multiple sense organs, it is appropriate that the Sūtra aims at resolving that very point in order to refute the atomicity of the mind (*manas*), rather than being intent on investigating the teeth of a crow. || 32 ||
Having summarized the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), he first shows them for the purpose of demonstrating that they are the cause of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*):
"The modifications are fivefold; they are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) and unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*). (YS 1.5)

Whether the fluctuations (*vṛtti*) be afflicted (*kliṣṭa*) or unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*), they are fivefold—that is, of exactly five types and no more. The afflicted are those worldly fluctuations that cause suffering. The fivefold nature of the fluctuations is stated in the *Pātañjala-sūtra* [in the *Samādhipāda*], beginning from the sūtra: "The five fluctuations are right knowledge, misconception, conceptualization, sleep, and memory" (YS 1.5), up to: "Right knowledge consists of perception, inference, and valid testimony" (YS 1.7); "Misconception is false knowledge, which does not abide in the true form of the object" (YS 1.8); and so on.

Thus, in the Yoga Sūtras [it is said]: "Cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory. Among these, the cognitive function (*pramāṇa-vṛtti*) has been explained here as well. Error (*viparyaya*), however, for us is simply the non-apprehension of discrimination (*vivekāgraha*), since the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*) is to be rejected. Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is knowledge such as "the head of Rāhu" or "the consciousness of a person," which occurs even at the time of perceiving a specific object. Sleep (*nidrā*) is the mental state (*buddhi-vṛtti*) occurring during deep sleep. Memory (*smṛti*) is knowledge produced by latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). All of this has been formulated in the Pātañjala Sūtra.

These mental modifications (*buddhi-vṛtti*) that have been described constitute only a conditioned state of difference for the *puruṣa*, not its own nature; and upon their cessation, the *puruṣa* abides in its own true form. By this direction as well, he defines the nature of the *puruṣa*:
"Upon their cessation, with its coloring stilled, it is established in itself" (34).

The meaning is that during the state of cessation of those mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), the Self, being free from their reflection, becomes established in its own nature, as if in liberation (*kaivalya*), even at other times. And thus there are three *Yoga-sūtras*: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind"; "Then the seer abides in its own nature"; and "In other cases, it conforms to the form of the fluctuations. This alone is the self-abiding state of the Puruṣa, namely, the cessation of the reflection of the fluctuations of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). Such a state of the Puruṣa is illustrated by an analogy in the *Vāsiṣṭha*:
"Just as [the sky remains] when no reflection of mountains and the like has been reached..."
In the mirror, the nature of the mirror may exist as nothing other than its own essential self-nature.
"When the delusion of the visible world—such as 'I', 'you', and 'the universe'—has been stilled, there arises that state of absolute oneness (kevalatā) when the Seer remains without seeing. (34)
He explains this very point by means of an illustration:
"And like a gem with a flower. (35)

The word *ca* (and) indicates the reason. The meaning is: "like a gem by means of a flower. Just as a crystal gem becomes disordered (*asvastha*) by means of a *japā* flower—[in the reading *svaniṣṭhasvābhāvikadharmavān na bhavati*, the meaning is that it does not possess its own inherent quality]—and upon the removal of that [flower], it becomes free from coloration and returns to its natural state, so it is in this case. This very point is stated in the *Kūrma Purāṇa*:
"Just as a pure crystal is perceived by people as being red..."
"In the same way, [the Supreme Person appears] through the proximity of passion and the like. (35)
Now, one might ask: by whose effort would the collection of instruments be set in motion, given that the Puruṣa is immutable and the Lord has been refuted? To this, he says:
"The emergence of the instruments is for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose, arising from the manifestation of the unseen (adṛṣṭa). (36)

The emergence of the instruments [of perception and action] occurs for the sake of the Puruṣa, just as the activity of Pradhāna does. The meaning is that the activity of the instruments also arises solely from the manifestation of the Puruṣa's unseen merit (adṛṣṭa). And this unseen merit belongs only to the limiting adjunct (upādhi). 36.
He provides an illustration for [the Buddha's] spontaneous engagement for the sake of others: "Like a cow toward her calf. (37)

Just as a cow flows with milk of her own accord for the sake of her calf, without depending on any other effort, in the same way, the instruments (karaṇas) operate spontaneously for the sake of the master, the Puruṣa. Furthermore, it is observed that from deep sleep, the intellect (buddhi) awakens by itself. This very point has also been stated in a verse: "Each instrument adopts its respective function, which is caused by mutual intention; the purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause, and no instrument is set in motion by anyone else. (Kārikā 37)
In response to the inquiry as to how many instruments there are when the external and internal ones are combined, he says:
"The instrument is of thirteen kinds due to its intermediate subdivisions. (38)

The three internal organs together with the ten external organs make thirteen. With the intention that even among these there is a distinction, it is said: "due to internal subdivisions. This means that although the instrument called *buddhi* is one, it possesses a plurality of instruments [within itself]. || 38 ||

Now, one might object: since it is *buddhi* (the intellect) alone that primarily serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the person by presenting objects to him, the status of being an instrument for the others is merely secondary (*gauṇa*). To address the inquiry as to what excellence (*guṇa*) they possess [to be considered instruments], he says:
"Because of their connection with the quality of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), like an axe, in relation to the sense organs. (39)

The connection with the previous sūtra is as follows: because the quality of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*) for accomplishing the goals of man resides in the sense organs, this quality exists in the instrument that is the intellect (*buddhi*) through a mediated succession; therefore, it is established that the instrument is of thirteen kinds. Regarding the phrase "like an axe": just as, although the blow alone is the primary instrument in the act of cutting because it is the factor whose non-connection with the result is excluded, the axe is nonetheless considered an instrument due to its possession of the quality of being an excellent means (*prakṛṣṭasādhanatva*), so it is here. Intending to maintain the unity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the status of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) as a secondary instrument has not been mentioned here. || 39 ||
He states specifically the distinction regarding the primary and secondary status:
"Of the two, the mind is the principal, just as in the world [the master is principal] among the ranks of servants. (40)

Between the two—the external and the internal—intellect (*buddhi*) alone is the primary or principal [faculty]. That is to say, it is the direct instrument of apprehension, because it presents objects to the *puruṣa*. The meaning is that just as among a group of servants only one person becomes the chief minister of a king, while others such as village headmen become subordinate to him, so it is here. In this context, the word "mind" (*manaḥ*) does not denote the third internal organ (the *manas*). This is because the capacity to retain all latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), which will be described later, is impossible for anything other than the intellect; or, if it were possible, the postulation of a separate intellect would be redundant. || 40 ||
He states the reasons for the primacy of the intellect (buddhi) through three sūtras:
"Because of non-deviation" (41).
The meaning is: because it pervades all instruments [of action], or because the result is not deviant. || 41 ||
Likewise, because it is the substratum for the remaining formative forces (saṃskāra). || 42 ||

The capacity to serve as the substratum for all latent impressions (saṃskāra) belongs to the intellect (buddhi) alone, and not to the eyes and so forth, nor even to the ego (ahaṅkāra) and the mind (manas); for otherwise, the recollection of objects previously seen, heard, and so on, would be impossible for those who are blind or deaf. Furthermore, since recollection is observed even when the ego and the mind have been dissolved through the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna), it follows that the intellect alone is the most preeminent of all, by virtue of being the substratum for the entirety of latent impressions. This is the meaning. || 42 ||
And because of memory and inference. (43)

The meaning is that [it is known] primarily through inference based on memory, which is a mental modification (vṛtti) consisting of reflection. For the reflective modification called meditation (dhyāna) is superior to all other instruments of mental modification; this is the sense. || 43 ||
[Objection: "But surely the activity of thought must belong to the Puruṣa alone. To this, he says: "It could not [arise] spontaneously. (44)

Memory cannot arise from the *puruṣa* by itself; the meaning is that this is because of its immutability (*kūṭasthatva*). Or, it may be explained in this way: anticipating the objection—"In that case, let the intellect (*buddhi*) alone be the instrument; what is the use of intermediate organs?"—the author says: "It could not [arise] by itself. The meaning is that without the mediation of the eyes and other [senses], the intellect's status as an instrument in all operations would be impossible, as this would lead to the absurd consequence that even the blind and others could perceive forms and so forth. (44)
Now, if it is the case that the intellect (*buddhi*) alone is predominant, how is it that the mind (*manas*) was previously described as having a dual nature? To this, he says:
"The status of being subordinate or predominant is relative, depending on the specific activity. (45)

With respect to specific actions, there is a relative relationship of primary and subordinate among the instruments. In the operations of the eyes and other senses, the mind is primary; in the operation of the mind, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is primary; and in the operation of the ego-sense, the intellect (buddhi) is primary. || 45 ||
Now, one might ask: "What is the basis for this established rule that for this person, this very intellect is the instrument, and not another intellect? In response to this expectation, he says:
"Because it is acquired through its own karma, it exerts effort for its own sake, as is seen in the world. (46)

Because the instrument (*karaṇa*) arises from an action performed by a particular person, its activity—its entire operation—is for the sake of that person, as is seen in the world. The meaning is that, just as in the world, whatever axe or other tool is acquired by a person through such actions as labor, its function, such as cutting, exists solely for the sake of that person. Therefore, the sense is that there is a fixed order regarding the instruments.

Although there is no action in the *puruṣa* due to its immutability (*kūṭasthatā*), nevertheless, because it is the means of experience and possesses the *puruṣa* as its owner, action is attributed to the *puruṣa*, just as victory and so forth are attributed to a king. If it is asked, "What is the determining factor for that action belonging to that specific *puruṣa*? [the answer is: it is simply another such action. Because this process is beginningless (*anādi*), there is no fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). As for what some undiscriminating person says—that action belongs to the *puruṣa* reflected in the intellect (*buddhi*)—that is not correct.

Because the *Yogabhāṣya* describes only the method we have stated, any other method lacks authoritative validity; furthermore, since a reflection is not a real entity (*avastu*), it is impossible for it to possess karma and so forth. Otherwise, if one were to admit that a reflection possesses karma, its experience thereof, and so on, the uselessness of postulating a Puruṣa conceived as the "original" (*bimba*) has already been demonstrated. || 46 ||
He concludes in order to manifest the preeminence of the intellect:
"In the performance of an identical action, the preeminence of the intellect is like that seen in the world. (47)

Although the activity of all the instruments (karaṇas) is indeed equal insofar as it serves the purpose of the Puruṣa, nevertheless, the primacy belongs to the intellect (buddhi) alone, as is seen in the world. For in the world, even though there is no difference in their service to the king, among the village overseers and others, the minister alone possesses primacy; such is the meaning. Therefore, it is proclaimed in all the scriptures that the intellect alone is the "Great One" (mahat). [This concludes the chapter with the repetition. 47.
That subtle primary effect, which consists of seventeen components and constitutes the constituent of the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), has been described here in this chapter. || 1 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, on the effects of Pradhāna, in the commentary on the *Kāpila Sāṃkhya Pravacana* composed by the venerable teacher Vijñānācārya.
Now begins the third chapter. || 3 ||

From this point forward, the gross effects of Pradhāna—the great elements and the two types of bodies—must be described. Furthermore, the various courses of birth and so forth must be explained for the purpose of inducing supreme detachment by demonstrating that these are caused by the practice of the means of knowledge. Consequently, all the means of knowledge must be taught for the sake of supreme detachment; thus begins the third chapter.
The commencement of a specific [quality] occurs from that which is non-specific. || 1 ||

That in which there is no distinction—such as the forms of being peaceful, terrible, or delusive—is the "undifferentiated" (*aviśeṣa*), namely the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*) known as the five *tanmātras*. The meaning is that from that [undifferentiated state], the gross great elements (*mahābhūta*), which possess distinctions such as the forms of being peaceful and so forth, originate. For the nature of pleasure and the rest—which constitutes the forms of being peaceful and so forth—is manifested only in the gross elements through degrees of intensity and so on, but not in the subtle ones; because those [subtle elements] are manifested to yogis solely by way of their uniform, peaceful nature. || 1 ||

Thus, having explained the production of the twenty-three principles starting from the previous chapter, he now states the production of the two bodies from that: "From that, [the production] of the body" (1.2).
Therefore, the meaning is that from these twenty-three principles, the two bodies—the gross and the subtle—are originated. || 2 ||
Now, he provides proof for the impossibility of transmigration otherwise within the system of twenty-three principles:
"From that seed comes transmigration" (3).

From the seed of that body—the subtle cause consisting of the twenty-three principles—the transmigratory existence of the *puruṣa*, its coming and going, occurs; for since the immutable (*kūṭastha*) self is all-pervading, movement and such are impossible for it by itself. This is the meaning. Established within the twenty-three principles, the *puruṣa* migrates from body to body through this very adjunct (*upādhi*) for the sake of experiencing the fruits of previously performed actions:
"He experiences with the mind alone the mental [results], whether auspicious or inauspicious;
with speech, the action performed by speech; and with the body alone, the bodily action."

By such Smṛti passages as these, it is established that, as a general rule, the atoms belonging to a previous creation continue to provide enjoyment in subsequent creations. For this very reason, the Brahma-sūtra concludes with the words: "enveloped" (sampariṣvakta). || 3 ||
He also states the limit of transmigratory existence:
"And the activity of the non-specific [evolutes] continues until discrimination. (SK 4)

For all persons alike—whether they possess the distinction of being lords or non-lords—transmigration is inevitable until the attainment of discriminative discernment (viveka); however, after discernment, it no longer exists. This is the meaning. || 4 ||
Regarding this, he states the reason:
"Because of the experience of the other. (Sūtra 5)
The meaning is that for the other, namely the non-discriminating one alone, there is the inevitable necessity of experiencing the fruits of his own karma. || 5 ||
He states that even while the body exists, there is no experience at the time of transmigration:
"Now he is liberated from both" (6).

The meaning is that, at present, during the time of transmigratory existence, the person becomes liberated from the two pairs of opposites, such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and so forth. This very point has been stated in the verse:
"The subtle body (liṅga), permeated by latent dispositions (bhāvas), transmigrates while being devoid of experience."
The entities (bhāvas) are dharma, adharma, latent impressions (vāsanā), and so forth. || 6 ||
From here on, he begins to speak specifically regarding the two bodies: "The gross body is generally born of mother and father; likewise in other cases. (7)

The "gross" [body] is born of mother and father, for the most part; this is because even the gross body that is not born from a womb is remembered [in tradition]. The other, however, is the subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*), which is not so—it is not born of mother and father, because it arises at the beginning of creation. This is stated in the *Kārikā*: "The *liṅga* (subtle body), which has arisen previously, is unattached, constant, composed of the principles from *mahat* down to the subtle elements, migrates without experiencing [sensory objects], and is permeated by dispositions (*bhāva*). Thus it is said.

It is certain that [the subtle body] is eternal, even though it lasts for two *parārdhas*; however, this is a "conditional eternity" (*gauṇanityatva*), because it would be cumbersome to assume the production of a new subtle body (*liṅga*) for every individual body. At the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*), its destruction is accepted on the authority of the Śruti and Smṛti. The statement regarding the absence of experience during the journey is intended as a general rule (*utsarga*). But sometimes, due to entering a body made of air (*vāyavīya-śarīra*), experience occurs even at the time of travel; therefore, the scriptural statements concerning the experience of suffering on the path of Yama are justified. || 7 ||
Between the gross and subtle bodies, by which limiting adjunct (upādhi) does the Puruṣa undergo the conjunction with the pairs of opposites? He determines this:
"Because it was produced first, that [subtle body] is its effect; experience belongs to one [of them], not to the other. (8)

The subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) which first arises in *larga* and other such states is precisely that which possesses the quality of being an effect—namely, the quality of producing the effects of pleasure and pain. Why? Because the experience known as pleasure and pain belongs solely to the single subtle body, and not to this gross body (*sthūla-śarīra*). This is because it is universally accepted that pleasure, pain, and so forth are absent in a dead body; this is the meaning. He now states the essential nature of the aforementioned subtle body: "The subtle body consists of seventeen principles. (9)

The subtle body (*sūkṣmaśarīra*) is also twofold by way of the relationship between the support and the supported. Among these, the seventeen [constituents] combined constitute the *liṅgaśarīra*. The meaning is that at the beginning of creation, it exists as a single collective whole (*samaṣṭi*). These seventeen consist of the eleven organs, the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the intellect (*buddhi*). Ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is included within the intellect itself.

Based on the authority that will be stated in the fourth sutra, these seventeen alone should be understood as the *liṅga* (mark), and it should not be explained as eighteen by treating the seventeenth and the [first] as one; for the unity of the *liṅga* is established here by the subsequent sutra demonstrating the distinction between individual instances, and because the intent of the word "one" (*eka*) is thus determined.
That person whose nature is action, who is joined with bondage and liberation,
is also joined with the group consisting of seventeen.

Thus, because it is established in the *Mokṣadharma* and other texts that the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) consists of seventeen components—the meaning of "seventeenfold" being that there are seventeen parts here—the word "aggregate" (*rāśi*) refutes the idea that the subtle body is a composite whole (*avayavin*), as in the case of the gross body. This is because postulating a distinct substance in the form of a composite whole would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Furthermore, the gross body is postulated as a composite whole in accordance with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of its unity and so forth.

In this context, with the intention that intellect (*buddhi*) alone is the primary constituent of the subtle body (*liṅgadeha*), the experience of the subtle body was previously described. Furthermore, vital breath (*prāṇa*) is merely a specific modification (*vṛttibheda*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); therefore, the pentad of vital breaths is also included within the subtle body. He himself will later state that this [subtle body], consisting of seventeen components, possesses the nature of a body in the aphorism: "The teacher Sanandana says it is caused by the subtle body. Consequently, being the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*) is the primary definition of a body.

However, its status as the body in this context is due to its being the substratum for that [consciousness]; this will become clear later. Furthermore, the definition "the body is the substratum of purposeful movement, the sense organs, and their objects" has also been formulated in the Nyāya system. || 9 ||
If the *liṅga* (the subtle body) is indeed one, then how can there be diverse experiences according to the difference between individuals? To this he says:
"The distinction between individual manifestations arises from the particularity of karma. (10)

Although at the beginning of creation there is only one subtle body (*liṅga*) in the form of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of Hiraṇyagarbha, nevertheless, after that, through its manifestation as individual entities, it also possesses a partial plurality in the form of individuals. Just as now, from a single father’s subtle body, a plurality arises partially in the form of the subtle bodies of sons, daughters, and so forth. He states the reason for this: "due to the distinction of karma. This means due to the karma and other factors that serve as the cause for the experiences of other individual souls.

Here, because of the specific statement, it follows that the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*) of living beings occurs through their common karma (*sādhāraṇa-karma*). Furthermore, this distinction between individual manifestations (*vyakti-bheda*) is also stated by Manu and others. As it says in the *Manusmṛti*, following the production of the six sense organs of the collective person (*samaṣṭi-puruṣa*): "He then fashioned all beings from the subtle constituent parts (*avayava*) of those [organs], which possess the power of the six elements, into the measures of the primary qualities (*mātrā*)."

The phrase "of the six breaths" (ṣaṇmāṇām) is an elliptical indication for the entire subtle body (liṅgaśarīra). The meaning is: "having joined them to the portions of the Self within the consciousness-elements. And so, there is another statement in that very same [text]:
"Together with those effects and instruments produced from that body, the knowers of the field (kṣetrajñas) were born from the limbs of that wise one. (10)

Now, if the subtle body (*liṅga*) alone is the "body" by virtue of being the locus of experience, how is there the conventional usage of the term "body" with respect to the gross [body]? To this he says:
"Because it rests upon that as its substrate, the designation 'body' is applied to the gross body through metaphorical transfer from the former. (11)

The meaning is as follows: for whichever subtle body (*liṅga*) there is a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), which is its support—the five elements to be described—within that support, namely the body composed of the six sheaths (*ṣāṭkauśika-deha*), there is the "discourse on the body" (*dehavāda*). This means that because of the discourse on that [support] which is designated by the term "substratum," there is the discourse on the body. The ultimate sense is that the substratum becomes the "body" through its connection with the subtle body, and the gross [body] becomes the "body" because it is the support of that substratum. It will be explained that the substratum is not the subtle [body] consisting of the five elements; thus, the three bodies are established. As it is said: "There is one *ātivāhika* (conveying) body, and another is the *ādhibhautika* (elemental) body."
Is there indeed only one Brahman for all classes of beings?

In such scriptures as these, only two bodies are mentioned; this is because the subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) and the body that serves as its substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna-śarīra*) are intended to be treated as one, due to their mutual necessity and their subtlety. || 11 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what proof there is for another body—distinct from the six sheaths—which serves as the substratum for the subtle body (liṅgaśarīra), he says:
"Not by its own independence; without that [gross body], it is like a shadow and like a painting. (12)

That subtle body (*liṅga-śarīra*) does not exist independently without a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), just as a shadow cannot remain without a support, or as a painting [cannot exist without a canvas]. Thus, the sense is that for the purpose of departing for another world after abandoning the gross body, another body that serves as the support for the subtle body is established. Its nature is stated in the *Kārikā*: "The specific elements (*viśeṣas*) are of three kinds: the subtle, those born of mother and father, and those produced together with them.
Among these, the subtle ones are constant, while those born of mother and father cease. Thus it is said.

In this context, that which is the effect of the subtle elements (*tanmātra*)—the five gross elements (*bhūta-pañcaka*) which are subtler in relation to the body born of parents—is said to be the support of the *liṅga* (the subtle body) even until the dissolution of the *liṅga* itself; thus, by another verse, it is established that this very [body] is the "body as the substratum of the *liṅga*": "Just as a painting cannot exist without a support, and just as a shadow cannot exist without a post or other such object."

In the same way, [the subtle body] does not exist without the subtle elements (sūkṣma), meaning without the internal subdivisions of the gross elements. In this verse, since the distinction between the subtle elements—which are called "subtle"—and the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra) is understood, the meaning of the previously cited verse beginning with "That which was produced first, unattached, constant, from Mahat down to the subtle elements" is not that everything up to the subtle elements constitutes the subtle body; rather, it refers to the subtle body in the form of Mahat and the rest. If one asks how many constituent factors (padārtha) comprise this subtle body, [the answer is:
"The latent impressions (vāsanā), the subtle elements, karma, and likewise ignorance (avidyā)."
The ten sense organs, the mind, and the intellect—the wise know this to be the subtle body (liṅga).

Thus, based on statements from the *Vāsiṣṭha* and other texts, it is intended that the "eightfold city" (*puryaṣṭaka*) should be explained precisely through the presentation of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) here; with this in mind, there is a separate mention of the attributes of the intellect—namely, latent impressions (*vāsanā*), karma, and ignorance (*vidyā*). Furthermore, the intention here is that the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) consist of the ten sense-faculties (the five organs of knowledge and the five organs of action) which constitute the two cities. As for the fact that the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādinaḥ*) substitute the pentad of breath (*prāṇa*, etc. for the place of the subtle elements and conceive the eightfold city otherwise, that is without scriptural authority. || 12 ||

[Objection: "But surely, since it is a corporeal substance, just like air and so forth, space itself may be the support of the subtle body (liṅga) through non-attachment; thus, the postulation of attachment elsewhere is useless. To this, he replies:
"Even though it is corporeal, because of its connection with a composite structure, like the sun. (13)

The meaning is that even though it is of the nature of urine, it exists in an unattached state due to its independence, because it is inferred to have contact with a composite aggregate by virtue of its luminous form, like the sun. All luminous bodies such as the sun are seen to exist only through contact with earthly substances; and the mark (liṅga) consists of the manifestation of sattva, which is conjoined with the elements. || 13 ||
He determines the dimension of the subtle body (liṅga): its dimension is atomic, because of the scriptural statement regarding its being "smaller than the small. (14)

That subtle body (*liṅga*) is of minute dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) and limited, but it is not absolutely minute (*atyanta-aṇu*). Why? Because it has been stated to possess parts. From what [is this known]? From the scriptural mention of action (*kṛti-śruti*), that is, the mention of movement (*kriyā-śruti*). The meaning is that, because of such scriptural passages as, "Consciousness (*vijñāna*) extends the sacrifice and also extends ritual acts," the subtle body—predominantly consisting of the intellect (*buddhi*) known as consciousness—is heard to perform all ritual acts. If it were omnipresent (*vibhu*), action would not be possible. The reading *śruteḥ* (from scripture) is the more standard one.

Furthermore, there is scriptural testimony regarding the movement of the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*): "As he departs, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) follows after him; as the vital breath departs, all the vital functions follow after it. He becomes endowed with consciousness (*savijñāna*); indeed, he departs possessed of consciousness. The meaning is that he is born accompanied by the intellect (*buddhi*), and he transmigrates in such a way that he remains endowed with consciousness. [The author] states another argument for its limited nature:
"And because of the scriptural statement that it consists of food (*annamaya*). (Sūtra 3.1.15)

Because that indicative mark (liṅga) is stated in scripture to consist of food (*annamaya*) only in part, its all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) is not possible; the meaning is that if it were all-pervasive, it would follow that it is eternal. And that scriptural passage is: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food, breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire," and so forth. Although the mind and the other organs are not material (*bhautika*), nevertheless, the designation of them as "consisting of food" and so on should be understood as being due to their being filled by portions of the same class that are conjoined with food. || 15 ||
In response to the doubt as to why there is the transmigration—the movement from one body to another—of these insentient subtle bodies (liṅga), he says:
"The transmigration of the subtle bodies is for the sake of the purpose of the Puruṣa, like a cook [serving] a king. (16)

Just as the movement of a king’s cooks among the kitchens is for the sake of the king, so too the transmigratory journey of the subtle bodies (liṅga-śarīra) is for the sake of the Puruṣa; this is the meaning. || 16 ||
The subtle body has been examined in its entirety; now he examines the gross body in the same manner: "This [body] consists of the five elements. (17)
The meaning is that the body is the transformation (pariṇāma) of the five elements when they are combined. || 17 ||
He states another opinion: "Some say it consists of the four elements. (18)
This is stated with the intention of establishing that space is not a productive cause. 28.
Others say it consists of a single element. (19)

The meaning is that the body is indeed composed of earth (pārthiva), while the other elements are merely auxiliary; or else, it means that each body is composed of a single element (ekabhautika). In the bodies of humans and others, there is "earthiness" due to the predominance of the earth-element portion, whereas in the worlds of the Sun and others, there is "fiery-ness" (taijasatā) and so on due to the predominance of the fire-element and the rest, just as in the case of gold and other metals. This very position will be established as the final conclusion (siddhānta) in the fifth chapter as well. || 19 ||
He states what is established by the fact that the body is composed of the elements:
"Consciousness is not innate, because it is not observed in each [element] individually. (20)

When the elements are separated, consciousness is not observed; therefore, the consciousness of the elemental body is natural [to it], yet it is actually adventitious (aupādhika)—this is the meaning. || 20 ||
He states another refutation:
"And there would be an absence of the world, of death, and so forth. (21)
