The meaning is that if the body possessed an inherent consciousness (*svābhāvikacaitanya*), there would be an absence of death, deep sleep, and so forth for the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). For death, deep sleep, and the like constitute the insentience of the body; and that [insentience] is not possible if inherent consciousness exists, because an essential nature (*svabhāva*) persists as long as the substance itself does.
Regarding what was stated previously—that [consciousness] is not observed in each [atom] individually—the author raises a doubt and refutes it:
"If it is argued that, like the power of intoxication, its emergence occurs in the aggregate even though it is not perceived in each individual part. (22)

If it is argued that just as intoxicating power (*mādakatā*), though not residing in each individual substance, exists in the combined substances, so too might consciousness (*caitanya*) be; we reply: no. For the emergence of such a property in a composite state would be possible only if it had been observed in each individual component. In the present case, however, there is no such observation in each individual part. Therefore, in the given example, since intoxication is established as existing subtly in each substance through its own nature and so forth, what is proven is merely the manifestation of intoxication at the time of their combination.

In the case of the subject under discussion (the dārṣṭāntika), however, consciousness is not established by any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) as existing subtly within individual elements; this is the meaning. Now, one might object: "Since consciousness is observed when [elements] are combined, the existence of a subtle power of consciousness in each individual element must be inferred. To this we reply: because it would be cumbersome (*gaurava*) to postulate multiple powers of consciousness for multiple elements, it is more appropriate—due to parsimony (*lāghava*)—to postulate only a single, eternal nature of consciousness.

[Objection: But surely, just as functions such as containing water and performing measurement—which do not exist in the individual parts—are observed in objects like jars, so too consciousness might belong to the body. [Reply: Not so; because the specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) residing in the elements are produced by qualities of a similar kind in their causes, consciousness cannot exist in the body in the absence of consciousness in its cause. || 2 ||

It has been stated that the transmigratory existence of the subtle bodies (liṅga) is for the sake of the human goal (puruṣārtha). Regarding this, the specific human goal of each birth—characterized by the movement of the subtle bodies through gross bodies—which is accomplished by which particular activity, is stated in two aphorisms:
"Liberation arises from knowledge. (23)

The meaning is that through the transition of the *liṅga* (the subtle body), by means of birth, there arises the direct realization of discrimination (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*), from which results the human goal consisting of liberation. Furthermore, knowledge and the rest are defined in the *Kārikā* as the "creation of mental states" (*pratyaya-sarga*): "This creation of mental states consists of error, incapacity, contentment, and attainment. Thus it is said.

The misconceptions and so forth will be explained later. In this context, however, the distinction is that the very same creation of the intellect is stated in the Sūtra by way of its purpose. || 23 ||
Bondage [arises] from the reverse. || 24 ||

The meaning is that, through the reverse process, the purpose of the Puruṣa, which consists of pleasure and pain and takes the form of bondage, arises from the migration of the subtle body (liṅga). || 24 ||
Liberation and bondage are said to result from knowledge and its opposite, respectively. Regarding this, he first examines liberation through knowledge:
"Because there is a fixed cause, neither a combination nor an option [of means] is possible. (25)

Although such scriptural passages as, "He who knows both knowledge and ignorance together," are heard, nevertheless, since knowledge has a fixed cause by virtue of being established in the world as that which brings about the cessation of non-discrimination (aviveka), there can be neither a combination (samuccaya) nor an option (vikalpa) regarding the production of liberation through knowledge in conjunction with the karma known as ignorance; this is the meaning.

From such scriptural passages as, "Only by knowing Him does one pass beyond death; there is no other path for the journey," and "Not by action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality," it follows that action is not the direct cause of liberation. The performance of the combination [of knowledge and action] is justified in the scriptures through their relationship as primary and subordinate factors (aṅga-aṅgibhāva) and so forth. || 25 ||
He provides an illustration for the absence of both conjunction and alternative:
"Just as through both dreaming and waking, so there is no liberation for the person through both the illusory and the non-illusory. (26)

Just as a single human purpose cannot be accomplished through the mutual cooperation of dream-objects and waking objects—whether they be illusory or non-illusory—so too, when both illusory and non-illusory actions and knowledge are performed, liberation for the person is not tenable; this is the meaning. "Illusory-ness" (māyikatva) means unreality, that is to say, instability; and this exists in the case of dream-objects. However, a waking object is indeed real in comparison to a dream-object.

Because it is unstable and therefore unreal when compared to the immutable Puruṣa, the dream state is distinct from [waking] activities such as bathing; likewise, action (karman) is illusory (māyika) due to its instability and because it is an effect of Prakṛti. The Self (Ātman), however, is non-illusory because of its stability and because it is not an effect. Therefore, only that which is non-eternal is properly an effect. || 26 ||

[Objection: "But even so, since that which is to be meditated upon is not illusory (*amāyika*), there would still be the possibility of either a combination (*samuccaya*) or an option (*vikalpa*) between the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) and the knowledge consisting in the meditation on the Self (*ātmopāsanā*). To this, he says:
"And for the other [knowledge], there is no absolute [certainty]."

Even for the other object of worship, there is no absolute absence of illusoriness (*māyikatva*). The meaning is that this is because objects superimposed upon the self of the object of worship are also included therein.
He states in which respect the worship is illusory: "The same applies even to that which is mentally constructed. (28)

"In that which is mentally conceived"—that is, in the aspect of the object of meditation (*dhyeya*)—even so, the meaning is "it is also illusory" (*māyikatva*). For in the object of worship described in such scriptural passages as "All this, indeed, is Brahman," the phenomenal aspect (*prapañca-aṃśa*) is precisely illusory. || 28 ||
Then, in response to the inquiry as to what the fruit of meditation is, he says:
"Through the accumulation of cultivation, for the pure one, everything is as in the case of primordial nature. (29)

The meaning is that through the perfection of the worship known as *bhāvanā*, all sovereignty arises for the person who is purified and free from sin, just as it does for *prakṛti*. Just as *prakṛti* performs creation, maintenance, and dissolution, so too the *buddhisattva* (the pure intellect) of the practitioner becomes the agent of creation and so forth through the impulsion of *prakṛti*. || 29 ||
It has been established that knowledge alone is the means to liberation. Now, he states the means for attaining knowledge: "The destruction of passion is meditation. (30)

The meaning is that meditation (*dhyāna*) is the cause of the destruction of that coloring of the mind by objects which acts as an obstacle to knowledge. This is a designation of identity between cause and effect used figuratively, because the destruction of passion cannot itself be meditation. Here, by the word "meditation," one should understand the three stages mentioned in Yoga—concentration (*dhāraṇā*), meditation (*dhyāna*), and absorption (*samādhi*)—since it is heard in the Pātañjala [Yoga-sūtras] that these eight limbs of yoga alone are the causes for the direct realization of discrimination (*viveka*). The specific internal distinctions among these should be sought in that very [text]. And he himself will explain the other five limbs later. (30)

With the intention that the arising of knowledge occurs only through the perfection of meditation and not by its mere commencement, he states the definition of the perfection of meditation: "Its accomplishment results from the cessation of mental fluctuations. (31)

The meaning is that through *samprajñāta-yoga*, which consists of the cessation of mental fluctuations other than those directed toward the object of meditation (*dhyeya*), the perfection of meditation occurs in the form of being endowed with the fruit called knowledge. Therefore, the intention is that meditation must be practiced until that point is reached.

It should also be understood that yoga is a cause for knowledge, just like meditation (*dhyāna*) and other limbs of yoga; for it is held that when other mental activities are ceased, the direct realization of the object of meditation occurs due to the removal of the obstacle known as the wandering toward other objects. This is understood from such scriptural and traditional texts (*śruti-smṛti*) as: "Having realized the Divine through the attainment of internal yoga, the wise man leaves behind both joy and sorrow. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.12) || 31 ||
He also states the means for achieving meditative absorption (dhyāna): "Its accomplishment is through concentration (dhāraṇā), postures (āsana), and one's own duty (svakarma). (32)
The meaning is that meditation (dhyāna) arises through the triad of concentration (dhāraṇā) and the others, which will be described hereafter. 32.
He defines the triad beginning with *dhāraṇā* (concentration) in succession by means of three aphorisms: "Cessation [of breath] occurs through vomiting and retention. (33)

The term "of breath" (prāṇasya) is understood through common usage, since the author of the commentary on the *Yogasūtra* has explained *prāṇāyāma* as "either by means of exhalation (*pracchardana*) and retention (*vidhāraṇa*) of breath. Here, *chardi* means vomiting; *vidhāraṇa* means restraint, which is to say, cessation. By this, inhalation (*pūraka*) and exhalation (*recaka*) are obtained. Furthermore, *vidhāraṇa* refers to *kumbhaka* (retention). Thus, the meaning is that it is the common method for the restraint or mastery of breath through inhalation, exhalation, and retention.

Since the actions of sitting and [posture] are to be indicated later by their own specific terms, they remain unmentioned in the Sūtra; thus, because Dhāraṇā alone is obtained as the object of definition, the word "Dhāraṇā" was not included [in the definition of Yoga]. It has been stated that the concentration (dhāraṇā) of the mind is already grasped by the very term "Dhyāna," just like Samādhi. || 33 ||
He defines the seat (āsana), which follows in the sequence:
"The seat is that which is firm and pleasant. (34)
The meaning is that *āsana* refers to that which, being stable, becomes a means for attaining happiness, such as the *svastika* posture and others. 34.
He defines one's own duty:
"One's own duty" is the performance of the duties prescribed for one's own stage of life (āśrama). || 35 ||

This is easy to understand. In this context, by the word *sarma* (comfort/well-being), the restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are included. Furthermore, withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*), which consists of the mastery of the senses, should also be incorporated among the duties because it is common to all stages of life (*āśrama*). Thus, the eight limbs of yoga taught in the Patañjala Sūtra as means to knowledge are also found here. As that Sūtra states: "The eight limbs are restraint, observance, posture, breath-control, withdrawal, concentration, meditation, and absorption. Their specific definitions should be sought in that very [text].

For one who possesses primary qualification, there is no requirement for the five external limbs beginning with *yama*; rather, the established doctrine of Patañjali is that knowledge and yoga arise from *saṃyama* alone—consisting solely of the triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*. This is also observed in the cases of Jaḍabharata and others. Therefore, following that tradition, the Teacher also says:
"From dispassion and from practice. (36)

The meaning is that for those of the highest qualification, knowledge and its means—yoga—arise from the practice of meditation alone when accompanied by dispassion (*vairāgya*). This has also been stated in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Procedures regarding postures and locations do not accomplish yoga;
all such elaborations are proclaimed to cause delay."
Śiśupāla attained perfection through the weight of his practice in constant remembrance. Thus it is said.

Alternatively, detachment (*vairāgya*) and the practice of meditation (*dhyānābhyāsa*) are stated here as the causes of meditation itself; the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include concentration (*dhāraṇā*). Thus, liberation through knowledge has been explained. || 36 ||
Beyond this, it was stated that "bondage [arises] from error"; thus, error, which is the cause of bondage, will now be explained. First, he states the essential nature of error:
"The varieties of error are five" (Kārikā 37).

Ignorance (*avidyā*), egoism (*asmitā*), attachment (*rāga*), aversion (*dveṣa*), and the clinging to life (*abhiniveśa*)—these five, as stated in Yoga, are the sub-varieties of error (*viparyaya*), which is the cause of bondage. Therefore, there is no deficiency even if errors consisting of the cognition of mother-of-pearl and the like are not included therein. Among these, ignorance is defined in Yoga as the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self. Likewise, egoism is the notion of identity between the self and the non-self, taking the form that "there is no self distinct from the body and so forth. Ignorance, however, is not of this specific form.

Even though the self possesses both embodied and disembodied forms, the notion of "I" (ahaṃbuddhi) is possible only with respect to the body. Attachment and aversion are well-known. Clinging (abhiniveśa) is the fear of death and so forth.
Because attachment and the others are effects of error (viparyaya), they themselves possess the nature of error. || 37 ||
Having stated the nature of error, he now states the nature of its cause, incapacity:
"Incapacity, however, is of twenty-eight kinds. (38)
This is easy to understand. This too has been explained by the following verse:
"The destruction of the eleven organs, together with the destruction of the intellect, is designated as incapacity (*aśakti*).
There are seventeen such destructions of the intellect, resulting from the inversion of contentment (*tuṣṭi*) and attainment (*siddhi*). Thus [it is said].
Deafness, leprosy, blindness, dullness, loss of smell, as well as muteness,
lameness, crippledness, impotence, upward movement of wind (udāvarta), and stupidity.

Thus, there are eleven incapacities (*aśakti*) belonging to the eleven organs, and seventeen capacities belonging to the intellect (*buddhi*) itself. The meaning is that just as there are nine obstructions to the nine contentments (*tuṣṭi*) to be described hereafter, so too there are twenty-eight incapacities of the intellect to be described. The word "but" (*tu*) is intended to indicate the specific distinction between these [incapacities] and [the other categories]. He states in two aphorisms those contentments and perfections (*siddhi*), upon the obstruction of which the incapacities of the intellect arise: "Contentment is ninefold. (39)
He himself will explain the state of the nine elements. || 39 ||
The accomplishments (siddhis) are eightfold. 40.
He himself will also state this later. || 40 ||
In order to investigate the specific distinctions among the aforementioned opposites—namely incapacity (aśakti), contentment (tuṣṭi), and attainment (siddhi)—four aphorisms proceed in succession:
"The intermediate subdivisions are as before" (YS 3.41).

The intermediate subdivisions of the misconceptions (*viparyaya*), which were stated generally as five, are to be understood exactly as they were previously described by the ancient masters (*pūrvācāryas*) without further distinction; the meaning is that they are not stated here for fear of prolixity. Furthermore, those [factors] beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*) have been explained by me also only in their general sense as five; specifically, however, there are sixty-two varieties. As it is said in the *Kārikā*:
"The division of delusion (*moha*) is eightfold, great delusion (*mahāmoha*) is tenfold;
likewise, darkness (*tāmisra*) is eighteenfold, and so too is blinding darkness (*andhatāmisra*)."

This is its meaning: ignorance (*avidyā*) is eightfold, consisting of the notion of self (*ātmabuddhi*) with respect to the eight non-self *prakṛtis*—namely, the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*). The notion of self regarding the purely evolved (*vikṛti*) principles is also included here by virtue of the non-difference between cause and effect. Thus, because ignorance is eightfold according to the distinction of its objects, the delusion called "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*), which has the same objects, is also eightfold.

Because there are ten objects—sound and the rest—divided into divine and non-divine, the great delusion (mahāmoha) called attachment (*rāga*) directed toward them is tenfold. Ignorance (*avidyā*) and egoism (*asmitā*) have eight objects, while hatred (*dveṣa*) called darkness (*tāmisra*) is eighteenfold, being directed toward the eighteen things that obstruct those [other] ten objects of attachment. Likewise, the fear called the "darkness of darkness" (*andhatāmisra*), which is the clinging (*abhiniveśa*), is eighteenfold, arising from the perception of the destruction of those eighteen [objects]. And they bear the names "darkness" (*tamaḥ*) and so forth because they are the causes of those [states]. 41.
The same applies to the other [vow]. || 42 ||
Thus the Sūtra has been explained by means of the Kārikā:
"The internal [contentments] are four, known as Nature, Means, Time, and Fortune;
the external are five, due to the cessation of objects; thus nine contentments have been declared."

This is its meaning: the four internal contentments (*ādhyātmikī tuṣṭi*) are so called because they function with reference to the aggregate (the body) of one who possesses contentment regarding the Self. Among them, the contentment called "Nature" (*prakṛti*) is as follows: "Every transformation, up to and including direct realization, belongs to Nature alone; Nature alone performs that, and Nature alone effects it, while I am immutable and complete."

Thus, satisfaction arising from the cultivation of one's own self is called *tuṣṭi* (satisfaction) and is designated as *ambhas* (water). Furthermore, the satisfaction derived from undertaking the life of renunciation (*pravrajyā*) is called *upādāna* (acquisition) and is designated as *salila* (fluid). Next, the satisfaction resulting from the long-term practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) within that state of renunciation is called *kāla* (time) and is designated as *ogha* (flood). Finally, when the *dharmamegha-samādhi*—the cloud of dharma—is reached, which constitutes the ultimate pinnacle of wisdom, the satisfaction therein is called *bhāgya* (fortune) and is designated as *vṛṣṭi* (rain). These are the four internal forms of satisfaction.

The five external contentments arise from the cessation of the defects—such as acquisition, preservation, loss, enjoyment, and injury—with respect to the five external objects, beginning with sound. These contentments are designated, respectively, as *pāra*, *supāra*, *pārapāra*, *anuttamāmbhas*, and *uttamāmbhas*. However, someone has explained this verse in another way, as follows:

The contentment that arises from the view that "even the direct realization of discrimination (*viveka-sākṣātkāra*) is merely a transformation of primordial nature (*prakṛti*); therefore, enough with the practice of meditation" is called *prakṛti*. The contentment that thinks, "Liberation will come simply by adopting the life of a wandering mendicant; what is the use of meditation and the like? is called *upādāna*. The contentment that thinks, "Even for one who has performed renunciation, liberation will occur in due time; enough with this agitation," is called *kāla*. [And the contentment that thinks] "Liberation will come through destiny alone."

"The satisfaction derived from such fallacious reasoning, rather than from the means taught in the scriptures of liberation, is called 'luck' (bhāgya)," and so forth—this is the meaning [of the opponent's view]. That is not correct; for it is inappropriate to designate that absence of the satisfactions explained therein as "lack of capacity" (aśakti), since its nature is conducive to knowledge and the other [means of liberation]. || 43 ||
Success is achieved through the *ūha* and other [subsidiary sciences]. || 44 ||
The meaning is that perfection (siddhi) occurs in eight ways through reasoning (ūha) and the other [means]. This sūtra has also been explained by the following verse:

"Reasoning (ūha), oral instruction (śabda), study (adhyayana), the three types of removal of suffering (duḥkhavighāta), acquisition of friends (suhṛtprāpti), and generosity (dāna)—these are the eight perfections. The former three are the threefold goad (aṅkuśa) for perfection. Thus.

This is its meaning: here, because they are the opposites of the threefold suffering—internal and so forth—the three "destructions of suffering" (*duḥkhavighāta*) are the primary accomplishments (*siddhi*). The others, however, are secondary accomplishments because they are the means to those [primary ones]. Among them, *ūha* (reasoning) is as follows: the independent inference of a truth by oneself, even without instruction and the like, due to the force of practice from a previous birth. *Śabda* (verbal testimony) is as follows: that knowledge which arises either by hearing the recitation of another or by personally studying the scriptures. And *adhyayana* (study) is as follows: [the study of the Vedas].

Knowledge arises from studying the scriptures through the relationship of disciple and teacher. As for "attaining a friend": it is the acquisition of knowledge from one who has come to one's home out of supreme compassion for the sake of giving instruction. And as for "giving": it is the acquisition of knowledge from one who is fully satisfied by the gift of wealth and so forth. Among these, the first three—consisting of reasoning (*ūha*), verbal testimony (*śabda*), and study (*adhyayana*)—are the hooks that pull forth the primary accomplishment. This [latter] statement was made in order to demonstrate that attaining a friend and giving are weaker means when compared to the triad beginning with reasoning.

However, some explain that there is a "goad" for these eight perfections—a restrainer—which consists of the three previously mentioned forms of error, incapacity, and contentment, because they act as bondages; but that is not correct. For since the absence of contentment is itself a form of incapacity, like deafness and so forth, it follows that it is an adversary to perfection; thus, it is impossible for both contentment and its opposite (discontent) to be adversaries to perfection simultaneously. || 44 ||

But how can it be said that perfection is achieved through *uḍḍīyāna* and the other [bandhas] alone? For it is established in all the scriptures that the eight perfections, such as *aṇimā*, are attained through mantras, austerity, meditative absorption (*samādhi*), and so forth. To this he replies:
"Not without the abandonment of what is derived from other [means]. (45)

The accomplishment of asceticism (*tapas*) and the like—distinct from the five beginning with the removal of the other—is not ultimate. Why? Because it occurs without the removal of the other. Since that accomplishment arises even without the removal of its opposite, it does not stand as an obstacle to *saṃsāra*; therefore, that accomplishment is merely a result of practice, but not an ultimate accomplishment. Thus it has been stated in the *Yoga-sūtra*: "These are obstacles in *samādhi*, but accomplishments in the state of emergence (*vyutthāna*)."

Thus, beginning with the statement "liberation comes from knowledge," the evolution of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which consists of its various qualities (*guṇas*)—has been explained in detail along with its bondage consisting of effects, together with the human goal that is liberation. These two evolutions, consisting of the intellect and its qualities, exist in the form of a continuous flow as mutual causes, like a seed and its sprout. Accordingly, the *Kārikā* states: "Without the objective entities (*bhāvas*), there is no subtle body (*liṅga*); without the subtle body, there is no manifestation of objective entities. Therefore, the two-fold evolution proceeds: that called the subtle body and that called the objective entities."

The "existent" (bhāva) consists of the intellect (buddhi) in the form of latent impressions (vāsanā), characterized by qualities such as knowledge; this is the Great Principle (mahat-tattva), which is the intellect. Thus, the collective creation (samaṣṭi-sarga) and the creation of cognition (pratyaya-sarga) are completed. || 45 ||

Now, it has been stated in brief that the differentiation of individual beings arises from specific karma; thus, the creation of the individual (vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi) is set forth in detail according to its divisions, beginning with the divine (daiva) and so forth. 46.
The remainder of the sentence is "creation is such," meaning that its intermediate divisions consist of the divine and so forth. This very point has been explained by the *kārikā*:
"The divine creation is of eight varieties, the animal creation is fivefold, and the human is of one kind; thus, in brief, is the elemental creation."

The divine creation is of eight kinds: Brāhma, Prājāpatya, Aindra, Paitra, Gāndharva, Yākṣa, Rākṣasa, and Paiśāca. The animal creation is of five kinds: domestic animals, wild beasts, birds, reptiles, and immobile beings. The human creation is of one kind. This refers to the elemental creation—the creation of individual living beings from Virāj. (46)
He states that even the intermediate creation which has been described serves the purpose of the Puruṣa:
"From Brahmā down to a blade of grass, creation exists for his sake until the dawn of discrimination. (47)

Beginning from the four-faced Brahmā down to the stationary beings, even the individual creation (vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi) serves the purpose of the person (puruṣārtha), just like the cosmic creation (virāṭ-sṛṣṭi); that is to say, until the discriminative discernment (viveka-khyāti) of those respective persons is attained. 47.
He also describes the division within the individual creation (vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi) by means of three aphorisms:
"Above, it is vast with sattva" (48).
The meaning is that above the Bhūrloka, the creation becomes characterized by a predominance of *sattva*. || 48 ||
It is vast with darkness from its very root. || 49 ||
The meaning is: "from the very base," that is, from the world of earth (bhūrloka) downwards. || 49 ||
In the middle is Rajoviśālā. || 50 ||
The meaning is "in the middle of the Bhūrloka. || 50 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to what cause accounts for the diverse creations arising from the expansion of the qualities such as *sattva* within that single *prakṛti*, he says:
"Due to the variety of karma, the activity of *pradhāna* is like that of a slave in the womb. (51)

The aforementioned activity of *pradhāna*, which takes the form of the diversity of effects, arises solely from the cause of diverse karma; as for the illustration regarding this diversity, it is like that of a gardener's servant. The meaning is that just as, beginning from the stage of being in the womb, a servant performs various kinds of activities and service for the sake of his master due to the intensity of his latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of servitude, so it is in this case. || 51 ||
Now, one might object: "If there exists a vast creation of beings extending upwards, then since the person's purpose is fulfilled by that alone, what is the need for liberation? To this, he says:
"Even there, because of the application to ever-higher births, it must be abandoned. (52)

Even there, although there is upward movement, there is still a return; because of the application to ever-higher births, there is descent to lower births. The meaning is that even that world is to be abandoned. || 52 ||
The suffering arising from old age, death, and so forth is common to all. || 53 ||

Furthermore, for all beings from Brahmā down to the stationary objects, who move between higher and lower states, the suffering born of old age, death, and so forth is common; for this reason also, [suffering] is to be abandoned—this is the meaning. 53.
What more need be said? He states that even through dissolution into the cause, one has not yet achieved the goal:
"One does not achieve the goal by dissolving into the cause, just as [a diver] does not [achieve his purpose] by emerging from the water. (54)

When, in the absence of discriminative knowledge (*viveka-jñāna*), dispassion toward the principles beginning with Mahat arises through the practice of meditation on *prakṛti*, then dissolution into *prakṛti* occurs, according to the statement: "From dispassion comes dissolution into *prakṛti*. Therefore, even from dissolution into the cause, there is no fulfillment of one's purpose, because [the soul] rises again like one who has dived. Just as a person submerged in water emerges once more, even so those persons dissolved in *prakṛti* reappear by virtue of their status as the Lord (*īśvara-bhāva*). The meaning is that since the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) and so forth have not been destroyed, there is no burning away of defects; thus, without discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*), a future manifestation is inevitable. || 54 ||
[Objection: Surely no cause is itself caused by anything; therefore, being independent, how can it bring about for one who is asleep the rising that is the source of suffering? To this, he says:
"Even though it is not caused, its connection [to the result] occurs due to dependence on another. (55)

Even though *prakṛti* is not an effect, is not impelled, and is not dependent on the will of another, there is its "conjunction"—namely, the fitness for re-emergence of that which has dissolved [into it]. Why? Because of its dependence; that is, because it is subject to the purpose of the *puruṣa*. The meaning is that by the power of the *puruṣa*'s purpose, which consists in discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), *prakṛti* causes that which had dissolved into her to emerge again. Furthermore, the purposes of the *puruṣa* and so forth are not the actual impellers of *prakṛti*; rather, they are merely the instrumental causes for the activity of *prakṛti*, whose nature is to be active. Thus, there is no loss of her independence.

And likewise, the *Yogasūtra* states: "The efficient cause is not the motivator of the primal natures (*prakṛtis*); rather, it is the removal of their obstruction, like a farmer. Here, "removal of obstruction" means the cessation of hindrances. (55)
He also states the proof for the emergence of the Puruṣa from dissolution into Prakṛti:
"For he is all-knowing and the doer of all. (56)

For he, having been dissolved into the causal state during the previous creation, becomes in another creation the omniscient, all-creating Lord, the Primordial Person (Ādipuruṣa), because it is appropriate that he alone attains the state of Prakṛti upon the dissolution of Prakṛti. This is the meaning based on such scriptural passages as, "Attached, together with his karma," and, "Wherein his subtle body (liṅga) and mind are cast. || 56 ||
If it is objected that, in this way, the refutation of God is untenable, he says in response: "The proof of such a God is established. (57)

The proof of the Lord who is produced from primordial nature (*prakṛtilīna*) is indeed established for all, based on such scriptural passages as, "He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving, whose austerity consists of knowledge. The meaning is that only the eternal Lord is the subject of dispute. Having explained these two sūtras, he also establishes [the Lord's] dependence through the sūtra beginning with "sa hi" (for he...). For that Supreme One is the commonality of the Puruṣas, possessing the power of omniscience and the power of being the agent of all.

The meaning is that it acts as an impeller by its mere proximity, like a magnet. And in that case, because the purpose is not yet completed due to the proximity of the Puruṣa, the activity of Prakṛti—even though it is independent of any desire for that purpose—is necessary.

Indeed, if this were so, there would be a contradiction with the refutation of God; to this he replies: "The proof of such a God is established. The meaning is that the proof of God's existence by His mere presence is universally accepted in the Śruti and Smṛti.
A person the size of a thumb dwells in the center of the self;
he is the lord of what has been and what is to be, and from him the pervasive one does not transcend.
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) creates all the qualities (guṇas) and observes them;
yet the Lord (īśvara), remaining like a neutral witness, is not transformed by those qualities.
And such scriptural and traditional texts as these are the means of valid knowledge regarding such a Lord. || 57 ||

Beginning from the first sūtra of the second chapter up to this point, the primary creation (*pradhāna-sṛṣṭi*) has been completed through the arrangement of aphorisms. Hereafter, for the sake of establishing liberation, the absolute cessation of the primary creation with respect to the liberated person—the so-called "absolute dissolution" (*atyantalayā*)—must be explained. To establish that, he first demonstrates in detail the purpose of the primary creation, which was stated only in brief in the initial sūtra of the second chapter:
"The primary creation is for the sake of another (the Spirit), because, though it exists by itself, it is not an enjoyer, like a camel carrying saffron. (SK 58)

Although the creation of Pradhāna proceeds from itself alone, it is nevertheless for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of the experience and liberation of another. It is like a camel carrying saffron for the sake of its master. Why? Because, being non-enjoying and insentient, experience and liberation are impossible for it; this is the meaning. Now, if it is argued that "creation is for its own sake" based on the statement "for the sake of the liberation of the emancipated," that is true. Nevertheless, even the status of being for its own sake is not established without the ultimate purpose being the welfare of the Puruṣa.

For the self-interest of *pradhāna* consists in the liberation of the Self (*ātman*) from the Puruṣa once enjoyment and liberation have been accomplished. Now, one might object: "If *prakṛti* is like a servant, then why does she act even for the sake of the suffering of her master? This is not so; for suffering arises as an inseparable concomitant of activity directed toward the attainment of pleasure, or because she is like a wicked servant. || 58 ||

But surely, since it is an insentient entity, it is not possible for the "giving" (pradāna) to be a creator by itself, as we observe that chariots and such things function only through the effort of another; to this, he says:
"Even though it is insentient, the activity of the Pradhāna is like that of milk. (59)

"Just as milk transforms itself into the form of curd independently of human effort, so too, despite being insentient, the transformation of the *pradhāna* into the forms of the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest occurs even without the effort of another. This is not redundant with the sūtra "Like a cow for its calf" (Sāṅkhya Kārikā 7), because in that case the activity of the instruments alone was examined, and cows are sentient beings. || 59 ||
He states the reason for the point already explained by first presenting another illustration:
"Or, because time and so forth are perceived like karma. (60)

The activity of time and so forth is established either as being like an object (*karman*) or as being primary in itself, because it is observed [to be so]. Now, regarding the statement "one goes": here the intended meaning is this—just as the six seasons, such as spring and summer, are described in the scriptures in accordance with the specific movements of the single sun, yet the sun alone is the cause of everything.

This very point is clearly established in the *Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa*, and the scriptural passage (*śruti*) is as follows: "The sun, indeed, is all the seasons: when it rises, that is spring; when it is the time of the cows returning (*saṅgava*), then it is summer; when it is midday, then it is the rainy season; when it is afternoon, then it is winter and the cool season. The meaning is that just as another season proceeds and so forth, such actions pertaining to time and so on occur spontaneously; in the same way, this would also apply to the Pradhāna, because conceptualization must follow what is observed.

[Objection: Even so, since there is an absence of the recognition "this is my means for enjoyment and so forth," there would never be any activity on the part of Prakṛti, who is [otherwise] deluded, or at least her activity would be contrary [to the goal]. To this, he says:
"And her activity proceeds from her own nature, due to a lack of conscious intention, like a servant. (61)

Just as for a distinguished servant, service to the master proceeds from his very nature and from past impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone—being both specific and necessary—and not with the intention of personal enjoyment; even so, the activity of *prakṛti* proceeds from past impressions alone. This is the meaning. || 61 ||
Or because it is drawn forth by karma. || 62 ||

The word "vā" here signifies conjunction. The meaning is that since karma is beginningless, and because of the attraction exerted by karmas, the activity of *pradhāna* is both necessary and established. || 62 ||

Thus, since it has been established that the primary cause (pradhāna) acts as a creator for the sake of another, liberation is accomplished through the cessation of the primary cause by its own accord once the purpose of the other has been fulfilled. He states this in the following section:
"From the realization of [its] distinction [from Puruṣa], there is the cessation of the primary cause's creation, just as the activity of a cook ceases upon the completion of the cooking. (63)

Through the knowledge of the isolated Puruṣa, when the purpose of the Puruṣa is accomplished by means of supreme detachment, the creation of Pradhāna ceases. The meaning is that just as the activity of fire ceases once cooking is complete, so too does this process stop; this very state is called ultimate dissolution (*atyantika-pralaya*). And thus says the Śruti: "From meditating upon Him, from union with Him, and from the realization of His true nature, there follows at the end the cessation of all cosmic illusion (*viśva-māyā*). (63)

But surely, if the creation of Nature were to cease for the sake of producing discriminative knowledge in one person, there would be the undesirable consequence of universal liberation; to this he replies:
"The other [is] like the other, because of that same defect. (Sūtra 64)

The other, however, being devoid of discriminative awakening, remains by its very nature bound, just like the others. Why? Because of that defect. The meaning is: because of that defect of the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) known as the "accomplishment of the purpose of the *puruṣa*" (*puruṣārthasamāpāna*). As it is stated in the *Yogasūtra*: "Though it has ceased with respect to one whose purpose is fulfilled, it has not ceased, because it is common to others."

And thus, the sense is that the cessation of *pradhāna* mentioned in the preceding sūtra occurs only with respect to the isolated *baddha-puruṣa*. The scriptural text regarding "the illusion of the universe" (*viśvamāyā*) should also be understood as referring only to the knower (*jñānin*), because it forms a single syntactical unit with the scriptural text "the unborn" (*ajā*). || 64 ||
He states the result of the cessation of creation: "Liberation is the indifference of either one of the two. (65)

The indifference and solitude of the two—the primary matter (pradhāna) and the spirit (puruṣa)—is what is meant by their mutual separation; that is liberation (apavarga). Alternatively, it is the absolute isolation (kaivalya) of the spirit alone, for the purpose of the spirit is seen to consist solely in the realization: "May I be liberated. || 65 ||

[Objection: Surely, once Nature (prakṛti) has become dispassionate toward a particular person through a mental modification (vṛtti) in the form of discriminative discernment upon that person's liberation, how could she again engage in creation for the sake of another person? Nor should it be argued that there is no fault because Nature possesses distinct parts, for we observe the creation of objects of enjoyment for one person even by means of the earth and other elements that have already served as instruments for a liberated person. To this, he says:
"Even when colored by the creation of others, she does not become dispassionate, just as a snake does not cease to be a snake for one who has recognized the true nature of the rope. (66)

Even though *pradhāna* has become detached from one person due to that person’s discriminative awakening (*viviktabodha*), it does not become detached from creating for any other person; rather, it continues to create for him alone. The meaning is this: just as a snake no longer produces fear and so forth for one who has awakened to the reality of the rope, yet continues to produce them for the deluded person; and the similarity of *pradhāna* to the snake is due to its being superimposed upon the person, who is like the rope.

Failing to understand the intended meaning of such examples as the rope-snake and others, certain ignorant persons who merely claim to be Vedāntins weigh the primordial nature (prakṛti) as being either utterly non-existent or mere mind. By this [verse], the meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti should be understood through the example cited by the Sāṅkhya proponents of the reality of prakṛti; for this matter is not established by the mere existence of an example. || 66 ||
And because of the connection with the causes of karma. || 67 ||
The meaning is that even due to the connection with that karma which is the cause for creation, [the Lord] creates for the sake of another person's purpose. || 67 ||

Now, an objection is raised: since all *puruṣas* are equally indifferent and lack any desire, there being no distinction in their independence, what is the determining factor for the *pradhāna* to proceed toward one particular *puruṣa* and desist from another? Nor can karma be the determining factor, because there is no means of determining which karma belongs to which *puruṣa*. To this, the author replies:
"In the case of indifference, non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is the cause for the service of *prakṛti*. (68)

The meaning is that when there is no independence among persons—that is, due to the lack of discrimination such as "this one is my master" or "this one is indeed I"—Prakṛti assists the Puruṣas through creation and so forth. Thus, the intention is that the regulator is simply this: Pradhāna proceeds toward that Puruṣa for whom a latent impression (*vāsanā*) exists to manifest itself without having been discriminated from him. || 68 ||
Since its very nature is active engagement, how can cessation be possible even when there is discernment? To this he says:
"Like a dancer, even for one who has engaged in activity, there is cessation because the purpose has been fulfilled. (69)

The inherent nature of the activity of *pradhāna* is solely for the sake of the *puruṣārtha* (the purpose of the Spirit), and not in a general sense. Therefore, even though *pradhāna* has begun its activity, its cessation is logical once the purpose of the *puruṣa* is accomplished and it has attained its goal. This means that just as a dancer who has begun performing for an audience ceases her performance once that task is fulfilled. || 69 ||
He states another reason for its cessation:
"Even when defects are recognized, there is no further approach by the Pradhāna, just like a virtuous wife. (70)

Due to her perception of defects such as being subject to transformation and having suffering as her very nature, Prakṛti does not approach the Puruṣa again, just like a woman of good family (*kulavadhū*). The meaning is that just as a woman of good family, feeling ashamed because she has been judged at fault by her husband, does not approach him again, so it is here. As it is said in the *Nāradīya*:
"Though she was full of modifications and had long enjoyed [him] through her delusion in the form of the *guṇas*, this Prakṛti, once her faults have been known, withdraws as if out of shame."
This very point has also been stated in a verse:
"It is my conviction that there is nothing more delicate than Nature (prakṛti), which, once seen [by the Puruṣa] thinking 'I have been seen,' does not again come into the sight of the Puruṣa. (70)

Now, if the activity of primordial matter (pradhāna) is for the sake of the person’s purpose, then it follows that through bondage and liberation the person would undergo transformation; to this he replies:
"Bondage and liberation do not belong to the person in an absolute sense, except through non-discrimination. (71)

Bondage and liberation, consisting of union with and separation from suffering, do not belong to the person (puruṣa) absolutely in reality; rather, the meaning is that they arise solely from non-discrimination (aviveka), in the manner that will be explained in the fourth aphorism. || 71 ||

But from the perspective of ultimate truth, it is said that both bondage and liberation belong to *prakṛti* alone: "Because of its directness and because of its state of being associated [with the Puruṣa], like a beast. (72)

In reality, bondage and liberation from suffering belong to *prakṛti* alone, because it is characterized by attachment and is smeared by *dharma* and other factors that are the means to suffering. The meaning is that just as an animal undergoes bondage and liberation through being smeared by a rope, so it is with *prakṛti*. This has been stated in the *Kārikā*:
"Therefore, the *puruṣa* is certainly not bound, nor is he liberated, nor does he transmigrate;
it is *prakṛti*, which has various supports, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated."

And as for the liberation of the Puruṣa mentioned in the Sūtra, "Liberation is the indifference of one or the other of the two," that is simply the separation from false suffering in the form of a reflection. || 62 ||
In this regard, in response to the inquiry as to by what means there is bondage and by what there is liberation, he says:
"Pradhāna binds itself through seven forms, like a silkworm; it liberates itself through a single form. (73)

By means of these seven forms—dharma, vairāgya, aiśvarya, adharma, ajñāna, avairāgya, and anaiśvarya—which are the causes of suffering, *prakṛti* binds itself with suffering, just like a silkworm. Just as the activity of a silkworm binds itself with its own constructed dwelling, so it is here. And it is that very same *prakṛti* which, through knowledge alone of a single form, liberates itself from suffering; this is the meaning. || 73 ||

As for what was stated—that bondage and liberation result from non-discrimination—that is incorrect, because non-discrimination is neither to be abandoned nor to be adopted. This is because, in the world, suffering and its absence (such as happiness) are inherently to be avoided or sought; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with observed experience. Anticipating this objection, he himself explains what was stated in the fourth sūtra:
"Non-discrimination is merely the instrumental cause [of bondage]; there is no contradiction with observed experience. (74)

The meaning is that it was previously stated that non-discrimination (*aviveka*) alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for persons, but that non-discrimination itself is not those two states; therefore, there is no contradiction with what is observed. This is clear in the sūtras of the first chapter:

"The conjunction of Nature (*prakṛti*) and Spirit (*puruṣa*) is caused by non-discrimination. And from that conjunction, the reflection of the primordial suffering (*prākṛtaduḥkha*) arising within the Spirit is what constitutes the experience of suffering—that is, the connection with suffering. The cessation of that [connection] alone is the purpose of the Spirit known as liberation (*mokṣa*). || 74 ||

Thus, it has been explained in detail across two chapters that all transformations, from the initial creation until ultimate dissolution, belong solely to the *pradhāna* and its evolutes; the *puruṣa*, however, is merely pure consciousness, like a spectator on the sidelines. Regarding the means for achieving this discrimination (*viveka*), he states the essential practice:
"The perfection of discrimination arises from the practice of the principles through the renunciation [of them] as 'not this, not this. (75)

The perfection of discrimination arises from the practice of reality (*tattvābhyāsa*) consisting in the relinquishment of the conceit [of agency] regarding all insentient things up to primordial nature (*prakṛti*), by means of the formula "not this, not this" (*neti neti*). Everything else is merely an auxiliary (*aṅga*) to that practice; for such is the meaning. And thus says the Śruti: "Now, therefore, the instruction is 'not this, not this. For there is nothing else higher than this 'not this. This Self is 'not this, not this,'" and so forth.

"When this transformation, beginning with the unmanifest (avyakta) and ending with the non-specific (aviśeṣa), has been described, knowledge is said to consist in the discernment of the difference between the conscious and the unconscious. Thus [it is said].
For example:
"This body is a pillar of bones bound together by sinews, plastered with flesh and blood,
covered with skin, a foul-smelling abyss filled with filth, an abode of disease, and miserable."
"One should abandon this abode of the elements, which is full of passion and impurity, just as a tree leaves a river-pile or as a bird leaves a tree;
thus, by abandoning this body, one is released from the crocodile of suffering. Thus it is said.
This very point has also been stated in a verse:
"Thus, from the practice of the principles, there arises the complete knowledge—'I am not,' 'nothing is mine,' 'I do not exist'—which is pure and free from error, being absolute. Thus it is said.

The negation of agency does not apply to this Self; "not mine" is the negation of attachment; "not I" is the negation of identity. "Kevalam" (alone) is explained as "pure because free from error. Thus, the meaning is that it is not corrupted by error in the interim. This very state of being "alone" is expressed by the word "siddhi" (accomplishment) in the Sūtra. By the Yoga Sūtra, "The means of abandonment is discriminative knowledge that is uncorrupted," it is established that such knowledge alone is the cause of liberation. || 75 ||
He states a specific point regarding the attainment of discernment:
"There is no fixed rule because of the different types of qualified aspirants. (76)

The meaning is that because there exist differences among practitioners such as the dull-witted (*manda*) and others, there is no fixed rule that the perfection of discrimination (*viveka*) will occur in this very birth even when practice is being performed. Therefore, the intention is that one should strive to attain the highest level of qualification through proficiency in practice. || 76 ||
He says that liberation occurs only through the perfection of discernment (*viveka*), and not otherwise:
"Through the persistence of what has been sublated, there is still enjoyment even from intermediate discernment. (77)

The meaning is this: after the direct realization of the Self (*ātma-sākṣātkāra*) through the yoga of once-and-for-all discriminative awareness (*sakṛt-samprajñāta-yoga*), one remains in a state of middling discrimination (*madhya-viveka*). Even while in that middling discrimination, although suffering and other afflictions have been sublated, they continue to persist in the form of reflections within the Puruṣa due to the force of *prārabdha* (commenced karma); thus, experience (*bhoga*) still occurs. Furthermore, the perfection of discrimination arises only from non-discursive concentration (*asamprajñāta*) which prevents re-arising; therefore, it is stated "from middling discrimination" (*madhya-vivekataḥ*) to demonstrate that when that [perfection] exists, there is no more experience. The distinction is that "weak discrimination" (*manda-viveka*), however, consists merely of hearing, reflection, and meditation prior to direct realization. (77)
And he is liberated while living. || 78 ||
The meaning is that even one who is liberated while living remains in a state of intermediate discernment. || 78 ||
He states the proof for one who is liberated while living (jīvanmukta): "Its establishment [is known] from the fact of being the teacher and the taught. (79)

The meaning is that the attainment of liberation while living (jīvanmukti-siddhi) occurs because the relationship between teacher and disciple is heard of in the scriptures regarding the subject of discrimination (viveka);
for it is only one who is liberated while living who can possibly function as a teacher. || 79 ||
And there is also scriptural authority. || 80 ||
And there is scriptural authority regarding the one liberated while living:
"By initiation alone a man may be liberated; though liberated, he may remain in the body.
Like a pot situated in the middle of a potter’s wheel, it continues to spin even after the impulse has ceased."
"Being Brahman, he merges into Brahman," and so forth. The Nāradīya-smṛti also states:
"By the power of previous practice, neither worldly nor Vedic duties are performed;
free from merit and demerit, the universal self is called one liberated while living. (80)
But would not the status of a teacher be established even by mere hearing? To this he says:
"Otherwise, there would be a succession of the blind. (81)

Otherwise, if even one of dull discernment were to act as a teacher, there would result a succession of the blind; this is the meaning. If one were to teach without knowing the reality of the Self through the totality [of means], one might, due to one's own delusion regarding some part, cause the disciple to fall into error as well. He too would teach another, and he another—thus proceeds the succession of the blind. || 81 ||
Now, one might ask: "If karma is destroyed by knowledge, how can there be continued life? To this he replies:
"The body is maintained like the spinning of a potter's wheel. (82)

Even when the potter's work has ceased, the wheel continues to spin by itself for some time due to the momentum of its prior motion; likewise, even though no new karma arises after the attainment of knowledge, the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta) remains, sustaining the body as it moves under the force of previously commenced karma (prārabdha-karma). This is the meaning. || 82 ||

[Objection: But surely, when the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of enjoyment and so forth have been destroyed by means of *samprajñāta-yoga*, which has knowledge as its cause, how can the maintenance of the body be explained? Nor should it be asked: "If yoga possesses the power to suppress mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), what need is there for [the practice of] silence (*mauna*)? For this is established from the *Yogasūtra*: "The suppression-transformation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*) consists in the sequence of the mind characterized by suppression, wherein the impressions of emergence (*vyutthāna*) and suppression alternate between being suppressed and appearing. Furthermore, it is experienced even in the world that a long-standing absorption in one object suppresses the impressions of other objects. To this, he replies: "Its accomplishment is due to a remnant of impressions" (83).

The meaning is that the maintenance of his body is accomplished because only a small remnant of those latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of sense-objects—which serve as the causes for maintaining the body—remains. In this regard, the existence of even a trace of the latent impression of ignorance (*avidyā*) is not required; for ignorance is a cause only for the initiation of the ripening of karma in the form of birth and so forth, as explained by Vyāsa in the *Yogabhāṣya*, and according to the maxim: "Because birth is not observed in one who is free from passion. This does not apply, however, to the experience of karma whose fruit has already begun (*prārabdhaphala*).

Furthermore, that specific kind of effort constituting experience (*bhoga*), which necessarily depends upon ignorance (*avidyā*), exists only among the deluded; it has been stated previously that for those liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), there is merely a semblance of experience. As for the claim made by some that even a trace of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of ignorance remains in the one liberated while living—that is not so. For it would entail the production of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), it would result in a blind tradition (*andhaparamparā*), and there is no purpose in postulating the existence of a trace of the impressions of ignorance. This has been explained in detail in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā-bhāṣya*. || 83 ||
He summarizes the meaning of the treatise’s statement:
"Through discriminative discernment, when all suffering has ceased without remainder, there is the state of having accomplished all that was to be done;
not otherwise, not otherwise. (84)

From the aforementioned attainment of discriminative discernment (*viveka-siddhi*), by means of supreme dispassion (*para-vairāgya*) and the cessation of all mental fluctuations (*sarva-vṛtti-nirodha*), when all suffering—whether already sublated or not—is completely removed through the commonality of total sublation, at that very moment the *puruṣa* becomes one who has accomplished his purpose (*kṛta-kṛtya*). The meaning is that this does not occur through anything else, such as liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) and so forth. The repetition "not through anything else" (*netarāt... netarāt*) marks the conclusion of the chapter. 84.
The dissolution of the unmanifest (avyakta) must be carried out until its ultimate end, but not that of the Self (ātman).
Thus has been described here this discernment, which is the means for attaining supreme detachment. || 1 ||
Thus ends the third chapter, on Dispassion, in the commentary on the *Sāṅkhya-pravacana* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu. || 3 ||
Now begins the fourth chapter. 4.
Now, the fourth chapter is commenced for the purpose of demonstrating the means for attaining discriminative knowledge by means of collections of stories established in the scriptures;
this is because [the truth] is taught through instruction, like [the case of] the prince. 1.1.1.

The distinction (*viveka*) found in the remainder of the preceding section of the sūtra continues here. The meaning is that discrimination arises from the instruction of reality (*tattvopadeśa*), just as in the case of a prince. In this regard, there is this narrative: A certain prince, having been cast out from the city due to being born under an inauspicious asterism (*gaṇḍarkṣa*), was raised by a certain Śabara and lived thinking, "I am a Śabara. Knowing him to be alive, a certain minister awakened him, saying: "You are not a Śabara; you are a prince."

Just as he immediately abandons the conceit of being a *caṇḍāla* and takes hold of his true royal nature, thinking "I am the king," even so, you—having been born from the Primordial Person who is manifested as pure, perfect Consciousness—are a portion (*aṃśa*) of Him. Through the instruction of a compassionate teacher, you abandon the conceit of *prakṛti* (material nature) and take hold of your own true nature, thinking: "Because I am a son of Brahman, I too am Brahman itself; I am not something different from Him, such as a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārī*). Thus is the meaning. Likewise, in the *Garuḍa Purāṇa*:
"Just as by a single piece of gold, the entire world is seen to be made of gold..."
In the same way, by the birth of the Lord, everything becomes born as well.
Just as a certain twice-born man possessed by a planet thinks, "I am a śūdra," yet upon the departure of the planet, he again recognizes his own true nature as a brāhmaṇa.
"Pervaded by Māyā, the individual soul (jīva) likewise thinks, 'I am the body';
through the destruction of Māyā, it again considers its own true nature: 'I am Brahman. || 1 ||

He shows another narrative for this purpose—that even women, Śūdras, and others may achieve their goal by hearing the instruction of a Brāhmaṇa from a Brāhmaṇa—even when the instruction is intended for someone else, as in the case of the Piśāca: "Even in the case of instruction intended for another, [the goal is achieved], like the Piśāca. (2)

The meaning is that even while Śrī Kṛṣṇa was imparting instruction on the ultimate reality for the sake of Arjuna, the ghost situated at the cremation ground attained discriminative knowledge; thus it may happen for others as well. || 2 ||

And if knowledge does not arise from a single instruction, then repetition of the instruction must also be performed; thus he says by means of another traditional narrative: "Repetition [is required] because of the repeated instruction" (Sūtra 4.1.3).

Instruction should also be repeated; the meaning is that in the Chāndogya and other texts, Āruṇi and others instructed Śvetaketu and others repeatedly, as evidenced by their laughter [at his initial lack of understanding]. || 3 ||
In order to induce dispassion, he demonstrates the fragility and other such qualities of the aggregate of the self by means of an illustration:
"Because both are seen to be like father and son. (4)

The meaning is that through detachment (*vairāgya*), discernment (*viveka*) arises because one's own birth and death are seen and inferred, just like those of one's father and son. As it has been said:
"One's own birth and dissolution are to be inferred from [the examples of] one's father and son. (4)
From this point onward, he demonstrates through the analogies mentioned in the narrative the factors for the perfection of knowledge for one who has arisen from ignorance and become dispassionate:
"Like a hawk, one experiences pleasure and pain through abandonment and separation. (5)

One should not engage in the grasping of objects, because through the renunciation of things one becomes happy, whereas through separation from them one becomes miserable, just like a hawk; this is the meaning. For a hawk possessing meat is made miserable by someone else snatching it away and separating it from that meat. When it relinquishes it of its own accord, then it is freed from suffering. As it has been said: "Other strong birds, being without meat, killed the meat-bearing osprey; having abandoned that meat, he attained happiness."
Likewise, it has been stated by Manu: "Just as a tree leaves the riverbank or a bird leaves a tree, so too one who abandons this body is liberated from the crocodile of distress. (5)

Like a snake casting off its skin; here, by means of both these scriptural passages, [the author] demonstrates the twofold nature of the one who abandons the body at the time of death for a practitioner of Brahman, since the karma of the commenced body is exhausted solely through experience. By the first [passage], he shows that one who awaits the falling of the body dependent upon karma is illustrated by the analogy beginning with "just as [a tree on] a riverbank," and so forth.

And by the second [verse], because of the combination of knowledge and action (*jñānakarmasamuccaya*), one—even though possessing mastery over death like Bhīṣma and others—abandons the body only by one's own will; this very point is illustrated by the simile beginning with "just as a bird leaves a tree," and it is likewise set forth in the *Bhagavadgītā*:
"Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes up others that are new, so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into other, new ones. (Gītā 2.22) || 6 ||

Just as a snake effortlessly casts off its worn-out skin with the thought that it is to be discarded, even so the seeker of liberation (mumukṣu) should cast off Prakṛti, which has been experienced for a long time and is now worn out, with the thought that it is to be discarded. Thus it is said: "Like a serpent casting off its worn-out skin. (6)
And regarding the point that one should not again accept what has been renounced, such as the primordial nature (prakṛti) and so forth, he says: "Or like a hand that has been cut off. (7)

Just as no one takes back a severed hand, so too one should not regard that which has been renounced as one's own again; this is the meaning. The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of "api" (also). || 7 ||
Contemplating that which is not a means to liberation leads to bondage, as in the case of Bharata.

Even if something should be a duty (*dharma*), if it is not an internal means (*antaraṅga-sādhana*) for discrimination (*viveka*), one must not direct the mind toward its contemplation or its performance; for that leads to bondage by causing the forgetting of discrimination, as in the case of Bharata. This refers to how the royal sage Bharata’s care—even though righteous—for the young fawn, who was helpless and destitute, [became a cause of bondage]. Thus, concerning Jaḍabharata, the Viṣṇu Purāṇa states:
"When he was restless, she was restless; when he went far away, she went far away."
"My heart was thus attached to that young deer. (8)
When there is conjunction with many [afflictions], there is contradiction with passion and the rest, like the maiden and the conch shell.

One should not associate with many; for in association with many, there arises quarreling due to the manifestation of passion and other afflictions, which causes a fall from yoga. The meaning is that just as a clanging sound (jhaṇatkāra) occurs when conch shells in the hands of young maidens strike against one another. || 9 ||
By both [means] likewise. || 10 ||
Even when two are joined together, there is likewise conflict; therefore, the meaning is that one should remain all alone. As it has been said:
"Among many there will be quarrel, and even between two there is talk [of discord];
therefore, one should wander alone, like a single bangle on a maiden's wrist. (10)
Indeed, when the mind is subject to desire, devoid of flavor, and bereft of contentment,
knowledge does not reflect within it, just as a face does not reflect in a tarnished mirror.
Based on this statement, he says that freedom from expectation should be practiced by the yogi:
"Free from expectation, one is happy, like Piṅgā. (11)

Having abandoned hope, a person should possess the happiness called contentment, like Piṅgalā. The meaning is that just as the courtesan named Piṅgalā, seeking a lover but failing to find one, became despondent and attained happiness by abandoning hope; so it is said: "Hope is indeed the supreme suffering, and freedom from hope is the supreme happiness; having utterly severed the hope for a lover, Piṅgalā slept in peace."

[Objection: Surely, with the cessation of hope there would be the cessation of suffering; but from what source would happiness come? [For] it would lack its means. [Reply: It is said: that innate happiness of the mind which, due to the predominance of *sattva*, remains covered by hope—that very happiness, upon the disappearance of hope, becomes manifest. Just as the coldness of water is obstructed by fire, there is no dependence on external means in this case. And this alone is called "happiness in the object" (*artha-sukha*). || 11 ||
Since even the undertaking [of action] is an obstacle to yoga, one should not act for the sake of enjoyment, as that can be accomplished otherwise; thus he says:
"Even without undertaking [action], one is happy in another's house, like a snake. (12)
The ellipsis "may he be happy" is to be supplied. The remainder is easy to understand. As it has been said:
"The undertaking of a house leads only to suffering, never to happiness;
a snake, however, enters a dwelling built by another and thrives in comfort. (12)

One should grasp only the essence from scriptures and teachers; otherwise, due to dogmatic assertions and the like, partiality, mutual contradictions, and the profusion of topics, one-pointedness of mind becomes impossible. Thus he says:
"Even while attending many scriptures and teachers, one should extract the essence like a bee. (13)
The word "to be done" (*kartavyam*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The rest is easy to understand. As it has been said:
"A skillful person should extract the essence from all these great treatises, just as a bee [gathers honey] from flowers."
And in the Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa:
"One should practice that knowledge which is the essence and which accomplishes one's own goal;
for this multiplicity of knowledges is indeed an obstacle to yoga."
"He who wanders about thirsty, thinking 'this is to be known, this is to be known,' shall not attain knowledge even in thousands of eons. (13)
Let other means of practice be as they may; the direct realization of discernment must be accomplished solely through the preservation of samādhi by means of one-pointedness. Thus he says:
"Like the arrow-maker, there is no loss of samādhi for one whose mind is single. (14)

Just as for an archer whose mind is fixed on the creation of an arrow, there is no obstruction or loss of his activity even by the passing of a king nearby, so too for one whose mind is one-pointed, there is no loss of concentration (samādhi) even through the flow [of breath], because the cessation of other activities has been achieved. Consequently, in the absence of movement toward other objects, the direct realization of the object of meditation (dhyeya) necessarily occurs; thus, the meaning is that one should practice one-pointedness. As it has been said:
"Thus, with the mind restrained within the self, one knows nothing either external or internal."
"Just as the arrow-maker, with his mind fixed on the arrow, did not see the king walking by his side. || 14 ||

When the capacity [to follow the rules] exists, the transgression of the rules established by the scriptures through the power of knowledge is in vain. Then, due to the non-attainment of knowledge, ruin befalls the yogin; thus he says: "From the transgression of what has been prescribed, there is ruin, as in the world. (15)

The purpose known as the perfection of knowledge does not arise from transgressing the rules established for yogis in the scriptures; it is like the case in the world. Just as in the world, when one transgresses the prescribed wholesome diet and so forth regarding medicine and the like, the respective success is not achieved—this is the meaning. However, if there is a transgression due to incapacity or for the sake of protecting knowledge, there is no obstruction to knowledge. But one who has cast off ritual observances and actions, remaining solely established in Brahman, having become Brahman, is called a "brahmacārī" in this world at the end.

Thus it is stated in the *Mokṣadharma* and other sections, as well as in the *Smṛtis* of Vasiṣṭha and others. For this very reason, in the *Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other texts, those who abandon ritual action in vain are censured as heretics (*pāṣaṇḍas*), with such statements as: "For men who have already shaved their heads, the wearing of matted hair is indeed useless," and so forth. || 15 ||
He states that there is futility even in the forgetting of the observances:
"Even upon forgetting that, like a female frog" (16).

This is easy to understand. This is the story of the frog: A certain king, having gone hunting in the forest, saw a beautiful maiden. When she was requested by the king to become his wife, she made a condition: "When water is shown to me by you, then I must go. Once, however, being exhausted from playing, she asked the king, "Where is the water? The king, forgetting the agreement, showed her the water.

Then that daughter of the frog-king, capable of assuming any form at will, became a female frog and entered the water. Thereupon, although the king searched for her with nets and other means, he did not find her. || 16 ||

He tells a historical anecdote regarding the necessity of investigating the teacher’s words even after hearing them, just as in the case of hearing [the Vedas]: "Even upon hearing the instruction, one does not achieve the highest fulfillment without reflection, as was the case with Virocana. (17)

*Parāmarśa* is the deliberation that determines the intended meaning of the guru’s words. Without it, there is no certainty regarding the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), even upon hearing the words of instruction. This is because, despite both Indra and Virocana hearing the instruction of Prajāpati, Virocana was heard to be deluded due to his lack of *parāmarśa*. Therefore, one must also engage in reflection (*manana*) upon what has been taught by the guru. Indeed, even today we observe that the single instruction "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) can be conceived in various ways:
as being partless (*akhaṇḍatva*), as non-difference characterized by the absence of dissimilarity (*avaidharmya-lakṣaṇābheda*), and as non-division (*avibhāga*). || 17 ||
And for this very reason, he states that a reflective awareness (parāmarśa) is observed [of them]: "The perception of those two is by means of the sense organ" (18).

The word "that" (tat) refers back to what was previously mentioned and what is being mentioned. The meaning is that between those two, Indra and Virocana, it is observed that Indra [attained success];
and he states that one who seeks correct knowledge must serve the teacher for a long time:
"Having performed prostrations, observance of celibacy, and attendance, success is attained after a long time."
It is the same as that. || 19 ||

In the same way, for anyone else as well, success—the dawning of the realization of the true meaning—occurs only after performing prostrations, the study of the Vedas, service, and so forth toward the Guru, and not otherwise; this is the meaning. And thus says the Śruti:
"For that high-souled one who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and who regards the Guru as he does the Divine, these meanings declared here truly shine forth. (19)
There is no restriction regarding time, as in the case of Vāmadeva.

The arising of knowledge does not depend on a fixed temporal rule regarding the practice of this life alone; it is like the case of Vāmadeva. The meaning is that just as knowledge arose for Vāmadeva even while in the womb due to practices from previous births, so it may arise for another as well. And thus says the Śruti: "Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I [am...]"

"I was Manu, I was the Sun"—this [statement] also applies even now to one who knows thus: "I am Brahman. He becomes all this, and so forth. The passage beginning with "I was Manu" either refers to a distinction characterized by a lack of difference (avaidharmya-lakṣaṇa-bheda), or it refers to the state of being Brahman known as omnipresence (*sarvavyāpakatā*), according to the traditional teaching (*smṛti*): "You pervade everything; therefore, You are everything. As for the statement "He becomes all this," it refers to the absolute destruction of the limitation caused by adjuncts (*aupādhika-pariccheda*). || 20 ||

[Objection: But since it is heard that even the meditation on [Brahman] with attributes (saguṇopāsanā) is a cause of knowledge, knowledge will arise from that alone; what is the purpose of the difficult and subtle practice of yoga? To this, he says:
"From meditation on a superimposed form, [knowledge arises] through a traditional succession, as in the case of those who worship the sacrificial post. (21)

The word "success" (siddhi) is supplied [from the previous verse]. Through the worship of deities such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Hara—who possess superimposed forms—there is the accomplishment of knowledge either indirectly by way of attaining the worlds of Brahmā and others in succession, or through the purification of the mind; it is not direct. This is the meaning, as in the case of ritualists (yājñika). || 21 ||
He states that there is no fixed rule for the attainment of knowledge even through the succession of worlds beginning with Brahmā:
"Even upon obtaining the other [worlds], there is a return, because of the scriptural teaching of rebirth resulting from the practice of the five fires. (22)

Even upon attaining everything up to the world of Brahmā (brahmaloka)—which consists of superimposed forms belonging to the Self that is devoid of qualities (nirguṇātman)—there is still a return. Why? Because even for one who has gone to the world of Brahmā by the path of the gods (devayāna), birth from the fivefold oblations is heard of in the sequence of heaven, rain-cloud, earth, celestial nymphs, and fire. This is the meaning of the passage beginning with "That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire" in the fifth prapāṭhaka of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad.
And as for the statement regarding non-return from the world of Brahmā, that refers primarily to a person in whom knowledge has arisen right there [in that world]. || 22 ||

He provides an illustration for the fact that the perfection of knowledge belongs only to one who is dispassionate: "For the dispassionate person, there is the abandonment of what is to be discarded and the acquisition of what is to be acquired, like a swan [separating] milk. (23)

Only for one who is dispassionate does the abandonment of the things to be discarded, such as primordial nature (prakṛti) and the rest, and the acquisition of the self, which is to be accepted, take place. The meaning is that this is like the case of milk and water that have become mixed; only a swan, and not a crow or the like, can discard the essenceless water and acquire the essential milk. || 23 ||
