He states that both of these also arise from association with perfected beings (siddhapuruṣa): "Or likewise, through yoga that has attained excellence. (24)

The meaning is that he by whom an excellence has been attained—that is, the pinnacle of knowledge—speaks even through association with such a person, just like a swan; for it is said that in the case of Ālarka, discrimination arose spontaneously from the mere company of Dattātreya. || 24 ||
He says that one should not associate with those possessed by passion:
"One who is afflicted by passion should not act according to his own whims, like a parrot. (25)

One should not, out of desire, form an attachment to a person afflicted by passion, just like a parrot. The meaning is that just as a parrot bird, despite being of excellent beauty, does not act according to its own will because of its fear of captivity due to the greed of those lusting after its form, so it is here. || 25 ||
He states the fault in associating with those possessed by passion:
"Bound by the connection to qualities, like a parrot" (26).

But by associating with them, one becomes bound due to the connection with their qualities—that is, through the connection with their passion (*rāga*) and so forth—just like a parrot. The meaning is that just as a parrot bird is bound by the snares, which are the qualities (strings), of a hunter, so it is here. Alternatively, the meaning is that one is bound by those who are greedy for qualities (*guṇa-lolupa*) because of one's own possession of qualities, just like the parrot. On this very point, Saubhari said: "This meditative absorption (*samādhi*) of mine, which was my friend during my dwelling in the water, has been suddenly destroyed by association with fish. This attachment of mine was caused by social contact, and from such attachment arise great desires for possessions. (26)
He determines the means for detachment as well by means of two [verses]:
"Passion is not pacified through enjoyment, as in the case of a sage. (27)
The meaning is that just as Saubhari the sage found no pacification of passion through enjoyments, so it is not for others either. This was stated by Saubhari himself:
"I have realized today that there is truly no end to desires until death;
the mind of one who is intent on the fulfillment of desires can never become attached to the supreme reality. (27)
Rather, [it is abandoned] because faults are seen in both. || 28 ||

The pacification of attachment occurs precisely through the perception of defects—such as the nature of being subject to transformation and the essence of suffering—in both the primal nature (prakṛti) and its effects. The meaning is that it is just like the sage [Saubhari]. Indeed, it is heard that Saubhari attained detachment from worldly association simply by perceiving the defect in such association:
"Whatever suffering is born from even a single body, that same amount is produced when there are half that number;
and through the possession of the daughters of kings, that suffering was multiplied manifold by numerous sons. (28)
He states that one who is afflicted by defects such as passion lacks the qualification even for receiving instruction:
"The seed of instruction does not sprout in a mind that is defiled, just as [it does not sprout] in a stone. (29)

The sprout of that seed of the tree of knowledge, which consists of instruction, does not even germinate in a mind defiled by passion and other impurities. It is like the case of King Aja; just as when King Aja’s mind was clouded by grief for his wife, no sprout of the seed of instruction arose despite its being spoken by Vasiṣṭha—this is the meaning. || 29 ||
What more need be said?
It does not even possess a mere reflection, like a soiled mirror. || 30 ||

Even initial knowledge does not arise from instruction in one whose mind is defiled, because of obstructions such as the wandering toward other objects. The meaning is that just as an object does not reflect in a dirty mirror due to being obstructed by impurities, so it is in this case. || 30 ||
Or even if some kind of knowledge were to arise, it would still not correspond to the [true] instruction; thus he says:
"Even for that which is born from that, there is no identity with its form, like a lotus [grown in mud]. (31)

Therefore, even for knowledge born from instruction, there is no conformity to that instruction, because it is not understood through the totality of conditions (*sāmagrya*), like a lotus. The meaning is: just as a lotus, despite the excellence of its seed, does not conform to the seed due to the defect of the mud, so it is here; the student's mind occupies the place of the mud. || 31 ||

[Objection: But surely, since the status of being the human goal is already accomplished through sovereignty in the world of Brahmā and other realms, what is the purpose of producing knowledge for the sake of liberation through such great effort? To this, he says:

"Even when there is union with supernatural power (*bhūti*), there is no sense of having accomplished all that was to be done (*kṛtakṛtyatā*); it is like the attainment of the object of worship (*upāsya-siddhi-vat*). (32)

Even when endowed with sovereign power (*aiśvarya*), there is no state of having accomplished one's purpose (*kṛtakṛtyatā*) or fulfilled one's aim (*kṛtārthatā*), because it is followed by decay, excess, and suffering, just like the success of those who are worshipped. Just as even for those such as Brahmā and others who are objects of worship, there is no state of having accomplished one's purpose despite their possession of supernatural powers (*siddhi*), since it is heard that they too engage in the practice of yoga during the "yoga-sleep" (*yoganidrā*) and so forth; in the same way, this applies to one who has obtained that sovereignty through the worship of them. 32.
This is the internal limb of the discernment taught in the three preceding chapters.
In this chapter, it has been briefly declared by means of narratives. || 1 ||
Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Chapter on Narratives, in the commentary on the *Sāṅkhya-pravacana* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu. 4.
Now begins the fifth chapter. || 5 ||

The established tenets of our own system are sufficient. Hereafter, the fifth chapter is commenced in order to refute the prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) of others regarding our own system. Therein, at the outset, he resolves the objection that the auspiciousness performed by the word *atha* in the opening aphorism is superfluous—namely: "The performance of an auspicious rite is [justified] because it is the practice of the learned, because its fruit is observed, and because of scriptural authority. (1)

The meaning is that the necessity of performing the introductory benediction (*maṅgalācaraṇa*) which has been made is established by these proofs. The word "iti" serves to exclude any further expectation for additional reasons. || 1 ||

The objection raised—that the existence of God is unproven—is untenable, because His existence is established by His being the bestower of the fruits of action; [the author] refutes those who hold such a prima facie view:
"The production of the fruit does not depend upon the superintendence of God, because that [superintendence] is established through the action itself. (2)

It is not logical that the accomplishment of the transformation into the form of the fruit of action occurs when the cause is presided over by a Lord; for the meaning is that the production of the fruit is possible through action alone, which is necessary. ||2||
He states through the aphorisms that even the Lord's status as a bestower of fruits is not tenable:
"Presiding [over the world] occurs for the sake of His own benefit, as in the case of worldly beings. (Sūtra 3)
The meaning is that if God were an agent of superintendence, His superintendence would be for the sake of His own benefit, just as in the case of worldly beings. ||3||
Anticipating the objection that "let there be benefit even for Īśvara; what is the harm?", he says: "Otherwise, [it would be] like a worldly lord. (4)

If even the Lord were to accept assistance, then like a worldly lord, he too would be subject to saṃsāra; the meaning is that this would result in suffering and the like due to his desires being incomplete. || 4 ||
Anticipating the objection that "let it be exactly so," he says: "Or it is technical. (5)

If God were also a being within saṃsāra, then for you, as for us, the term "Lord" would be a mere conventional designation applied to a person produced at the beginning of creation. The meaning is that because there is a contradiction between being subject to saṃsāra and having unimpeded will, eternal sovereignty is logically impossible. || 5 ||
He states another objection to [the claim that] God is the presiding controller:
"Its establishment is not possible without passion (rāga), because of the necessity of specific causes. (6)

Furthermore, without passion (*rāga*), the state of being a presiding agent (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) is not established; the meaning is that passion is the specific cause for activity. [Now, one might object: what was stated in the third sūtra—that the presiding is "like in the world" and solely for the sake of one's own benefit—is precisely what is stated here as "not without passion, its establishment occurs. Thus, there is tautology. To this, he shows the distinction between benefit and passion: Benefit is the accomplishment of a desired object, whereas passion is an intense desire; thus, there is no tautology. || 6 ||
[Objection: "Let it be so that there is passion (rāga) even in the Lord. To this, he says: "Even in connection with that, He is eternally liberated. (7)
Even if the conjunction with passion were admitted, he would not be eternally liberated; consequently, there would be a loss of your own tenet—this is the meaning. || 7 ||

Furthermore, sovereignty over *prakṛti* is not possible through desire and so forth, which are transformations of *prakṛti*, because that would involve mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Nor is it logical for eternal desire and the like to exist in *prakṛti*, as this would contradict the state of equilibrium established by *śruti* and *smṛti*. Therefore, only two alternatives remain. They are as follows: Is sovereignty due to the power of *pradhāna*—that is, through a direct connection with consciousness as we maintain in the case of desire and the rest—or is it due to its being a stimulator merely by its presence, like a magnet? Regarding these, he refutes the first position:
If it is argued that [the Self] incurs attachment through connection with the power of Pradhāna, [we reply: no. 8.

The meaning is that because the desire and other qualities of the power of *pradhāna* would attach to the *puruṣa* through conjunction, the *puruṣa* would also incur the association with attributes (*dharma*). Consequently, there would be a contradiction with such scriptural passages as: "Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it; for this *puruṣa* is indeed unattached. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.15). || 8 ||
Regarding the latter [view], he says: "If [the Lord's] universal sovereignty were due to mere existence alone... (Sūtra 9).

If the sovereignty of the conscious being consists merely in its presence, like a magnet, then the very sovereignty we intend to establish is proven without distinction for all male souls who are enjoyers in their respective creations; for the Pradhāna creates the Mahat and the rest solely through conjunction with every enjoyer. Consequently, the meaning is that your own tenet—that there is only one Lord—is abandoned. || 9 ||

It might be argued: "Those [arguments] are merely fallacious reasonings (asattarka) because they contradict the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that establish God; otherwise, it would be possible to refute even the Primal Matter (pradhāna) by means of thousands of other such fallacious reasonings. To this he replies:
"Because there is an absence of a means of valid cognition, there is no establishment of that [God]. (10)

Regarding the proof of that [existence], since there is no perception of an eternal Lord, inference and verbal testimony alone must be stated as the means of valid cognition; however, the meaning is that these two are not possible. 10.
He demonstrates the impossibility itself through two sutras:
"Inference is not [possible] because of the absence of a relationship" (11).

The relation [of pervasion] is *vyāpti*; its absence is *asiddhi*. Thus, in inferences such as "the great principle (*mahat*) and so forth have an agent because they are effects," there is no inference regarding God due to the lack of pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*), resulting from the reason being non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*). This is the meaning. || 11 ||
Nor is there scriptural authority [for this], as he says:
"Even scripture [does not support] the state of being an effect of the Pradhāna. (12)
In the case of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), there is scriptural authority for its being the effect of *pradhāna* alone, but not for its having a conscious being as its cause. As it is said:
"The one unborn female, red, white, and black, producing many offspring of similar form..."

The meaning is as follows: "In the beginning, this was indeed undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form," and so forth. Furthermore, the scriptural passage regarding the sentient cause, such as "It thought: May I become many," refers to the knowledge produced in the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa) who possesses the adjunct (upādhi) of the principle of Mahat at the beginning of creation. Alternatively, in accordance with the desire to become manifold, it is figurative (gauṇī) with respect to Pradhāna itself, like the expression "the bank wishes to fall."

Otherwise, the non-modifiability of the Puruṣa as declared by such scriptural passages as "The witness, the cognizer, alone, devoid of qualities" would be untenable. Furthermore, it has already been explained that this refutation of God is merely a bold assertion (prauḍhavāda) intended either for the sake of cultivating detachment from sovereignty or to establish liberation even without knowledge of God. Moreover, there is the conceptual burden (kalpanā-gaurava) of assuming that the eternality of God and other attributes—which distinguish Him from the individual soul (jīva)—are merely figurative.

The justification for [the existence of] qualities such as permanence, based on the acceptance of eternal knowledge, will, and so forth as being conditioned (*aupādhika*), as well as the transformations into the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, should be examined in the *Brahmamīmāṃsā*. || 12 ||
Regarding the conclusion established in the first chapter—that there is no bondage through ignorance—the author refutes the opposing view at length with this section:
"There can be no connection with the power of ignorance for that which is free from attachment. (13)

Others say: "Pradhāna does not exist; rather, there is a power called beginningless ignorance (avidyā) which is destroyed by knowledge and resides in the conscious principle (cetana). From that alone comes the bondage of the conscious one, and upon its destruction, liberation. To this, it is said: A connection with the power of ignorance is not possible directly for the conscious principle because of its state of non-attachment (niḥsaṅgatā). For ignorance is the assumption of the form of another thing; and that, being a specific modification, is not possible without attachment in the form of conjunction, which is the cause of [continued] agency. || 13 ||
Surely, the connection with ignorance must be said to arise solely through the power of ignorance; and since it is thus not ultimately real, there can be no attachment to it. To this, he replies:
"If its connection [with ignorance] were established by that [ignorance], there would be the fallacy of mutual dependence. (14)

Furthermore, if the accomplishment of knowledge were to arise from the conjunction with ignorance, there would be either mutual dependence, self-dependence, or an infinite regress; this is the remainder [of the argument]. || 14 ||
Anticipating the objection that "the infinite regress is not a fault, just as in the case of the seed and the sprout," he says:
"It is not like the seed and the sprout, because of the scriptural teaching that saṃsāra has a beginning. (15)

The infinite regress [of ignorance] is not possible, like that of a seed and its sprout, because it is heard in scripture that the cycle of transmigration (saṃsāra) for individual persons—which consists of all misfortunes such as ignorance—is itself beginningless; the meaning is that it is heard that this [transmigration] is absent during dissolution, deep sleep, and so forth. For by such scriptural passages as, "Being a mass of consciousness alone, having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them," it is established that at the time of dissolution and so on, due to the absence of mental modifications (buddhi-vṛtti), the state of pure consciousness—devoid of all transmigratory existence such as ignorance which is conditioned by those [modifications]—belongs to the persons.
Therefore, the claim that "ignorance too is caused by ignorance" is a mere verbal assertion. || 15 ||

Now, one might object: "Our ignorance (*avidyā*) is technical in nature and not the kind defined in Yoga as the notion of self in what is not-self; thus, just like your *pradhāna*, even though our ignorance is partless and beginningless and resides in the *puruṣa*, there is no loss of its being unattached. Anticipating this doubt, [the author] refutes it by analyzing the conceptualized meaning of the term "ignorance": "If it were other than knowledge (*vidyā*), there would be the consequence of sublation (*bādha*) of Brahman. (16)

If the very meaning of the term "ignorance" (avidyā) is simply its difference from knowledge (vidyā), then it follows that the Self, which is Brahman, would also be subject to sublation or destruction, because it would be distinct from knowledge; this is the sense. || 16 ||
If there is no obstruction, there is fruitlessness. || 17 ||

If, however, that which consists of the nature of ignorance were not sublated by knowledge, then knowledge would be futile; the meaning is that it would lack the capacity to remove ignorance. || 17 ||
He refutes another alternative:
"If the world were sublated by knowledge, it would be exactly like this. (18)

If, on the other hand, ignorance (*avidyātva*) is defined as being merely that which is sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*), then it would follow that the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—including its material cause (*prakṛti*), the Great Principle (*mahat*), and so forth—is likewise ignorance. The meaning is that, according to scriptural passages such as "Not this, not this" (*neti neti*) and "neither gross nor subtle" (*asthūlam anaṇu*), material nature (*prakṛti*) and the rest are taught to be [superimposed] upon the Self just like false cognition (*mithyājñāna*). And thus, if the entire phenomenal world were indeed ignorance, then since ignorance is destroyed for one person through knowledge, the world would no longer be perceived by others either. This is the intended sense.

It cannot be said that the nature of ignorance (*avidyātva*) consists in being destroyed by knowledge (*vidyā*); for since it is impossible to apprehend that which is destroyed by knowledge through its being destroyed by knowledge, it cannot be said that the Self is ignorance, because [such an apprehension] would involve the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). (18)
If it were of that nature, it would be beginningless. || 19 ||

Or, let it be granted in some way that ignorance (*avidyā*) is precisely that which is sublated by knowledge (*vidyā*). Even so, such a thing must have a beginning among persons; its beginninglessness is not possible. The meaning is that according to scriptural passages such as "He is indeed a mass of consciousness," the person is established as pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). Furthermore, in our system, even though the person is free from transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) during dissolution, rebondage is demonstrated to occur due to the conjunction with the independent and eternal *pradhāna*.

Likewise, it has also been stated that even in the case of conjunction with *pradhāna*, the cause is precisely the non-discrimination (*aviveka*) belonging to a previous birth, acting through the medium of the unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*) and so forth. Therefore, there is no ignorance other than that which is described in the Yoga system. And it is established that this [ignorance] is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*) alone, not a property of the self (*puruṣa*). || 19 ||
In this very chapter, regarding what was stated—that the activity of *pradhāna* is caused by *karman*—the author refutes the opponent's prima facie argument with the following section:
"There is no denial of *dharma*, because of the diversity of the effects of *prakṛti*. (20)

The denial of *dharma* is not possible on the grounds of its imperceptibility; for it is inferred from the fact that the diversity observed in the effects of nature (*prakṛti*) would otherwise be inexplicable. This is the meaning. || 20 ||
He states another means of valid cognition as well: "Its establishment is through direct revelation, indicative marks, and so forth. (21)

The meaning is that its existence is established by such scriptural passages as "One becomes virtuous through virtue and sinful through sin," by the indicative mark (liṅga) consisting of injunctions and the like such as "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Aśvamedha," and by the direct perception of yogis and other means of knowledge. || 21 ||
He renders the opponent's argument—"the non-establishment of dharma because of the absence of perception"—into a fallacious reason:
"There is no such restriction, because there is scope for other means of valid cognition. || 22 ||
There is no rule that the non-existence of a thing follows from the absence of its perception; for things can be distinguished by other means of valid cognition as well—this is the meaning.
Just as with dharma, it establishes adharma too; thus it is the same in both cases. || 23 ||
The meaning is that, just as with dharma, these are the means of valid knowledge regarding adharma as well. || 23 ||

[Objection: "But surely the establishment of *dharma* occurs through *arthāpatti* (presumption), which consists in the impossibility of explaining an injunction otherwise; since that [presumption] does not exist for *adharma*, how can there be an extension (*atideśa*) of the Vedic indicative mark (*liṅga*) to it as *adharma*? [Reply: No, he says—"If the establishment is by way of implication (*artha*), it is the same for both. (24)

For there exists an equal mark (*liṅga*) for both dharma and adharma; the meaning is that the very prohibitive injunction such as "one should not go to another's wife" serves as the mark for adharma. || 24 ||

Now, one might raise the objection: "If dharma and the other qualities are accepted [as real], then since persons possess dharma and so forth, it would follow that they undergo transformation and the like. He dispels this doubt:
"Dharma and the rest are attributes of the internal organ" (25).

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), all the specific qualities of the self (ātma-viśeṣa-guṇa) mentioned in the Vaiśeṣika scriptures are included. Nor should it be argued that, in the case of dissolution (pralaya), since the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is absent, where would dharma and the other qualities reside; for, like space, the internal organ does not undergo absolute destruction. Indeed, it has already been explained that the internal organ consists of both effect and cause. Therefore, while in its causal state, dharma, adharma, mental impressions (saṃskāra), and so forth, reside within the internal organ as a particular portion of primordial nature (prakṛti). || 25 ||

It might be argued as follows: "The establishment of *dharma* and so forth [is possible] because of the diversity of the effects of *prakṛti* and because of the Veda and other authorities. This is incorrect, because your own scripture itself sublates both *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*, and its effects. For instance, [the scripture states]: "The witness, the knower, solitary and devoid of qualities" (*sākṣī cetā kevalo nirguṇaśca*); "Now, therefore, the instruction: 'not this, not this'" (*athāta ādeśo neti neti*); and "That which is soundless, touchless, formless, undecaying, likewise tasteless, eternal, and odorless" (*aśabdamasparśamarūpamavyayaṃ tathārasaṃ nityamagandhavacca yat*), and so forth.
"Neither destruction nor origination; modification is a mere verbal handle, a name based on clay, and 'clay' alone is the truth"—thus they [the Mādhyamikas] say. He refutes this as follows:
"And there is no absolute sublation of qualities and so forth. (26)

There is no sublation (bādha) of the qualities (guṇas), such as *sattva* and the rest, nor of their attributes, such as pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest, nor even of their effects, such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, by way of their essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*). However, sublation occurs in consciousness (*cetana*) only through association (*saṃsarga*), just as heat is sublated [in water]. Likewise, the meaning is that for all transforming things, beginning with the *guṇas*, sublation occurs only through time (*kāla*) by means of states (*avasthā*) and so forth. But why does sublation not occur by way of essential nature itself, as in the case of objects in dreams, mental desires, and the like? In response to this expectation, he says:
"The perception of pleasure arises from the conjunction of the five constituents. (27)

Here, for the purpose of specifically making it the subject (*pakṣa*), the mention of "mere pleasure" (*sukhamātra*)—which is one part of the object of dispute—is intended to indicate all objects [of experience]. The reading "the cognition of pleasure and so forth" (*sukhādisaṃvittiḥ*) is indeed correct. The five members of the syllogism (*nyāya*) are the proposition (*pratijñā*), the reason (*hetu*), the example (*udāharaṇa*), the application (*upanaya*), and the conclusion (*nigamana*). The meaning is that from their conjunction—that is, their combination—the establishment of all categories such as pleasure and so forth follows. And the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: pleasure exists, because it performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*). Whatever performs a causal function exists, just like the conscious self (*cetana*).

Furthermore, pleasure is "existent" because it performs a causal function (arthakriyā) in the form of horripilation and so forth; and even though sentient beings are unchanging, the illumination of objects is itself their causal function. Against the nihilist (nāstika), one should employ a negative inference (vyatireki-anumāna), and in that case, the horn of a hare and the like serve as the illustrative example. || 27 ||

The Cārvāka further objects: "There is no means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) other than perception, because [properties] such as being pervaded (vyāpyatva) are unestablished"—namely, that the relation [between smoke and fire] is not established by a single apprehension. (28)

The meaning is that because the relationship of pervasion (*vyāpti*) cannot be established through the apprehension of a single concomitance, and because multiplicity (*bhūyastva*) is not universally applicable (*ananugata*), the object cannot be proven by means of inference due to the impossibility of grasping pervasion. || 28 ||
He provides the definition: "Pervasion (vyāpti) is the necessary concomitance of two properties, or of one of the two. (29)

The "concomitance" (*sāhitya*) of properties (*dharma*) is their concomitance within the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); that is to say, it is their co-occurrence (*sahacāra*). Thus, the meaning is that *vyāpti* (pervasion) is the necessary, non-deviant co-occurrence of two things—the probandum and the probans—or of the probans alone. The phrase "of both" is stated according to the view of symmetrical pervasion (*samavyāpti*); and since the rule [of pervasion] is apprehended through favorable reasoning (*anukūlatarka*), the sense is that there is no impossibility in the apprehension of pervasion. || 29 ||
He states that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not a distinct category of reality (*padārthāntara*) in the form of the "power" (*śakti*) and so forth to be described hereafter:
"It is not a separate principle (*tattvāntara*), because that would entail the unwarranted postulation of a new entity. (30)

Pervasion (vyāpti) is nothing other than the concomitance of necessary factors; for otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to postulate a real entity as the substratum of pervasion. Our position, however, is that we merely postulate the status of pervasion for an already established entity—this is the meaning. || 30 ||
He states the opinion of others: "The teachers [say] it arises from one's own power. (31)

Other teachers, however, say that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is indeed a distinct category (*tattvāntara*), consisting of a specific power (*śaktiviśeṣa*) produced by the inherent power of the pervaded (*vyāpya*). Mere inherent power, however, is not pervasion because it persists as long as the substance exists; for even smoke that has moved to another location is not pervaded by fire. Furthermore, since that power is destroyed by moving to another location, there is no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) of the definition [to such cases]. In our own view, however, the intention is that smoke must be qualified by being delimited by the time of its production. || 31 ||
Pañcaśikha says it is the connection with the capacity to be supported. || 32 ||

The meaning is that Pañcaśikha [states] that because there is a conventional usage of the pervasion of *prakṛti* and so forth with respect to intellect (*buddhi*) and the rest, the power of being a substratum is the pervader, and the state of possessing the power of being the contained is the pervaded. || 32 ||

Now, one might ask: for what purpose is the "power of being contained" (ādheya-śakti) postulated? Let the pervasion simply be the inherent power of the nature of the pervaded entity itself. To this, he replies:
"The restriction [of pervasion] is not the power of the nature [itself], because that would entail the fallacy of circular reasoning. (33)

However, the power of essential nature (*svarūpa-śakti*) is not a restriction or a pervasion (*vyāpti*), because that would entail the fallacy of tautology. Just as "pot" and "jar" refer to the same thing, so too in the case of "intellect is the pervaded," the meaning is that there is no difference in substance. While one could simply say "essential nature," the inclusion of the term "power" (*śakti*) is intended to establish that pervasion is a property of the pervaded. || 33 ||
He explains the tautology himself:
"Because it would result in the uselessness of the qualifiers. (34)
This has already been almost fully explained in the Pūrva-sūtra itself. || 34 ||
He states another objection:
"And because it is untenable in the case of sprouts and the like" (Sūtra 35).

The state of being pervaded by a tree and so forth exists in the sprout and other parts. However, its definition as "mere intrinsic power" (svarūpa-śakti) is not possible; for since that intrinsic power does not depart even when the sprout is cut, it would follow that the state of being pervaded still exists at that time—this is the meaning. The point is that while the "power of being supported" (ādheya-śakti) is destroyed at the moment of cutting, there is no pervasion at that time [by virtue of that power]. || 35 ||

Now, one might object: why does Pañcaśikha not state that pervasion (*vyāpti*) is simply the emergence of one's own power (*nijaśakti*), such that since smoke lacks the status of being a superstratum (*ādheya*) with respect to fire, it would follow that smoke is not pervaded by fire? To this he replies:
"When the power of being a superstratum is established, the connection with one's own power [is also established] by the same logic. (36)

When the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the power residing in the locus (*ādheya-śakti*) is established, the emergence of its own power (*nija-śakti*) is likewise established as pervasion by virtue of the same principle; that is to say, because the reasoning is identical. Furthermore, the lack of a single common form (*ananugama*) is not a defect, just as in the case of words with multiple meanings (*nānārtha*). Thus, even in our own system, various kinds of concomitances (*sahacāra*) themselves should be understood as the pervasions. Nor should it be argued that, even so, there would be a lack of uniformity among the pervasions as causes of inference; for this is explained by the fact that the effect possesses a specific diversity (*vaijātya*), just as in the case of grass, flint, and a gem [all producing fire].

The objection to the validity of inference has been refuted by defining pervasion (vyāpti) in order to establish that which was stated: that the establishment of qualities and so forth results from the employment of the five-membered syllogism. || 36 ||

Now, in order to establish that a word consisting of five members (the syllogism) is capable of generating knowledge, the opponent’s objection against the validity of verbal testimony—which consists in the impossibility of such generation—is refuted by defining the power of words and so forth:
"The relationship between a word and its object is the relation of the signified and the signifier. (37)

In the object there is the power called denotability (vācyatā), and in the word there is the power called denotative capacity (vācakatā); this alone is their relation, like that of the correlate (anuyogitā). The meaning is that from the knowledge of that [relation], the object is presented by the word. || 37 ||
He states the means of apprehending the expressive power (śakti):
"The establishment of the relationship [between word and meaning] is achieved through three [means]. (38)

The meaning is that the relationship is grasped through these three: the instruction of a reliable person (āptopadeśa), the linguistic usage of elders (vṛddhavyavahāra), and the coreferentiality with well-known words (prasiddhapadasāmānādhikaraṇya). || 38 ||
There is no restrictive rule regarding the effect, because it is observed to occur in both ways. || 39 ||

The meaning is that there is no rule that the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) occurs only in relation to something to be accomplished (*kārya*), because in the world, the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) and so forth is observed not only regarding what is to be accomplished but also regarding what is already established (*siddha*). For instance, from a sentence directed toward an action such as "Bring the cow," the elder's activity of bringing a new [cow] is observed. And the intention is that once the validity of words referring to established facts (*siddhārtha*) is established through this discrimination, the validity of the Vedāntas is thereby established. || 39 ||

[Objection: "Granted that the apprehension of word-potency (śaktigraha) may exist in the world because we observe the cognition of meaning and so forth; but how will it be in the Veda, given that there would be the futility of teaching what is not to be done? To this, he says:
"The comprehension of the Vedic meaning belongs to one who is already proficient in the world. (40)

For a person who has mastered the power of words in common worldly usage, the comprehension of the meaning of the Veda occurs precisely by following that [worldly usage]. Indeed, the word-power (*śakti*) is not different in the world and different in the Veda; for according to the maxim, "those very [words] which are worldly are the same as those which are Vedic. Therefore, the meaning is that once it is established that [Vedic words] have already-accomplished objects (*siddhārtha*) as their primary referent in the world, that same status is established for them in the Veda as well.
Here, an objection is raised:
"No, because the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), and its meaning is also beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*). (41)

Is it not the case that the apprehension of word-potency (*śaktigraha*) through the three means—namely authoritative instruction (*āptopadeśa*) and so forth—is possible by means of the Vedic word? For, since the Veda is not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), authoritative instruction regarding its meanings is impossible. Likewise, because the meaning of the Veda is beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), it is impossible to apprehend either the usage of elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*) therein or the coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with well-known words; such is the meaning. || 41 ||
In this regard, he first refutes the claim that [dharma] has supersensible objects:
"Sacrifice and the like do not constitute dharma by their very nature, because of their specific qualification. (42)

What was stated is not correct. For sacrifice, charity, and so forth—consisting of the renunciation of substances intended for a deity and the like—are *dharma* by their very nature as being enjoined by the Veda, because they possess excellence due to yielding superior fruits. Furthermore, sacrifice and the like are not supersensible (*atīndriya*) because they consist of volition and other such mental states. However, it is not the *apūrva* (unseen potency) residing in the object of the sacrifice that is *dharma*, which would imply that what is enjoined by the Veda must be supersensible; this is the meaning. If it is argued that even so, there remains the fact that [sacrifice] is constituted by supersensible objects such as deities, we say no.
For it will be stated later that even in the case of supersensible objects, there is cognition by way of a universal form which serves as the delimitor of the objecthood [of those objects]. || 42 ||
Furthermore, he refutes the claim that there is an absence of authoritative instruction because [the Veda] is not of human origin: "One's own innate power is delimited by linguistic convention. (43)

Even though the Vedas are not of human origin (*apauruṣeya*), whatever inherent power (*śakti*) they possess regarding their meanings is delimited by authoritative persons (*āpta*) through a lineage of elders (*vṛddhaparamparā*) by means of linguistic instruction (*vyutpatti*) in the form: "this is the meaning of this word. It is taught to students as being excluded from other meanings; however, it is not itself arbitrarily assigned (*saṅketita*) like a modern word, such that there would be a dependence on human authorship. This is the sense. || 43 ||
[Objection: Even so, how could there be the apprehension of the expressive power (*śakti*) of Vedic words with respect to supersensible deities, fruits, and the like? To this, he says:
"Its establishment [occurs] because they generate cognition regarding both what is possible and what is impossible. (44)

The apprehension of capacity (śaktigraha) regarding both perceptible and imperceptible objects occurs by means of the presentation of a common property (sāmānyadharma), because it is established by experience that words generically produce cognition. However, the specific [property] is either beyond the senses or is simply the unprecedented meaning of the sentence (apūrvavākyārtha). The sense is that its apprehension is not required beforehand. || 44 ||
In the very course of establishing the authority of verbal testimony, he determines a specific characteristic pertaining to words:
"The Vedas are not eternal, because they are heard to be produced. (45)

The meaning is that the Vedas are not eternal, based on such scriptural passages as: "He performed austerity; from him, performing austerity, the three Vedas were born. Furthermore, those scriptural statements regarding the eternity of the Vedas refer to the non-interruption of the flow of a continuous succession of similar [recensions]. 45.
In that case, are the Vedas of human origin? No, he says:
"They are not of human origin because of the non-existence of a person who could be their author. (46)
The remainder, "because of the refutation of God," is easy to understand. || 46 ||
In response to the inquiry as to who else might be the agent, he says:
"No, because of the unsuitability of both the liberated and the unliberated. (47)

The meaning is this: Viṣṇu, the foremost among those liberated while living, although possessed of unsurpassed omniscience due to his state of pure being (viśuddhasattva), is nonetheless unfit for the composition of the Veda with its thousand branches because he is free from passion (vītarāga). On the other hand, one who is not liberated is unfit precisely because of his lack of omniscience. || 47 ||
[Objection: But in this way, because it is not of human origin (apauruṣeya), its very eternity (nityatva) follows; to this he replies:
"Eternity does not follow from being non-human, as in the case of a sprout and so forth. (48)
This is clear. 48.

"Surely, in the case of sprouts and the like as well, their being produced by a person (pauruṣeyatva) can be inferred on the grounds of their being effects, just like a jar; to this he replies: 'If those too were connected with that [agency], there would follow the sublation of what is perceived and so forth. (49)
The meaning is that the pervasion—that whatever is human is produced from a body—is observed in the world; if this were so, there would be a sublation of that very [pervasion]. || 49 ||
One might object that the Vedas are indeed human compositions because they were uttered by the Primordial Person; to this he says:
"That regarding which the notion 'it was created' arises, even when [the creator] is not perceived, is a human composition. (50)

The meaning is this: when, even with respect to an object not actually seen, a conviction arises that it was produced intentionally—that is, a cognition of its being preceded by intelligence—it is designated as "human" (pauruṣeya). This is what is intended: the status of being human-made does not consist merely in being uttered by a person, for if it did, there would be no designation of "human-made" in the case of inhalation and exhalation occurring during deep sleep; rather, it consists in being preceded by intelligence.

The Vedas, however, arise spontaneously from the Self-existent (Svayambhū) by the power of the unseen (adṛṣṭa), like a mere breath, and thus they are not of human origin. Accordingly, the Śruti states: "This Ṛgveda is the breath of that great Being," and so forth. || 50 ||
[Objection: "In that case, since it would not be preceded by a cognition of the sentence-meaning as it truly is—just like the speech of Śuka—the Veda too would lack authority. To this, he says:
"Its authority is intrinsic, because it is manifested through its own power. (51)

The meaning is as follows: since the innate, natural power of the Vedas to produce true knowledge is observed to be manifested in the *mantras*, the *Āyurveda*, and so forth, the authority (*prāmāṇya*) of all the Vedas is established as being intrinsic (*svataḥ*), and not based on the fact that they are rooted in the true knowledge of a speaker, and so on. Accordingly, the *Nyāyasūtra* states: "And its authority is like the authority of the *mantras* and the *Āyurveda*.

Having proposed the thesis that there is no absolute sublation (*atyantabādha*) regarding qualities and the like, one reason has been presented and elaborated upon: that pleasure and other such things are established through reasoning (*nyāya*). || 51 ||
Now he states another reason for that very point:
"There is no manifestation of what is non-existent, like a man's horn. (52)

Let it be for now that pleasure and the like are established by means of the five-membered syllogism; they are established even from mere cognition alone. For if pleasure and the like were absolutely non-existent, cognition itself would not be possible, because [non-existent things] such as a man’s horn do not appear [in consciousness]. This is the meaning. And thus says the Brahma-sūtra: "There is no non-existence, because of perception. Furthermore, in cases such as mother-of-pearl appearing as silver, dreams, and mental fantasies, an object consisting of a transformation of the mind is what is perceived; he will state later that "it is not absolutely non-existent. (52)

[Objection: "In that case, let qualities and so forth be absolutely real; thus, there would be no absolute sublation (atyantabādha), and the word 'absolute' (atyanta) would be redundant. To this, he replies:
"Not [so], because sublation is observed even for what is real" (na sato bādhadarśanāt). //53//

The appearance of even an absolutely non-existent entity, such as a quality (guṇa) and so forth, is logical, because sublation is observed at the time of its destruction; and because sublation is observed within consciousness itself regarding the world appearing as consciousness. This is the meaning [of the statement] "Now, therefore, the Self... and so forth, according to both scripture and reasoning. || 53 ||

[Objection: "Even so, let the world be simply different from both the existent and the non-existent; even then, the negation of absolute sublation is established. To this, he says: "No, because that [sublation] does not exist for that which is indeterminable. (54)

The appearance of such a thing as being indescribable in terms of both existence and non-existence is not tenable, because that [indescribable object] does not exist; the meaning is that a reality distinct from both existent and non-existent has never been established. The point is that conceptual construction must conform to what is actually observed. || 54 ||

Now, one might ask: "In that case, is it then *anyathākhyāti* (the theory of misapprehension) alone that is intended? He says, "No"—it is not *anyathākhyāti*, because it involves a contradiction with one's own words. (55)

Nor is it tenable that one thing appears in the form of another, for this contradicts its own statement. To say that the form of one thing in another is equivalent to a human horn—and yet, by the very word "appears," its manifestation is asserted—is a contradiction of one's own words regarding what is non-existent.

The meaning is that even by those who maintain the theory of "apprehension of what is otherwise" (anyathākhyāti), it is stated that there is no possibility of the appearance [of an object] without its being present. The point is that if the object is not present in front of one, its existence elsewhere cannot be the cause of its appearing. Nor should it be argued that in every case of the appearance of what is non-existent, the causal complex (samagrī) is impossible due to the absence of sensory contact (saṃnikarṣa) and so forth, and therefore some degree of existence must be required in certain instances; for it is possible for the stream of beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā) alone to serve as the cause of error. || 55 ||
Explaining the previously stated point that "there is no absolute sublation," he concludes his own established doctrine:
"The manifestation of the existent and the non-existent [occurs] due to sublation and non-sublation. (56)

The manifestation of both the existent and the non-existent (sadasatkhyāti) applies to all qualities and so forth. Why? Because of sublation and non-sublation. In that regard, there is non-sublation with respect to their own nature because all things are eternal; however, there is sublation with respect to their association [with other things] in relation to consciousness, just as redness and the like are [sublated] in the case of cloth and such. Likewise, there is sublation even by way of states for all transforming entities in relation to time and so forth—this is the meaning. Furthermore, "sublation" (bādha) is the state of being the object of a cognition of negation regarding a substrate already apprehended; whereas "non-existence" (asattva) is absolute absence.

That [substratum] too is the very nature of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Nor should it be argued that there is a contradiction between existence and non-existence, because there is no contradiction due to the difference in modes (*prakāra*). For instance, it is observed that redness exists as the form of the original object (*bimba*), yet does not exist as the form of the reflection (*pratibimba*) residing in the crystal. Or, for example, silver exists as the form found in the merchant's stall, yet does not exist as the form superposed upon the mother-of-pearl. As it has been said: "Even when the object is non-existent, transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*) does not cease;
for one who meditates on sense-objects, there is the arrival of misfortune, just as in a dream."

In this very way, existence and non-existence are not contradictory even with respect to different states (*avasthā*). For just as a tree or similar entity, while being existent through states such as full growth, is non-existent through states such as the sprout, so too primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the rest consist of both existence and non-existence. As it has been said:
"That which is the unmanifest cause is eternal and consists of both existence and non-existence;
that which the investigators of reality call *pradhāna* and *prakṛti*."
And this has been elaborated by us in the Brahmamīmāṃsābhāṣya and in the Yogavārtika; such is the direction [of our inquiry]. || 56 ||
This refutation is sufficient; now, this investigation of sound, which arose incidentally, is introduced at the end as a supplementary topic:
"Words are not of the nature of *sphoṭa*, because of [the impossibility of their] being perceived or not perceived. (57)

Grammarians (Yogins) accept that there exists an indivisible single word (*akhaṇḍaikapada*) called *sphoṭa*, which is distinct from the individual phonemes (*varṇa*), such as "jar" (*kalaśa*). It is like a whole (*avayavin*) such as a jar, which is distinct from its constituent parts such as the neck shaped like a conch (*kambugrīvā*). This specific sound, known as a word (*pada*), is called *sphoṭa* because it causes the meaning to burst forth clearly (*arthasphuṭīkaraṇāt*). That word is not established by valid means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*). Why? Because of both its perception and non-perception.

Is that sound perceived or not? In the first case, let the collection of phonemes itself—qualified by its specific sequence—be what conveys the meaning; what is the use of that superfluous [sphoṭa]? In the latter case, however, one who does not know the sphoṭa would have no capacity to convey the meaning; thus, the postulation of the sphoṭa is useless. This is the sense. 57.
The eternity of the Vedas was refuted previously; now he refutes the eternity of the phonemes as well:
"There is no eternity of sound, because it is perceived as something produced. (58)

The permanence of phonemes is not tenable on the strength of recognition such as "this is that very letter *ga*," because impermanence is established by the cognition "the letter *ga* has arisen. Furthermore, recognition refers to belonging to the same class (*tajjātīyatā*); otherwise, even jars and other objects would result in being permanent due to recognition. || 58 ||
He raises an objection:
"The manifestation of that which already possesses existence is like that of a jar by means of a lamp. (59)

Now, it might be argued that the object of our cognition is merely the manifestation (*abhivyakti*) of a word whose existence was already established prior to that time, brought about by sounds and other factors; and that manifestation is illustrated by the example of a jar being revealed by a lamp. (Verse 59)
He refutes this: "If [the opponent's position] is the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (satkāryavāda), then it is a case of proving what is already established (siddhasādhana). (60)

If "manifestation" is defined as the attainment of the present state by abandoning the future state, then the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is established; and since such permanence applies to all effects whatsoever, this results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Furthermore, if manifestation is said to be merely a cognition of that which already exists in the present, then it follows that even jars and other such things must be eternal; for the logical conclusion would be that through the operation of causes, it is the cognition itself that arises and becomes the object of perception—this is the intended meaning.
In order to present an objection regarding the non-duality of the self (*ātmādvaite*) that was not previously mentioned, the refutation of the non-duality of the self is commenced once again:
"There is no non-duality of the self, because its difference [from others] is perceived through its characteristic mark (*liṅga*). (61)

Although there are statements regarding the non-difference of the selves just as there are statements regarding their difference, nevertheless, non-duality—that is, absolute identity—is not established. The meaning is that difference alone is proven by the indicative marks found in passages concerning the ignorant and others, such as the abandonment or non-abandonment of *prakṛti*. For those indicative marks are not logically consistent with absolute identity. As for the statements of non-difference, they are consistent when understood as being in syntactic unity with scriptural texts on equality and so forth, having as their purport a non-difference characterized by the absence of distinct attributes (*vaidharmya*).
This is because it is determined that they have that as their purport through the impossibility of explaining them otherwise, namely, as the cessation of false egoism and the like. || 61 ||

An indicative mark (liṅga) that subverts [the opponent's view] has been stated regarding the non-difference of selves: "All this is indeed the Self; all this is indeed Brahman. However, he says that if there were non-duality of the Self with non-selves, even perception would be a subverting factor:
"Because perception also subverts [the claim] through the existence of multiple selves. (62)

Nor can there be non-duality of the Self with the manifold of objects of experience (*bhogyaprapañca*), even if that manifold is itself non-self, because this is contradicted by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). If the Self were non-different from all objects of experience, then there would be no difference between a jar and a cloth, since the jar and so forth would be non-different from the Self which is non-different from the cloth and so forth. And that [non-difference] is sublated by the direct perception that apprehends their difference; such is the meaning. (62)
Not by both; rather, by that very same [cause]. || 63 ||

The meaning is that there is no absolute non-difference between the self and the non-self, even though they are combined through repeated practice, for that same reason consisting of the two-fold cause. || 63 ||

[Objection: But in that case, what is the status of such scriptural passages as "The Self alone is this"? To this, he says: "For those lacking discrimination, [the scriptures] have another purpose in that regard. (64)

The meaning is that for those lacking discrimination—namely, undiscriminating persons—the statements regarding non-duality (advaita) are intended for something else; they are restatements (anuvāda) for the purpose of meditation (upāsanā). For in the world, due to a lack of discrimination between the body and the embodied, or between the object of enjoyment and the enjoyer, non-distinction is treated as a matter of common usage, such as "I am fair," "my soul is Bhadrasena," and so forth. Therefore, having restated that very usage, the Śruti prescribes meditation in that manner for those very people, for the sake of purifying the mind (sattva-śuddhi) and other goals.
For this very reason, the Śruti negates the selfhood of those objects of meditation in the state of ultimate reality: "That which the mind does not think, by which they say the mind is known..."
"Know that alone to be Brahman-hood, and not this which they worship," and so forth. || 64 ||
He states that even for those who maintain the doctrine of a single self (ekātmavāda), it is possible for there to be a material cause of the world:
"Neither the self, nor ignorance, nor both together can be the material cause of the world, because [the self] is devoid of attachment. (65)

Neither the pure Self alone, nor ignorance residing in the Self, nor both combined—as in the case of two potsherds—can possibly be the material cause of the world, because the Self is unattached (*asaṅga*). For it is only through that specific kind of conjunction called "attachment" (*saṅga*) that the transformation of substances occurs. Therefore, due to its unattached nature—and since the connection of ignorance with the Self has already been refuted on the grounds of that very unattachedness—the possibility of both being the material cause together is impossible for the same reason that each individually cannot be the material cause; this is the meaning.

If ignorance (*avidyā*) were held to be a substantial entity (*dravyarūpā*) residing in the person (*puruṣa*) or in space like the wind, then the non-duality of the Self (*ātmādvaita*) would be lost. Furthermore, if it were simply primordial nature (*prakṛti*), it would be a proof of what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). Moreover, such non-duality in the form of non-distinction (*avibhāga*) is indeed desired by us as well. Non-duality in the form of non-distinction is also taught by such scriptural passages as: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second" (*Chāndogya Upaniṣad* 6.2.1). This is because another scripture states: "But there is no second thing existing after it, distinct from it, that it might see. And so it has been said: "In the beginning, the object consisted of knowledge alone, one only, undifferentiated."
For one of these two is the object, and the primordial nature (prakṛti) consists of both.
"But knowledge is one particular state; that is designated as the Puruṣa. Thus [it is said].

It is undivided and free from conceptual construction. Therefore, the meaning of the Vedāntas is not an indivisible non-dual Self (*akhaṇḍātmādvaita*). Nevertheless, modern Vedāntins imagine that the very collection of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) presented here constitutes the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā. However, since that [position] is neither stated in the Brahma-sūtras and, on the contrary, contradicts them, we have already refuted it in that very place. In this regard, the siddhānta of the Brahma-mīmāṃsā remains unimpaired; rather, it should be remembered that only those meanings which appear plausible at first glance in the Vedāntas are being refuted. This is likewise the case with the subsequent sūtras. (65)

It has been established by us that the Self is of the nature of light. In this regard, [the author] refutes the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa) that bliss also is the very nature of the Self, based on the scriptural text, "Brahman is consciousness and bliss" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28):
"Not so, because if one [entity] were both bliss and consciousness, there would be a distinction between the two. (66)

A single substratum cannot possess the dual nature of both bliss (*ānanda*) and consciousness (*caitanya*). The meaning is that because there is no experience of pleasure at the time of experiencing pain, pleasure and the cognition thereof must be distinct. Furthermore, it cannot be said that pleasure is a particular kind of cognition, because the cognition of the self's own nature is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). For this very reason, it cannot be said that there is an obscuration of pleasure even at the time of experiencing consciousness; for if the indivisible [self] were obscured, the experience "I am experiencing pain" would be untenable.

For there is no division of parts within the Self such that, even when the aspect of bliss is veiled, the aspect of consciousness might still appear. Nor should it be argued that these [objections] are merely fallacious reasonings (asattarka) on the strength of scripture; for since the absence of bliss is also established by such scriptural passages as "neither bliss nor devoid of bliss," and by such Smṛti texts as "Brahman is neither suffering nor happiness, consisting of the past, the future, and the present," it is precisely reasoning that must be respected in this matter. || 66 ||
If it is asked, "In that case, what is the status of the fact that [liberation] consists of bliss? he says: "The status of bliss as consisting of the cessation of suffering is figurative. (67)

The meaning is that the word "bliss" (*ānanda*) used in the Veda with respect to the Self, which is essentially the cessation of suffering, is figurative. As it has been said: "Bliss is the transcendence of pain and pleasure. The scriptural statement that the Self is not "without bliss" refers to bliss conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*), just like the scriptural statements regarding its "truthful resolve" (*satya-saṅkalpatva*) and so forth. As for the inference made by some that the Self is of the nature of happiness because it is dear without any limiting adjunct—that is incorrect; for affection is possible even through the form of the absence of suffering. Furthermore, being the Self (*ātmatva*) is a cause of affection just as much as being happiness and so forth;
otherwise, affection would result even toward the happiness of others. || 67 ||
He states the reason for the figurative application:
"The praise of liberation is for the sake of those who are dull-witted. (68)
The meaning is that the Śruti praises liberation—which is the nature of the self consisting in the cessation of suffering—as being "happiness" for the sake of inspiring those of dull intellect.
To establish the aforementioned logical consistency of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he refutes the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding the all-pervasiveness of the mind (*manas*):
the mind is not all-pervasive, because it is an instrument (*karaṇa*) or because it is a sense-organ (*indriya*).
Like an axe and so forth, and like the eye and so forth. || 69 ||

The mind, which is the general internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa-sāmānya*), does not possess all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*). This is because it is an instrument (*karaṇatvāt*), like the sense of smell and other organs. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative restriction (*vyavasthita-vikalpa*). The meaning is that even by virtue of being a sense-organ (*indriyatvāt*), this third specific internal organ does not possess all-pervasiveness. Furthermore, the fact that cognition and so forth pervade the body is compatible only with a medium size (*madhyama-parimāṇa*). || 69 ||
Regarding the doubt that this [reason] is not probative, he states the supporting argument (anukūlatarka):
"Because it possesses activity, on account of the scriptural mention of its movement. (70)

The meaning is that, since the activity of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which serves as its limiting adjunct, is established by the scriptural accounts of the self's transition to another world, its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva) is not possible. || 70 ||
He also refutes the partlessness of the mind in order to establish its status as an effect:
"It is not partless, because it possesses conjunction, like a jar. (71)

The word "that" (tat) refers back to the "sense organ" (indriyam) mentioned in the preceding sūtra. The mind does not possess partlessness; rather, because it is simultaneously in contact with multiple sense organs, its meaning is that it possesses parts and has a medium dimension (madhyama-parimāṇa), like a jar. Furthermore, it should be understood that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) in its causal state is indeed atomic (aṇu). || 71 ||
He negates the eternality of the mind, time, and so forth:
"Everything other than primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa) is impermanent. (72)

This is easy to understand. Furthermore, that which exists in the causal state—the internal organ, ether, and so forth—is called *prakṛti* alone; however, the mind (*manas*) and other faculties are not so called, because they lack specific attributes such as determination (*vyavasāya*) and the like. || 72 ||
But surely it is said: "One should know Māyā as Prakṛti and the Great Lord as the wielder of Māyā;
by its constituent parts, this entire world is pervaded."

Thus, by such scriptural passages, both the person (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti) would also be impermanent due to their having parts. To this, he replies: "There is no acquisition of parts for the experiencers, because of the scriptural teaching of their partlessness. (73)
It is not logical for the individual soul or the primal matter (pradhāna) to possess parts, because of the scriptural teaching that they are partless:
"It is actionless, tranquil, faultless, and stainless."

The meaning is as stated by these and other such passages. Furthermore, the cited scripture teaches the relationship of part and whole (aṃśāṃśibhāva) through mere distinction, like that between space and water, or like that between the consciousnesses of father and son. || 73 ||
It has been stated that liberation is the cessation of suffering. To determine this, he refutes the views of others regarding that liberation:
"Liberation is not the manifestation of bliss, because [the self] is devoid of attributes. (74)

In the Self, there exists no attribute in the form of bliss nor in the form of manifestation; and since its own nature is eternal, it is not something to be accomplished by means of a causal instrument. Therefore, the meaning is that liberation is not the manifestation of bliss. || 74 ||
The destruction of the specific qualities is not like that. || 75 ||

Even the destruction of all specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is not liberation; it is for that very reason [not liberation], because [the self] is devoid of attributes (*nirdharmatva*). If it is objected: "In that case, why is the cessation of suffering alone called liberation, since even the absence of suffering is an attribute? We reply: No, because we state that the absence of suffering is a human goal (*puruṣārtha*) only by virtue of its connection with being an object of experience (*bhogyatā*). Thus, there is no attainment of specific qualities for one who is inactive. (76)

Even going to the world of Brahmā is not liberation, because there is no movement for the Self due to its being devoid of action; and if a subtle body (liṅgaśarīra) is admitted, then liberation is not possible—this is the meaning. || 76 ||
There is no eradication of the defilements of the aggregates because of faults such as momentariness. || 77 ||

The view held by the nihilists—that the self is merely momentary cognition, that its bondage consists in assuming the form of objects, and that liberation is the destruction of the coloring known as its latent impressions (vāsanā)—is also not tenable; the meaning is that because of defects such as momentariness, liberation would fail to be a goal for man (apuruṣārtha). || 77 ||
He refutes the notion of liberation for the nihilist alone: "There is no cessation of the outflows [for the nihilist], because of defects such as it not being a human goal. (78)

Even the total destruction of the self, which is of the nature of consciousness, cannot be liberation; for in the world, the annihilation of the self is not observed to be a human goal (puruṣārtha), and so forth—this is the meaning. || 78 ||
In the same way, emptiness also [is not established]. || 79 ||

The meaning is that even if the entire phenomenal world, which consists of the objects of knowledge, were to perish within knowledge, it would not constitute liberation, because such self-destruction is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha). || 79 ||
Since unions end in separations, there is no lasting gain even from the acquisition of place and other such things.

Even sovereignty over excellent lands, wealth, women, and so forth is not liberation; for it is heard [in scripture] that "unions end in separation, and life ends in death. Thus, because it is perishable, sovereignty is not liberation. || 80 ||
There is no connection with a part for that which has no parts. || 81 ||

The merging of the part—the individual soul (jīva)—into the whole—the Supreme Self (paramātman)—is not liberation. This is because of the stated reason that "all unions end in separation," and because [the opponent] does not accept the existence of a Lord (Īśvara). Furthermore, the meaning is that such a merging into one's own self is not a human goal (apuruṣārtha). || 81 ||
Even the yoga of the powers such as *aṇimā* must necessarily come to an end, just like other forms of yoga, because it is subject to transformation. || 82 ||

Even the connection with sovereign powers such as *aṇimā* (minuteness) and so forth is not liberation; for, just like the connection with other forms of sovereignty, that too is necessarily subject to cessation—this is the meaning. Likewise, even the attainment of the status of Indra and the other gods is not [liberation]. 83.
The meaning is that even the attainment of sovereignty over Indra and others is not liberation, because—like other forms of sovereignty—it is subject to decay. || 83 ||
Regarding what was stated—that the sense organs are derived from the ego (ahaṅkāra)—he refutes the opposing misconception therein:
"The sense organs do not have the elements as their material cause, because of the scriptural statement that they are derived from the ego. (84)
The interpretation is easy to understand; this has been explained previously as well. || 84 ||
With the intention that principles such as *śakti* and the rest also exist, he refutes the opponents' restriction of categories and their claim that liberation arises from knowledge of those alone:
"There is no fixed rule of six categories; there is no liberation through knowledge of them. (85)

The restriction of the Vaiśeṣikas that "the categories (padārthas) are only substance, quality, action, generality, particularity, and inherence," as well as their tenet that "liberation results from the knowledge of them," is unauthoritative. This is because [the categories] exceed [their list] by virtue of power (śakti) and so forth, and because primordial matter (prakṛti) exceeds the nine substances such as earth and the rest—this is the meaning. For the conventional usage of "earth" and so forth occurs solely on account of possessing smell and other qualities; yet smell and the rest do not exist in the state of equilibrium (sāmyāvasthā). Therefore, even the genus "earth-ness" and so forth, like "pot-ness" and the like, exists only in effects. As it has been said:
"There was neither day nor night, nor sky nor earth; there was neither darkness nor light, nor anything else.
At that time, there existed only the Pradhāna-Brahman, the Puruṣa, which is the singular object of perception through sound, intellect, and so forth. (85)
The same applies to the sixteen [fingers] and so forth as well. 86.

In the systems of Nyāya, Pāśupata, and others—such as those consisting of sixteen categories and so forth—there is no fixed rule, nor is liberation attained through knowledge of those categories alone; the meaning is that this is because they include additional categories in the manner already described. In our own system, however, there are only two eternal categories. There is a fixed rule that the categories common to both the eternal and the non-eternal are exactly twenty-five. This is because qualities (guṇa), actions (karman), universals (sāmānya), powers (śakti), and so forth, are all included within these twenty-five substances. || 86 ||

In order to establish that the five elements possess the effects previously described, he refutes the eternality of the atoms of earth and the other elements as accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others: "There is no eternality of the atoms, because scripture declares them to be effects. (87)

The atoms of earth and the other elements are not eternal; the meaning is that even those atoms are heard in scripture to be effects. Although we do not see that scriptural passage ourselves—due to its having been lost over time and so forth—it can nevertheless be inferred from the words of the Teacher (Ācārya) and from traditional recollection. As Manu says:
"The five [elements] which are remembered as consisting of minute, perishable particles—from these together with them, this entire universe arises in due succession."

"Of the five elements," meaning the five elements beginning with earth. Nor should it be said that in this sentence the word *aṇu* (atom) refers only to the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and so forth; for there is no evidence for such a restriction. Here, the word *aṇu* refers specifically to the atoms of the elements as conceived by the Vaiśeṣikas and others, and their eternity—which they maintain—is refuted by this aphorism. It does not, however, refute the eternity of the general category of substances possessing atomic dimension (*aṇuparimāṇa*). This is because the status of being atomic is established in accordance with the restlessness of the quality of *rajas*;
for if [the atom] were of medium dimension, its eternity would be untenable, and if it were all-pervading (*vibhu*), its activity would be impossible. || 87 ||
Now, one might ask: how can a partless atom possess the nature of a body? To this, he says:
"It is not partless, because it is an effect. (88)

The meaning is that the atoms of earth and the other elements cannot be partless, because their being effects—as established by scripture—is otherwise inexplicable. For this very reason, it was demonstrated by the venerable Vyāsa in the *Pātañjala-bhāṣya* that the subtle substances called *tanmātras* are indeed the constituent parts of the earthly and other [gross] elements; this is intended with reference to the ultimate limit of the diminution of earth and the other [elements]. Therefore, there is no contradiction even if the state of being an atom extends as far as *prakṛti*.

Although smell and the other qualities exist even in the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), nevertheless, because they are imperceptible, they do not serve as the determinants for [the classification of] earth-ness and so forth. This is because earth-ness and the rest are established solely through the manifest smell and other qualities. Therefore, the subtle elements are not earth and the others. Furthermore, it should be understood that the conventional designation "subtle element" applied to them is based solely on their being the direct causes of the gross elements. || 88 ||
He refutes the objection of the nihilist—that the direct perception of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is impossible because the perception of a substance is caused by its form—by stating:
"The restriction that perception [occurs] is not based on form. (89)

There is no rule that perceptibility arises from visible form (*rūpa*) alone; the meaning is that direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) can also occur through other qualities such as *dharma*. This is because there is no fault in the lack of restriction regarding manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*), as this is observed in the case of eye-salve (*añjana*) and the like. Therefore, the intention is that for external substances, only manifested visible form (*udbhūta-rūpa*) is the manifesting agent with respect to ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*). || 89 ||
Now, in response to the inquiry as to whether or not there exists a substance of atomic dimension, he establishes the determination of dimension:
"The fourfold division of dimensions does not [apply], because it is connected with two [of them]. (90)

The fourfold classification of dimension—as minute (*aṇu*), large (*mahat*), long (*dīrgha*), and short (*hrasva*)—does not exist; rather, only a twofold classification truly persists. This is because those [other dimensions] arise from the combination of two [primary ones], and it is only through the two dimensions of minuteness and largeness that the fourfold classification is possible. For "short" and "long" are merely internal subdivisions of the dimension of largeness.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of an infinite regress of dimensions such as those of a wheel and so forth. Therefore, in our system, the atomic dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇa*) of space should be understood—excluding the specific quality [of sound]—as residing in the fundamental causes of the elements and sense organs, namely the qualities of *sattva* and the rest. Elsewhere, however, there are dimensions ranging from the intermediate up to the ultimate great (*paramamahat*), as appropriate; and these are merely subdivisions of the quality of greatness (*mahattva*) itself. || 90 ||

The oneness of the *puruṣa* has been stated explicitly as a generality (*sāmānya*), whereas the oneness of *prakṛti* has been stated implicitly. To that end, he refutes the nihilist's misconception regarding generalities: "Because stability is impossible if there were impermanence, recognition belongs to the generality. (91)

Even though individuals are impermanent, that recognition which occurs through the connection with stability in the form "this is that very same one" belongs to the universal (*sāmānya*). The meaning is that such recognition has the universal alone as its object. || 91 ||
Therefore, he says that the denial of the universal is not tenable: "Hence, there is no denial of that. (92)
This is easy to understand. || 92 ||

[Objection: But surely recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) can be accounted for by non-existence (*abhāva*) itself in the form of the exclusion of that [other]; let that very thing be the meaning of the word "universal" (*sāmānya*). To this, he replies:
"The cognition of a positive entity (*bhāva*) does not have the nature of the exclusion of others. (93)

The meaning is that the universal does not consist in the nature of the non-cessation of the abstract suffix (bhāvapratyaya), such as "this is that very same [thing]. For otherwise, one would simply perceive it as "this is not a non-pot. Furthermore, the word "exclusion of others" (anyavyāvṛtti) must mean "exclusion of the non-pot" (aghaṭavyāvṛtti). In that case, since "non-potness" would be the state of being distinct from the universal of pot (ghaṭasāmānya), the very admission of a universal would result. || 93 ||
[Objection: "But surely recognition will be based on similarity. To this he replies:
"Similarity is not a distinct entity, because it is perceived through direct perception. (94)

The meaning is that there is no similarity existing apart from the commonality of parts and so forth, because it is perceived through direct perception itself as having the nature of a universal (sāmānya).
Anticipating the objection that "similarity may simply be an inherent power (śakti) and not a universal," he refutes it:
