"Or rather, it is the manifestation of its own inherent power, because it is perceived through its specific distinction. (95)

Furthermore, even the production of a specific inherent power (*svābhāvikī śakti*) in an object does not constitute similarity, because the apprehension of power is distinct from the apprehension of similarity. For the cognition of power does not depend upon the cognition of another substratum (*dharmin*), whereas the cognition of similarity, like the cognition of absence (*abhāva*), requires the cognition of a counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*); such is the distinction between the two cognitions. Moreover, the general power of a substratum is not similarity, for otherwise it would follow that a child possesses similarity to a youth even during his childhood stage.

However, it must be said that the specific power belonging to the young and so forth is what constitutes "similarity to the young. Thus, rather than postulating an infinite number of powers for each individual instance, it is more logical to postulate a single universal (sāmānya) common to all instances. || 95 ||
[Objection: Even so, let it be that the similarity of individual objects such as jars consists precisely in their having names such as "jar" and so forth. To this, he says:
"Nor even the relationship between the name and the named. (96)

The relationship between the name and the named, as previously described, is also not based on similarity; the meaning is that it arises from the perception of the specific distinction itself. This is because even one who does not know the relationship between the name and the named can have knowledge of similarity [based on that distinction]. 96.
Moreover:
"No, because the relation is not eternal and both [the related terms] are non-eternal. (97)

Since both the designation (*saṃjñā*) and the designated object (*saṃjñin*) are impermanent, their relationship cannot be permanent either. Therefore, how could there be a similarity between a present object and a past object by means of that [relationship]? This is the meaning. || 97 ||

[Objection: "But even if the related entities are non-eternal, the relation itself might still be eternal; what is the subverting argument (bādhaka) here? To this he replies: "No, therefore [the relation is not eternal], because it is sublated by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (dharmin). (98)

A relation is established only when there is occasional division [of the related entities]. Otherwise, since the matter would be accounted for by the very nature of the entities as they will be described later, there would be no occasion to postulate a relation. That occasional division is not possible if the relation were eternal; therefore, the meaning is that the relation is not eternal, because it is sublated by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends the relation. || 98 ||

[Objection: But in that case, an eternal inherence between two eternal entities—the quality and the qualified—would not be possible. To this he replies: "There is no inherence, because there is a lack of evidence. (99)
This is easy to understand. || 99 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that the perception of a qualified entity and the impossibility of accounting for a qualified cognition otherwise constitute the means of valid knowledge? To this, he says:
"In both cases, since there is an alternative explanation [for these], there is neither perception nor inference [as proof]. (100)

The meaning is that both perception and inference regarding the specific qualification (*vaiśiṣṭya*) [of inherence] are not valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) for inherence (*samavāya*), because they are established otherwise (*anyathāsiddha*) by the very nature of the thing itself. This is the point: just as the cognition of the specific qualification of inherence is accepted as being due to the very nature of inherence itself—out of fear of an infinite regress (*anavasthā*)—in that case, perception and inference are established otherwise. Likewise, let the cognition of the specific qualification of qualities, possessors of qualities, and so forth, also be accepted as being due to the very nature of the quality and so on.

Therefore, even in that case, perception and inference are established otherwise. [Objection: But in this way, even conjunction (*saṃyoga*) would not be established; for the cognition of a jar and so forth on a ground and so forth would also be established otherwise by their own nature alone. [Reply: No, because even at the time of disjunction, since the own-nature of the ground and the jar remains as it was, there would follow the undesirable consequence of a qualified cognition [of them as conjoined]. Furthermore, in the case of inherence (*samavāya*), there is never a disjunction of the inherent object from its own substrate; thus, this fault does not apply.

However, some argue that inherence (*samavāya*) is established otherwise (*anyathāsiddhi*) here through the relation of identity (*tādātmya*). That is not so; for there is merely a difference in terminology. Indeed, absolute identity cannot be asserted here, because the substrate (*guṇin*) exists even when the quality (*guṇa*) is absent, and because there is the cognition of distinction (*vaiśiṣṭya*). Rather, one must inevitably postulate a specific type of relation that governs the cognitions of both difference and non-difference. Thus, whether it is called "inherence" or "identity," the difference is merely nominal.

The relation, moreover, is indeed established as distinct from the two related entities. And if identity is said to be nothing other than the very nature [of the entities], then that is exactly what we have also stated; thus, the difference is merely verbal. || 100 ||

From the agitation of *prakṛti* arises the conjunction of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*; from that comes the action of something. Since every entity is momentary—perishing in the very place where it arises—an action inferred from conjunction with another location cannot be established. To this, he replies:
"Action is not merely inferable, because that which possesses the [result], being most proximate, is perceived directly. (102)

Action is not merely inferable from [the observation of] conjunction with another location; for even to a nearby observer situated close by, there is a perception of both the action and the agent through direct perception, as in the case of "the tree moves," and so forth. This is the meaning. || 101 ||

In the second chapter, only the various conflicting views regarding the body—such as its being composed of the five elements and so forth—were stated, but no definitive conclusion was established. Here, he refutes the opposing position:
"The body is not composed of the five elements, because it is impossible for many [elements] to serve as its material cause. (102)

In instances such as a jar or a word, it is not observed that multiple heterogeneous substances can serve as the material cause; therefore, the material cause must be of the same class (*sajātīya*). Furthermore, the other four elements serve as supporting factors (*upaṣṭambhaka*), and it is with this intention that the conventional designation "composed of the five elements" (*pāñcabhautika*) is used. Even though there is only a single material cause, he will state later that the earth alone is the material cause of the entire body.
Some maintain that the body is merely gross (*sthūla*); he refutes that by stating: "It is not necessarily gross," for there is also a subtle body (*ātivāhika*).
Because of its existence. || 103 ||
The state of being a body is the state of being the substratum of the sense faculties.
The six subtle parts of that form resort to the Umās;
therefore, the wise call that form of his "the body" (śarīra).

This is according to the statement of Manu. Furthermore, there is no rule that such a body must be gross and perceptible. Why? Because there exists another, subtle, elemental body—the *ātivāhika*—which is imperceptible. The meaning is that it is called *ātivāhika* because it carries this [individual] from one world to another by means of the *liṅga*. For it has already been stated that movement is impossible, like a painting and so forth, without a substratum consisting of the elements (*bhūta*). And this sūtra is intended merely for clarification.

Furthermore, it should be understood that the subtle body (*liṅga*) constitutes the "body" [of the self] by virtue of being the locus of experience or the locus for the reflection of the *puruṣa*. And the proof for the existence of the transportive body (*ātivāhika-śarīra*) is as follows:
"The *puruṣa*, the inner self, the size of a thumb, is eternally seated in the hearts of men."

"By force he drew out the person the size of a thumb from the waters"—so state the Śruti and Smṛti. For it is not possible for the subtle body (liṅga-śarīra), which pervades the entire body, to be inherently the size of a thumb. Therefore, by implication, the support [of that body] is established as being the size of a thumb.

Just as a lamp, although it pervades the entire house, has the form of a flame because the subtle portion consisting of oil, the wick, and so forth—along with the condensed earthly element upon the wick—takes the form of a flame; in the very same way, although the subtle body (liṅgadeha) pervades the physical body, its measurement of one thumb's breadth is to be inferred from the fact that the subtle elements have the measurement of one thumb's breadth. || 103 ||
The sense organs were previously stated to be distinct from the globes (golaka). To establish that, he refutes the view that the sense organs illuminate objects without reaching them:
"The sense organs do not illuminate what they have not reached, because either [the object] is not reached at all, or else everything would be reached. (104)

The sense organs do not manifest objects with which they are not in contact, because they have not reached them; for it is observed that lamps and the like do not illuminate what they have not reached. Furthermore, if they were to illuminate what they have not reached, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that they would illuminate all things, including those that are obstructed and so forth. Therefore, the implication is that the sense organ must be something distinct from the physical globe (golaka) in order to establish a connection with distant objects such as the sun. Moreover, the capacity of the instruments (karaṇa) to manifest objects occurs only by way of presenting the object to the Puruṣa, because they are inherently insentient (jaḍa), just as a mirror manifests a face [only by reflecting it].
Alternatively, the very apprehension of the reflection of the object is what constitutes the manifestation of the object. || 104 ||

An objection is raised: "In that case, it is more logical that the eye is composed of light (taijasa), because it is observed that light alone travels rapidly to a distance in the form of rays. He refutes this doubt:
"The eye is not composed of light merely because of the travel [of rays]; its nature as light is established through its function (vṛtti). (105)

One should not say that the eye is composed of light (taijasa) on the grounds that the departure of light is observed [from it]. Why? Because even if it were not composed of light, its departure would be possible through a modification of its function (vṛtti), just as in the case of the vital breath (prāṇa). For just as the vital breath, without leaving the body, departs to some distance outside the tip of the nose by means of its function called "breathing" (prāṇana), so too the eye—even though it is not a substance composed of light—would instantly reach a distant object by means of a specific modification of its function called "activity" (vṛtti), without leaving the body. What is the proof for this? He says:
"The existence of the function is established from the mark (liṅga) of the illumination of the object upon contact. (106)
This is easy to understand. || 106 ||
He demonstrates the nature of the *vṛtti* (functioning) so that it may proceed even without abandoning the body:
"The *vṛtti* proceeds toward another principle by means of its parts and qualities for the sake of establishing a connection. (107)

The meaning is this: because it "creeps" (*sarpati*) for the sake of establishing a connection, the function (*vṛtti*) of the eye and other organs is neither a part—like a spark from a divided whole—nor a quality—like color and so forth. Rather, the function is something distinct from both parts and qualities, being a constituent portion of that [organ]. For if there were a division [of the organ], a connection with the sun and other objects through that [function] would not be possible; and if it were a quality, the action known as "creeping" would be untenable.

By this, it is established that the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) is also a transformation in the form of a substance, like the flame of a lamp, which assumes the form of an object due to its transparency, just like a clean cloth. (107)

Now, if the *vṛttis* (mental modifications) are indeed substances (*dravya*), how can they be designated as "modifications" (*vṛtti*) on account of being qualities (*guṇa*) such as desire and so forth? To this, he says:
"There is no restriction regarding substance, because of their connection with that [the Self]. (108)

There is no rule that *vṛtti* (function) is exclusively substance (*dravya*). Why? Because of its connection with it—that is, because the etymological meaning exists within that function. For this word is etymologically derived from the root *vṛt*, meaning "to exist" or "to live. And "living" is an activity that causes one's own maintenance, according to the grammatical rule: *jīva* [is used] in the senses of strength and sustaining life. This is also evident from common usage such as "the livelihood of a Vaiśya" or "the livelihood of a Śūdra. In that regard, just as the intellect lives by means of a function consisting of substance, so too does it live through desires; therefore, those [desires] are also functions. The meaning is that by the complete cessation of these, the mind dies. || 108 ||

Since it is also heard that the sense organs are composed of material elements (bhautika), one might occasionally suspect that the arrangement of the Vedas varies according to the differences between specific worlds; to this, he says:
"Even though there is a difference of location, there is no restriction [regarding their origin] such that they must have a different material cause, as is the case with us and others. (109)

The sense organs do not have as their material cause anything other than the *ahaṅkāra*, even due to differences in location such as the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*) and so forth; rather, there is a rule that for all beings—just like those of us who dwell on the earth—their origin is from the *ahaṅkāra*. This is because scripture teaches that it is only this subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), despite its movement through different locations, that transmigrates. || 109 ||
But in that case, how is the scriptural statement regarding its being composed of the elements (bhūta) to be explained? To this he says:
"The designation of that [Self] as such is due to the designation of its instrumental cause. (Sūtra 3.1.10)

Even when something is merely an instrumental cause (*nimitta*), one may employ the designation of being a material cause (*upādāna*) by intending to emphasize its predominance, as in the expression, "fire from fuel. Therefore, the meaning is that there is a designation of the elements as the material cause. For indeed, the sense organs such as the eyes arise from the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) which is permeated by them, only through the support of the elements such as fire; just as fire arises from light that is permeated by it through the support of the earth element. The scriptural passage, "The mind, my dear, consists of food," and the reasoning stated therein serve as the authority for this. Now, he incidentally determines the specific characteristics pertaining to the gross body:
There is no fixed rule [regarding the origin of bodies], which may be born from heat, from an egg, from a womb, from a sprout, through mere volition, or as a result of perfection. || 111 ||

Indeed, for these beings, there are only three types of origins: egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), viviparous (*jīvajam*), and soil-born (*udbhijjam*). This statement in the Śruti is made with the intention of indicating that bodies are generally of three kinds, such as those beginning with the egg-born; it is not, however, an absolute rule, because the body is actually of six kinds, including those born from heat (*ūṣmajā*) and so forth. Among these, "heat-born" refers to biting insects and the like; "egg-born" refers to birds, snakes, and the like; "womb-born" refers to humans and the like; "soil-born" refers to trees and the like; and "will-born" refers to Sanaka and others.
The innate ones (*sāṃsiddhika*) are those born from the attainment of mantras, asceticism, and so forth; for example, the body produced from the body of Raktabīja and others. (111)
By means of the very same reflection mentioned previously, he states specifically, as a corollary, that the body has earth alone as its material cause:
"In all [bodies], earth is the material cause; because it is the non-common [cause], there is designation by that [name], as before. (112)

In all bodies, earth alone is the material cause, because of its predominance—due to its superiority through qualities such as preponderance. Here too, the designation of being composed of five, four, or other elements is as before; the meaning is that it is by way of mere support, just as the sense organs are said to be elemental. || 112 ||
Now, one might object: "Since the vital breath (prāṇa) is predominant in the body, let the vital breath alone be the initiator of the body. To this, he says:
"The vital breath is not the initiator of the body, because its establishment [as such] is due to the power of the sense organs. (113)

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not the initiator of the body. This is because, through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), it is established that the vital breath arises solely from a specific power of the sense organs (*indriya*); that is to say, without the sense organs, the vital breath cannot persist. The underlying point is this: the vital breath, which consists of the functions of the instruments (*karaṇa*), does not remain when separated from those instruments. Therefore, since the vital breath is absent in a dead body due to the absence of the instruments, the vital breath is not the initiator of the body. || 113 ||
Now, if it be argued that since the vital breath (prāṇa) is not the cause of the body's form, the body might be produced even without the vital breath, he says in response:
"The construction of the abode of experience occurs because of the presiding presence of the enjoyer; otherwise, there would be the consequence of putrefaction. (114)

The formation of the body, which is the locus of experience for the living being who enjoys [the fruits of karma], occurs solely through the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa). Otherwise, in the absence of the activity of the vital breath, there would be the undesirable consequence of the semen and blood putrefying, as in the case of a dead body; this is the meaning. Thus, by means of specific activities such as the circulation of the nutritional essence (rasa), the vital breath is the efficient cause (nimittakāraṇa) of the body because it sustains it; this is the intended sense. || 114 ||

Now, it might be argued that the status of being a locus (adhiṣṭhānatva) is possible only for the vital breath (prāṇa), because it possesses activity, and not for the living being (prāṇin), because he is immutable (kūṭastha) and because there would be no purpose for an inactive being to act as a locus; to this, he says: "The presiding over [the breath] by the master is not absolute, as in the case of [control exercised] through a servant. (115)

The presiding presence (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the conscious Lord, in the form of activity during the creation of the body, does not occur directly and exclusively; rather, it occurs through the medium of the servant that is the vital breath (*prāṇa*). This is the meaning: as in the case of a king’s construction of a city. Thus, it is established that while the vital breath possesses direct presiding power, the person’s presiding power over it exists merely through conjunction with the vital breath. The same applies to potters and others in the making of jars and so forth. However, this is the distinction: in those cases, there is also the employment of the conscious intellect (*buddhi*) and other faculties, because their creation is preceded by deliberation (*buddhipūrvaka*).

Although the construction of the body occurs solely through the presiding presence of the vital breath (prāṇa), nevertheless, the conjunction with a living being is also required by way of that vital breath. With the intention that the body is constructed by the vital breath specifically for the sake of the person's purpose, it is said: "due to the presiding presence of the enjoyer. || 115 ||

It was stated previously that liberation is the cessation of suffering for the primary principle (pradhāna). In response to the objection of others—asking how the Self can be eternally liberated given the perception of bondage—the author says the following in order to establish its eternal liberation:
"In samādhi, deep sleep, and liberation, there is the nature of Brahman. (116)

Samādhi is the state of non-cognitive [samādhi] (*asamprajñāta*). Deep sleep here refers to complete deep sleep, and liberation refers to bodiless isolation (*videhakaivalya*). In these states, the Puruṣas possess the nature of Brahman; due to the dissolution of the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), the limitations imposed by its adjuncts (*upādhi*) disappear, and they abide in the fullness of their own essential nature. This means that just as the space within a jar becomes whole upon the destruction of the jar, so it is here. This has been stated: "Upon the cessation of that [fluctuation], being free from the coloring [of objects], one is established in oneself."

And thus, the very nature of persons is Brahman-hood itself, because it is not adventitious, just as whiteness is the nature of a crystal. However, at the time of connection with the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), there arises the conceit of limitation through manifestation as a limited form of consciousness; likewise, by virtue of the reflection of those modifications, there appears as if there were impurity such as suffering. All of this is merely conditional (*aupādhika*), because it follows the presence and absence of the causes known as limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just like the redness of a crystal. This is the intended meaning.

And likewise, the *Yogasūtra* states: "In other cases, there is conformity with the mental modifications" (*vṛttisārūpyam itaratra*). Furthermore, in our own system, the word *brahman* denotes the universal consciousness that is free from limitations, impurity, and so forth caused by adjuncts (*upādhi*); it should be distinguished from its usage in the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā*, where it denotes merely the Person characterized by sovereignty (*aiśvarya*). On this point, these verses are spoken for the sake of the student’s proficiency: "When the sky of consciousness (*cidākāśa*) has not yet manifested, the intellect (*dhī*), wandering here and there in various forms along with its manifestations, reveals the wandering consciousness itself."
In reality, however, the sky of consciousness is eternally full and of a single nature;
it does not perceive objects in those regions devoid of mental modifications because of the absence of anything visible there.
For the activity of the person is indeed perceivable by the eye as having form, and not otherwise;
since that [activity] does not exist during meditative absorption and similar states, the person is then complete [in its true nature]. (116)
In that case, what is the distinction between deep sleep (suṣupti) and meditative absorption (samādhi) on one hand and liberation (mokṣa) on the other? To this he says:
"In two cases there is a seed; in the other, its absence. (117)

The meaning is that in the two states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is "with seed" (*sabīja*), meaning accompanied by the seeds of bondage; whereas in liberation (*mokṣa*), there is the absence of such seeds—this is the distinction. Now, one might object: if the seeds of bondage exist during these two types of meditative absorption, then because of that very limitation, how can there be Brahman-hood? We say no. This is because the seeds of bondage, such as karma and so forth, at those times reside only within the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), namely the intellect (*buddhi*), and not in the conscious self (*cetana*). For they do not reflect upon the Puruṣa. It has been stated more than once that in states such as waking, bondage is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), resulting from the reflection of the modifications of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) [upon the self].

If it is objected: "In the *Pātañjala* [Yoga-sūtras] and its commentary (*bhāṣya*), asamprajñāta-yoga is said to be 'seedless' (*nirbīja*); how then can it be called 'with seed' (*sabīja*) here?"—it is not so. For the statement there that it is "seedless" is made with the intention that the destruction of the seeds occurs gradually within asamprajñāta. Otherwise, if every individual instance of asamprajñāta were seedless, the impossibility of re-emergence (*vyutthāna*) from that state would follow. || 117 ||
He refutes the objection of the nihilist: "Surely deep sleep and meditative absorption are observed [in experience], but what is the proof for liberation?"—[by stating]:
"Because all three are observed, just as the two are; it is not that there are only two. (118)

Since liberation is both seen and inferred by means of the analogy of deep sleep (*suṣupti*) within the various states of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it is not the case that the state of being Brahman which exists during deep sleep and so forth is abandoned due to the influence of defects such as attachment residing in the mind. If that defect is destroyed by knowledge, then a stable state similar to deep sleep and so forth comes to be; that very state is liberation. || 118 ||

[Objection: Granted that even when the seed known as latent impression (*vāsanā*) exists, due to the obstruction of that impression by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*) and so forth, let there be no mental modification (*vṛtti*) bearing the form of an object during *samādhi*. However, it is logical that the state of being Brahman should occur in deep sleep (*suṣupti*). To this, he says: "By the latent impression, there is no manifestation of its own object; even when there is a conjunction with defects, the secondary cause does not subvert the primary cause. (119)

Just as in the case of dispassion (*vairāgya*), so too when there is the presence of the defect of sleep (*nidrā-doṣa*), there occurs no manifestation of its own object nor any recollection of its own domain by means of the latent impression (*vāsanā*). The meaning is that it is not possible for a latent impression—which is subordinate to the cause—to overcome a more powerful defect such as sleep. The point is that only a more powerful defect renders a weak latent impression incapable of performing its own function. || 119 ||

It was stated in the third chapter that the maintenance of the body by one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) is due to a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāraleśa*). Regarding this, an objection is raised: "The enjoyment of even a single object, as seen in those like us, is observed to occur constantly for one who is liberated while living; this is untenable. For, upon the initial production [of knowledge], the previous impressions are destroyed, and no other impression arises—just as [no new] karma arises—due to its being obstructed by [perfect] knowledge. To this, he replies: "A single impression effects the action, but there is not a distinct impression for every individual action, because that would entail the fault of postulating too many [impressions]. (120)

The single *saṃskāra* by which the enjoyment of a body as a deity or other [being] has been initiated is itself the one that brings to completion that commenced enjoyment to be accomplished by that body. And that [saṃskāra], like karma, is destroyed only by the completion of the enjoyment; it is not the case that there is a multiplicity of *saṃskāras* for every action or every manifestation of enjoyment, because that would entail the fault of postulating an excessive number of entities (*kalpanā-gaurava*). This principle should be understood to apply even in the case of the spinning of a potter’s wheel: there is only a single *saṃskāra* called momentum (*vega*) that persists until the completion of the rotation. (120)

It has been stated that there exists a body born from a sprout (*udbhijja*). In response to the objection of the nihilists (*nāstika*) that such a thing lacks the status of a "body" because it lacks external cognition, he refutes this:
"There is no rule [that a body] must possess external cognition. (121)

Even for trees, shrubs, creepers, medicinal herbs, forest giants, grasses, climbing plants, and so forth, there is the state of being the enjoyer and the locus of enjoyment, as previously described. 122.

There is no rule that only that which possesses external cognition is a body; rather, one must consider that even trees and the like, though possessing internal consciousness, are bodies because they serve as the locus of experience for an enjoyer. For, just as previously stated—that the putrefaction of human and other bodies occurs in the absence of the presiding enjoyer—in the same way, withering and so forth occur in the bodies of trees and the like. This is the meaning.

And thus says the Śruti: "When the living self (jīva) leaves even one branch of this [tree], then that branch withers," and so forth. Although the portion beginning with "there is no restriction regarding external cognition" (*na bāhyabuddhiniyama*) could have been treated as a separate sūtra, these two sūtras should be explained as a single unit in this very manner. It should be understood, however, that the division into separate sūtras was made out of fear of excessive length. (121–122)
And because of the Smṛti. || 123 ||
Through defects of action born of the body, a man goes to the state of stationary beings;
through those of speech, to the state of birds and wild animals; and through those of the mind, to the state of the lowest castes.
The meaning of such Smṛti passages as these is that trees and other such things possess both the capacity for experiencing and the state of being a locus for experience. || 123 ||
[Objection: But if this were so, would it not follow that even trees and the like possess consciousness, thereby resulting in the production of merit and demerit in them? To this he says:
"The qualification for performing ritual action does not arise from the body alone, because of scriptural statements regarding [the soul's] distinctness. (124)

The individual soul (jīva) does not possess the capacity for the production of merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) by means of the body alone. Why? Because of the scriptural teaching of its distinction (vaiśiṣṭya). The meaning is that its qualification [for ritual action] is heard in scripture only as being distinguished by a body originating from Brahman. || 124 ||
Demonstrating that the qualification for dharma occurs precisely through the differentiation of the body, he states the threefold nature of the body:
"The arrangement of the three is threefold: the body of action (karmadeha), the body of experience (upabhogadeha), and the body of both (ubhayadeha). (125)

The meaning is that for all living beings—whether superior, inferior, or middling—there is a threefold division of the body: the *karmadeha* (body of action), the *bhogadeha* (body of enjoyment), and the *ubhayadeha* (body of both). Among these, the *karmadeha* belongs to the supreme sages (*paramarṣis*), the *bhogadeha* to Indra and others, and the *ubhayadeha* to the royal sages (*rājarṣis*). This is the primary threefold division; otherwise, everything would result in being merely a *bhogadeha*. (125)
He states the fourth type of body as well: "There is no body whatsoever for one who possesses latent dispositions. (126)

"One should know that *anuśaya* is the object of aversion in the states of remorse and repentance"—from this statement, *anuśaya* means dispassion (*vairāgya*). The meaning is that for those who are dispassionate, this body is distinct from these three [states], as in the case of Dattātreya, Jaḍabharata, and others. || 126 ||
In order to establish the aforementioned absence of a Lord (īśvara), he refutes the permanence of knowledge, will, and action as accepted by the opponent:
"There is no permanence of intellect and so forth, even though the substratum is not distinct [from the individual], just like fire. (127)

In this context, "intellect" (buddhi) refers to the function known as determinative cognition (adhyavasāya). Thus, even though others accept [intellect] as an attribute (upādhi) of God (Īśvara) residing in a specific substratum, it lacks eternality. This is because, by means of the example of the intellect of persons like us, one can infer the non-eternality of all intellects, desires, and so forth. The meaning is that just as the non-eternality of the veiling light is inferred by means of the example of ordinary fire, so too is the case here. || 127 ||

Let alone for now the permanence of knowledge, desire, and so forth; their substratum, namely the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of God, is itself unestablished because God himself is unestablished. To this he says:
"And because of the non-establishment of the substratum" (128).
This is easy to understand. || 128 ||

Now, one might object: "In that case, how could omniscience and other such qualities capable of creating the cosmic egg and so forth even be conceived as produced, since such sovereignty is not observed in the world through the adjuncts of yoga? To this, he says:
"The perfections of yoga, like the perfections attained through herbs and the like, are not to be denied. (129)

The meaning is that, by the example of the attainment of medicinal herbs and so forth, the supernatural powers (*siddhis*) born of yoga—such as *aṇimā* and the rest—which are useful for creation and other purposes, are likewise accomplished.
Because it is contrary to the attainment of the true Self (*puruṣa*), he refutes the proponent of the doctrine that consciousness belongs to the elements (*bhūtacaitanyavādin*):
"There is no consciousness in the elements, because it is not observed in them individually, nor even when they are combined."
And also in the case of a composite [whole]. || 130 ||

The meaning is that even in the state of being combined, consciousness does not exist within the five elements, because consciousness is not observed in each one individually at the time of their separation. This has been stated in the third chapter as part of our own established doctrine (*svasiddhānta*). Here, it is stated for the purpose of refuting the views of others (*paramata*), so there is no fault of redundancy (*paunaruktya*). At the conclusion of the chapter on repetition (*vīpsā*), those who are false disputants (*kuvādinaḥ*) speak matters contrary to our own established doctrine.
In the fifth [chapter], having refuted those [opposing views], his own established doctrine is firmly established. || 1 ||
Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Conquest of Opposing Positions," in the commentary on the *Kāpila Sāṅkhyapravacana* composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu. || 5 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter. || 6 ||

Having set forth the entire meaning of the treatise through four chapters, and having established it in the fifth chapter by refuting the positions of opponents, he now concludes by summarizing that very essence of the treatise with the sixth chapter. For when a detailed expansion known as a *tantra* is made of matters already stated, a firmer understanding—free from doubt and error—arises in the disciples. Therefore, according to the maxim of "driving in a post," and because of the presentation of arguments not previously mentioned, repetition is not a fault here.
"There is a self, because there is no proof for its non-existence. (1)

The person is already established in a general sense by the very fact that he is perceived as thinking "I know"; since there is no subverting evidence (bādhaka-pramāṇa) to the contrary, the meaning is that only the discrimination of him [from the body and so forth] remains to be accomplished. || 1 ||
Regarding that isolation (*viveka*), he states two proofs by means of two aphorisms:
"This [Self] is distinct from the body and so forth, because of its diversity. (2)

This Self, the seer, is absolutely distinct from [the categories] beginning with the body and ending with primordial nature (*prakṛti*), because of its diversity; that is to say, because of the difference in properties such as being subject to transformation (*pariṇāmitva*) versus being immutable (*apariṇāmitva*). Primordial nature and the others are established by perception, inference, and scripture as being exclusively subject to transformation; however, the immutability of the Puruṣa is inferred from the fact that it is an object that is always known [by the intellect]. For instance, it is postulated on the basis of the resulting evidence that the eye has only color-and-form (*rūpa*) as its object, and not any other thing, even though the conditions for contact are equal.

Rather, another object becomes an object of experience for the *puruṣa* only by being mounted upon a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), and not by itself; otherwise, there would be the consequence of everything being perceived at all times. Furthermore, those modifications of the intellect do not remain unperceived; for if one were to admit the existence of knowledge, desire, pleasure, and so forth while they remain unknown, then—just as with a jar or other objects—there would arise doubts and the like regarding them as well, in such forms as "Do I know myself or not? or "Am I happy or not? Since these [mental states] are always known, it follows that their witness, the conscious principle (*cetana*), is unchanging (*apariṇāmī*).

If the intellect were subject to transformation like the conscious self, then at times, due to a transformation into blindness, there would be the occurrence of doubt and so forth, because even though the activity of the intellect exists, it would not be perceived. In this way, the previously mentioned collection of dissimilarities, such as being for the sake of another or not being for the sake of another, should also be understood. ||2||
Also because of the designation by the genitive case. || 3 ||

The self is distinct from the body and other such things, even because of the use of the genitive case by the wise in expressions such as "this body is mine" and "this intellect is mine. The meaning is that the genitive case would be untenable if there were absolute non-difference. As it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa:
"Are you this head, or is the head yours? Likewise, are you the belly, or is the belly yours? Are you indeed the feet and so forth, O King, or do these belong to you?"
"O King, having become distinct from all your constituent parts and remaining thus, reflect skillfully upon this: 'Who am I? Thus it is said.

Nor should it be argued that expressions such as "I am fat" also constitute a designation of the wise; for, since they are not sublated by scripture, such usage is explained as being merely figurative, like saying "Bhadrasena is my self. || 3 ||

[Objection: "But surely this [expression] may be like such designations as 'consciousness of the person,' 'the head of Rāhu,' or 'the body of a stone statue. To this, he replies: Not so, because, unlike the case of the stone statue, it is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (dharmin). (4)

This use of the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhīvyapadeśa) is not like the expression "the body of a stone statue" (*śilāputrasya śarīram*) and so forth. In cases such as the stone statue, it is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) because it is sublated by the very means of valid cognition that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇena*). However, in the designation "the body is the same [as the self]," there is no sublation by valid cognition; the meaning is that only the identity of the body and the self is what is sublated. As for the prohibition of the sense of "mine-ness" (*mamakāra*) found in the scriptures, the intention is that it refers only to the unreality of that notion—viewing it as mere conventional speech (*vācārambhaṇamātra*) due to its own inherent impermanence.

Regarding the statement "consciousness belongs to the person" (puruṣasya caitanyam), there is also sublation by the means of knowledge that apprehends the substratum (dharmigrāhakamānabādha). This is because, when the self is established as distinct from the body and so forth due to the fear of infinite regress and the principle of parsimony (lāghava), it is understood to have consciousness as its very nature. || 4 ||

Having ascertained the Puruṣa as distinct from the body and so forth, he ascertains its liberation: "The state of having accomplished all that was to be done results from the absolute cessation of suffering. (5)
This is easy to understand. || 5 ||
But surely, since pleasure also ceases with the cessation of suffering, it cannot be the goal of man because the gain and loss are equal; to this he replies:
"As there is no affliction for a person from suffering, so there is no longing from pleasure. (6)

In the case of causality by way of being an object (*viṣayavidhayā*), two ablative cases are used. Here, "affliction" (*kleśa*) refers to aversion (*dveṣa*). Just as aversion toward suffering is more powerful, desire for pleasure is not equally powerful; rather, it is weaker in comparison. Thus, even while overriding the desire for pleasure, aversion toward suffering generates the very wish for the cessation of suffering; therefore, there is no equality between the gain and the loss. As it has been said:
"Out of fear of the rejection of one's request, a seeker maintains neutrality even toward a desired object."
However, that engagement in trivial pleasures even while beholding the sufferings of hell and other realms occurs solely through the power of defects such as passion (rāga). || 6 ||
He states that the cessation of suffering alone is the human goal because suffering is far more abundant than happiness: "Nowhere is anyone happy. (7)

The meaning is that, among the infinite number of grasses, trees, animals, birds, humans, and so forth, only a very few—such as humans and gods—attain happiness; "iti" is used here in the sense of a reason. || 7 ||

Even that pleasure, being occasional and localized like food mixed with honey and poison, is to be rejected by those who possess discernment; thus he says: "Even that is variegated with suffering," for the discriminating ones cast it into the category of suffering. (8)

The meaning is that even that pleasure mentioned in the previous sūtra is mixed with suffering; therefore, those who discern between pleasure and pain cast it into the category of suffering. This has been stated in the Yoga Sūtra: "Because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict among the functions of the guṇas, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person."
In the Viṣṇupurāṇa as well:
"O Maitreya! Whatever object arises that is pleasing to men, that very thing becomes the seed of the tree of suffering. (8)
He refutes the view that the mere cessation of suffering is not the goal of human life (*puruṣārtha*), but rather that it must be colored by pleasure:
"If it is argued that [the cessation of suffering] is not a *puruṣārtha* because there is no acquisition of pleasure, we say no, because of its twofold nature. (9)

If it is argued that because happiness is absent, the absence of suffering known as liberation (mokṣa) cannot be a human goal (puruṣārtha), we say no; for human goals are of two kinds—meaning they are of two types, namely, by way of being happiness and by way of being the absence of suffering. Indeed, the aspirations of people are seen to be distinct: "May I be happy" and "May I not be miserable. || 9 ||
He raises an objection: "The self possesses no qualities, because of scriptural texts such as its being unattached. (10)

Now, is it not the case that the qualitylessness of the Self—the state of being eternally devoid of all qualities such as pleasure, pain, and delusion—is already established? This follows from the scriptural teaching of its "unattached" nature (*asaṅgatva*) and from the hearing of the absence of contact with the causes of modification; for without that [contact], modifications known as qualities cannot possibly arise. Therefore, the cessation of suffering also cannot logically constitute a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). If it is argued: "Let there be modification by itself, even without contact," we say no. Fire does not burn for the sake of fire, nor do waters moisten for the sake of water;
because a substance indeed does not bring about a modification of that very same substance.

Furthermore, if [the self] were itself subject to modification, liberation would not be possible at all, because there would be the consequence of bondage again through its own modification by delusion. Thus it is said.
And so it is said in the Kūrma Purāṇa:
"If the self were by its very nature impure, unclean, and subject to modification, there would be no liberation for it even through hundreds of future births. (10)
He provides the solution: "Even though it is the property of another, its establishment occurs due to non-discrimination. (11)

The meaning is that although qualities such as pleasure and pain are attributes of the mind (*citta*), they [come to the Puruṣa] through the medium of the conjunction between *prakṛti* and the Puruṣa. This has been established in the first chapter, and also in the third chapter sūtra: "The cause is non-discrimination; there is no loss of what is perceived. Thus, just as redness appears in a crystal, suffering exists in the Puruṣa by way of reflection; therefore, the cessation of that [suffering] alone is the goal of the Puruṣa (*puruṣārtha*). Since experience consists precisely in the connection with suffering via the medium of reflection, it is by way of reflection alone that suffering is to be abandoned. || 11 ||
When the question arises—"The bondage of the qualities (guṇas) to the person has non-discrimination as its root; but what is this non-discrimination?"—he says:
"Non-discrimination is beginningless, for otherwise two defects would follow. (12)

Non-discrimination (*aviveka*) is a cognition that does not grasp the non-connection [between the Self and the mind] and which has both as its object. It is a property of the mind (*citta*) that is beginningless by way of a continuous flow and persists in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) during dissolution (*pralaya*). Otherwise, if it were beginningless, two faults would follow. For if it were beginningless, then if it arose spontaneously, bondage would result even for one who is liberated. Furthermore, if it were produced by karma and so forth, then in seeking another non-discrimination as the cause of that karma and so forth, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This is the meaning.

And this non-discrimination, being of the nature of a mental modification, appears as if it were an attribute of the Puruṣa by way of reflection; therefore, it is the cause of bondage for the Puruṣa, as has been stated previously and will be stated again. || 12 ||
If it is argued that what is beginningless must therefore be eternal, he says in response:
"It cannot be eternal like the Self; otherwise, there would be no cessation. (13)

It is not eternal, indivisible, and beginningless like the Self; rather, it is beginningless in the form of a continuous stream. The meaning is that otherwise, the destruction of a beginningless entity would be impossible. || 13 ||
Having stated the cause of bondage, he states the cause of liberation:
"Its [bondage's] being destructible by a specific cause is like that of darkness. (14)

Regarding this non-discrimination (aviveka), which is the cause of bondage, its destruction is brought about by that specific cause of destruction which is discrimination (viveka), just as darkness is destroyed by light. For darkness is destroyed only by its specific counteragent, light, and not by any other means; this is the meaning. As it is stated in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa: "O Viprarṣi! Ignorance is like blinding darkness, and that which arises from the senses is like a lamp;
but knowledge born of discrimination is like the sun. (14)
He also states the evidence for this specific rule—that non-discrimination is destroyed by discrimination alone:
"In this case as well, the specific rule is established through positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka). (15)

The meaning is that, just as there is a fixed rule between darkness and light, so too in the present case, the specific determination regarding shell-silver and the like must be grasped precisely through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*). Alternatively, it may be explained thus: [An objection is raised] "But what is the fixed cause even for discrimination (*viveka*)? To this he says: "In this case, too—regarding discrimination—the restriction of causes is established only through positive and negative concomitance; namely, that the cause consists specifically of hearing, reflection, and meditative absorption (*śravaṇa-manana-nididhyāsana*), and not ritual action (*karman*) and the like. The meaning is that ritual action and so forth are merely external factors (*bahiraṅga*). || 15 ||
He recalls what was stated in the first quarter [of the verse], that bondage cannot be something inherent and so forth:
"Because no other possibility exists, bondage is simply non-discrimination. (16)
In this context, "bondage" refers to the cause of bondage known as the conjunction with suffering; the remainder is easy to understand. 16.
Now, one might object that since liberation (mukti) is an effect, it would be subject to destruction, and thus there would be a recurrence of bondage; to this he says:
"There is no possibility of the liberated one being bound again, because of the scriptural teaching of non-return. (17)

Since only that which is produced as an effect is subject to destruction, there is no destruction of liberation; this is the meaning based on the scriptural text, "He does not return again. The word "api" (also) serves to include the matter stated in the preceding sūtra. || 17 ||
Otherwise, it would not be a human goal. || 18 ||

Otherwise, even for one who is liberated, there would be bondage again; thus, liberation would be like dissolution (pralaya) in being a non-goal of human endeavor, or it would lack the status of being the supreme goal of human endeavor—this is the meaning. || 18 ||
He states the reason for its not being a human goal: "Because both would result in being indistinguishable. (19)

Due to the equality of being bound by existence (bhāvi-bandhatva), there would be no distinction between the two—the liberated and the bound. Consequently, it would follow that [liberation] is not a human goal (apuruṣārthatva); this is the meaning. || 19 ||
[Objection: But if a distinction between the bound and the liberated is thus admitted, how can "eternal liberation" (nityamuktatva) be asserted? To this, he says:
"Liberation is [nothing more than] the destruction of obstacles; it is not something else. (20)

The meaning is that liberation is not some ontological entity distinct from the destruction of the obstacles to be described hereafter. For instance, the redness of a crystal—which is naturally white—is caused by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of a *japā* flower; it is merely an obstruction that conceals its whiteness. However, the whiteness does not perish because of the presence of the *japā* flower, nor does it arise only upon the removal of the *japā*.

In the same way, the reflection of suffering belonging to the self—which is by nature devoid of suffering—is merely an obstacle consisting of the form of its veiler, conditioned by the intellect (buddhi); it is not that suffering is produced by the conditioning of the intellect, nor does it perish upon the removal of that conditioning. Therefore, the self is eternally liberated, and bondage and liberation are merely conventional; thus, there is no contradiction. || 20 ||

[Objection: "But if bondage and liberation are thus unreal, does this not contradict the Śrutis and other authorities that establish liberation as the goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha)? To this he says:
"In that case also, there is no contradiction. (21)

The meaning is that even if liberation (*mokṣa*) consists in the destruction of obstacles (*antarāya*), there is no contradiction in its being a human goal (*puruṣārtha*). For it is only the conjunction with and disjunction from suffering that are attributed to the Self (*puruṣa*), and not the experience of suffering itself; moreover, "experience" is a connection with suffering by way of reflection (*pratibimba*). Therefore, the cessation of suffering by way of reflection is indeed a real human goal. That very thing is the destruction of obstacles. And such a liberation is indeed real—this is the point. || 21 ||

If liberation were merely the destruction of obstacles, then its accomplishment would occur through hearing alone, like the discovery of gold around one's neck that was previously obstructed by ignorance. To this, he says:
"There is no such rule, because of the threefold nature of eligibility. (Sūtra 22)

There are three types of those qualified for knowledge: superior, middling, and inferior. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no rule that mental direct realization (mānasasākṣātkāra) occurs for everyone immediately after mere hearing (śravaṇa). Consequently, due to the defect of being of duller capacity, mental knowledge capable of dissolving the mind did not arise for Virocana and others from mere hearing; however, this was not because mere hearing lacks the power to generate knowledge. || 22 ||
He says that not only hearing alone is the observed cause for knowledge, but there is another as well: "For the sake of strengthening the subsequent [stages]. (23)

The rule is to be understood as applying for the sake of the absolute firmness, characterized by the destruction of obstacles, of the subsequent stages such as reflection (manana) and meditative absorption (nididhyāsana), following upon hearing (śravaṇa). || 23 ||
He states further means of accomplishment:
"The seat (āsana) is that which is steady and pleasant"—this is not a restrictive rule. || 24 ||
There is no restriction regarding the posture, such as the lotus posture (padmāsana) and so forth; for the meaning is that whatever is steady and comfortable is itself the proper posture. || 24 ||
He states the primary means: "Meditation is the mind free from objects. (25)

When the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) becomes devoid of mental modifications (vṛtti), that alone is meditation (dhyāna); the meaning is that it is yoga, consisting of the cessation of the modifications of the mind (cittavṛttinirodha). This is because meditation will be described as the means for achieving this state. || 25 ||

Now, one might object: "Since the person remains of a single nature whether in a state of yoga or non-yoga, what is the use of yoga? Anticipating this, he provides the following resolution: "If it be argued that there is no distinction in either case, it is not so; for there is a distinction due to the cessation of the coloring [of the intellect]. (26)

The meaning of the sūtra’s concluding portion is that, due to the cessation of the coloring (uparāga) and the removal of the reflection of the fluctuations, there is a distinction of the Puruṣa in the state of yoga from its state of non-yoga. The rest has already been largely explained. || 26 ||
Now, one might ask: how can there be an "affliction" (uparāga) in that which is unattached? To this he says:
"Even in the unattached, there is affliction due to non-discrimination. (27)

Although there is no ultimate coloring (uparāga) in that which is free from attachment, nevertheless, because it appears as if colored, those who discern coloring conventionally designate the reflection itself as the coloring; this is the meaning. || 27 ||
He explains this very point:
"There is no coloring [of the self] as between a japā flower and a crystal; rather, there is identification (abhimāna). (28)

Just as there is no actual coloring (*uparāga*) between the hibiscus flower and the crystal, but rather there is merely the conceit of coloring due to the reflection of the hibiscus—as in "the crystal is red"—so too there is no actual coloring between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the *puruṣa*. Rather, the meaning is that there is merely the conceit of coloring due to the reflection of the intellect, caused by non-discrimination (*aviveka*). Therefore, the final conclusion of the two sūtras is that the coloring of the *puruṣa* is actually the reflection of the mental modification (*vṛtti*), by virtue of its similarity to coloring.

And that very taint of the mental modification consisting of suffering is the obstacle to liberation, which is termed the cessation of suffering; its destruction occurs through the dissolution of the mind. And that dissolution of the mind occurs by means of asamprajñāta-yoga, known as the cessation of all mental modifications; therefore, it is the established doctrine of the Yoga-śāstra that the destruction of obstacles arises from yoga alone. || 28 ||

"Concentration is the mind devoid of objects"—thus yoga has been defined. Desiring to know its means of accomplishment, [the author] states the method for the cessation of the aforementioned coloring:
"Its cessation occurs through meditation, concentration, practice, dispassion, and so forth. (YS 1.29)

Through the door of concentration (samādhi), meditation (dhyāna) is the cause of yoga, and the cause of meditation is retention (dhāraṇā). The cause of that [retention] is practice (abhyāsa), which is the performance of the means for steadying the mind; the cause of practice is detachment from sense-objects (viṣaya-vairāgya); and the cause of that [detachment] is the perception of defects [in objects], as well as the observances (yama) and restraints (niyama), according to the method taught in the Pātañjala [Yoga-sūtras]. Thus, by way of yoga—which is called the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind—the cessation of those [fluctuations] occurs, meaning the cessation of their coloring (uparāga). || 29 ||

By means of meditation (*dhyāna*) and other practices that bring the mind to its ultimate state, the obstruction of the soul’s coloring (*uparāga*) is removed; [the author] shows the gateway established by the ancient masters:
"By turning away from both dissolution (*laya*) and distraction (*vikṣepa*)," so say the teachers. (30)

The meaning is that the ancient teachers have stated that through meditation (*dhyāna*) and other means, by the cessation of the mind’s function of sleep as well as its functions such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there occurs the cessation of the reflection of activity upon the *puruṣa* as well; for when the original object (*bimba*) ceases, the reflection (*pratibimba*) also ceases. Patañjali expresses this very point in three *sūtras*: "Yoga is the cessation of the functions of the mind; then [the *puruṣa*] abides in its own nature; in other states, it conforms to the form of the functions. Likewise:
"The Self (*ātman*) is eternal and all-pervading, yet by virtue of its proximity to the intellect (*buddhi*), in whatever way the intellect becomes, the Self is considered to be so."
Smṛtis such as these also declare this very point. Thus, the meaning of this section is that the destruction of the obstacles to liberation occurs solely through asamprajñāta-yoga. ||30||
He states that there is no restriction regarding places such as caves for meditation and so forth:
"There is no restriction of place, because of the clarity of the mind" (YS 2.31).

Meditation and the like arise solely from the clarity of the mind; therefore, the meaning is that there is no restrictive rule regarding places such as caves for that purpose. However, the scripture prescribes forest retreats, mountain caves, and so forth as the locations for yoga only with a general intention. For this very reason, the *Brahma-sūtra* concludes its inquiry into liberation with the aphorism: "Wherever there is one-pointedness [of the mind], there [is yoga], because there is no distinction. Now, he investigates the cause of the world in order to establish the unchanging nature of the Puruṣa:
"Primordial Nature (Prakṛti) is the original material cause, because other things are heard in scripture to be effects. (32)
The meaning is that since the Great One (mahat) and the other principles are heard to be effects, Primordial Matter (prakṛti) is established as their ultimate cause. || 32 ||
Let it be that the person alone is the material cause; to this he replies:
"Even though [the self] is eternal, it is not so because of the absence of its being a conjunction. (33)

The meaning is that since the Puruṣa lacks both possession of qualities (guṇavattva) and the state of being connected (saṅgitva)—the two factors required for suitability as material cause (upādānayogyatā)—it cannot be a material cause despite its eternity.

Now, one might object: "Since scriptures such as 'Many creatures have been born from the Puruṣa' establish the Puruṣa as a cause, doctrines such as the theory of illusory transformation (vivarta) must be accepted. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Because it contradicts scripture, no room can be found for this base of fallacious reasoning. (34)

The meaning is that all the various positions proposed regarding the Puruṣa as the cause are contrary to the Śruti; therefore, those base logicians and others who accept such views do not possess knowledge of the true nature of the Self. By this, it should be understood that those who argue that the Self is the material cause (upādāna) of qualities such as pleasure and pain are likewise mere logicians; they too lack knowledge of the Self as it truly is. Furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning the Self as the cause are intended solely for the purpose of meditating on the non-difference between power and the possessor of power.

This is because the status of *pradhāna* as the cause is established by such scriptural passages as "the one unborn [female]" (*ajāmekām*). Furthermore, if it is argued that space is the causal substrate for clouds and the like, we do not refute that; for our refutation applies only to the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāma*). || 34 ||
Since earth and the other elements are seen to be the causes of stationary and moving things, does it follow that *prakṛti* is the material cause (*upādāna*) of everything? To this he replies:
"Even in a mediated succession, there is a persistence of the primary cause (*pradhāna*), as in the case of atoms. (35)

Even though [Pradhāna] is a cause in a successive series with respect to stationary objects and the like, its status as the material cause (upādānatva) remains unimpaired because it is inferred to exist within them. The meaning is that just as atoms of earth and other elements possess the status of material cause in stationary objects and the like through their presence in sprouts and so forth, so too does Pradhāna. || 35 ||
He states the proof for the all-pervasiveness of primordial nature (prakṛti) by means of inference: "Its omnipresence [is established] because its effects are observed everywhere. (36)

Because the word "not" (na) is observed everywhere without restriction, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the Pradhāna [is established], meaning that it pervades even minute things such as jars; this has already been explained previously. || 36 ||
[Objection: Even if it is limited, one must say that it goes to wherever the effect arises; to this he replies:
"Even when there is connection with motion, its status as the primary cause remains like that of an atom. (37)

The meaning is that even if motion is admitted, there is an absence of being the primal cause due to its being limited, as illustrated by the example of earth-atoms and the like. Alternatively, it may be explained thus: An objection is raised—surely, in the Śrutis and Smṛtis, activity called "disturbance" (kṣobha) is heard of regarding Pradhāna, which consists of the three guṇas, for the sake of their mutual conjunction; and because of possessing activity, like the examples of threads and so forth, there is an absence of being the primal cause. Anticipating this, he provides the rebuttal: "Even if motion is joined [to it], there is no loss of the status of being the primal cause, just as in the case of atoms. Motion is activity; the meaning is that even when that exists, there is no loss of the status of being the primal cause, just as in the Vaiśeṣika system, the earth-atoms and others [are considered primal causes despite possessing motion]. || 37 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: since only nine substances, beginning with earth, are observed, how can a substance called *pradhāna* (the primordial cause), which is devoid of the nature of earth and the rest, be possible? Nor should it be said that *pradhāna* simply does not exist as a substance at all; for its status as a substance is established through conjunction, disjunction, transformation, and so forth. To this, he replies: "The addition [of *pradhāna*] is well-known; there is no fixed rule. (38)

The meaning is that there is no fixed rule that there are exactly nine substances, because the addition of the well-known nine substances [to the eight] is precisely what constitutes the primary [pradhāna]. The intention is that the scriptural mention of only eight as being effects (kārya) serves here as a logical argument (tarka). || 38 ||

In response to the doubt—whether the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth are themselves *prakṛti*, or whether *prakṛti* is the substance that serves as the substratum for the three qualities—he determines:
"Sattva and the others are not properties [of prakṛti], because they are its very form. (39)

The meaning is that qualities such as *sattva* do not constitute the nature (*dharmatva*) of *prakṛti*, because they are the very essence (*svarūpa*) of *prakṛti*. Although both [views] are heard in the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, nevertheless, through reasoning (*tarka*), it is determined that they are the very essence, and not merely attributes. To explain: are the three, beginning with *sattva*, attributes of *prakṛti* in the form of its effects, or are they eternal attributes by mere conjunction, like wind is to space?

In the first case, it is impossible for the three diverse qualities to arise from a single primordial nature (prakṛti) without the conjunction of other substances, and such a hypothesis contradicts observed reality and is therefore improper. In the second case, since all diverse effects can be accounted for by eternal *sattva* and the other qualities through their mutual association, the postulation of a primordial nature distinct from them is redundant. Statements that *sattva* and the others are effects of *prakṛti* merely indicate their manifestation as being conditioned by effects such as illumination;
this is just as one speaks of the emergence of islands from the earth. || 39 ||

He determines that the activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of providing experience, because if one were to accept activity without a purpose, liberation would be impossible—thus, even in the absence of [the Puruṣa's] enjoyment, the creation of the Pradhāna serves the goal of the person, like a camel carrying saffron. (40)
This has been explained in the sūtra beginning with "The creation of the primary matter is for the sake of another," which is located in the third chapter. || 40 ||
He states the efficient cause for the diverse creation:
"From the diversity of karma arises the diversity of creation. (41)
Karma consists of merit (dharma) and demerit (adharma); the rest is easy to understand. || 41 ||
Now, let it be granted that creation proceeds from Pradhāna; but why does dissolution occur? For two contradictory effects cannot arise from a single cause. To this, he says:
"The two effects [arise] through equilibrium and disequilibrium. (42)

The three qualities, beginning with *sattva*, constitute *pradhāna*. Their "inequality" (*vaiṣamya*) is their combination in states of deficiency or excess; their "equality" (*sāmya*) is the absence of that [inequality]. The meaning is that from this single cause, through these two conditions, two contradictory effects in the form of creation and dissolution arise. As for maintenance (*sthiti*), since it is included within creation, the causality of *pradhāna* with respect to it has not been discussed separately. || 42 ||
[Objection: Since the primary cause (pradhāna) has the inherent nature of creating, would it not continue to create even after [the soul] has attained knowledge? To this, he says:
"Due to the realization of liberation, there is no further creation by the primary cause, as in the world. (43)

Because the Puruṣa has been directly realized through liberation, there is no further creation by the Pradhāna for the sake of that Puruṣa, since its purpose has been fulfilled. This is like the world: just as ministers and others, having accomplished the king's business and having achieved their own purpose, do not again engage in service for the king's sake; such is the meaning regarding the Pradhāna. For it has been stated that the activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of the liberation of the liberated soul, and that [liberation] has been accomplished through knowledge—this is the sense. || 43 ||

[Objection: Surely the Pradhāna has no purpose other than creation, since it is observed to cause the cycle of transmigration for those who are ignorant. Furthermore, through the creation of the Pradhāna, even one who is liberated would undergo rebondage. To this, he says: "Even upon approaching another [cause], there is no experience for the liberated, due to the absence of a cause. (44)

Even when the Pradhāna approaches others through the creation of the aggregate of cause and effect and so forth, there is no experience for the liberated one, because of the absence of the necessary conditions. The meaning is that the conditions for experience—namely, the specific conjunction with one's own limiting adjunct (upādhi) and the non-discrimination of its causes—are absent. Indeed, this very cessation of the Pradhāna’s creation with respect to the liberated one consists in the non-production of that specific transformation of the limiting adjunct called "birth," which is the cause of [continued] participation in that [creation]. || 44 ||

Now, one might object: "This systematic arrangement would only be possible if there were a plurality of Puruṣas; however, that very plurality is contradicted by the scriptural texts on the non-duality of the Self. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"The plurality of Puruṣas [is established] from the systematic arrangement. (45)

The meaning is that the plurality of persons is established precisely from the scriptural determination of bondage and liberation, as stated in such passages as: "Those who know That become immortal, while others go toward suffering. (45)

Now, if a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is accepted, then by the very establishment of that adjunct, non-duality (*advaita*) is once again destroyed; this is the meaning. However, in reality, even if there is a difference in limiting adjuncts, a systematic order (*vyavasthā*) is not possible, as was already explained at length in the first chapter. 46.
Now, one might object: "Since the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) are also products of nescience (*avidyā*), there is no destruction of non-duality (*advaita*) by them. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By both [views], there is contradiction with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). (47)

The meaning is that the contradiction with the Śruti, which is the means of knowledge for non-duality, remains exactly as it was by both these [arguments], "The person" and "Ignorance," which have been formulated as constituent parts. || 47 ||

He states two further objections: "Because there is no contradiction with either [of the two], the former is not [the case] and the latter is not [the case] due to the absence of a means of proof. (48)

Your prior prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) based on both accepted reasons is untenable; for we too accept only two [principles], namely *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Furthermore, since we also accept that transformation (*vikāra*), being impermanent, is merely a matter of verbal designation (*vācārambhaṇamātra*). Anticipating the objection that "there is indeed a contradiction with our position because you admit the plurality of *puruṣas* and the permanence of *prakṛti*," he states another refutation beginning with "And the subsequent... and so forth.

The reply and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Advaitins are untenable because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the Self; and if such a means were admitted, non-duality (*advaita*) would be lost by that very fact—thus, the proponents of selflessness (*nairātmyavādin*) have won, such is the meaning. || 48 ||

[Objection: But surely the self will be established through its own self-luminosity; to this, he replies: "If it were established by being luminous, there would be a contradiction between the object and the agent. (49)

Furthermore, if consciousness were established through the manifestation of the nature of consciousness, there would be a contradiction between the object and the agent; for manifestation is observed in things such as light only when there is a relationship between the illuminated and the illuminator. Moreover, a direct relationship of a thing with itself is a contradiction. In our view, however, because we accept the instrument of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) known as the modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*), a relationship of the self—in the form of a reflection—within the self—in the form of the original object (*bimba*)—is possible by means of that [modification].

The sense is that, just as the sun has a connection with its own reflection by way of water, so it is here. Furthermore, the scriptural texts concerning the self's self-luminosity (svaprakāśatva) should be understood as referring to a luminosity that is not dependent on any other limiting adjunct (upādhi). || 49 ||

[Objection: Is it not the case that there is no contradiction between the object and the agent? For, by means of the attribute of light residing in itself, it is possible for it to have a relation with itself, just as for the Vaiśeṣikas, by means of knowledge residing in itself, the self is its own object. To this, he says:
"The conscious nature, being distinct from the insentient, illumines the insentient. (50)

In consciousness (*cetanā*), there is no attribute (*dharma*) consisting of luminosity (*prakāśa-rūpa*), as is the case with jars and other objects; rather, it is the very nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*) that illuminates insentient things. For the reason that it is called "consciousness" merely by its exclusion of the insentient (*jaḍa-vyāvṛtti-mātra*), and not because it possesses attributes distinct from the insentient—this is the meaning. Therefore, due to its being devoid of attributes (*nirdharmatā*), it is pointed out by the Śruti as "This is not, this is not" (*sa eṣa neti neti*), and not by way of positive affirmation. Thus also says the Smṛti: "Even by a teacher, it cannot be pointed out as 'this is that'."

Even if the reading is *jaḍavyāv� consciousness reveals only the insentient (jaḍa), but not itself*, this is the same meaning, since the locative case here denotes the logical reason (*hetu*). Furthermore, in this aphorism, it is not the sense that "the nature of consciousness reveals only the insentient, but not itself. For if that were the case, the opponent would be unable to raise the objection that [consciousness] is unknowable due to the absence of a means of proof, because the same logic would apply to oneself as well. || 50 ||

Now, if duality is thus established in accordance with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth, what is the status of the scriptural texts on non-duality (*advaita-śruti*)? To this he says:
"There is no contradiction with scripture, because that [duality] is established for the sake of generating detachment in those possessed of passion. (51)

There is no contradiction with the scriptures on non-duality (advaita-śruti), for the scriptures establish non-duality solely for the sake of producing detachment in passionate persons toward that which is other than the Self. This is because, unlike the knowledge of the Self, no independent further fruit is heard of in the knowledge of the absence of duality. And that detachment is established only through the non-duality of Being (sadadvaita). "Being" (sattva) means the state of being immutable (kūṭasthatva). Therefore, the intention is that even the Śruti itself has propounded only the non-duality of Being in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad. || 51 ||

The proponent of non-duality (advaitavādin) is to be rejected not only on account of liberation alone, but also because of the absence of any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehends the unreality of the world; thus he says:
"Because it is produced by an internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) and so forth afflicted by defects such as sleep, and because there is no sublater [of that perception]. (52)

In the world, it is observed that objects in dreams—such as the yellowness of a conch shell—are unreal because they are produced by an internal organ (antahkarana) and other factors corrupted by defects such as sleep. However, that [unreality] does not apply to the phenomenal world (prapañca) consisting of Mahat and the rest, because its cause, namely Prakṛti and the intellect (buddhi) of Hiraṇyagarbha, is not defective, as is known from the scriptural text: "He fashioned [the worlds] as before. [Objection: But surely, since this world is sublated by such scriptural texts as "There is no diversity here at all," one must postulate some beginningless defect called "ignorance" (avidyā) and so forth. To this, he replies: "Because there is no sublater" (bādhakābhāvāt).
