This is the intended meaning: The sense is as follows: [The opponent argues that] the world cannot be real because it is sublated by the aforementioned scriptural texts. To this we reply: No, for there is no sublater. It is true that the world is sublated by those texts; however, that very sublation itself is sublated by the scriptural text: "I am Brahman. Therefore, the world is not unreal. Furthermore, the world is not sublated by the cognition "this is a snake," which arises when a rope is mistaken for a snake, because that [latter] cognition is itself sublated by the subsequent cognition "this is a rope. Moreover, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul" (saṃsārī). Consequently, since there is no sublater, the world is real. And because it is real, it is not produced by a defect. Thus, the world is not false. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul. Therefore, since there is no sublater, the world is real. And because it is real, it is not produced by a defect. Thus, the world is not false. This is the meaning. Moreover, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul. Therefore, since there is no sublater, the world is real. And because it is real, it is not produced by a defect. Thus, the world is not false. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul. Therefore, since there is no sublater, the world is real. And because it is real, it is not produced by a defect. Thus, the world is not false. This is the meaning. Moreover, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul. Therefore, since there is no sublater, the world is real. And because it is real, it is not produced by a defect. Thus, the world is not false. This is the meaning. Furthermore, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul. Therefore, since there is no sublater, the world is real. And because it is real, it is not produced by a defect. Thus, the world is not false. This is the meaning. Moreover, the world is not sublated by the cognition "I am Brahman," because that [cognition] is sublated by the cognition "I am the transmigrating soul. Those scriptural passages such as "There is no diversity here whatsoever," which others intend to be sublaters of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), actually only prohibit distinctions and so forth according to their specific context; they do not aim at the absolute unreality of the phenomenal world. For if they were so intended, they would themselves be sublated, resulting in the undesirable consequence that they could not establish their own meaning. Indeed, when a word from the time of a dream is sublated, the object signified by it is not thereby rendered free from doubt.

Therefore, since they do not cause harm to the Self, the Śrutis do not intend the absolute negation of the phenomenal world (prapañca). In this regard, the meaning of such Śrutis as "There is no diversity whatsoever here" is that nothing exists as distinct from Brahman, because this is consistent with Smṛtis such as "You pervade all, therefore You are everything. As for Śrutis such as "The modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is real," their meaning is the absence of ultimate reality in the form of permanence, for otherwise the analogy of clay would be untenable.
For in the world, it is not established that modifications of clay are absolutely non-existent, such that they could serve as an illustrative example.
There is neither cessation nor arising, neither one who is bound nor one who would be liberated.
Neither one who seeks liberation nor one who is liberated—this is the ultimate truth.

The meaning of such scriptural passages as these is that there is an absence of absolute ultimate reality—characterized by unchanging permanence—for anything other than the Self. Furthermore, the meaning is the absence of cessation and so forth in the Self; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the teaching that knowledge of this kind results in liberation (*mokṣa*). For no prudent person, having established that liberation is illusory, would then teach that it is a fruit [of spiritual practice]. As for those scriptural texts concerning the unity of the Self, they have already been explained in the first chapter.
In the *Brahmasūtrabhāṣya*, these and other scriptural passages have also been explained by us; this is the general direction of the argument. || 52 ||
He states that the manifestation (prapañca) is not only real during the present state, but is real at all times:
"Because no other possibility exists, there is the production of the existent" (53).

Because the production of what is non-existent is impossible due to the arguments and modes of operation previously stated, that which is already existent arises in a subtle form and becomes manifest; this is the meaning. || 53 ||
He establishes the systematic arrangement [of experience] even though agency and enjoyership reside in different substrates, by means of two sūtras:
"The ego (ahaṅkāra) is the agent, not the Puruṣa. (54)

The internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) whose function is self-identification (*abhimāna*) is the ego (*ahaṅkāra*). That alone is the possessor of volitional activity (*kṛtimān*), because it is generally observed that activity follows immediately after self-identification. It is not the *puruṣa*, however, because of its lack of transformation (*apariṇāmitva*); this is the meaning. Furthermore, what was previously stated—that merit (*dharma*) and so forth belong to the intellect (*buddhi*)—was said with the intention that they are merely different functions of the single internal organ. 54.
Experience ends with consciousness, because it is acquired through that karma.

Even though the agency belongs to the *ahaṅkāra*, experience ultimately culminates in consciousness alone, because the *ahaṅkāra*—being a composite entity—is for the sake of another. [Objection: If this were so, there would be no restriction to a specific person regarding experience through an action residing in something else; to this he says: "Because it is acquired by that action. [This means] that which is accumulated by the *ahaṅkāra* belongs to that consciousness (*cit*).

The meaning is that experience arises from that [specific] action. Thus, when a particular ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) takes up a particular person and produces the non-conscious functions of "I" and "mine," the action of that ego-sense is said to belong to that self. And by that very action, experience is acquired for that self; therefore, there is no over-extension [of the principle]. This is the intended sense. || 55 ||
He shows the reason for what was stated previously—that there is no final liberation even for those whose destination is as far as the world of Brahmā—by stating:
"Even in the worlds of the Moon and others, there is return because the causal conditions still exist. (56)
The "cause" (nimitta) consists of non-discrimination, past actions, and so forth; the rest is easy to understand. || 56 ||
[Objection: "But surely, non-return would result from the instruction of the inhabitants of those respective worlds. To this, he says:
"The accomplishment does not come from the instruction of the world, as before. (57)

Just as in the case of the previous human world, perfection—the accomplishment of knowledge—does not occur through mere instruction, so too in each respective world, the accomplishment of knowledge for those residing there does not occur through mere instruction; this is the meaning. || 57 ||
If it is objected, "What then is the status of the scriptural statement that 'from the world of Brahman there is no return'?", he says in response:
"When that [returnlessness] is established through a traditional succession, the scripture speaks of liberation. (58)

The meaning is that for those who have gone to the world of Brahmā and other such realms, liberation is heard of when knowledge is generally established through the succession of hearing, reflection, and so forth, and not merely by the act of going there directly; because this is the general rule, it is distinguished from other worlds. || 58 ||
He establishes that even though the Self is all-pervading, the scriptural accounts of its movement are justified:

"And because of the scriptural accounts of movement, even though [the Self] is omnipresent, the attainment of the place and time for experience occurs through connection with limiting adjuncts (upādhi), just like space. (59)

Even though the Self is all-pervasive, its movement is established as occurring in the place of experience due to the force of time; the meaning is that this occurs through association with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just like space. For just as space, though omnipresent, is conventionally said to move to a particular location through association with limiting adjuncts such as a jar, so too does the scripture declare:
"Just as when a jar containing space is carried away, it is the jar that is moved and not the space, even so is the individual soul (*jīva*) comparable to space. (59)
He elaborates upon the statement that "the creation of the body, the locus of experience, occurs through the presiding presence of the enjoyer," by means of two aphorisms:
"That [creation] is not established because there would be the consequence of putrefaction for that which is not presided over. (60)

The meaning is that since semen and other such substances would necessarily undergo putrefaction if they were not presided over by an enjoyer, the previously mentioned establishment of the body as the locus of enjoyment cannot be proven. 60.

"Surely, even without a presiding deity, the creation of the body as a locus of experience for the enjoyers may occur through the medium of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa); to this, he replies: 'If it were by way of the unseen force, that would be impossible for one who is unconnected [to it], just as [the unseen force] is not [the cause] of a sprout in relation to water and so forth. (61)

The meaning is that since the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which is not directly connected to semen and so forth, cannot serve as a medium for the enjoyer in the production of the body and other things—just as water and other factors unconnected to a seed cannot produce it except through the mediation of a farmer and so on. Alternatively, one must state that there is a connection to semen and the like by way of conjunction with its own substratum (the soul). And thus, it is established that the presiding agent’s causality in the production of the instruments of experience consists in its conjunction with the soul possessing the unseen force; this is the intended sense. || 61 ||

According to the system of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, the self's status as a supervisor is established by virtue of its acting as the connector of the relationship with the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*); however, in his own established doctrine, since the unseen force and so forth are properties of the self, it is impossible for the enjoyer to be the cause through that medium. Thus he says:
"Because [the self] is devoid of qualities, that is impossible; for these are indeed properties of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*). (62)

Furthermore, because the enjoyer (bhoktṛ) is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) cannot exist [in him]; thus, the enjoyment does not occur by means of the unseen force. For these factors, such as the unseen force and so forth, are attributes of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is the general internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa)—this is the meaning. Consequently, in our view, the presiding over (adhiṣṭhāna) by the enjoyer is established directly through mere conjunction (saṃyoga) alone, without dependence on an intermediate instrument (dvāra); this is the intended sense. || 62 ||

If the Puruṣa is indeed all-pervasive, then it is said: "The individual soul (jīva) should be known as a portion of the hundredth part of the tip of a hair divided a hundredfold; yet it is capable of infinity."

Thus, the limitation of the individual soul (jīva) established by the Śruti is untenable; likewise, because the Lord is denied and because all persons are of a uniform nature, even the scriptural distinction between the individual self (jīvātman) and the supreme self (paramātman) is untenable. To dispel this doubt, he says:
"The state of being the individual soul belongs to the qualified [Self], due to positive and negative concomitance. (63)

By the etymological derivation "that which possesses strength (*bala*), vital breath (*prāṇa*), and movement (*naya*)," there is the state of being a living being (*jīvatva*) or the state of being endowed with life (*prāṇitva*). And this is a quality of the *puruṣa* as qualified by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), but not of the isolated (*kevala*) *puruṣa*. Why? Because of positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*). For it is observed that only those possessing the ego-sense exhibit excellence of capacity and the maintenance of the vital breaths; whereas among those devoid of it, only the cessation of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛttinirodha*) is observed. The meaning is that [in the latter case], the ego-sense—which is the cause of activity and the producer of attachment—is absent.

Thus, the sense is that the individual soul's (jīva) limited nature and its distinctness from the Supreme Person known as the Paramātman are due to the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). By this Sūtra, neither the status of being an enjoyer nor the state of being the object of the notions "thou" and "I" is predicated of the qualified [self], because enjoyment in the form of direct perception does not possess the quality of being a property of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), and because it is impossible to effect discrimination by prioritizing the attributes of "thou" and "I. However: "When there arises the realization of non-difference between the individual self and the Supreme Self, O best of sages! then the severance of the bonds will occur."
They maintain that the self is twofold, distinguished as the higher and the lower;
the higher is said to be devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), while the lower is endowed with the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).

Thus, by means of hundreds of such statements, the very distinction between the individual soul (jīvātman) and [the Supreme Self] has been demonstrated; herein, within the state of being a living soul, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) serves as a defining characteristic. 63.
Now, intending to demonstrate the difference in the effects of the Great Principle (mahat) and the I-principle (ahaṅkāra), he first states the effect of the I-principle:
"The accomplishment of an effect depends upon the agent who is the I-principle, not upon God, because there is a lack of evidence [for the latter]. (64)

The agent who is of the nature of *ahaṅkāra* (ego) is that upon whom the accomplishment of effects—the completion of creation and dissolution—depends; for such power is the product of *ahaṅkāra*, since its capacity is not observed in those who are devoid of *ahaṅkāra*. However, it does not depend on a Supreme Lord devoid of *ahaṅkāra* as asserted by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; the meaning is that there is no proof for either a creator devoid of *ahaṅkāra* or for an eternal Lord.

For it is heard in scripture that creation is preceded by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), as in: "May I be many, may I procreate. In this context, there is no evidence that the word *aham* is used merely as a phonetic imitation (*anukaraṇa*). By this Sūtra, it is established that the agency of Brahmā and Rudra in creation and dissolution, though already proven by Śruti and Smṛti, is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of the ego-sense. || 64 ||
"But let the ego (ahaṅkāra) be the agent of other things; who, however, is the agent of the ego itself? To this he replies:
"It is sufficient [to say] that it is equal [to others], like the manifestation of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa). (65)

Since the manifestation of the karma that disturbs primordial nature (prakṛti) at the beginning of creation and so forth occurs solely from a specific point in time—because postulating another activating karma would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress—in the same way, the ego-sense and the sprout arise from the cause of time alone; there is no other agent for them either. This is the meaning of the phrase "the equality of existence. || 65 ||
Anything other than the Great [Self] is [the Self]. || 66 ||

The functions such as preservation (pālana) and so forth, which are distinct from creation and the like that result from the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), arise from the principle of the Great One (mahattattva). The meaning is that, because it consists of pure sattva and is devoid of pride, passion, and the like, its sole purpose is the mere favoring of others. By this sūtra, Viṣṇu’s role as the preserver, conditioned by the principle of the Great One, is established. Furthermore, because he has the principle of the Great One as his limiting adjunct (upādhi), Viṣṇu is celebrated as "the Great One" (Mahān), the Supreme Lord (Parameśvara), and Brahman.
As it has been said: "That which they call the mind named Vāsudeva is essentially the Great One."

In this treatise, however, the causal Brahman is intended to be the universal Puruṣa, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), because the existence of an Īśvara is not accepted. In that context, it should be understood that the term "cause" (kāraṇa) refers either to the Puruṣa as qualified by its own power, namely Prakṛti, or to the instrumental cause (nimitta-kāraṇa), since the Puruṣa is the impeller of Prakṛti for the sake of the Puruṣa's purpose. || 66 ||

It was previously stated that the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is caused by non-discrimination (*aviveka*). To the inquiry as to what causes that very non-discrimination—and to the objection that postulating a continuous stream of non-discrimination would lead to an infinite regress (anavasthā)—the following reply is given, which is common to all schools of thought, since such a [causal] basis is established by authoritative means of knowledge:
"The relationship of owned and owner between *prakṛti* and [the *puruṣa*] is also beginningless, being caused by karma, like the seed and the sprout. (67)

In the view of those followers of a branch of Sāṅkhya for whom the relationship between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*—as that of master and servant, or enjoyer and enjoyed—is caused by karma, even in their system that [relationship] is indeed beginningless in the form of a continuous stream (*pravāha*), because it is established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), like the seed and the sprout. Otherwise, if it were accidental (*ākasmikatva*), there would be the undesirable consequence of enjoyment occurring again even for one who is liberated. || 67 ||
Even on the view that [the world] is caused by non-discrimination (*aviveka*), this beginninglessness is the same; thus he says: "Or Pañcaśikha [holds it] to be uncaused by non-discrimination. (68)

Pañcaśikha says that the relationship between property and owner is caused by non-discrimination (*aviveka*). In his view as well, the meaning is that it is beginningless (*anādi*). This alone is his own position, because it was stated previously. Furthermore, non-discrimination exists even during dissolution (*pralaya*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), just like karma. However, in the view that non-discrimination is the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of discrimination, its beginninglessness—like that of the seed and the sprout—is not tenable; for it is only an undivided prior non-existence that serves as the cause for all experience. || 68 ||
"It is caused by the subtle body," says Sanandanācārya. (69)

But Sanandanācārya says that the relationship of enjoyer and enjoyed between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* is caused by the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*), stating: "Because experience occurs only through the medium of the subtle body. According to his view as well, the meaning is that this [relationship] is beginningless. Although the subtle body does not exist during the dissolution (*pralaya*), nevertheless its causes—such as non-discrimination (*aviveka*) and karma—produced by the subtle body of the previous creation, do exist. The intention is that, by means of those [causes], the relationship of seed and sprout exists between the relationship of owner and owned and the subtle body. (69)
He summarizes the meaning of the treatise’s statement:
"Whether this or that [is the cause], the cessation of that is the goal of human life; the cessation of that is the goal of human life. (70)

Whether the relationship between primordial matter (*prakṛti*) and the self (*puruṣa*) as the enjoyed and the enjoyer is caused by karma or caused by non-discrimination (*aviveka*) and so forth, in any case, its eradication—which is difficult to achieve due to its beginninglessness—is the supreme goal of human life; this is the meaning. This was first stated in the initial proposition: "The absolute cessation of the threefold suffering is the ultimate goal of human life."

[Objection: Is it not the case that here the human goal (puruṣārtha) is stated as the cessation of experience common to both pleasure and pain, whereas there [in the previous sūtra] it was the cessation of pain alone? How, then, can what was stated there be concluded here? [Reply: No, because although there is a difference in words, there is no difference in meaning. For pleasure, having been relegated to the side of pain, the experience of pleasure is indeed nothing but the experience of pain. Furthermore, since the experience of pain is reflected in the Puruṣa, what is intended is the cessation of that pain; thus, the meaning of the opening and concluding sūtras is one and the same. The repetition of the majority of the text is for the purpose of marking the completion of the treatise. || 70 ||
The extensive meaning of the primary subject matter of the Śāstra is [established] through the completion of what was not stated in that which is called Tantra.
In the sixth chapter, [the analysis] was completed, and subsequently the meaning of the sentence was summarized. || 1 ||

This very Sāṅkhya scripture was revealed by the Lord Viṣṇu in the form of Kapila for the welfare of the entire world. Regarding this, some who merely claim to be Vedāntins say: "The founder of Sāṅkhya, Kapila, is not Viṣṇu, but rather another Kapila who was an incarnation of Agni—'He is Agni named Kapila, the promulgator of the Sāṅkhya scripture,' according to the Smṛti. That is nothing but a delusion of the people.
This birth of mine in this world is for the purpose of enumerating the principles for those seeking liberation, who are weary of false desires, so that the vision of the Self may be attained.

This is because the aforementioned Smṛtis establish that the incarnation of Viṣṇu who was the son of Devahūtī alone was the teacher of Sāṅkhya, and because postulating two Kapilas would involve the fault of unnecessary complexity (*kalpanā-gaurava*). Furthermore, in that context, the word "Agni" is employed precisely due to the entry (*āveśa*) of the power (*śakti*) known as Agni; just as in the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, "I am Time (*kāla*), the destroyer of worlds, grown great," the word "Time" is used solely due to the entry of the power of Time. Otherwise, even for Kṛṣṇa when manifesting his universal form (*viśvarūpa*), [the same logic would apply].
Because it would result in the fallacy of difference from Kṛṣṇa, who is an incarnation of Viṣṇu; such is the direction [of the argument].
Having filled the channels of Sāṅkhya with the nectar churned from Vedānta.
In ancient times, the sage Kapila, whose sacrifice was knowledge, nourished the seers.
Through faith in those words and through a steady disposition toward that guru.
By a mere fragment of his grace, this treatise has been explained by me.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, the Tantrādhyāya, in the commentary on the Kapila Sāṅkhya Pravacana composed by the venerable Vijñānabhikṣu, the teacher of Sāṅkhya.
Thus ends the Commentary on the Exposition of Sāṅkhya.
Thus concludes this Sāṃkhya philosophy and its commentary on the authoritative teaching.
